DISCLAIMER / PROTIP: IF YOU SUFFER FROM EPILEPSY OR ARE VERY SENSITIVE TO FLASHING LIGHTS AND COLORS,  DON'T BUY OR PLAY THIS GAME... YOU'LL PROBABLY DIE.
So after earning the achievement for playing a single round for 20 minutes and landing myself 4th on the global leaderboard, I suppose I can adequately evaluate this game:
It's simple.
It's fun.
It will cook your eyes and strenghten your fingers.
This game reminds me a lot of Super Hexagon for its simplicity; if you liked that game then you will probably like this one, but it is also a bit more... bizzare. The premise is simple: use the space bar to control a colored bar between the upper and lower limits on a "gauge" while the background flashes alternating colors and patterns. The closer to the top of the gauge you are the more points you earn per second, but if you TOUCH the top or bottom you lose a score multiplier A.K.A. your lives (think the Bit Trip series: reach zero multipliers and its game over). Periodically you can collect score bonuses near the bottom of the gauge and, if you so elect, press the CTRL button to start controlling 2 bars at once for twice the points.
Problem is, the game doesn't like it when you start scoring high and progressively speeds the rate of color flashing, swaps patterns more quickly, stretches/shifts/flips the screen orientation, moves the location of the upper and lower limits, changes music, and even flashes text questions and pictures of cats when you least suspect it.
It gets very difficult and I don't recommend playing for extended periods of time, especially on a large screen. That being said this can be a really fun game in small doses and getting put on the leaderboard is satisfying. In addition, after playing certain amounts more and more game modes unlock for you to try, tweaking one aspect of the game at a time to keep it fresh.
In conclusion I would give this game an 8/10 as a casual, but challenging, lunch break spender. The only detracting aspects of this game for me are:
-The music is good, BUT it could be better. I prefer something even more aggresive in this type of game to keep me focused.
-The agressive strobing of bright colors for minutes on end make this game difficult to play for more than 10-15 minutes, basicaly forcing the player to stop playing after a short time (and thats saying something because I have a pretty decent tollerance for this stuff).
All in all, for 4 bucks I'd say its well worth the money.

This is a bubble shooter game - a casual strategy/puzzle genre where you shoot things at other things, if the colours match then they pop. The aim is to clear the level, in this case of cute (but evil) creatures known as the Minax. Supermagical has added some depth to the genre, with a simple story that drives the levels forward, and RPG elements such as (fairly limited) equipment (hats) and ingredients you have to collect to craft spells (character upgrades). You can use "soda" to activate special abilities, "sweets" to change the colour of your gun and "chococoins" to purchase quest items, crafting ingredients and more sweeties. Yeah, the whole thing just screams "I'M CUTE." There are a couple of mini-games such as a memory-pair game and hidden object games (find the treasure for each stop).
The art is great - extremely bright, attractive cartoon / comic book style. I love it, but in limited doses please. The animations are smooth and satisfying and the sound is appropriately upbeat to match. There are a lot of levels, and you can replay them to max out your stars (although this seems to be purely for an achievement) but after playing it for a while I did find the levels felt fairly similar. Definitely a game better played in small chunks than long gameplay sessions. The whole cuter-than-cute style won't suit everyone as well - but would definitely be a good family-friendly game and age appropriate for just about anyone.  My four month old son watched me play this and was enthralled. Start em young, right?
Unfortunately, here's the reason I won't be recommending it at full price. This was originally released on the mobile market as a free to play game with in-app purchases. The developers say the controls have been changed to adapt to PC, but the UI has not been updated and it's clear that the "swipe and shoot" mechanic is very much a direct port from a touchpad and not the standard way you would expect to play a game with a mouse and keyboard. It's not an intuitive movement at all. Graphical improvement is listed for the PC - but it seems to be a simple upscaling to 1080p, there are no resolution options or window options at all. This must be played in fullscreen, as there are zero options, which does not cater to different monitor sizes or the fact that a lot of people like to alt tab and multi-task whilst PC gaming, especially when the game is this casual. It does not feel like any real effort was made to accomodate PC players and the basic updates I would expect from a mobile port are simply missing.
Something that I noticed is that the three reviews featured on the store page are from 2012 - 2 reviews of the mobile game and 1 from the PS Vita. The awards listed on the side are for the various mobile versions. I feel this is somewhat misleading.
That does not mean I feel the same about it being a $5 Steam game with no PC customization or options. It's disengenous for a developer to list a positive quote from a review or a sleugh of awards for a different version of the game and not clearly state that. This isn't the first developer to do it, and since Steam doesn't police the content of the store pages, it won't be the last - but it's something I think folks should be aware of.
I would like to thank Super Awesome Hyper Dimensional Mega Team (try saying that fast three times) for giving me a copy of the game to review.

It's a free to play game hiding behind a buy to play price tag.
I've had some issues with the game that we talked over with the publishers handling this western release of the game.
For anyone wanting to play pure support and those dedicated healers amongst you online RPG gamers, you won't get any XP in groups. XP is only shared with the DPS. Deal damage, get rewards, heal your group and get nothing. Some people are okay with that, as a healer it doesn't sit well with me.
Respeccing is locked behind either a pay wall or daily missions. They cost 25 empire coins each or 99 if you go for the loot orb for a chance at a mount or pet. You get 10 empire coins for each daily. May not seem like a problem but with a choice of 2 specs, plenty of skills and needing to tweak builds for different things it's going to get costly.
Those I could tolerate but what I just found, and the reason I can't recommend this at all, is RPG's give ways to customise your character and Guardians of Ember is no different.
What the problem is with this buy to play game is that in order to save items for costumes it costs 100 frozen ember per item which is cash bought currency.
That would be fine for a free to play game but I can't accept that in a buy to play game.
Mounts are temporary unless you get a permanent one in a loot orb (another free to play staple).
Pets are temporary unless you find a permanent one in a loot orb.
If paying £15, £20 or £40 for a free to play game is okay with you then go ahead, the game itself isn't bad but there are just too many cash drains for me to recommend this to anyone. If they dropped the price tag or the silly cost for things in game it would be one of the best games i've bought recently but it's greed holding it back.
Shame really.

After a pretty bad pc launch (the game WAS removed), the supposedly "final" game in the Arkham trillogy made quite a comeback. This review will be separated in 3 parts; one for the game at it's core, one for the DLC/Season pass worth and the last stating my opinion about it's performance on pc.
One year after Batman: Arkham City, Scarecrow wants to fill Gotham with his notorious fear toxin (who knew) and there is only one man able to stop him, Batman. If you are familiar with the previous games, you'll feel right at home here. The dark knight has been practicing his moves! He moves quicker, hits harder and looks scarier by doing so (thanks Mr. Fox), all thanks to the new [amazing looking] batsuit. He has most of his gadgets from the previous  games right for the get-go and throughout his adventure he will find old and new ones to help him on his quest. After a couple of minutes of gameplay, we get introduced to this game's greatest feature: the batmobile! It goes fast, has a boost and blasts through everything on it's way! If a simple car is no match for Batman, this one can transform into a mobile tank that shoots non-lethal bullets and rockets!
The story is nothing of legendary, but it's on par with a classic Batman box-office movie. Scarecrow teams up with the *ahem* MYSTERIOUS ARKHAM KNIGHT to take down our cowled hero. After some time, more and more exciting side missions become availiable, weather if it's to save firefighters from low-life thugs to following penguin to his clandestine hideouts. In some of these missions, you can even team up with other characters such as catwoman and nightwing or even fight as them! Unfortunately, they are only playable here and in the DLCs I'll talk about later.
To not spoil anything about the story, I won't say anything, but some people might be dissapointed with the choices they made. I was not of of those people, but I've seen many shake their heads, so you'll be warned.
Some points that annoyed me in the main campaign were few, but still present. After a while, using the Batmobile for the same tasks becomes redundant (Thanks Nigma...) and might bore the completionists away, but it's not that bad in the main story. Even for a Batman Arkham Veteran (I just played arkham asylum so much on the windows live version), the combat gets very hard. You can have shield mobs, stun baton mobs, medic mobs, electrified mobs and big mobs all at the same time. In these situations, keeping a combo going is sometimes impossible. It does not mean that it is bad (I think it's the best even), but beginners beware, and read up a bit about the prequels because the game will start rough. Other than that though, it's a great game!
Rough score: 9/10
Now for the Dominion Leprechaun Curriculum: If you are a fan of the Batman mythos and/or want to use the freeroam mods, I definitely recommand the season pass. There are a bunch of little stories that tie up into the main game. They are not very long, but the content and detail are more than worth their price. You play as other characters with their own moves and arsenal (wanted to play as red hood, well now you can murder people :), while elaborating on some deus ex machina-ish stuff in the game. I have nothing else to say, but this is nor excellent nor aweful. Pick it or not, it's up to you.
DLC score: 7/10
Now for the controversial part of the review; here comes the PC port... with a vengeance?
Yes this game has high system requirements for a reason: it was made for consoles at first. I have a decent Nvidia 860m 2gb and 16gb of ram, but my cpu sucks. I can play at 60fps with pretty much no slowdown on low settings and 30 on medium (there is an option to limit the framerate). I had a single crash and some aweful slowdown on some boots, but I think that was my hdd freaking out like it always does. I didn't buy it on pc after hearing about the performances, so I waited. I tought it was still going to run 40fps with multiple crashes, but it looks like they fixed most of the issues. Play this on console if you are worried, but if you want it on pc and have the machine capable of taming the dragon, go for it :P
Performance grade: better than anticipated.

If you were looking for a super casual bubble pop style game, this game is for you at its low low price.
The rest of the review and some gripes/ technical PC related problems:
Your typical "touch to shoot" badly ported mobile game comes to pc, but it has a remastered soundtrack!!!.
The only way to quit while on the map is to start a game, "touch" pause, choose main menu and quit from there.
Actually, I don't even remember if there was an actual quit button on the main menu... Not sure anymore.
There's no audio settings, and if there are it's not in the options menu.
But what it does have:
The game is a horizontal bubble pop game, but you shoot "Minix".
You can click (tap) your minix to change the color of at the cost of a candy of that color that can be bought in the shop.
There's other beings that use "soda" to provide certain abilities / power ups to help.
In some scenarios you have to use them to pass, but the game drops more soda if you do.
No microtransactions as far as I can tell. You can always grind levels for in-game currency.
3 continents and 71 levels, and other bosses and secrets...
65 or so of the like I will choose not to see. 0.4 hours is all I needed to give the game a chance.
It does what it says it does.
The game seems to have a pretty solid storyline from what little of my time I invested into it. The story goes that you messed up pretty badly, cast the wrong spell as is the cliche and now the underworld minix things are trying to eat your worlds magic energy. The first boss fight I didn't actually do anything - I clicked a few dialogue options and the map ended with a victory screen.
I didn't leave the first continent because I saw all I needed to.
The art is nice though. Charming, clean and well done. And the soundtrack is also fairly nice.
Just the gameplay is really dull, and even at such a low price I'm not recommending it.
Perhaps if it were a better port, and not a direct slap of the game from phone to steam.

Book of Demons is a hack & slash which pays homage to Diablo with a few twists - it is set in a paper-cut universe like in a pop-up book, and everything you can equip, use, do comes in the form of cards that you assemble into your loadout to conquer the said Paperverse. You start out with 3 card slots out of the maximum of 10 available. Card slots are unlocked using gold and cost incrementally more. As of the build I played (0.75.11062+), only the Warrior class is available. The other 2 classes - Mage and Rogue will be released at a later date according to the
but apart from this the game is pretty complete for an Early Access game. The total of 32 cards in the Warrior's arsenal are divided into Artifacts (equipment - e.g. weapons, armor, trinkets), Items (e.g. potions, bombs, town portal scroll) and Spells (e.g. Mighty Blow, Charge, Blade Storm). All Artifacts have a mana cost which effectively reduces your mana pool available for using Spells (Items have no mana cost). Leveling up allows you to increase your health or mana, which translates to taking more hits / casting more spells. You do not actually grow stronger by levelling up. Instead you increase in strength by discovering new cards or upgrading your existing cards using gold and runes you find.
Your goal is of course to take care of The Archdemon that awaits you in the depths of hell. At major intervals you'll find 3 familiar main bosses of Diablo I - The Archdemon being the final boss. So how do the dungeons play out?
The Flexiscope system let's you decide how big / long a session you wish to play and randomly generates an appropriate dungeon of that size / depth. The range available for selection goes from Very Small (2 floors, ~8 mins) to Very Big (~4-7 floors, ~40+ mins). Note that the progress / rewards are balanced across all sizes that you choose. What it really means is, even if you have only a few minutes Flexiscope will give you a dungeon that still fits your needs. Pure awesome! =)
You traverse the dungeons in set paths and eliminate the various enemies that you come across by clicking on them. Enemies with elements will have their own quirks e.g. fire enemies are easier to take out with a ice weapon equiped. Boss monsters are pretty fun too. They are like multi-stage enemies in that each stage brings out a different attack pattern / attribute. Having said that, being constrained to a set path can be annoying but for the most part the game has designed it's way around it fairly well. Unlike you, the enemies can swarm at you from all directions however you are given spells / items to get out of those difficult situations.
The one thing that did trouble me was the fact that
. So if you're surrounded the only way you're getting out is to clear the enemies on either side. It sounds trivial but the combat mechanics of later enemies compound this problem. Shielded enemies can only be damaged after you take out their shields, enemies may charge at you or teleport onto you and archers will be raining death on to you whilst summoners add to their growing numbers. I think you can see how a situation can quickly get out of hand especially when your auto-attack can only hit 3 enemies at a time with a fully upgraded Shadow Sword (Artifact).
Once you complete Adventure Mode (by taking out The Archdemon), you unlock Freeplay mode and slowly you will unlock the higher difficulties which are made more difficult by forcing you to use a certain number of random cards during a session, having bosses which curse your cards rendering them useless while the boss lives and having harsh penalties for dying (gold loss, card loss, etc). Lastly if that isn’t enough of a challenge there’s Daredevil mode (equivalent of Diablo’s Hardcore mode) and a leaderboard for that.
The NPCs available - Healer, Barmaid, Sage, Fortune Teller all have clear counterparts to Diablo (except The Healer). The links to Diablo are fairly obvious but are done tastefully in my opinion and I would think they must have chose the voice actors carefully. Reason being they sound remarkably similiar to the voices in Diablo but at the same time are clearly different (hope that makes sense!). It's a pity that they have limited lines of gossip to go through. There are cutscenes for each major boss and I think nobody gives the devs enough credit for the rhymes they put in there. =)
All in all, it’s a good game that I hope becomes better with the remaining features on the roadmap. I think it would definitely help to have more cards and better balance (some upgrades feel less meaningful). Some have complained about the difficulty / lack of variety in the enemies and / or procedurally generated dungeons but personally I did not find this a problem. For the record, I did not encounter any bugs during my entire time with the game.
[EDIT] Although Adventure Mode can be completed without experimenting with the card combinations, the late game at higher difficulties requires understanding what combos are viable with the imposed hand. For example, if Blade Storm gets imposed. Do I build a powerful crowd control build - Blade Storm + Shadow Sword + Burning Axe / Frozen Flail or a more flexible build – Blade Storm + Dagger + Amulet of Mana? In either case, you are still free to swap out cards on the fly to adjust your build to the enemies you are currently facing. Conclusion : Late game is surprisingly well balanced and those hardcore achievements (no equiped cards / no healing) are truly difficult BUT achievable.

So I've been playing this game for about a week or so now, and so far, it's easily the best Zombie I've ever played, hands down. At first glance it may just seem like another Dead Island, but trust me, Techland learned a hell of a lot from their previous title, and made something that truly stands out to rival Far Cry 3 or even Skyrim.
The game has a brilliant Fight or Flight setup, where you can either tear through the mobs of zombies with swords, blunt weapons, or guns. Or run use the parkour to avoid fights altogether, as well as little traps and noise makers to draw the zombies' attention while you do something else (lockpick, quick time event to open doors, etc). It's a interesing contrast to the Stealth vs Mayhem you normally see in most games.
The Parkour itself really does deserve a mention here, it's a little odd at first as you can't wall run like in Mirror's Edge. But you can climb buildings by jumping from window ledges or other parts of the architecture that jut out and give you something to grab onto. Almost feels like Assassin's Creed honestly, which is really nice as it does feel like real parkour, using the environment to your advantage and improvising your path as you go.
The day and night mechanic is also pretty solid, during the day the game feels like a free for all, go nuts. But at night it's closer to a true horror game with the Volatiles (think of Verdugo from RE4). And these things don't ♥♥♥♥ around, they are TOUGH to kill, and even harder to fight, to a point where you just need to run and get to the nearest safehouse. Plus the game has a sound mechanic, where loud noises like explosions, gunshots, car alarms, etc all draw in zombies, which adds to the tension and adds a risk factor to balance out Pistols, Rifles, and Shotguns. The end result is a drastic contrast in gameplay as time goes by, with daytime being all about having fun and starting a riot, and night being a more stealthier horror driven experience.
The story, yea the voice acting isn't perfect but it is interesting enough to keep me playing, if just to find out what happens next. And there are some likeable characters, like Brecken, Rupert, Jade, Troy, Spike, etc. Each of them has some trait or two that I like about them, but they are minor traits that are underplayed and easily missed if you're not paying attention at all.
Graphics wise is a bit iffy......while I am sure it looks great when it's running on the right system, it ran like♥♥♥♥♥♥for me until I got ahold of the Dying Light Manager from LeavesOwnZ, you really do need to have at least i5 4690K and GTX 970 or better to really make this game run beautifully. But then again graphics aren't everything as long as the game is playable, and with the Dying Light Manager it runs pretty decently, even on an older system like mine.
As for other criticisms I do have a few, one, in a game with melee combat, what do you expect to do besides striking someone.....block right? Guess what you can't do....BLOCK or at least a freaking parry function, press mouse2 to parry attacks, it may degrade my weapon twice as fast but at least I have the freaking option to do it, especially against human enemies. And yea they do have a shield but it is♥♥♥♥♥♥ it would have been nice to have some sort of parry button in the game at the very least, so it's skill based and still has drawbacks.
Another criticism I have so far is with the more unique zombies, like the toads, bombers, and goons. They certainly add variety but are kind of annoying to deal with at times. Like the goons for example, dodging their melee attacks is a bit weird, you think you are out of range of the hammer smash that they use, but it still knocks you off your feet, which if you get surrounded means you are boned. Bombers are just what they sound like, they explode when hit, but the developers put these guys in spots where you'll accidentally melee them by accident, which kills you instantly. As for toads they just shoot you from afar with toxic sludge, which isn't bad until you encounter more than one. I love a challenge as much as anyone else, but only as long as it's a fair one, and the challenge here with these types of enemies is ok...but it could've been done a bit better. The volatile for example was done fantastically, as it's an enemy that only appears at night, and it's best to run to the safehouse and evade them rather than fight them head on. That leaves room for you as the player to figure out how to deal with. The other 3 I mentioned just seem to be thrown in as an annoying obstacle rather than an enjoyable change of pace.
Guns in the game are also something that I think could be improved on, while the fact that they do have a risk of drawing in more zombies to you when fired, they could have a few other interesting mechanics added in. Basically what happens is when you get the guns, they do not change at all even with a higher quality, not even damage. It would be nice if they had a few other stats or things added in, like attachments replacing upgrades, a wear mechanic where the gun overtime would get dirty and need to be cleaned or you risk it jamming on you in the middle of battle (ala Far Cry 2). Heck let us build a Silencer that wore down over time, so you only get like 10-15 shots out of it before it breaks and your gun makes noise again. Just a little more attention to the guns would have been nice, to make them really stand out from melee weapons.
Overall the game does have some issues and room to expand on, but it's a solid ground work for an outstanding zombie sandbox game. If you thought Dead Island was meh...and was hoping for something more, or just love sandbox games and parkour, this is absolutely worth buying.

I have played over 30 hours and I haven't yet finished the game. (It can be finished faster, if you do only story missions. I have done side missions and challenges.)
Pros:
- Freerunning/parkour, you can go almost everywhere and pretty fast too. It needs little practice, but when you get hold of it you run like master.
- Zombie killing at it best. Nothing gives more pleasure than mashing and slashing zombie heads and bodies. Fighting is enjoyable and fun.

- First person view offers jumpscares (at least for me) when you turn and zombie is in your face.
- Use of weapons and every sound done calls more zombies and more dangerous zombies.
- Day/Night cycle is awesome and make this game stand out from other zombie games. Offers different gamestyles at day and at night. (or you can do as I and play always reckless no matter time of day.) Game encourages to play at night, because your skills advance faster.

- Open world and no fast travel, you have to run from point A to point B.
- Excellent graphics and sound, world looks and sounds great.
- Some funny characters and funny conversations.
- Side quests and collectibles. Side quests are pretty intresting and offers different kinds of thing to do.
- Can be played 4 player coop (not tested) and you can be the zombie and invade other players game at night. It was pretty fun to be zombie.
- Not seen bugs in 30 hours of playing.
Cons:
- Story is decent, but nothing special.
- Characters are pretty much all looking the same and faces look some kind of static when talking.
- Framerate drops and screen freezing (Can be fixed and can be depend by your hardware).
I give game 10/10 as zombie and action game, but if you find great and deep story it ain't here. All in all I have enjoyed every minute and I recommend you to buy it sooner or later.

Let's get the obvious thing out of the way: yes, this is a Hearthstone clone. If you've ever played Hearthstone before, the interface during a match is essentially identical, almost down to the animations and sound effects. The crafting system also follows a similar template, as does the solo campaign that serves as a lengthy tutorial. However, and this important -- while Cygames has copied most of the look and feel, they've also created enough different keywords and game mechanics that it's not just a reskinned version of Hearthstone. This is a different situation from that Hex TCG that basically took Magic: The Gathering and just changed all the names.
If you're already deep into Hearthstone, there isn't really much here that might entice you to switch. Maybe if you prefer the style, which is anime through-and-through (complete with bad English dubbing). But if you're new to CCGs, this is a good F2P title for you -- there aren't that many cards yet, so you're less likely to be overwhelmed, and won't need to grind/pay as much to catch up to veteran players.

A game that can only be described as delightfully cruel.
Word of warning, if the acts of the RNG and the need to load a save to "fix" things enrage you. Don't play this and most of all don't complain about this game. It wasn't meant for you.
Being said the permanent deaths of squand members, the failure of missions and ultimately the fate of the entire earth hang on your shoulders, commander. Provided of course the the mighty RNG wills it. This game is a delightful mix of turn based tactical combat combined with the rush of the roulette wheel. Each action a soildier makes has a chance of success, will you play those odds or make a new plan. Remember, for every mile long alien crit kill through full cover, there is the 12% chance to hit miracle shot success to save the mission before the colonel bleeds out. The dice roll both ways try to remember teh success as well as the failures they all make great stories. At a glance or in a rage haze the mechanics may seem unfair (they acctually are on classic and impossible, but only crazy people play that way) but normally they aren't. Once you figure out the system and begin closing the tech gap, the casualties slow and the sweet taste of victory makes you complacent and kills your favorite colonel reminding you that tech parity is no reason to get sloppy. Stay sharp, roll with the punches and remember, "its a game, have fun".
Overall it was a blast, played it twice through, once vanilla and once fully dlc-ed and expansioned. Give it a try if you are willing to pick apart some juicy mechanics and use them to save the world. Just never forget the foundation made of slaughtered rookies. Time for me to go try out some second wave options!

This was a surprisingly good game. It's not great by any means, but if you can be forgiving of its shortcomings, the plot will reward you.
PROS
+ Excellent story. The setup drags a little bit, but once you're into the meat of things, it keeps you hooked.
+ A solid script, characters who are less heroic than your average shooter, and nice voice-acting add a lot of gravitas.
+ There are some truly great setpieces worth experiencing, namely a shootout in a crowded nightclub and a moving daylight shootout through the streets of Tokyo. They're reminiscent of Michael Mann movies like Collateral and Heat.
+ The squad commands allow you to employ some complex tactics in firefights, advancing under covering fire, guarding each other's flanks, etc.
+ Some inspired moments of art direction.
CONS
- The weakest levels and least polish - including an atrocious driving level - are all up front, meaning that if you bounce off the game you'll bounce off hard.
- The A.I. isn't terrible, but the things that it does well - flanking and maneuvers - are limited by linear level design that doesn't cater to it and exposes its weaknesses.
- The cover system is inconsistent. You'll abandon it pretty quickly, not that it makes a huge difference in the gameplay.
- Lack of polish abounds. Jagged edges, texture bugging on an early level, some too-simple level design.
- Games for Windows. We all know why.
PRO OR CON???
There are some nasty difficulty spikes, even on Easy mode. It takes some trial and error. Normally, that kind of unevenness wears thin very quickly for me, but something about the story kept me going at it anyway.
This is a SOFT RECOMMENDATION. It's not a big money risk, given its sale prices now, and you can finish it in a few evenings max, so it's not a big time sink either. Story's worth it, and a few moments are very memorable.

I had put this off for a bit when I initially saw it pop up in EA and decided to pick it up after finally getting a little hands on with the demo to actually get a feel for what it is. Everything about this game just feels "comfy". The papercraft assets all pop into place with nice little sounds, the clicks and pops of the UI all have a nice feel as you go through them, and theres a lot of little touches to the UI and play experience that show some definite thought was put into the player experience beyond the gameplay. As far as the gameplay itself, its a more straightforward ARPG thats more about staying alive, reacting appropriately to enemy types and managing your cards as you progress, rathe than furiously clicking and seeing huge numbers pop up everywhere. Character advancement is more about gathering the cards, upgrading them, and making subtle adjustments over grinding gear (there is no "gear" to speak out outside of the cards which have rarity). Its a bit more laid back but definitely pleasant. The setting and story have kept pretty true to having that "storybook" feel it's going for, with the game maintaining its own sense of identity and charm while not feeling overly cheesy with references.
I've still got quite a bit to go with it as of this review, but it's a damn charming game and I wanted to say something about it. I actually had no idea about the Return 2 Games project part of all this until I had booted up the game for the first time and it's a very neat concept. I'd love to see what they do with the other books planned in the future. The planned "popup sandbox) looks like it will also be an amusing addition. As someone who's a sucker for unlocking, collecting, and arranging trophies, having a little popup book area you can pose and screenshot your own little papercraft unlocks is a cool plan I hope ends up panning out.
tl;dr: Solid little ARPG that looks and feels like a storybook, definitely worth giving the demo a shot if you remotely seem into it.

In a breve explanation, this "Lite" version includes the game mode myClub in a standalone version, it also includes exhibition match mode but it has only few specific teams which obviously is understandable but the main focus of this is the myClub game mode.
Now the main question, do i recommend this game? Yes and no. Don't get me wrong, the game itself is a lot of fun and definitely is the best version of PES we got in a very long time but a few problems still persist in its core gameplay.
I'm gonna talk about certain aspects of this version, as well as the full version of the game which i own on my Playstation 4 console, after all, the Lite version is the same in its core gameplay as the full version.
The AI still suffers from certain clumsiness and noticeable scripting and on top of it all, an absurd reliability on RNG. But for the most part, these problems mentioned above, only seem to occur in higher values of difficulty. There isn't a sweet spot of balanced gameplay with equal terms on both sides (When playing against COM). Top Player difficulty seems to be balanced but somewhat easy, everything above this difficulty is scripted and unfair, it lacks balance. Legendary and Superstar hardly have any difference.
On a player vs player note,
Playing offline against a friend on a exhibition match, the game is hell of fun, there is no input lag, player movement is smooth, game pace is fantastic, the game just feels great overall.
The same cannot be said about playing against other players in online matches.
Playing online against other players is what ruins the experience for me, not because of the skill gap between each player, but how the game's core drastically changes.
While developing the game, KONAMI specifically said that they slowed down the pace of the game, comparing it to their previous titles which is a nice addition overall BUT while playing online, the game slows down even more to the point of it becoming immersion breaking, players are slow, counter-attacks are slow, the ball flies and stays up in the air as if it's a balloon, you get the picture, to put it simple, controls have input lag due to the game's player/server latency. Persistent bad netcoding is still a thing sadly, which is absolutely unacceptable for this day and age, specially for a competitive driven game AND specially for a game that one mistake can be easily punished.
In summary, i do recommend this game if you just want to chill and play a few matches every once in a while but i don't recommend playing this game if you want to invest a lot of time in it, which is what myClub is about, grinding and investing a lot of time to make your ultimate team, ranking up in division matches, etc.

I actually put aside Grim Dawn to beat this game before, of course, jumping back to Grim Dawn. I missed the awesomeness that was Diablo II. But I've tried to make up for that by playing Diablo III, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile, etc. When I found this game, I was immediately drawn to the ability to set managable time limits for dungeon crawling. You set how long you want to play for and the game will unfold a series of paths that are approximately the amount of time you have.
The whole card thing is a little played out, but fits really well with the paper craft style. Upgrading cards, unlocking new slots, constantly becoming more powerful as you venture into Hell is all very well done. Is the a little more involved than casual, and not "holy crap" complicated like Path of Exile's point system. It's a nice middle ground for people who want to kill stuff, level up, and dungeon crawl on a time limit. Have to study? Have a kid? This lets you set the length of your adventure! Stop any time, or make it longer. I love that about this game.
I cannot wait for the other classes to be added! This is a very polished early access. It's missing two classes and perhaps a bit more cards. Other than that, I haven't experience any bugs of glaring issues.

This game is good, but it's beyond infuriating. You're constantly getting things thrown at you nonstop. There's not a single moment where you can rest and relax unless it was right after you got killed. This game seems to shift between forcing you to focus on what's coming toward you, and muscle memory depending on what patterns are coming your way. Shifting between these mindsets constantly seriously makes me feel like my brains going to implode.
I enjoy this game, but I also hate it. It's fun to kill some time to at first, but eventually it grates your nerves.
Even though this game is probably going to surface some anger issues I didn't know I had, it's still good enough to be worth full price. It's very satisfying to be able to reach your next goal, even if you're not very good. Dying sucks in this game, but once you start bettering yourself and reaching more and more outstanding milestones, you'll feel like you've accomplished something worthwhile, even though you really haven't (I mean, it's just a high score in a game).
The soundtrack is actually extremly good. It fits the game's flashy colors and quick gameplay and it makes it sound like your in a retro rave. There are enough songs to keep the sound from getting too repetitive, but it does have the tendency to distract you, and distraction is something you can't have when playing this game. Hell, I don't think I even blink.
The character is cute too. I don't know what it is about being a Hexagon and taking control of a small arrow, but for some reason, it just adds a much needed "d'aww factor".

Let's get the obvious thing out of the way: yes, this is a Hearthstone clone. If you've ever played Hearthstone before, the interface during a match is essentially identical, almost down to the animations and sound effects. The crafting system also follows a similar template, as does the solo campaign that serves as a lengthy tutorial. However, and this important -- while Cygames has copied most of the look and feel, they've also created enough different keywords and game mechanics that it's not just a reskinned version of Hearthstone. This is a different situation from that Hex TCG that basically took Magic: The Gathering and just changed all the names.
If you're already deep into Hearthstone, there isn't really much here that might entice you to switch. Maybe if you prefer the style, which is anime through-and-through (complete with bad English dubbing). But if you're new to CCGs, this is a good F2P title for you -- there aren't that many cards yet, so you're less likely to be overwhelmed, and won't need to grind/pay as much to catch up to veteran players.

I am reviewing the immortal version of  this game.  I will keep in mind that this is an early access game.
At the time of this review, I have played for 11 hours.  I will break this review down by sections.
Graphics:
Overall, this game looks decent.  I am playing at 4K with a high end computer, so this may be skewed.  A major bug is the textures being stuck at medium (the devs are addressing this), but even with this taken into account the game is overall looking good.
Sound:
The sound effects are not very immersive.  There is no voice acting implemented (which is not a negative, just something I would expect at final launch for $50).  The clash of weapons against flesh is not satisfying, nor is the sound of me dodging an attack.  The enemies make generic noises, and there's no significant audio cues if an enemy is about to make patterns of attacks.  These small features would add a lot of depth to the game.  On a positive note, I  think the music is well done and fits the theme of the game.
Gameplay:
This is the meat and potatoes, and it's a small meal right now.  There is a clear delay (about 1 second) between keystroke and on screen effect.  Using a game like Diablo 3 as the standard for smooth gameplay, this game lacks  significantly in execution.  I found myself purposely pausing between attacks to make sure my last one landed properly or to make sure my buff/debuff actually was implemented.  Does it take away from the overall immersion?  Absolutely not.  I think back to when I played Path of Exile (which was horrible in beta) and this reminds me of it.  As long as this gets addressed before final launch, that's fine.
Getting a little deeper into gameplay - I like the option to click move or use wsad.  There is some skill required to dodge certain attacks or to strategically place myself during a fight.  This has potential to be very useful in the long run should the devs decide to implement it with boss mechanics etc.
As a side note, you can build a house and customize it similar to Rift.  It's a nice addition and adds a level of customization/personalization to your character.  This is also where you can trade items between characters on the same account.
Character building:  The character building is very limited at this time from a skills point of view.  There's a left/right click skill, and 1-4 (plans to implement 5-6 in the future).  There is some variety (using the knight class as the example) to your build.  I can choose to go pure DPS, a mix of DPS and healing, a party buff build (creating shields/healing/increasing attack speed of party members), and it seems there's a tank spec as well (increasing taunt, etc).  There are also passives  that can be used to supplement your main spec, and I think there are good choices/variety.
The nice thing is the ability to add a secondary class which opens the unique playstyle you want.  I think one of the nicest features is the ability for all classes to use all weapons.  It encourages interesting builds and allows for viability should the devs decide to add certain boss fights or mechanics that require the player to switch between ranged/melee, sword/board, etc.  I think this feature adds a lot of potential to the game's growth.
Itemization:
With all of that said, another interesting feature (although not to everyone's liking) is the loot system.  Any item can roll any variety of stats.  There is no "smart loot" like some of the more recent games.  This is a double edged sword.  If I wanted to make a knight that held a gun in 1 hand and a sword in the other, it would be beneficial to me to have a sword roll extra pistol damage.  However, the items can roll all sorts of stats that may not apply to your class.  You'll see a 2 handed crossbow roll +wand damage for example.  It's dealer's choice when it comes to this kind of feature.  There is a diablo 3 style stat re-roll system, although it's expensive after a while.  There are some features I have not experienced yet like the rune system.  I can edit this after further play.
On the same topic is the orb system.  Think of this as a mainly cosmetic RNG loot bag.  Sometimes you get a mount, a pet, ability/attribute resets, fireworks,  clothing, etc.  If you just pay for the base game, you can earn currency through daily quests and in a month's time you can accumulate quite a few orbs.  If  you buy one of the other packages, you get 20/30/50 orbs.  Once you get a mount, it makes the process worth it as it's much easier to get around the maps.  If it's not your thing, you can progress through the game and not be at a major disadvantage versus someone else.
Servers:
I am from the US, and I played on a European server.  There have been some horrible reviews based on other players' laggy experiences.  I have a great connection at home, and in 11 hours I had literally 3 lag spikes that lasted less than 5 seconds.  It didn't get me killed, and I barely minded.  There are US servers coming soon, so that issue will be moot.
In conclusion, I think this game shows a lot of promise.  I think one of the most important things that influenced me getting the $50 version is the developers/support from the community.  This team is willing to listen and take ideas to help make the game better.  They answer you on the forums and don't sugarcoat anything - they are people like you and I.  If they feel like your idea is good, but something else in development is taking precedence, they will come revisit it and I've seen that many times  in their prior posts/topics.  If this community and company continues to communicate well, there is a bright future ahead for this game.  While it is in EA and it's not "polished", it's still a fun game to play and I recommend you give it a shot.

People give Arkham Knight allot of♥♥♥♥♥♥ And I understand this because I know Arkham Knight had possibly one of the worst launches of all time, Rocksteady out-sourced the PC port of this game to a cheap and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Chinese company who had no passion for the game and only cared about meeting the crteria of being able to launch the game on a PC so they could make their pay-check.
As Shigeru Miyamoto said:
This was the reason for Arkham Knights not-so-welcoming reception on launch, on PC anyway. And why it's still considered a bad game by most.
But since it's launch people have neglected Rocksteady's dedication to this game. They didn't leave it in a broken state and cut their losses like many other triple A developers would have (Ubisoft is a perfect example). They worked effortlessly to make this game a true ending to the acclaimed Arkham series, and they have, the game runs perfectly on PC now after many patches since launch, and the DLC they've produced for the game adds many hours worth the couple dollars you spend on it.
While the DLC was also surrounded by controversy and was very poorly reviewed for being incredibly overpriced at the time of its release, that is certainly not the case anymore. The only complaint about the DLC was the cost - so Rocksteady halfed the cost of the season pass and made the many individual items dirt cheap, while I don't care about $1 cosmetics I do care about the many story packs that were added as DLC, allowing you to play as a whole array of characters including villians such as Red Hood. The DLC wasn't a bad thing - it was just way too expensive when it was introduced and Rocksteady asked allot for very little for a long time, but this is not the case anymore.
I loved City, but I couldn't find myself enjoying it as much as Knight. It's one thing to enjoy City but once you've played Knight and have a feel for the overhauled movment system and batmobile you get seriously annoyed going back for a playthrough of City. Frankly City feels so restricted, small and slow. By god did Knight improve on all the existing areas, frankly the only area Knight feels short is on the areas it innovated in, not improved on. The areas of the game that had been done before like fighting, movment and AI have been elevated to an entirley new plane of brilliance compared to City and Asylum. Once you've got your teeth into Knight you seriously can't go back to City without wishing you could chain grapple, jump into the batmobile or face some actually adaptive and smart AI. In City the extent of the AI adapting is going to an unconcious character who you just knocked out, in Knight the system was expanded to make the AI act independly and with direction; when directed by a boss the AI will group together, read your style and take steps to stop you and even be tricked into thinking your the boss when you emulate their voices later on in the game, but hell they even figure that out if you abuse it.
When you go through the reviews for this game despite allot of them being negative you will only really find 1 common complaint: the Batmobile was too forced into the game and main story. And I agree, it was too forced into the game, hell the insanly built up boss fight for Deadshot was a tank fight we'd done 3 times before that you can finish in less than a minute with a fully upgraded batmobile, this really annoyed me esspecially after how awesome previous encounters with deadshot were in the other Arkham games.
It was just way too forced into the story.
The game is quite cheap now and the DLC is basically a steal, if you're willing to goto third party websites you can pickup this game for about $5. Come on, for $5 you can just try it, it's the price of a cup of coffee for what might be the best arkham experience you might have; at the very least a great Batman experience.

Guardians of Ember
Guardians of Ember is an early access game which plays like a combination of Diablo and Wow. Is it good enough to be on your watch list or should be dumped in the sale bin of steam? Let’s find out:
Guardians of Ember is a Hack’n’slash MMORPG set a fantasy medieval world. As is the norm in typical MMORPG, you start out by selecting a race and then classes from those races. There are four races available and then multiple classes within them. While it is not much for a typical MMORPG, it does give you a good customizable character to tinker around with. The lore of Guardians of Ember borrows heavily from well known stories like Game of thrones and Lord of the rings. There are races of elves, humans, dwarves and children of the woods(might be the ones who were killed by the white walkers and ended up in this world).
Despite knowing that this is copied, I was actually invested in the story for the first couple of hours. That may be because I’m a person who will eat any story featuring medieval times and fantasy. The story does get boring and there is no real reason to pursue only the major quests. Despite being in early access, Guardians of Ember has heaps and heaps of content. Though none of them are there to keep you hooked, those are fun little time wasters which include Housing and fishing. These things add another layer of busywork on the top of the game.
The levelling system for Guardians of Ember is fine enough and slowly eases you in on the difficulty. Though you might defeat first couple of bosses standing at one place and attacking, later on you really need to apply your brains to take some difficult ones out. The loot is nice and diverse and the combat feels smooth and rewarding when it works properly.
Despite having loads of content, what Guardians of Ember really lacks is the amount of polish on the game. There is a huge amount of lag when attacking or moving which can prove crucial when you’re fighting an especially difficult boss or group of enemies.
There are numerous amount of glitches which include enemies just glitching through walls or you falling through the floor into the eternal abyss. These are made extra frustrating by the fact that the game is highly unstable. It crashed on me four times in 17 hours and disconnected me from the server a couple of times. The UI is also very clunky and difficult to navigate. These problems keep Guardians of Ember from achieving a level of greatness that it strives for.
Guardians of Ember has a nice variety of visuals. The environments are diverse and look good. Though there is a lot of empty spaces in every part of the map, the areas where the action takes place are densely packed and richly detailed.
The character models though are god awful when looked up close but serve the purpose in the game. The enemy designs are nice even though its fairly generic and the same goes for the armor and weapon design in the game. Overall, Guardians of Ember features nice visuals but nothing that will make you gape in wonder.
Guardians of Ember has a nice assortment in its sound design. The soundtrack is excellent and bang on mark and the other sound effects are done nicely enough which help in the solidifying the environment. There were a few audio bugs but nothing too distracting.
Guardians of Ember needs a huge amount of polish right now. It has a good amount of content and fairly nice levelling system. There are plenty of things to do inside the game but all of it is marred by the plethora of glitches and bugs in the game. The devs should look to fix these issues before trying to stuff in more content. Guardians of Ember has potential to be a really good game but is held back by these issues.
Note: I tested out the Immortal edition of the game which game me a head start in the game. While the game does feature microtransactions, it does not feel like a free to play game. Most of the stuff that is purchasable while real money is cosmetic and does not affect the stats of the character.

This game is what it says it is- an arena-based roguelite platformer-shooter. Its parts don't really come together.
The game has really stylish presentation and hints at a deeper story than "space wizard blows up cargo ship", but it really clashes with obvious VIDEOGAMES elements like everything being on cooldowns and enemies spawning in plain sight as a timer counts down and the difficulty meter goes up. You spawn into a room and dudes also start to spawn. Nothing is explained to you, except that you have to find a teleporter. The fact that it doesn't play or look like a plot-driven experience makes it bothersome that lore tomes are dropping in the middle of gunfights, but trying to enjoy the story and atmosphere they're presenting is muddled by it being pushed off to the side as arenas to kill lizardmen in.
The gameplay flow isn't great either. Keyboard controls use the arrow keys, with abilities mapped to Z/X/C/V. Enemies are too difficult (read: have far too many HP) to be reasonably taken on in a stand-up gunfight and spawn faster than you can kill them off, so it seems like you should get to the clean-cut goal the game presents you and move on, but once you defeat the boss you still have to kill everything else in the level before you can leave. (For scale: your starting attack does ~5-6 damage for two hits and fires about three times a second. The first enemy you'll encounter has 100 HP.) There are flying enemies, but you can only shoot left or right, and even though they apparently have the least HP of any enemy, that just means they only have a little more than half health after a hit from the starting character's most powerful ability. The first boss I encountered is just a large version of this enemy that moves towards you and tries to sit on you and kill through contact damage, making it identical to its smaller versions save that its sprite is too large to be jumped over and it has in excess of 5000 HP. The evasive roll gives you i-frames, but using it with good enough timing to avoid incoming attacks moves you so far away that you can't use it to hold your ground, and most actual attacks are easily avoided by jumping anyway. Everything costs money and progressively gets more expensive, but you don't carry any over between levels. Altogether, the result isn't a horrible experience, just a tedious and grindy one. It's usually not so terribly unfair that I blamed the game for my losses. It's just that I don't lose because I get tired after fighting the same teleporting elite enemy for six minutes and alf-f4 out instead of killing the other 59.

Thing Trunk, the developers behind Book of Demons, has undertaken a large multi-game series project named Return 2 Games. This series of 7 games (Books) take heavy inspiration from the "golden days" of gaming, each a tribute to a single hit game from the 90s. Although these Books will be self-contained and unique in their own right, they will all share a "grand vision," set in a stylish paper-cut universe. Book of Demons marks the release of the first Book in the Return 2 Games project.
Book of Demons is a fully voiced, Hack & Slash ARPG dungeon crawler coupled with deck-building aspects. Collect skill cards and upgrade them in order to save the world from demonic annihilation. Currently in Early Access, this ARPG manages to provide a very fun take on a popular classic many know and love, Diablo. In its current state, only one of three classes are unlocked (Warrior); however, the single-player campaign is complete, and nearly all of the spell cards are available. The story is mostly provided in bits and pieces through NPC gossip and creature descriptions throughout the duration of the campaign, along with minor cut scenes from the 3 major bosses. The bulk and core content comprising the gameplay focuses on pure, unadulterated, Hack & Slash dungeon crawling with intermittent trips to the town for healing and upgrades.
When you first venture into the deep unknown, the Flexiscope system will make itself known. This system aids in tailoring the upcoming set of procedurally generated dungeon levels to match a desired playtime. Although it will take a few tries to hone in on your playstyle, this innovative system manages to do a great job designing to your needs. Almost every end-game dungeon generation and boss fight length approximation was spot on. The game increases your time in the dungeon based on increasing the dungeon's physical map size, creature density, and number of creature types. Larger dungeons will reward you with more obtainable gold and chests.
Book of Demon's combat is fairly simplistic. With only your health and mana to manage, BoD's take on Diablo's combat system takes shape in the form of a static deck-building system (deck is not randomized), along with predetermined and confined movement paths. As opposed to a traditional skill bar filled with skills and consumables, BoD utilizes unlockable card slots to equip skill cards. These skill cards come in the form of pseudo-consumables that must be recharged, spells, and equipment. They must also be individually discovered as loot from your dungeon crawling expeditions. In an ARPG with minimal story elements, the goal is to foster a loot/combat-based addiction in order to motivate progression, and I feel that the developers did a great job in making me feel like a loot junkie. Almost every droppable item will be useful in some shape or form, and the creature mechanics are extremely varied between races. Certain creatures have shields that must be physically targeted with your cursor before damage can be dealt directly to the creature itself. Other monsters can be categorized by their tendencies to jump, charge, warp, spell cast, or spawn henchmen.
After defeating the Archdemon, you will unlock Freeplay along with 4 different difficulty levels (Normal, Hard, Nightmare, and Massacre). Everything carries over, and the new mode allows you to generate dungeons from each of the 3 different locations (Labyrinth, Catacombs, Hell). Defeating the bosses in higher difficulties, collecting all remaining cards, player levels, and achievements will add a lot of extra playtime while waiting for the rest of the Early Access content to unlock.
There is an aspect of micro-management in combat that is very fun, and it revolves around the poison, dazed, disrupt, and knocked loose mechanics. These mechanics are implemented by: breaking your poison status (click on health pool), recovering the stars (floating around when dazed), interrupting enemy spell casts (by discharging their cast bubbles), and re-orientating your cards when knocked loose. These mechanics help break up the Hack & Slash monotony; however, this can quickly turn into a clicker game when swarms of creatures start to overwhelm you. For most ARPGs, a single auto attack will instakill grunt-type enemies. Imagine the tedium when a basic grunt takes 3+ hits to kill, while managing a swarm of them on top of much deadlier, spell casters, bowmen, or boss creatures mucking things up. To make things worse, you are also confined to a 2 directional path, so strafing is out of the question. There are certain items that will alleviate the strain when under a swarming ambush (extra phantom attacks, etc.); however, there needs to be a scatter auto-attack weapon, a weapon with a skill shot/aoe placement, or a weapon that can instakill enemies so that the fighting doesn't begin to feel tiresome. Providing more cards that can alter the character’s auto attack properties is also desirable.
Regarding the dungeons themselves, one major downside I have seen in almost every procedurally generated game is the lack of hand-crafted or detailed scenery and events, and upon closer inspection, Book of Demons shows this with too similar environments regardless of room layouts. It takes a little too long to change locations, and combat begins to feel like a chore since nothing special really happens until you reach the area boss (only 3 in the game). A new creature here or there really helps stem this feeling of repetitiveness, although if only for a short while. More interaction with the dungeons would also alleviate some of the strain, such as incorporating puzzle, lever, or switch-type elements along with dynamic tile-changes (moving platforms, trap doors, etc.).

With so many weaknesses covered regarding combat mechanics and procedural generation, it's important to know that Book of Demons still does a lot of things well. Don't let my previous scatterbrained thoughts paint a dreary image about this game, because I still had a blast making my way to the Devil's hot tub. The Antipope fight and lair leading up to the boss contained some really fun gameplay elements. In that specific area, your first encounter with the Antipope starts with him scattering all of your cards throughout the dungeon, forcing you to trek through the darkness recovering them all. This was a definite stroke of genius on the developers’ part, as it not only provided a unique twist, but it also made me appreciate cards that I never thought had much usefulness.
The most important thing to take away from this is that Book of Demons still has an amazing and very solid foundation for improvement, and since the game is still in development, there is a chance that the developers will manage to improve the weaker areas. Adding more cards and classes will already make the game have much more replayability, but to improve the depth, it really needs more story, side objectives, locations, and true boss fights. Fortunately, these ideas are listed in their long-term roadmap of planned features. Going back to what the game does right, the card-based combat and equipment system is fairly refreshing to use, and enables an addictive loot-based progression system. The Flexiscope system also manages to create dungeons in such a way to match your available playtime. Taking all of this into consideration, I am able to confidently recommend Book of Demons to fans of the dungeon-crawling/Hack & Slash ARPG genres.

Honestly, I've never sworn so much at a game. I've never really sworn at a game out of frustration. That may be just me; but in contrast the amount it offers easily overpowers my lack of peace with it. The freedom you're given when crossing the city skyline, skyscraper to looming skyscraper via a plethora of long jumps, ziplines and wall propulsion lets the game belong to a unique genre of parkour. BRINK and several other games (of which I am yet to sample) do explore the concept of parkour over firearms, but really Mirror's Edge deserves the credit for all the merits in achieving it as superbly and integrally as it does. (The BRINK parkour hasn't really any need for the parkour features; it always seemed so limited and underwhelming in the first instance). Finally, to top it all, there's nothing labouring about it: the storyline isn't overly long, and so you don't find yourself taking midway breaks that result in you never resettling into the game again. The beauty is in its replayability. So to conclude, it addresses the parkour predicaments that are instantly faced in competitive titles to Mirror's Edge stunningly. Really worthy of a playthrough, and really sets up a sequel that gives more freedom from a fairly linear storyline.

Before I start the review, a note on the censorship of this game in Australia: After playing the uncensored version (in Sweden) from start to finish I think there are many scenes that are far more affronting and potentially offensive than those the OFLC chose to have removed. Moreover, when you look at these censored scenes in a greater context including other games that have been banned or censored the selection of what is and what isn't ok seems completely arbitrary. Yes I know they have "guidelines". I guess expecting a censorship regime to be coherent, no matter how supposedly civilised the country is, doesn't make any sense.
Now for the review. TLDR; extremely funny(same type of humour as show), good quality RPG that perhaps was a couple of hours too long.
This game is a product of a practised studio together with Parker and Stone. The gameplay, visuals and sound are finely polished as to be expected. The graphics and visuals really put you into the series in a way that I haven't seen done for cartoon to game conversions.
The RPG elements (character skills, items, etc) are well designed but if you are a completionist you may find that you max out your skills and have the best items a few hours before the end of the main story. This matches the game difficulty which is entertaining early on before plateuing mid game, its about as hard as a sponge late game.
By far the best thing about this game is the humour. There are ideas in this game which I haven't seen anywhere else and which we unfortunately probably won't see for a while. Travel up a guys ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, perform abortions, beat up homeless people and meth addicts, deftly matrix dodge out of the way of a pair of gigantic testicles and much, much more. This game has it all, most of which you can still experience in the land down under. The laughs are very much in this same vein as the TV series so if you found the humour there tired you will probably not enjoy this game.
Thanks for reading,

Nostalgia really is a funny thing.
I've been a Looking Glass Studios fan since the 90's with System Shock 2, and a Thief fan for a long time. Thief II: The Metal Age (the sequel to the critically-praised Thief: The Dark Project) brings players back into the world of master thief Garrett, this time with a bunch of new missions and antagonist in the form of Karras, the leader of the Mechanists.
The one thing I loved most about this game was that the scale just felt bigger in (almost every way). While I still have an issue with the fact that roughly half the levels are strictly linear, the missions that open up to you (like "Stonemarket First Bank", "Life of the Party" and "Masks") offer a wide array of alternate routes and secret passages to accomplish your goals, as well as give a far grander sense of the City and the threat Karras poses to its inhabitants.
Likewise, the variety of weapons and items you can acquire is great and allows for lots of experimentation, although (since I'm a purist) I still stuck to water arrows for the majority of the game.
Admittedly, I found much more joy in the levels where I could pick off guards at will with hit-and-run tactics. I think it's fair to say that the AI in this game alternates between hypersensitive and woefully inept. When the guards aren't aggro-ing on you from far distances, they're complete morons in combat. It is exceptionally easy to take advantage of the combat system. When a sword-wielding guard runs at you, walk backwards and swing like mad, or circle-strafe and hit his back. Bow-wielders are an automatic win - just mash the attack button if you get one cornered. The only real challenge came from the Mechanist robots and groups of enemies, which sometimes stacked up in doors and got stuck or ran around the mansion in the "Masks" mission chasing me (all that was missing was the Benny Hill music).
Likewise, the voice acting is either really good (in the case of Garrett's voice actor and some of the minor antagonists) or near-laughable (the nobles, who sound like they're reading from a script). I couldn't take Karras seriously as a villain because of his nasally voice, which made me laugh more than get freaked out whenever I heard his voice.
I vaguely remembered a lot of buzz and praise for "Life of the Party", which sees Garrett take to the rooftops to rob every building in sight and infiltrate Karras' tower, Angelwatch - and that mission did not disappoint. Easily the best in the game, it had everything I consider to be so great about the genre - lots of expansive areas and alternate routes to take, lots of secrets and hidden goodies to find, great level design, the works. I wish more of the missions had those kinds of additional areas or features to make them worth replaying, because I didn't feel much compulsion to go back and do much besides replay the missions that were either "loot everything" or "steal and/or kill everything".
All in all, though, Thief II is still a standout in the stealth genre. I haven't played Deadly Shadows yet (as of this writing), but the improvement in scope in this game makes me excited to see what's next.

Antichamber. It looks and sounds so simplistic. But it isn't.
Antichamber is a puzzle game that challenges your mind. What seems simple isn't so, and what seems complicated is easy. Return to places different than you remember. All of what Antichamber is as a game, is to screw you mentally. That's why I love it.
You are in a pseudo-sensory-deprivation chamber. You navigate your way through a simple world.
W for forward.
A for left.
But wait. It gets way more complicated. Some pathways are straightforward and simple. Some require meticulous observation. Some require you to take a step back, look in a certain area, move in a certain way. As the game moves forward, the complexity increases.
Pick up and move blocks.
Solve puzzles.
Turn around.
Shift blocks forward.
Destroy them.
Multiply them.
Fly.
Soon, your ability augments even more: you learn more new tricks, but continue to use the old.
Swap perspectives.
Expand.
Solve.
Extract.
And finally, presented with the final problem. you need to outsmart it. You need to use everything you know, from the basic WASD and jump, to the complex techniques that you have learned from the Manipulator. To destroy the final dark force. To escape.
10/10 - IGN.
While I wouldn't say it has too much replayability, it certainly is possible. It's fun! You can stretch your brain to its limits, and spend hours upon hous figuring out one piece to the worldly puzzle. It has a pretty short campaign, though the speed all depends on how fast it takes you to figure out each puzzle. There are hidden secrets in-game, hidden perspectives, and hidden meanings. Pick up this game now, and understand everything!
Explore. Play. Observe. Destroy. Antichamber.

Of all the stealth based games I've played, "Thief II: The Metal Age" is by far the best. It's stealth mechanics make use of both light and sound which is pretty amazing for a game that came out in 2000. It also features a great story with possibly the coolest main character of any videogame series out there, Garrett.  Voiced by an awesome dude called Stephen Russell, Garrett is a sarcastic thief whose commentary you hear throughout the entire game and it is a joy to listen to. You might know Stephen Russell from the game "The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim" where he voices a large number of characters including the leader of the Thieves Guild, Mercer Frey, which is a nice nod to the Thief series.
Unlike it's predecessor, "Thief: The Dark Project" (AKA "Thief Gold"), Thief 2  knows what it wants to be, a stealth game, and ditched all the combat focused, "Tomb Raider-esque" missions that were so prevalent in it's predecessor, making it the superior title. Large open levels, even more tools than the first one, amazing atmosphere, a great stealth system, and awesome sound design make "Thief II: The Metal Age" the holy grail of stealth games.

So I've been playing this game for about a week or so now, and so far, it's easily the best Zombie I've ever played, hands down. At first glance it may just seem like another Dead Island, but trust me, Techland learned a hell of a lot from their previous title, and made something that truly stands out to rival Far Cry 3 or even Skyrim.
The game has a brilliant Fight or Flight setup, where you can either tear through the mobs of zombies with swords, blunt weapons, or guns. Or run use the parkour to avoid fights altogether, as well as little traps and noise makers to draw the zombies' attention while you do something else (lockpick, quick time event to open doors, etc). It's a interesing contrast to the Stealth vs Mayhem you normally see in most games.
The Parkour itself really does deserve a mention here, it's a little odd at first as you can't wall run like in Mirror's Edge. But you can climb buildings by jumping from window ledges or other parts of the architecture that jut out and give you something to grab onto. Almost feels like Assassin's Creed honestly, which is really nice as it does feel like real parkour, using the environment to your advantage and improvising your path as you go.
The day and night mechanic is also pretty solid, during the day the game feels like a free for all, go nuts. But at night it's closer to a true horror game with the Volatiles (think of Verdugo from RE4). And these things don't ♥♥♥♥ around, they are TOUGH to kill, and even harder to fight, to a point where you just need to run and get to the nearest safehouse. Plus the game has a sound mechanic, where loud noises like explosions, gunshots, car alarms, etc all draw in zombies, which adds to the tension and adds a risk factor to balance out Pistols, Rifles, and Shotguns. The end result is a drastic contrast in gameplay as time goes by, with daytime being all about having fun and starting a riot, and night being a more stealthier horror driven experience.
The story, yea the voice acting isn't perfect but it is interesting enough to keep me playing, if just to find out what happens next. And there are some likeable characters, like Brecken, Rupert, Jade, Troy, Spike, etc. Each of them has some trait or two that I like about them, but they are minor traits that are underplayed and easily missed if you're not paying attention at all.
Graphics wise is a bit iffy......while I am sure it looks great when it's running on the right system, it ran like♥♥♥♥♥♥for me until I got ahold of the Dying Light Manager from LeavesOwnZ, you really do need to have at least i5 4690K and GTX 970 or better to really make this game run beautifully. But then again graphics aren't everything as long as the game is playable, and with the Dying Light Manager it runs pretty decently, even on an older system like mine.
As for other criticisms I do have a few, one, in a game with melee combat, what do you expect to do besides striking someone.....block right? Guess what you can't do....BLOCK or at least a freaking parry function, press mouse2 to parry attacks, it may degrade my weapon twice as fast but at least I have the freaking option to do it, especially against human enemies. And yea they do have a shield but it is♥♥♥♥♥♥ it would have been nice to have some sort of parry button in the game at the very least, so it's skill based and still has drawbacks.
Another criticism I have so far is with the more unique zombies, like the toads, bombers, and goons. They certainly add variety but are kind of annoying to deal with at times. Like the goons for example, dodging their melee attacks is a bit weird, you think you are out of range of the hammer smash that they use, but it still knocks you off your feet, which if you get surrounded means you are boned. Bombers are just what they sound like, they explode when hit, but the developers put these guys in spots where you'll accidentally melee them by accident, which kills you instantly. As for toads they just shoot you from afar with toxic sludge, which isn't bad until you encounter more than one. I love a challenge as much as anyone else, but only as long as it's a fair one, and the challenge here with these types of enemies is ok...but it could've been done a bit better. The volatile for example was done fantastically, as it's an enemy that only appears at night, and it's best to run to the safehouse and evade them rather than fight them head on. That leaves room for you as the player to figure out how to deal with. The other 3 I mentioned just seem to be thrown in as an annoying obstacle rather than an enjoyable change of pace.
Guns in the game are also something that I think could be improved on, while the fact that they do have a risk of drawing in more zombies to you when fired, they could have a few other interesting mechanics added in. Basically what happens is when you get the guns, they do not change at all even with a higher quality, not even damage. It would be nice if they had a few other stats or things added in, like attachments replacing upgrades, a wear mechanic where the gun overtime would get dirty and need to be cleaned or you risk it jamming on you in the middle of battle (ala Far Cry 2). Heck let us build a Silencer that wore down over time, so you only get like 10-15 shots out of it before it breaks and your gun makes noise again. Just a little more attention to the guns would have been nice, to make them really stand out from melee weapons.
Overall the game does have some issues and room to expand on, but it's a solid ground work for an outstanding zombie sandbox game. If you thought Dead Island was meh...and was hoping for something more, or just love sandbox games and parkour, this is absolutely worth buying.
