Returns is a wordy game to be sure but only to its benefit, a game full of text whether its dialogue or descriptive monologue backed up by a very able soundtrack. The tone, atmosphere and world are top-notch and ease you into its lore in a nifty way that doesn't bog down the pace of the story.
Speaking of story that ain't no shambles either, a noir murder mystery with body mods, elves, neon and magic throughout. What sounded like a real mess of themes in its description actually plays out really well in action. Combat is good too, a turn-based XCOM lite if you will, not as huge amount of challenge or depth to it though and this is where my issues with the game begin.
There simply isn't an overwhelming amount of stuff to do here. That itself is no crime but it does mean there is little room to go off the beaten track, do side-quests etc. As it is, it's a starting template that feels like it could use a little more work around the edges. It's happy to be a primer to the world of Shadowrun as opposed to a fully fleshed out game in of itself. Get past that and there's an enjoyable game to be had here. I'm certainly more than interested in playing Dragonfall after playing this and see its maker's take this template forward.

This game is what it says it is- an arena-based roguelite platformer-shooter. Its parts don't really come together.
The game has really stylish presentation and hints at a deeper story than "space wizard blows up cargo ship", but it really clashes with obvious VIDEOGAMES elements like everything being on cooldowns and enemies spawning in plain sight as a timer counts down and the difficulty meter goes up. You spawn into a room and dudes also start to spawn. Nothing is explained to you, except that you have to find a teleporter. The fact that it doesn't play or look like a plot-driven experience makes it bothersome that lore tomes are dropping in the middle of gunfights, but trying to enjoy the story and atmosphere they're presenting is muddled by it being pushed off to the side as arenas to kill lizardmen in.
The gameplay flow isn't great either. Keyboard controls use the arrow keys, with abilities mapped to Z/X/C/V. Enemies are too difficult (read: have far too many HP) to be reasonably taken on in a stand-up gunfight and spawn faster than you can kill them off, so it seems like you should get to the clean-cut goal the game presents you and move on, but once you defeat the boss you still have to kill everything else in the level before you can leave. (For scale: your starting attack does ~5-6 damage for two hits and fires about three times a second. The first enemy you'll encounter has 100 HP.) There are flying enemies, but you can only shoot left or right, and even though they apparently have the least HP of any enemy, that just means they only have a little more than half health after a hit from the starting character's most powerful ability. The first boss I encountered is just a large version of this enemy that moves towards you and tries to sit on you and kill through contact damage, making it identical to its smaller versions save that its sprite is too large to be jumped over and it has in excess of 5000 HP. The evasive roll gives you i-frames, but using it with good enough timing to avoid incoming attacks moves you so far away that you can't use it to hold your ground, and most actual attacks are easily avoided by jumping anyway. Everything costs money and progressively gets more expensive, but you don't carry any over between levels. Altogether, the result isn't a horrible experience, just a tedious and grindy one. It's usually not so terribly unfair that I blamed the game for my losses. It's just that I don't lose because I get tired after fighting the same teleporting elite enemy for six minutes and alf-f4 out instead of killing the other 59.

It's a lot like Dragon Quest 3 in slightly new wrapping; you choose from one of six classes to form a party of four characters, each class having different strengths and weaknesses in their statistics. Some can cast, some can fight, some do a bit of both. Instead of each class learning skills, you discover artifacts through the game that will each grant an ability. Turn-based combat, overworld map, dungeons, even the ubiquitous airship are all elements in this callback to the 80's and 90's.
I think this game could have done a lot more, for instance, the pool of enemy sprites is tragically limited (their 'humanoid' body gets reused pretty much twice or thrice per area) and there aren't any animations or backdrops that I know of which drags down the appeal because the presentation is brutally basic.
But if you're into the NES/early SNES era of turn-based RPG, you're looking for something that's worth more than a single play and something that won't grate your chest hairs off for turning it on (hello Souls and Monster Hunter), you may find Artifact Adventure right up your alley.

If you're a fan of oldschool RPGs from the NES era, like Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy, this is the Steam game you've been waiting for. It takes the core mechanics and concepts of those old RPGs, but applies the lessons of newer RPGs like the Elder Scrolls series to make a free-roaming adventure that you're sure to enjoy.
For starters, you're given a choice at the start of the game of one of three boons, and which one you choose will significantly alter the way you play. From there, you must hunt down various "Artifacts" that confer various abilities upon your party. It's important to switch who the party leader is before claiming an artifact, as most of them provide spells or other abilities that are permanently attached to the party member that picks it up.
This game is also packed with secrets. Some of them are fairly easy to figure out, others all but require a guide. One secret, in particular, took weeks for anyone to discover, and required a set of steps worthy of the most suspicious of playground rumors.
It's hard to really say much more about Artifact Adventure, as it boils down to a single, fairly simple question. Do you like oldschool RPGs? If so, buy it, right now.

If you were around to enjoy the original Neverwinter Nights or the Baldur Gate series, this is the MMO for you.  More MMO that ARPG, it has a sphisticated charm about it that will appeal to the MMORPG player.  There are a lot of systems in this game, and although at first it might seem very deep, those systems open up to you as you play.  The graphics are very good for this type of a game.  If you can turn them all up to max, I recommend you do so.  In fact, graphics go hand in hand with art style, and the cities and landscapes are immersive; which to MMORPG players is an important element.  The dungeons are fun and as you level you will have an option to run solo or whith a group for better rewards.  At end game you'll what to get in a good guild and run together.
I recommend giving this game a shot if you are a fan of both MMORPGs and ARPGs.  It's not a fast paced as Path of Exile, for example, but it's not instanced either.  So as you roam the world you will run into other people in which you can join together to tackle public quests, without actually having to form a group.
The skill system is in depth, and you can really customize the character you want to play.  Unfortunately I don't see this appealing to a ton of millenials, but the game has a strong community already, and I can see it being a sleeper hit for many years to come.

What all the reviews say is true about Flock.  But there are two features I did not find in any of them that make it a thumbs-down for me.  One, this is a score-game.  The point of playing is to generate a score, not to encourage good gameplay.  This is closely tied-in with the timer in the game - it isn't a game about abducting livestock well, it's a game about doing it fast.  This is a twitch game with no button mashing.  Second, the key to what gameplay there is depends on inefficient controls.  The controls deliberately are less accurate than the player's movements.  This isn't always bad in game - Banjo Kazooie Nuts & Bolts did a pretty good job of it, creating a zany (often hilarious) environment.  In Flock, I find it annoying.  The game is simply using time pressure + unreasonable control to create a frenzied atmosphere.  The concept and visual presentation are good.  The gameplay is lacking.  The soundtrack relentlessly insists that you keep raising your blood pressure, but the slow movements of the spaceship prevent you from achieving the frenzied pace that the music demands.  A secondary annoyance is that while gameplay is 98% mouse motions, you have to keep leaving the mouse to press Enter at all the menus (you cannot point at click at menu options), and you have to use the above-mentioned inefficient controls to select your next map (you must hover the spaceship over the map name, and it has the same tendency to miss the target as it does during gameplay.  The UI sometimes frustrates efforts to maneuver low enough to select certain maps).  The graphics are charming, but if you're trying to get the gold medal you won't have a half-second to appreciate them.  If you thrive on chaotic tension in a game and are not too concerned about gameplay depth, it might be a good buy.  The cuteness is there.

This is such an underrated game.
The characters are what really sold me on this game.  Unlike other series in which you play as "bad guys" who ultimately tend to do the right thing, Kane and Lynch are 100% scumbags.  Kane is a self-serving, traitorous sociopath and Lynch is just completely mental.  It's a real treat to see how they interact with each other and how their personalities affect the storyline.
The combat is good, not great.  The cover system is a little wonky and the AI is outright terrible at times, but I was always having enough fun that these issues didn't bother me much.  Shooting feels off at first, but as you progress and get a feel for the weapons, it becomes a total joy.  You really get the feel of desperation that would accompany a heist gone wrong leading into a frantic shootout with the cops (like I would know).  Kudos to whoever did the sound for the weapons, I haven't heard beefier sounding assault rifles in any other game!
The graphics are pretty mediocre, and look like what you'd expect from a non triple-A title in 2007.  That being said, the levels you play in are more than interesting enough to make up for it.  You'll go from banks and upscale office buildings to the streets and rooftops of Tokyo to Havana in the middle of a political revolution.  One of my favorite set pieces was a gunfight in a busy nightclub, which seemed to be lifted straight out of the movie "Collateral."
Overall, this is a solid game with a few flaws that stand out, but definitely won't ruin the experience of playing as such interesting characters in such interesting situations.  And for only $6.99 (down from $60 when it came out) you can't go wrong giving it a try!

Dying Light is a game that touches deep down into the inner soul of what makes a Zombie Apocolypse & captures every little inch of it in a very well crafted and spectacular game.
Dying Light is what i call a spiritual successor of Dead Island and in many different ways beats the absolutely crap out of it, this is the game Dead Island strived to be but did not live up to the hype it created.
Dying Light is developed by Techland the same guys who brought us Dead Island & published by Warner Brothers Interactive.
The story behind is that a viral outbreak has accured on the city of Harran, and you the player (Kyle Krane) have been sent into the thick of it by the GRE a government organization trying to recover a document & kill the leader of a thug group who was once mayor of the city before the outbreak.
Kyle is soon jumped by some thugs and after trying to dispatch of these thugs ends up being bitten by a Infected and becoming infected himself, soon after that you're on a battle of your own trying to survive and help keep the survivor group you're haulled up with alive as well as yourself.
After many events, you gain a feeling of security and home with the group of survivors you are bunked up with & feel the need to seek revenge after many of them perish to the hands of Rais the traitor and eventually lose focus on your primary mission. Soon after that it becomes apparent that things aren't what they seem with the GRE and this is where the story changes drastically.
The plot becomes a bit more sinister as the story goes on. You can read below for a more full story at your own risk.
(THERE ARE PLOT & STORY SPOILERS)

There's still much more to do in Harran.
The gameplay that Dying Light sets up is very solid and brings into play everything you should expect in a "Zombie Survival" game.

Earthworm Jim. If you are reading this, it is a game that you probably enjoyed as a child years ago (or maybe adult, I don't judge). This game is EJ2, no doubts about it. It is not however, the game that you want to play.
What is it then? This appears to be no more than the original code running in DOSBox. The game only supports the resolution of the era (640x480), fails to respond to mouse actions, and at times, fails to respond to basic keyboard actions. As other reviewers have stated, hit detection leaves a bit to be desired. This flaw turns Puppy Love from an adorable game of "aww, look, he is throwing puppies out the window" to "if that marshmallow misses another puppy in the middle I'm gonna lose it after Peter loses it on me." Also as other reviewers are saying, levels are missing (Lorenzen's Soil) or out of order (The Flyin' King).
To this day, I will pull out my Genesis and play some EJ2 to the last level. I would not however, play this game past the first level. This particular edition only serves as a last chance moneygrab from what once was a great enterprise. Do yourself (and your memories) a favor and play it on the consoles it was made for. Even if that means plugging in your old 386.

People on steam generally play games casually and live on with their daily lives. Most are however unaware of the true hardships of those who commit their lives to DotA 2 and the gaming industry. Whether it is the social stigmatisation, family pressures or psychological challenges, Free to Play is one of the most heartfelt and intense eye-o♥♥♥♥♥♥s to the intensities and obstacles professional players confront in the e-sports industry.
Personally, this stunning work brings into perspective a serious side of professional gaming that is not known to the vast public community. Beneath the tournament matches, streaming and skrims, the documentary features Dendi, Fear and hyhy and their respective real-life challenges they face to be a professional, personal determination to succeed and dramatic traumas that will completely overturn your impression of pro players. One of the highlights of this documentary in my opinion is its successes in capturing the vivid emotions and psychological challenges which all three players must confront. It is truly stunning especially on the scale of the immense hardships that they face whether it is financially, socially or psychologically. It conveys to us, viewers, the personal backdrops of these players and how this has developed their mindset when playing the game competitively. Indeed, for these players, the gaming industry is currently relatively niche and still undergoing structural development. It is most enlightening to delve into the lives of these personalities and grasp the psychological mindset of players like Dendi in face of unforseen cruelties.
As DotA 2 and the e-sports industry expands in the coming years, this documentary will serve as an inspirational message to all casual gamers, professional players and beyond on the realities of e-sports. At the heart of e-sports are the players. Watch this unique documentary on how e-sports has shaped their entire lives and, whether it is heartfelt sympathy or heartrendering tears, either way, you're up for a stunning adventure.

Heya,
Most people know me from my stream & YouTube content over at Path of Exile or WoW. Personally I've been looking for a proper MMO-ARPG for a very long time, Devilian failed me.. to say the least.. Instead, I have now invested 60-70h so far in this game and can't stop playing it.
I posted a rought Video Review as well:
----
Let's get to the actual review:
Pros:
* Devs listening and making changes based of the community feedback they get
* Huge ammount of possibilities & potential for the game to grow
* Intriguing gear modifying & enhancement system
* MMO features to the ARPG genre as the game is MMOARPG tagged. You can play Healer/Tank/Support, not just DPS class
* New ways of utilizing character stats compared to most games
* Very smooth & responsive fighting
* Devs who have publicly stated to not touch p2w features, several times
* A great community
----
Cons:
* It's in EA, there is some lag, even crashes & bugs to be expected. Far from all content is released
* PvP is rather♥♥♥♥♥♥due to balance not being focused for the low lvl we can reach atm (30)
* Class & Ability balances needs a good look at even at this low lvl, though this has lower priority over server issues
* Itemization can seem very odd to look at when a Bow can drop with an enhancement giving + to sword mastery
* Lacking a lot of guiding early on in the game
* Getting your horse stuck in the damn stairs every time (solves by jumping but still...)
* Chat functions reminds me of Path of Exiles chat system before they remade it
* Gender locked classes, for now
* Clunky movement with enemies or obstacles blocking your path
----
Conclusion:
To me, this game is the definition of what an Early Access game means, there are some bugs, lag issues and what not. However, the devs has so far shown their dedication to the community and their product and are not just solving issues but also paying attention to the feedback provided. For me, this is a game I want to grow with as long as the devs keeps up with their current path. Only thing that would steer me away is things not getting fixed within reasonable time.
What I want to see is heavy focus on the MMO features such as mini raids where your party needs a tank & healer to have a chance at making it, even with gear! Let's see what they got for us in the end-game content!
-----
Kind Regards,
GhazzyTV

First off, I should mention that this is, overall, a fantastic game. It has some significant problems, though, specifically in a few of the later levels. The game's strongest points are really those that focus entirely on the actual running aspect, and a lot of the platforming is surprisingly well done for a three-dimensional game, let alone a first-person game. The real issue is that the combat is kind of awful. There are several areas, most of them later on, where you are forced into combat scenarios, and they are probably the least fun parts of the game. The game's influences are clear. There are a few points that were more than a bit reminiscent of the Prince of Persia games. As a huge Prince of Persia fan, this is great for me, but a lot of the stunts that were needed for some of the harder sections are quite difficult to pull off from a first-person perspective. As a whole, very solid game, though some areas could have used a bit more polish. I look forward to seeing the sequel. 7/10

I'm going to start off saying that I love FTL. It's a modern take on a roguelike that is really quite fun. I love roguelikes. However, I'm going to focus on FTL's flaws.
Only by the severity of the flaws do we gain insight into the depth of the quality of the game. Only by investigating into the horribleness do we understand the goodness.
Firstly, the game is fairly short for a rougelike. While it still does fairly well in this regard when compared to most other games, It really should do a lot better. Roguelikes traditionally are next to impossible to clock, and have much more content. Leaving them with insanely long replayability  which cannot be matched by any other genre other than MMO's. I clocked FTL in little to no time on the easier setting, then again, not long after, on the harder difficulty. After this you can unlock all the ships if you want. But playing the game this way pales in comparison to playing the core storyline
Which brings me to the next flaw of the game (it actually doesn't, but it sounds cool). It really bugs me when a game gives you many options, but really only a select few are actually any good. FTL suffers from this, and it's annoying as hell. For example, not only does it apply to the weapons that you can find in FTL, with some being useless and others being OP, but also, the starting ships you can unlock.  They are horribly imbalanced. Some are next to useless and others are simply OP. luckily, it doesn't apply to the different races you can have. But I mean pheh, that was about the only thing left they could have messed up balance wise...
In my humble opinion, the game could have benefited from more content, more balance, More randomization, and one hard difficulty. I understand why they might want to let people clock the game. But they are detracting from the accomplishment, and replayability, and giving nothing back in return.

Revelations 2 start after the conclusion of RE 5. We play as our beloved Claire Redfield the sister of Chris Redfield, Moira Burton who is the daughter of Barry Burton who only features in two games (RE1/REHD and basicly if you get a perfect ending in RE3 he appears as a cameo in the ending where Barry flew of Jill and Carlos before the Racoon City destruction), and also we play as the one liner of lockpicking and sandwiches Barry Burton, and the mysterious little Girl Natalia.
Claire and Moira who is now part of Terrasave, is trapped and kidnapped by an unknown entity in a mysterious Island and they must Survive that's the first part of Episode 1, and we play as Barry and Natalia 6 months prior of Claire and Moira Kidnapping.
I have to say that i really like this game, From the first Revelations game i'm amaze how capcom listen to the fans by giving us the Survival Horror roots that Resident evil has stray away since 5 and 6 ( and boy was 6 is so Stupid ).
This is the Resident evil we want, and i applause how capcom move away from the comfort zone, and do a leap of faith in the franchise.
GAMEPLAY :
+ Gameplay mostly doesn't change from Revelations 2 , so if you love the Revelations 1 than you will love the Second one.
+ More Survival Horror than the First revelations.
+ Intense gameplay with the real survivor horror root, you must think before you shoot or react
- kinda wonky control especially when running and dodging
- stealth in Claire sections seems useless, especially that there's a completion medal in Claire section where we have to do a stealth kill
Story :
I can't give a Pro and Cons of the story, because it's basicly a 2.5 hours tutorial and story building episode, so i'm staying neutral and won't critic it
Atmosphere :
+ The important thing of Survival Horror is the atmosphere, and yes REV 2 deliver us the old scholl claustrophobic,horror, intense, scary atmosphere of old school RE, and also kind of open are in Barry section remind me of RE 4.
Graphic :
+/- an okay graphic really, not bad or that great. RE 5 still has the best graphic among all RE games
Price Value :
For a full value (even though i bought it at the 84% discount) i think episode 1 is worthy of the asking price, especially with the Campaign Replaybility and the addiction Raid Mode. With a 2.5 hours campaign and probably more than 4 hours of addicting Raid Mode that makes us into 8 hours of content so yeah it's worth of it full price.
Raid mode :
aaaaahhh the Raid More, the one i've been playing for 6 hours grinding to get that sweet weapons and parts. It's the same as REV 1 which is fun an addicting, and i love it so much. Trying different Character and weapons is satisfying as hell.
in the conclusion i give this game a 7.5 / 10
A solid and interesting start, i just love we finally get to play as Claire again since Code Veronica X, she's my favourite character in RE series, but the first episode sadly serve as a tutorial story and gameplay so that what makes the grade hurt for me. If you a RE fan and tired on feels RE 6 strips out of RE lore and Gameplay, this game is for you.
Can't wait to buy the rest of the Episodes

When it comes to the pinnacle of stealth gaming, some say Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, some say Hitman: Blood Money, and some even have the audacity to say Assassin's Creed. While they're all worthy contenders, Thief 2 stands fully erect as the throbbing crown jewel of an underappreciated genre.
They just don't make many games like this anymore. There are 15 glorious levels--each of which can take anywhere between 30 minutes to three hours depending on your level of Kleptomania. Even in 2014, I am still amazed at how goddamn huge the levels are, and the sheer amount stuff hidden in every nook and cranny. Sure, on a graphical level the game hasn't aged well at all, but from a gameplay standpoint, this game was (and still is) WAY ahead of it's time. Dishonored pointed its pinky in the right direction, but still wasn't able to capture the sheer size and replayability of this game. There are levels within levels within levels. It blows my mind.
Anyway, I'm surprised you made it this far in my review and haven't purchased this game yet. You're getting easily 20+ hours from this badboy...and that's undercutting it by a lot. This is the template for how to make a perfect stealth game. Period.

Let me just say up front that I am incredibly impatient. I cannot sit still in one place for very long if there isn't something going on to entertain me, and I get really antsy waiting for even a short amount of time. I'm also very bad at sneaking around. I would often try and sneak up on family members just for fun to startle them, but they'd always notice me, and often they'd beat me to the punch. With that said, Thief II is my favorite game of all time. Yes. A game as slow-paced and patience-testing as this one, which relies on you being very good at stealthing around to pass the levels even on normal difficulty, is my favorite game of all time, and also the only one I began again immediately after finishing for the first time. That should say everything you need to know about how perfectly designed this game is. I could talk about the absolutely gargantuan levels that reward exploration, or the deep gameplay with a huge variety of tools and ways of approaching any situation, or the amazing story, featuring excellent, writing, voice acting, and one of gaming's best protagonists and most underrated antagonists, but really, what else do you need to know? Thief II had the misfortune of coming out the same year as Deus Ex, and was thereby overshadowed (no pun intended). While it still sold well in it's day, it's fallen under a lot of people's radars over the years. Fix that. Get this game. Be it Steam, GOG, or physical CD, there is no excuse for any gamer not to have this in their collection. Go. NOW.
Edit: I forgot to mention this game also has fantasic sound design. The importance of sound is often neglected in games, and this game more than makes up for it's dated visuals in this aspect.

In theory, it only takes six minutes to beat the entire game.
In practice, though? Well... you WISH this were just in a bullet hell game. Each stage is harder than the last (and the first stage is "Hard"). You'll probably last a few seconds for your first few runs, as the disorienting colors, movement, and music throws you for a loop, but if you keep at it, you can claw your way up, second by second (literally), until you hear the blessed "HEXAGON!"Then your concentration will probably be thrown off, and you'll hear "GAME. OVER."
Seriously, "Begin. Game. Over." might as well be the mantra for this game.
As difficult as it may be, it's surprisingly addiciting, a la old school games like Tetris, and the music and colors really add to the game's charm. You'll find yourself playing for longer than expected each time, as you keep thinking "I can do better." and "It only takes a minute." In my experience, though, after about half an hour(!) the sensory overload will start to feel overwhelming, and you'll have to shelve the game for awhile. Good for relatively short playthroughs whenever you want to do something simple but challenging.

Some are present here, however the port wasn't a clean one.
Hit detection can be dodgy, missing levels, sounds that just aren't plumb there. Even among the poor ports out there this is probably the worst of the bunch.

Growing up, my grandparents had an NES. The squat gray box had been kicked out of my house after my father got addicted to Mario, and so I only got to see it on the rare occasions that I stayed over with my grandparents. It had quite a game library, too, since my mother had bought the console originally to play a few RPGs.
One of the games in the library was Final Fantasy.
I didn't really understand it at first. I'd load my inventory up with armor and then be puzzled when spiders took down my team with ease. I'd buy tons of weapons, but no one's damage would increase. I was utterly convinced that Blackbelts were the only good class in the game.
After a few lukewarm experiences with getting murdered by imps in the woods, I decided to leave it alone. I played Megaman and Star Tropics and had a grand time while it gathered dust on the shelf. Until one day when something finally clicked.
"Equip screen?" I wondered. "What's that about?"
What followed was an afternoon of the weirdest, most serene bliss I had ever felt.
Now, I tell that story because it's the easiest way to describe the effect that Artifact Adventure had on me when I booted it up. From the first menu, I felt like I had somehow stumbled back into that same insulating bubble of warmth and sound and small cups of instant butterscotch pudding. I don't usually like the nostalgia games market, but I'll make an exception for any game that can make me feel like I'm back in my grandmother's old house again.
I'm not sure I can do an unbiased review for this game, but if you ever had similar experiences, you might want to give Artifact Adventure a try.

As a documentary, it's relatively well crafted, and if the subject matter interests you (and let's face it, you're on Steam, there's a good chance that it will) this film should easily hold your attention from start to finish. The drama of the tournament is depicted quite well, and the individual characters are presented in a way that is designed to make you feel for them.
I use the word 'designed' deliberately. Documentary makers have to pick and choose from all the different elements of whatever it is they're studying in order to craft a narrative that works as a film. However, there are varying ways of doing this, some more subtle than others. The makers of this film have definitely gone in the non-subtle direction. The three main characters are all presented with such pathos that it almost becomes ridiculous. Their stories of struggle and perseverence in the face of adversity are dwelt on a bit too much, and the sappy music doesn't do much to help. There is too much sentimentality. That said, the actual narrative that is created is genuinely compelling and moving. I just question how much it really reflects reality.
Also, in many ways this film is an advertisement for DOTA. The specially made CG sequences of DOTA characters look much like something you'd see in a trailer, and it becomes jarring. But hell, it works. I want to play DOTA myself now, despite having all the skill and dexterity of a jellyfish with chronic fatigue syndrome.
Final verdict: good film, worth watching, too obviously going for the heartstrings.

There are a lot of unfair bad reviews for this game, and it makes me really sad.  So let's get that out of the way first.  YOU DO NOT HAVE TO BUY ANYTHING IN THIS GAME TO GET THE FULL EXPERIENCE.  EVER.  AT ALL.
When I heard respec scrolls were in the shop, I was concerned.  Then I found you can purchase respec scrolls (specifically, not as a random chance item) for the ingame currency at a ridiculously cheap price.  As in, just playing the game you will get way more than you would ever need.  You could respec four times a day, every single day, before you ever had to shell out a dime.  You can get in game inventory space relatively cheap too.  As in, you will unlock all your inventory slots, for free, just like I did, just by naturally playing the game.  The things people are saying about a paywall are completely false.  Grrr, makes me angry...  so now the game itself.
This is definitely an early access game, so no, it's not finished, and no, it's not polished.  What it is, however, is very fun.  I am personally really enjoying the dual class system, and exploring synergies between the two classes you pick.  Once you pick your primary class, starting at level 12 you can change your second class anytime you want.  There are a large number of abilities available, and for the time being, just experimenting with them all can be sort of fun.  The leveling is typical MMO style leveling, nothing special there.  I've heard other people aren't thrilled with the graphics, but I think they're fine.  One of the best features of the game, in my opinion, is actually how great the zones look.  Each zone has a nice, unique feel.  The combat is currently a little clunky (though I like it in spite of this) and the devs are working with the community to improve it.
The best thing this game has going for it are the devs.  They are incredibly active in the forums, personally responding to suggestions and concerns from the players.  So far they've already made major changes to the game based on customer feedback, and that's promising.
If you're looking for a finished, polished online experience, you should wait.  If you're looking to get in on a fun game that's being improved, and you want to be part of that improvement process, I'd say you should definitely jump at the chance.

The backstory of the game goes along your generic Diablo-esque trend: you are an adventurer trying to defeat the forces of evil. The subtle humour and gorgeous design (which reminds me a bit of Paper Mario) make it stand out from the crowd even further.
In brief:
At this stage I'd give it a 9/10, and strongly encourage you to buy it, if you want to be involved in the game's development, or keep an eye on it for when it's released.

Main points of the Game
- Itemization
Itemization in the game is about as complicated as mash potatoes, and even Devilian makes you think about things a bit more when it comes to stats which is already rather dull. Any item can have any stat, which some seem to get thrilled about, but that also means there needs to be FAR less actual mods available. General attack, specific weapon attack, Crit damage, dmg/block penetration, and hit points aka accuracy are about all you will find for offensive mods. The game also has a very very unforgiving diminished returns so min/maxing is rather punished than rewarded.
This also goes towards the issue of Light armor vs Heavy armor, as there is absolutely no benefit to Light armor whatsoever, but a huge penalty since your defenses will be minimal compared to wearing full plate. Full plate can have the exact same dps mods as light. This goes hand in hand with absolute open free to roll any mods on any type of base armor making one absolutely inferior. Armor value is a flat reduction, which goes hand in hand with the dull itemization.
The game also encompasses the, surprise, enhancing system in most non western games. However, in Guardians of Ember, enhancing only affects a few mods and base dmg or defense on an item. It's very basic, unfulfilling, and overall something that dulls you long before you thought it should. Even the generated pixels for weapon glow is... lackluster.
If you're a min/maxer, you will find no savior here.
If you're a themepark gear climber, you will find no satisfaction here.
If you're bored, then you might find something here to remind you how good you had it.
-PVE Content
First lets go with how you interact with the world; you collide with it.
Basically the game pushes collision between the player and monsters. This wouldn't be an issue if the hit boxes weren't so small on mobs that you often miss when you target a name. Classes that have PBAoE have a much easier time then those with mostly single target, and with the amount of holes in the worlds where you can be pushed into such as walls and corners which causes you to fall through the world it can get rather frustrating.
For skills you have 2 classes, a main and a sub. Plenty of skills, but you can only use one skill in a line of 4 which you unlock each new one by adding points to tiny little nodes. These nodes give very small passives such as 0.5% dmg, 0.5% crit chance, 1% healing, etc. So even if you like 2 of the 4 in a line, you can only use one.
Like Diablo 3... wait, no, not like anything else out there! You see you get 3 primary skill lines, 3 secondary skill lines, and by 30 around 7 advance skill lines. These all have 4 skills in them. That's a total of 52 skills, for one class, meaning over 100 for 2 classes leveled to 30.
You can use 6 skills, because the 5th and 6 th hotbar for skills is gated behind money. Now it might be changed here, but the fact that the game was originally made to revolve around buying hotbar skill slots to have more available skills is by far one of the most detrimental aspects of this game.
Remember, the game will not change drastically from the other versions that no longer exist.
You also have dungeons, which can be reset once every 30 minutes, or you can wait for a 3 minute timer to tick off after you've beaten the final boss. These dungeons have bonus chests at the end, and by accounts of some players they are only bonus chests, but in reality they are the main source of gear. I have ran hundreds upon hundreds of level 30 dungeons after farming keys and we will get to farming keys soon, and i can tell you even in a full party the epic loot drops are horrid.
Also, you will notice you get more junk/gold drops in a full party but less higher rarity gear, because people do actually roll on the same drops. The thing is just that you don't notice until you compare solo and party runs, since you only see drops for you, but rest assured you will lose on better gear running in a full party as far as ground drops go.
To get keys, you used to be able to buy them in the cash shop in other versions. They decided not to do that here, so now you need to fish. When you fish, you press X and wait for the fish to take hold and press X again. It is not automated, and you randomly pull up monsters as a anti macro feature. All fine and dandy until you've spend 4 hours fishing. Because the cursor needs to be where you wanna cast your lure and you only have 1-2 seconds to pull the lure when something hits your line, you have to simply divert all attention to this extremely dull activity. if you're lucky you can get 20 keys in a few hours, or 1 or 2.
-PVP Content
Hit first, pray you're on the south end since isomatric games really need to establish teams horizontally rather than vertically but Embers does not, and enjoy one shots to and from.
Stuff that won't ever be fixed, because it's why this is here.
-Mobs do not follow the same collision parameters as players, aka physics.
-Harsher itemization because the game was made to be a cash shop driven arpg.
-Graphic assets, such as animations and particles, or lack thereof.
However if you can get past all that, then the game has some merit to waste time. But you're gonna have to pay first. Yes, pay first.

A nice indie (yet solid) take on hack&slash genre.

instead of skills.

It offers the ability to create random dungeons in smaller or longer chunks. The game learns how you play and is quite accurate in estimating how long the next dungeon will take you to finish.
If you don't have too much time to grind in diablo, you can take 10 minutes of Book Of Demons and complete one dungeon, or you could dedicate more time if you wish. (Something similiar we could see in Dungeons of Dredmore).
There is a was array of enemies, that keep you from getting bored too quickly. Seeing as this is an Early Access game, I am relieved that there were no bugs I could find myself.
So far, you can play as a warrior, but it seems that two other classes are in the making.
I highly recommend watching this title as it progresses towards the full release.

This is a very, very good game. I don't think I need to describe what happens in it in any detail - you'll get a much better picture of that from the videos and other reviews. Instead, I should explain why I like it so much.
I'm not a big strategy game player. I used to play skirmishes on Red Alert way back in the day, but that's about it. FTL is not over complicated but that's not to say it doesn't have depth. It's fairly easy to get into and you can dip in and out of games when you have a free half hour or so.
People say FTL is hard, and I would say that is somewhat true. I would definitely recommend swallowing your pride and playing exclusively on 'Easy' until you can win consistently. The difficulty levels are misnamed - for 'Easy', read 'Hard' and for 'Normal', read 'Harder'. However, it gets less and less difficult with every playthrough.
I think many people get confused because they arrive at a battle they can't win and - not unreasonably - think that the game is too reliant on luck. However, I would strongly disagree with this. By the time you reach an unwinable battle, it's already too late. Your opportunity to make the right calls has passed. The skill is using what resources come your way to reduce the risk of opposing ships and increase your offensive ability.
Every playthough is slightly different. I don't see it as a hard game anymore, even though I still die on more than 50% of my playthoughs. Every time I die, I know what I could have done differently. Every game is different.
I play FTL virtually every night. It's relaxing (now that I know what I'm doing) but it can be horrendously exciting. I've had very good luck and not made the most of it, but my most memorable runs have been when I've had terrible luck but won through in the end. Those moments are the ones I play FTL for. I would buy it again in a heartbeat.
--------
For reference, I have about 400 games and a total of just under 2,000 hours played. I have played over 500 hours on FTL alone. I'm not weird, I'm not obsessive (at least, I don't think I am). I just enjoy playing FTL.

Kane & Lynch is certainly a controversial one. Famously responsible for getting Gamespot employee Jeff Gerstman fired, Kane & Lynch has earned a reputation for being a game that whilst being promising given the developer background (I.e Hitman series) ultimately led to dissapointment. However is this lukewarm reception justified? In a way, it sort of is.
The story is your standard revenge tale following main leads Kane and Lynch as Kane attempts to get his daughter back from an old gang that wants him dead. Nothing hugely inventive and with no real twists or turns in the plot it remains pretty uninteresting save for the ending which just happens upruptly and really leaves you with a feeling of "Is that it?". The most intreguing part of this story are its characters. Whilst Kane and Lynch themselves aren't hugely dimensional, the fact that they are often portrayed as bad people brings a nice, not often explored angle to the entire game. This portrayl lends itself well within the first half of the game with many heist like activites being the main goal, such things as bank heists, nightclub areas and prison breakouts. These areas prove to be where the game shows off the potential it could have had if more love and care went into the entire package.
The gameplay itself isn't all that exciting, just your standard third person action shooter affair. However the cover system isn't traditionally placed on a button in Kane & Lynch, instead they opted to make it an automatic cover system so you instantly stick to a wall. This sounds good in theory and for the first half of the game it works ok but it's in the game's second half where it falls apart. The problem is that the system doesn't work half the time leaving you running at the wall like a fool hoping you'll stick to it, this led to a small number of deaths that could have been easily avoided if the cover system was more competant. Also your partner AI is seriously dumb in most instances often getting themselves downed in need of saving because they stood out in enemy fire which again leads to numerous game overs.
The game's presentation is sloppy at best; pretty bad lip syncing in game, dialogue interupting other dialogue which causes them to over lap, bland visuals and design. That said however the voicework itself is pretty decent and varies up the locations to at least give some semblance of variety.
Overall Kane & Lynch isn't going to set the world on fire or win any awards, however it doesn't totally fail as there is some fun to be had with the servicable shooting. If you see it for sale at around £5 then it's probably worth the 3-4 hours of gameplay, just don't expect it to be all that great.

Thief II is a classic stealth game from a time when games were meant to actually challenge the player, force him to think, and punish him should he act hastily. This game will not hold your hand at all; there are no objective markers, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t x-ray vision that pervades modern stealth games, and no option to play like it's a generic shooter. The game is very non-linear, with multiple pathways and options for stealth, and even some secret passages for one with a clever mind and sharp eye. The ultimate goal, however, always remains the same: steal some priceless artifact and escape, leaving no trace.
The few downsides I can think of with this game just stem from it's age: the graphics are very dated, and the AI isn't very advanced, but the latter can be negated by thinking that the game's main challenge comes from the environment, not the guards. In addition, the Dark Engine that this game runs on is a little buggy, especially when it comes to dismounting from a ladder and climbing up objects, but it shouldn't impede your enjoyment too much.
If you enjoyed Dishonored (which was inspired by the Thief franchise) or the real Splinter Cell games (the series up until Double Agent), you can't go wrong with this game.

I want to be fair here and point out first off that I've only played a little less than two hours of this game.
That being said, the experience so far has been fantastic.  It bears some fairly normal cliches: the npcs are quick to trust someone they just met, you are abnormally good at something you've never done, etc.  Regardless, there is a barrier that usually exists between gameplay and story that I haven't seen in this one yet.  I walk into a safe area, talk to a guy, he gives me something to do, and I go out and do it.  It is all done with minimal control loss a'la Half-Life2, and it ledt me feeling a level of immersion that I haven't felt while gaming for a long time.
The controls are pretty smooth, and the game feels a lot like Mirror's edge, though there are some notable mobility techniques missing from the ME repertoire.  That's ok, though; there are some extras that ME doesn't have.  There is also a tad of added realism here and there, what with scaling walls taking a moment and a bit of effort, falls dazing you, and the physics of landing on weak or cushioning materials that either break when you land on them or otherwise break your fall more comfortably than the ground it is laying on.
Even with the graphic settings bottomed out (my vid card is getting up there in age), the game looks spectacular.  The lighting effects are slick, and the developer uses them very effectively.  I haven't found myself in utter darkness for long, which is a nice change from all the times when games overuse darkness as a hopeful attempt to scare players.  Textures are pretty detailed, and the pipe in my hand looks pretty spot on.
There are a lot of nice gameplay features that I like as well.  I looked forward to the parkour-around-zombies idea, but I didn't relaize that you can choose to either be a brawler or a runner.  If you want, you can slug it out with every infected you come across, and that will grant you abilities in that area faster, giving that style of gameplay more depth as a reward.  I have always been a fan of leveling your playstyle; it makes it feel more like the game was designed with your playstyle in mind.  Add to that equipment items that are actually useful and play a part in specific scenarios (firecrackers, for example), and what you have is a well-rounded gameplay toolkit.
I would comment on the music, but I usually ignore it.
All in all, I am very happy with this game purchase.

I've been playing this game for a while (I started playing on mobile during the japanese beta) and have grown to really like this game. When I compare this to most card games I've played (hearthstone, Yu-Gi-Oh!, Magic, Duel Masters) it holds its own very well, in some aspects even better.
The negatives you'd find in these games isn't present (RNG, overdrawing or underdrawing lands, text that requires a lawyer to correctly parse) but it still manages to capture a lot of the good points in its balancing act. There are some issues present, like;
-First vs Second is a bit of an issue in the game at the moment (some decks benefit too greatly from one or the other in terms of winrate)
-Paying for packs is reportedly underwhelming for the cost, although Cygames are really benevolent when it comes to giving you packs for free
-The game in steam uses default computer mouse icon
-game starts in windowed mode for some reason
-same UI from mobile version, nice and familiar if you're used to mobile but pretty sub-par for computer-only players
-UI is awful for deckbuilding
The positives of this as a card game:
-Excellent theming
-Cool cards
-Cool effects
-good deckbuilding design
-High levels of strategy in a variety of situations
-Far more benevolent with the number of card packs it gives you for free in comparison to competitors
-New expansions every 3 months
-Huge imbalance is rare/nonexistent, and if it were you can be assured Cygames would remedy it
-Cygames seem committed to running the game well, so future of the game should be fine
-Large playerbase in Japan and combined servers means you don't need to worry about playerbase size - it will always be large even with few steam players
-Take two is an interesting new arena-like mode and you get a tonne of tickets to play for free
In conclusion, as long as you like card games and don't mind anime artwork, Shadowverse is probably the best game on the market for you in terms of digital CCGs.

One of a long line of Final Fantasy retries, and it has the same failings that pretty much all of them have, along with the same strong points.  Strong points include an open world, LOTS of choices to make, and a combat system you'll either love or hate depending on how you feel about the old school Final Fantasy systems.
Weak points include awful balance, penalizing the player for not knowing what vague dialogue means (artifacts can't be exchanged between characters once acquired), and for me at least, I got rather bored of the game before I made it to the second boss.  Almost all combat is best handled by just pushing the Auto(-Resolve) button and letting it play itself.  No combat I encountered required any kind of thought or skill.  Your mages will even cast the appropriate type of damage spell to maximize damage done against the targeted enemies!  Though I did find my mage seemed to love casting the "dump all remaining MP into one big spell" spell quite a lot.
It's also worth noting that the game plays at its native, itty bitty resolution and doesn't have any kind of explanation of controls or what buttons do in the game.  I actually had to use Google to find answers about how to run the game in full screen, how to change party members, and all kinds of other things.  All of the in-game menus (accessed by pressing F1) are in Japanese.
I can't recommend this game at its asking price.  I think it'd be a decent enough buy for a few bucks, but even the $7 I paid for it felt like far more than it's worth.  It's not a bad game, but it's not really a GOOD game, either.

The combat is too basic to allow tactics; it is generally just as good (and MUCH faster) to have the game auto-pilot your party every fight. If you are unable to win a fight, your only real option is to grind a few more levels.
Three of the six classes on hand are useless. Hermits are too flimsy to be rank 2 and bows require ammo which costs money and take up space in your AGGRESSIVELY tiny inventory; meanwhile their damage is only marginally better than a Warrior's. Monks don't get to wear armor and don't have much HP, so putting one in rank 2 means they're going to require a lot of healing to stay on their feet. I would rather have a second Warrior with a two handed weapon in rank 2 so they don't put so much pressure on the healer. The Dreamer trying to be good at everything means they're good at nothing; if you need more defense you'd be better with a second Warrior, if you need more damage you'd be better with an Explorer or Shaman. The game does not give you enough information to determine this until you're several hours into a game and noticing the one party member who isn't pulling his weight. Your only recourse at this point is to start completely over or deal with having a 3 man party.
The UI is awful. If someone is dead you need to bring them to the front to be revived in towns. If you come across an item that grants a spell in the field, you have to bring the person you want to have the spell to the front of your party. If you choose the wrong person you have to reset your game to correct the mistake. The game *does not tell you this*, so I expect several players are going to give the first spell they find to the party Warrior, who has 0 MP and never gains any more. If you want to turn the music/sound off or get out of full screen, you have to press F1 and blindly guess which option does what, as the menu is in Japanese. I knew only from playing other RPGMaker games. And even when you turn sound off, attacks sometimes make a loud CLICK sound still.
The game loves springing choices on you without giving you any context for the choice. Five seconds in, you have to choose between getting an Airship, some artifacts, or the Key of Time. You are given zero explanation for what the artifacts do or what the key unlocks until you've already gone beyond the point of no return. There is a dungeon where going one direction closes the other off permanently, with zero forewarning. I rage quit the game when I approached an item in a cave a *long* way from my previous save, and some NPC I've never seen before walked up and asked me to give him the item. I do not know what this item does, who this person is, or what reward if any this guy is offering. This is not a decision, it is a guess. If you want to put these kinds of choices in your game, you owe it to the player to give them ways of getting more context on the sitaution. Let me ask this guy's name, what his quest is, why he's after this item, if he's willing to compensate me for passing what looks to be a powerful spell to him. I *want to know these things*. "Can I have that item? y/n" just ejects me from the experience.
The sprites suck. The music is repetitive. The environments are uninteresting. Combat looks sterile and stationary. There is a TON of reuse on display. If this game had been released in 1986 this would have been acceptable, even good. As-is, it's 30 years later and I'd rather just replay the original Final Fantasy. At least that game had more viable class choices than there were character slots.

I'm surprised at how much I'm enjoying Book of Demons, and I definitely recommend it. However, I do want to make sure that other buyers of the game understand what they're getting. I was looking for a new game with controller support in the dungeon crawling and hack and slash genres, and this game came up. That's not exactly accurate, though.
Book of Dungeons is understandably a dungeon crawler, because it takes place for the most part in dungeons that go deeper and deeper as the game progresses. However, it's also a CCG with turn-based combat. A variety of monsters are encountered and unlocked in the bestiary as you progress through the game, and cards of varying uses and rarity are obtained and utilized to build your deck. Players will be able to equip more cards as the game progresses and card slots are unlocked with gold and loot drops.
Combat is turn-based and automatic, so your only options as a player during combat are to move in a grid-like formation along a path to avoid and/or target enemies and projectiles, use consumable cards (like health and mana) click a button to disarm a shield or interrupt a spell to make an emeny vulnerable, or use an ability card, like a spell. No offensive combat happens while your character is in motion, so your choice is to be still and attack or maneuver around to avoid/engage enemies and obtain loot. That's not exactly, "Hack and slash" to me, and I have a hunch that this would be confusing to other players as well. Since I paid full price for my copy, and didn't get what I thought I was buying, I want to be very clear about what this game actually is.
In regard to controller support, the tag is accurate that this game currently provides partial controller support. You will still need a mouse and/or keyboard to access menus, such as those used to level up your character, switch out cards, and upgrade or identify cards. The controller support that is provided works very well. I didn't have any issues on that front, and I would bet that a Steam Controller or controller mapping program could be used for the remaining functions if a gamer was so inclined.
A positive aspect of the game is that it doesn't require a lengthy gaming session to enjoy. Games range from a few minutes to very long, and the player has the ability to set these parameters. Those with short attention spans and those who "bounce" between games will appreciate that the developers provided this feature. I know I certainly do.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. I love the angular features of the characters and scenery. It really does look like a world all its own, and it's fun to be a part of it. Overall, I'm having a lot of fun with it, and since I don't usually enjoy turn-based games of any kind, this is a testament to how very well this game has been developed.
It's a great combination of a lot of different elements, but it's really not categorized very well for browsing by tags. Of the dungeon crawling and hack and slash tags that have been attributed to this game, it's neither one nor the other. I'd classify it as a CCG with turn-based combat and dungeon crawling elements, with the dungeon environment and looting being fundamental to the game.
Most games have elements of other genres, like strategy, which is common and can be attributed to nearly any game, so I realize categorization isn't as simple as it once was. That's not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, a lot of great gaming combinations are available now, like one of my favorites which is actually an RPG/Pinball mashup. So while I don't believe these genre fusions are a negative thing, I do think that more attention should be paid to categorization, tags, and descriptions. Games like this with a $20 price tag aren't so easy to dismiss when "unwrapping" a game that isn't quite what you thought you had at the checkout.

The game is now in a playable state, but due to what appears to be a memory allocation problem, frame rate drops happen every now and again. Gameplay-wise it merges the best of AC and AO. The new stuff is welcome and adds well. The Batmobil is not just another option, though doesn't annoy as much as some complain.  The map is not as overwhelming as feared, but the story comes nowhere close to AC , still keeps you going. Special praise to the Riddler team: Riddler never felt that good before!
After finishing AC I couldn't wait to get my hands on AO and felt (as many others) utterly disappointed. AO basically served up a flat story and a game w/o love and silly new stuff together with a horrible level design and clunky game-mechanics. It took me a year to start playing AK after I bought it, mostly for the reason that AO kinda killed my love for the franchise.
AK also started as a disaster, horrible PC port and the complete scrapping of the Linux and Mac version - really sad.
But I can also feel the pain of devs who did an outstanding job in many parts of the game and it deserves more of a credit, than it received.
The map might be the biggest by size, but in reality it feels no different than AC due to a clever trick of the level and game designers: The buildings are far further apart from each other, but your gliding skills are far improved. If you have done paragliding in AC, you are now a full hang glider concerning your gliding capabilities.
AO even sucked at level design and had this tedious bridge to cross, theras AC used an upside down "U" shaped map with a no gliding zone at the end to make the map appear to be far bigger than it actually was. AK uses a more elegant version of the same trick having a donut shaped map with just a single grapple point in the middle and water around it (which is divided into 3 islands).
Interfaces were another major failure of AO and the ones of AK might not be the most beautiful, but else, they are the best concerning sense and usability. I can mouse-click the buttons again, like I was used to in AC - nice.
The progress gives even more freedom than in AC, only some gadgets are introduced quite late for my liking. All moves (including basic ones) are now explained by video which is great.
As mentioned above, gliding never felt that good in any of the Arkham games. You truly own the skies and the ceiling is far higher than in any other game before. Hence there are hardly any gliding challenges in the game. You start with the grapple boost and could add up to two upgrades for an extended boost.
I did the Pepsi challlenge and started a combat map before even reading through the key bindings and it felt familiar right away, which was very pleasing. But after a while I noticed more and more subtle differences, which is the best a dev could achieve by introducing new stuff: It fitted, wasn't overwhelming or silly as in AO (the flashbang thingy, anyone?) but also extended the gameplay. That being said not all is excellent.
The AO Remote Claw, the Shock Gloves and the Sonic (Shock) Batarangs are gone. The former replaced by the Batclaw, as we know it from AC and the other two by the ability to pick up baseball bats and knock through defences (until they break) and the voice synthesizer respectively.
The new combat moves are mostly extensions of existing moves and hence not overwhelming, like an "Aerial Juggle" would add a kick to an Ultra Stun with another attack click and things like that. Notably, the enemy AI has new options as a result of merging some of the AO combat with AC's. So you got some enemy charging at you which you can only evade and you have got AA style thugs which have permanent blades or even electrical stun attached to their bodies, so that a Disarm & Destroy would not work anymore.
Another new breed are medics, which occur in both Predator and Combat maps and have the ability to heal up to 3 unconscious thugs and also temporarily charge them with electricity on Combat maps.
In combat, you now got very cool looking Environmental Takedowns and some new special moves involving your quickfire gadgets, which are not really up to much. Basically most of the new combat moves are more of a filler than anything else.
There are only 3 special combat moves, so the Bat Swarm bit the dust. It was useful, but I found I triggered it far too often by accident. Generally, the combat feels not as broken as in AO, but also not as smooth as in AC - somwhere in between.
They also heavily worked on the predator maps, introducing a couple of new enemy types, which are mostly worth it. The best might be a drone operator and his drone, covering the high ground as well. Also there are thugs, which can track your detective mode besides the jammer and the mine thug we already knew from AC. Thugs might place sentry guns or wear deflective uniform which results in a colourless detective vision profile. - You can counter any of these threats with your upgraded disruptor, which becomes prep tool number one again. Else, the crypto sequencer got beefed up and is also capable of disabling turrets or triggering environmental traps. Enemies check grates and might hit you with thermobaric grenades, burning a whole grate system.
One novelty is the Fear TD, which is basically a noob friendly way of disposing of up to 5 enemies w/o being hit. You don't have to use it, so kinda ok.
The Batmobile, well truly the most controversial part of the game. I could see the marketing department and devs for once arm in arm, one side praising the great diversion in target groups, the other marvelling in their little "technological terror" as Darth Vader might have put it. How is it?
Personally, not the racing game type of person, but to my surprise, it felt quite good and after some trial & error on the challenge maps, I at least managed the two star times. The Batmobile is integral part of the story, but apart from the late game stages given in small doses and not as annoying as I feared (isn't the game about fear after all?).
Apart from the traversal or racing bit, you got a combat mode and challenges which aim to copy the combat w/o cars (as in combo and variation points). All in all manageable. The third version is a mix of the two and finally, you do some predator style hit and run against the heavy tanks, which I didn't really like - felt a bit like Killer Croc in AA: Too long.
I liked the boss fights in AC, especially Ras, Freeze and final one, wheras I found the endless Bane fight in AO really boring. Credit to them , they tried something new as in a racing and lesser used type of predator boss battle, but ultimately it fell short for me. The racing boss "fight" was tedious and the predator boss fight felt like playing the end of AC's Deadshot side quest about 4 times in a row.
Well, there is a reason that Joker was in most cases Batman's nemesis in movies over last 3 decades: The sadistical Clown Prince of Crime is simply irreplacable and ironically gave the Batman universe credibility and weight. It was the counterpart of the stiff Batman which was perfectly impersonated by Kevin Conroy's voice. It was the culmination of all these weird and crazy cartoon villains and made it enjoyable. British Rocksteady is at its best when indulging in Joker's dark, black humour. So the funny thug lines are back which change over the course of the main story and some of them are truly hilarious.
Batman on the other hand side gets taunted like never before and it is by any means the darkest of all Arkham episodes - not only concerning the humour. (
), but basically AC was too good to top. On AA level.

I don't write reviews often, but because of the incredibly mixed feelings this game left me with I decided to write one anyway.
The technical:
First of all, this game doesn't support resolutions over 1920x1200. If you have a 1440p or higher resolution monitor, be aware of this. I also do not know if it supports aspect ratios other than 16:10 and 16:9. If you have an ultrawide monitor, I cannot guarantee they offer a suitable resolution.
At the bottom of this review is a link to the game's discussions where the developers say higher resolutions aren't coming in the future either.
The good:
The game itself feels pretty innovative and I really liked the card system for your skills, equipment and consumables. The dungeon size slider is also a nice touch. The art style is very nice as well. It has a little "Don't Starve" influence, with everything being made out of paper, but in its very own way.
The bad:
Aside from the resolution problems mentioned under "The technical", the game suffers from immense swings in difficulty because of the procedural generation. Long corridors with archers can be a pain, as well as rooms being packed to the bring with monsters. This can be extra frustrating because monsters block your movement. Because you are "on rails" (can't walk off the paths) you do not have the freedom of movement to properly kite to deal with these packs.
The verdict:
Before the problems under "the bad" are fixed, I'd recommend holding off on this one. It shows a lot of promise, but still needs a few changes before it's ready.
The discussion regarding resolution:
Specifically, they say that because the 2D graphics they use are not made for higher resolutions, they will not be able to support 1440p or over without redoing all their art assets.

Kane & Lynch: Dead Men is probably more well known for the Jeff Gerstmann/Gamespot controversy than the actual game itself. I'm not going into what went on between Eidos and Gamespot but the game itself. Was it good? I thought so. Was it great? Well, no I can't say that. K&L is a third person shooter taking you through diverse locations such as a bank, a nightclub in Japan, a prison and finally Cuba. This part I really liked. I enjoyed the different locales even though they were extremely linear. The gun play is fun (this is a cover shooter) with plenty of weapons to pick from. The story was interesting and I enjoyed our protagonists. The bad? Well the enemy AI is AWFUL. There are times where they'll run at you or other times where they are staying behind cover while you fill them full of lead. My biggest issue was the hit detection. There were times, the guys you were shooting were bullet sponges. Other times one or two rounds would do it. Pretty annoying. The gameplay is pretty one note. Go from A to B shooting everything in sight. The levels are well done though. Especially the prison level, which was outstanding. I picked up K&L for $2.50 during the Square sale. Even with the brisk 6 hours it took me to finish it. It is well worth that and more. Recommended.

This is a very, very good game. I don't think I need to describe what happens in it in any detail - you'll get a much better picture of that from the videos and other reviews. Instead, I should explain why I like it so much.
I'm not a big strategy game player. I used to play skirmishes on Red Alert way back in the day, but that's about it. FTL is not over complicated but that's not to say it doesn't have depth. It's fairly easy to get into and you can dip in and out of games when you have a free half hour or so.
People say FTL is hard, and I would say that is somewhat true. I would definitely recommend swallowing your pride and playing exclusively on 'Easy' until you can win consistently. The difficulty levels are misnamed - for 'Easy', read 'Hard' and for 'Normal', read 'Harder'. However, it gets less and less difficult with every playthrough.
I think many people get confused because they arrive at a battle they can't win and - not unreasonably - think that the game is too reliant on luck. However, I would strongly disagree with this. By the time you reach an unwinable battle, it's already too late. Your opportunity to make the right calls has passed. The skill is using what resources come your way to reduce the risk of opposing ships and increase your offensive ability.
Every playthough is slightly different. I don't see it as a hard game anymore, even though I still die on more than 50% of my playthoughs. Every time I die, I know what I could have done differently. Every game is different.
I play FTL virtually every night. It's relaxing (now that I know what I'm doing) but it can be horrendously exciting. I've had very good luck and not made the most of it, but my most memorable runs have been when I've had terrible luck but won through in the end. Those moments are the ones I play FTL for. I would buy it again in a heartbeat.
--------
For reference, I have about 400 games and a total of just under 2,000 hours played. I have played over 500 hours on FTL alone. I'm not weird, I'm not obsessive (at least, I don't think I am). I just enjoy playing FTL.

When Thief II released, I had probably already spent over 300 hours (re)playing Thief: The Dark Project and Thief: Gold. Shortly after its release, I rebuilt my PC and dove in. The graphics were much improved from the first games, and the story was even better. The missions were even more expansive this time, and replaying the game always led to finding something new.
What made this game even more brilliant, was the opening of the Dark Engine to the users who wanted to mod/level build. Looking Glass Studios closed shortly after the release of Thief II and the sequel wasn't produced until 2004. In that period of downtime, hundreds of new, fan-made, missions were created and distributed in online communities like the Circle of Stone and Shadow. Some were better than others. And just a few may have been better than the game itself. In fact, one of the fan missions was so good, the developer was hired by Eidos to work on Thief III. Moreover, some fan mission developers ended up joining forces to release their own, unofficial sequel named Thief2x.
The game itself had its own replay value, but the fans who made these missions and mods increased the value tenfold.
Thief II is a must play. I'd definitely recommend playing Thief: The Dark Project or Thief: Gold first. When you're done, it's worth doing the investigation to find these fan-made missions and play them too.

TL;DR:
Note: This review doesn’t contain any spoiler.
What can I say? It’s your typical South Park look. Even though some effects seem dull, you’ll get what you expect. Every little detail is beautiful designed and there are some surprises. But don’t expect any graphical wonders. I love it.
I wish I could give more than 10/10. Some Soundtracks are damn good and remind you of certain games like Skyrim and such. But even funnier and better. Perfect synchro as in the series. Some weapon could sound more…”Damaging”, but overall you’ll feel mighty and strong and it is all accompanied by gorgeous music.
Normally I’d give here a 7/10, since the Story isn’t THAT innovative, but since it’s South Park, they managed to do fantastic things out of seemingly tedious things. It’s all well told and it doesn’t get boring at all. For me it was.. or is.. THE best South Park Episode I’ve experienced so far. And it gets weirder the further you get.
Oh boy where do I start? I’ll quote Smash Mouth here: “So much to do, so much to see.” And that’s on point. You have so many items to gather and equip, so many different enemy types to fight, so many places to visit… I could go on forever. I spent the first hour just walking through the whole town and visiting every building, talking to everyone. It was great.
The Fights are well done and you have a lot of ways to handle them. May it be through magical farts or combining your abilities with some heavy sword attacks. You even get to set who is accompanying you. You can choose wether it is Butters, Kyle, Cartman etc.. They all have different abilities and offering advantages in certain fights. So try them all out!
The options seem endless. The only thing I really didn’t like about it is that later on it gets so annoying to fight since it gets way too easy (I recommend a higher difficulty level). But you are greatly entertained for some hours.
The first half of the game was really challenging and some quest I had to leave out and do them later since I didn’t had a chance, but around Level 9 it starts getting way too easy. I played on normal (You can switch difficulty settings mid-game if you want) and I smashed just through the enemy lines. It’s easy for beginners, but don’t expect that much of a challenge. ♥♥♥♥ you Al Gore.
- I haven't come along one single bug. Just One or two minor lags that aren’t even worth mentioning.
- Funniest Game ever.
- ♥♥♥♥ you Al Gore.
- Lack of options, which is also not really worth mentioning because.. come on.. You didn’t really expect changing the graphic settings here, did you?
- Runs smoothly
- I completed it in around 16 hours and that is quite a lot! I left out 2 quests, which you can still complete after beating the game, but I was satisfied and happy at the end.
-
If you’re a fan of South Park: Get it.
If you’re no fan of South Park: Get it and become a fan.

The puzzles are well made and integrated into the story. Some puzzles might be a bit too hard for children, because the solution is not always showed immediatly. These harder puzzles do make it more entertaining for teenagers and mature people.
>Gameplay:
The Gameplay is nice and smooth, you don't need to have a very expensive PC to have nice graphics and good performance. One of the bad, yet importent thing in the gameplay is the fighting. Each hero or villain has his own special auto attacks that he or she will use from time to time.

Besides this the game is great! The game features a great open world based on New York City that you can explore, discover, collect and help people in. One thing I liked a lot about this game is that it features nearly every character in the Marvel Universe. Since this is a thing the movie world has problems with I found it great to play with aswell Iron Man and Wolverine. The game is also made in a way where diffirent characters need to use their abilities to help their team mates. It is impossible to do one level with just 1 character.
>Final Verdict:
The game is great and gives you more than enough content to play with for the price you are buying it for.  I recommend this game to everyone that likes Lego, Marvel or just puzzle games in general. I am still having a great experience with this game and I love the controller support which makes it so easy to play with my friend.
