Oh? Where was i? Ah yes, this game focuses on gun play and infantry combat more than awe and spectacular stuff, now with realistic thirdperson animations and AAA-quality first person animations. A few things i'd like to point out are:
+Lack of updates: while 314 arts doesn't update their game as much, at least they don't pump-out updates everytime something new is created, like most early access titles do. Rather, they would polish everything before they release an update. If it's quality we're getting, then i think it's worth the wait. One problem with this is that it kept players from coming back to the game as time progresses, my suggestion: put out a couple teasers every now and then to keep players up-to-date with what's going on behind the development of the game. It also shows that you're not slacking off.
+Performance: remember the old days of Police Infinity? Where the game barely has any optimizations for low-end computers? Well, now with the Extremely Low settings, even a toaster can run this game smoothly(ish).
+Gameplay: the gunplay is solid, feels like Modern Warfare and Counter-Strike decides to have a baby and named it Vengeance. The animations, the sound design and  the maps, they're all beautifully crafted.
+AI: the bots, they took a level in badassery and is now deadly assassins. Even early wave coop bots can do massive damage if you're not careful. Of course there's still some issues, like how accurate they shoot and sometimes they would stand next to each other not shooting anything, pathing errors, but yknow, they're multiplayer bots, they're aren't humans. Compared to Police Infinity's AI, i'd say they're somewhat better.
+Zombie mode: The usual generic stuff, zombies chases you and you kill them. For now it's generic. But i'm sure mars has got big plans ahead *wink*
+Networking: the netcode is decent, you can play on a german dedicated server with barely any lag. But just in case, if you die in a multiplayer match, just say it's a netcode thing :)
-Lack of players: Same as PI, you guys might need to step up your game in order to have a bigger playerbase.
-Missing content: Again, this is still an Early Access Alpha, and 314 arts isn't DICE. Wait as it develops and it'll have a campaign soon enough. I wonder what's the lore will be.
Overall: I'd say that this new update makes the game more playable than previous builds, kudos on that. If you want some fun with friends or if you're up for something fresh and not spacey shoot-em-up 2017. This is something you can get into.

I recently purchased super hexagon through a humble bundle sale containing FTL and Dustforce, both games I wanted a good deal, so I purchased the bundle a penny above the average price and got 6 games out of 5 and a half dollars, three of those games I’ll probably never play. I had heard about super hexagon before, often being praised as a very difficult game from both games journalists and regular people. Discussion of the game has died down quite a bit over the past year or so, and I rarely see it talked about. Now that I finally got my hands on the game I can actually voice my opinion.
Super Hexagon is a very minimalistic game. There are only two buttons you need to use for actual gameplay and three that you need to use to navigate the menus/restart the level. These buttons are the , , and space bar buttons.  moves you counter-clockwise around the hexagon, while  moves you clockwise it, and spacebar is reserved for menu selection. The game page describes it as a minimal action game, but there isn’t really much action to it. I’d probably say it’s closest to the rhythm genre of video games, although the controls don’t really specifically dictate any sort of rhythm and aren’t related to the rhythm of the song. The actual gameplay itself is controlling small triangle rotating around a hexagon (in the early part of the game, which is the first 20 seconds or so), and trying to avoid various blocks of light. The way the camera shifts, the hexagon pulsate, and the blocks fall are all related to the rhythm, furthering my point of this being closest to a rhythm game. Each level has its own song, each going at a quicker pace for each following level. That’s all there is to it, besides an arcade mode, which unlocks all the levels and keeps a scoreboard.
Unfortunately, the game seems to fail to deliver on a lot of basic concepts that the game holds. First is the actual “rhythm” part of the game, which is unfortunately awful. While the game does function on rhythm, there’s nothing in the controls that reflect that natural rhythm of the game, and there is no way to get in rhythm. Moving clockwise or counter-clockwise to avoid light blocks is easy enough, but when you start to get into the more advanced levels there are specific patterns that clearly need to be played “on rhythm”. These sections would be a bit easier if the controls weren’t hypersensitive. I can’t really fault them on that aspect though, as many areas of the game would be impossible to complete if the controls weren’t fast and sensitive, like the sections where there’s a set of light blocks that give you only one opening immediately followed by a similar set of blocks, but with the opening being on the opposite side of the hexagon. I often found myself dying to hypersensitive controls, because when I just try to tap either my right or left arrow keys, it sends me more than one side over, when I’m only trying to shift one side over, which is unfortunate, because the developers were clearly very lenient with the games hit detection, with a hitbox size being similar to that of a Touhou character, where only the very center of the triangle needs to be hit to be destroyed. These controls, are, however, tight and responsive, they are just too sensitive for me to accurately be able to move the triangle around the hexagon without dying from stupid mistakes. Thankfully the developers also realized many people’s tries at a level would only last mere seconds, so they made death as unobnoxious as possible. You die, you hit space bar, and you continue. The retry also starts you off at a different part of the song, depending how long your last try lasted, so it doesn’t run stale. The light blocks also seem to be a bit randomized also adding to the “fresh” factor of dying and retrying. I do feel that in some levels there are parts of the song that are much easier than other parts of the song.
Speaking of the music, the other aspect of the game that truly bothers me is the aesthetic of the game. The flashy visuals and annoying electronic music that play in each level make me almost nauseous at times. While my musical tastes are completely subjective, when I play a rhythm game I don’t want the visuals to be overly distracting (which is why I can’t play some songs on hard or expert in Project Diva), which they are. There are times in the game where I feel like I’m playing a level of Hotline Miami, because of the shifting camera, rotating hexagon, rotating light blocks, etc. This all makes the game very confusing to look at sometimes, and makes it nearly impossible for me to progress through the level past 5-10 seconds. Also the sort of monochromatic visuals (the whole level will just be different shades of green, red, grey, blue, purple, etc.) make it even more confusing to look at, and sometimes is hard to determine whether or not a certain color is a light block or if it’s just a part of the background. While I hate the term, these factors do end up adding to sort of an “artificial difficulty”, which is not only challenging, but also frustrating. If the game was more static, I’m sure the developers could’ve added something to make the game a bit more challenging and a bit less vomit inducing (this is seriously the first time I’ve ever gotten motion sickness from a game), because I truly do like the concept of the game.
One last thing I wanted to mention was playtime. The game time of each try lasts only a couple of seconds to a minute or two if you’re actually decent at this game, unlike myself. This quick play time and constant death make the game feel quicker than it actually is and I quit the game realizing that I only played 3-5 minutes, when I thought I was playing 10-15 minutes. This type of game is best suited for mobile device because of the quick pick-up-and-play style of the game and the simplicity of it. This isn’t a game that you sit down and play for hours at a time.
While Super Hexagon is undeniably a quick and relatively enjoyable experience I can’t help but fault it on a few flaws of the core aspects of gameplay like the hypersensitive controls, the bad music (which can be turned off, but will only hinder the gameplay), the vomit inducing visuals, the fact that the game grows tired very quickly, and the unnecessary difficulty that is added through many of those aspects. 4/10 – has potential/can be enjoyed, but many of the core aspects of the game are flawed/have problems that severely hinder core aspects of gameplay.

Calling Thief II the best stealth game I've ever played is an understatement. Thief II is quite simply the best game I've ever played, period, and is my go-to example of how to do game design right.
While it's old, ugly and more than a little cheesy, the game is thoughtfully and brilliantly designed. Every element has a reason to be there, its level design is simply the best I've even seen in a game, and despite having logged well over a hundred hours in it across various playthroughs I still find new surprises in familiar haunts. Thief II isn't big in the Witcher 3, "here's 50 square miles of monster-filled backwoods with no real reason to look around" sort of way. It's big in the way your neighborhood was big when you were a kid. You live here. You know this place. But somehow here's something you've never seen before.
On the gameplay side of things, Thief II is simply a lot more fair than most stealth games, which often seem deliberately designed to make you screw up, via twitchy paranoid guards, bottlenecking level design, or random arbitrary rule changes. Thief does none of that, and every time I get caught it genuinely feels like an error on my part and not because the AI randomly decided to spin around right as the blackjack was about to hit the back of their head. Hiding in shadows actually works, the levels are expansive enough that guard patrols take more than five seconds to loop back around, and there is very rarely only one way in.
Fans of stealth games and students of game design as an art form would both do well to give this game a look.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is an amazing game. You will spend hours, maybe even days, building the greatest civilization the world has ever known. Civilization V alone was good, but with the expansion packs and DLC, I couldn't tell you how amazing the game is. Civilization V is a turn-based strategy game where you are the leader of any civilization of your choosing, and there are different ways you can play the game. You can be passive and make allies with different civilizations and immerse them with your culture, or you can be aggressive by conquering nations and destroying entire civilizations. One nice thing is that you can also play with your friends, by becoming allies and working together, or completely go against each other and fight to the last man standing. I don't know how many times I told myself "Just one more turn", until I realized that I've been playing for 7-10 hours straight. I couldn't tell you everything there is to know about why you should get this game.
Pros and Cons
Pros:
- Civ V is like a tool box. It's not a game where everything is set a certain way which makes you feel constricted. Instead, you have the ability to edit the way the game is set up to your liking. This includes the number of civs in your game, or allowing only certain victory types, and whether resources are abundant or not. There are many more things you can do that I didn't even list.
- There are many, many different civilizations that you can choose to be. Each civilization has different and unique abilities, buildings, and units. For example, America has the B17 (Replaces Bomber) and Minutemen (Replaces Musketmen), and can purchase tiles for half the normal cost as well as all land military units gain +1 sight.
- There are different ways to beat the game. You can influence other civilizations, through culture and diplomacy, and become leader of the world. You can also grab resources, build up your military and conquer the world. There's also a scientific victory, which involves researching parts to build a spaceship. You can have a true space race!
- There's Steam Workshop. With Steam Workshop, there are many different things now that can enhance the game more than ever before. People have made new civilizations to play as, you can have new buildings for your civilization, or  have new ways to extend the game beyond the true ending of the game.
- Multiplayer is available. Some people might like the game, but not like being alone while playing. Well you can share the experience with your friends. You can create your own match, and make it public or private. Making each match is about the same as making a normal singleplayer match.
- The expansions are awesome. Gods and Kings was the first major expansion pack for the game, and it added many new civilizations, as well as a new game gameplay system. G&K added religion to the game, to which you can create your own religion and spread it across the globe. The second major expansion pack was Brave New World, which also added some new civilizations, but also changed the gameplay in many ways. The world is connected in more ways than ever before, with a new trading system, and the creation of a United Nations-like system, where all civs work together.
There are many more pros that I didn't list, but here are some cons
Cons:
- The A.I. is questionable. No matter how high you set the difficulty, and I've beaten the highest difficulty, I've never seen the A.I. make a logical or rational decision in a game. I've been denounced and attacked by nations that I've been allies with for thousands of years, just because I made one wrong move. If anything, the higher the difficulty, the more the A.I. cheats, as the A.I. doesn't get smarter, it just basically gets a better head start in the game than you.
- The multiplayer is also questionable. I know I said that the multiplayer was a cool thing in the game, but it does have its problems. You don't know how many times me and my friends have tried to start up a game of Civ, and the game crashes. We have had to restart a couple of games entirely because they seemed broken. So I'm hoping that maybe one day Firaxis or someone will fix the multiplayer, because when it works it really is fun.
Like I said before, Sid Meier's Civilization V is an amazing game. Though the game does have some problems, I think that you'll find that the pros outweigh the cons. Another good thing about Civ V I would like to mention is that you dont really have to of played any of the other Civilization games to know how to play this one. I was not a Civ veteran, I hadn't of even heard of the Civilization franchise until I saw this game. However, I do know a few people who played Civ IV and III, and they all say that they enjoy Civ V as well, so Civ V is good for old and new players. The last thing I would like to say to you is to buy this game now, and try to get it with the expansions.

When I have first seen the game on images, I didn't think much of it. It looked weird, yet I gave it a shot and after starting it up the first time, I played for several hours, untill that game started crashing on one level and I couldn't proceed (played before it was released, didn't encounter any crashes as of today). And I was crushed that I can't continue on, I've been enjoying my time with this title a lot! This day marks the release so I jumped right on it and finished the main story.
If you are seeing this title for the first time, let me tell you why it's worth your time.
This is a hack & slash done right, there's a big enemy pool the game is drawing from and you're seeing something new all the time from basic skeletons and zombies to crazy mages that will fill the screen with spawned enemies and then, if you escape, teleport all of them right on top of you again. You gain loot in the form of money, consumables and most importantly, relics and runes to upgrade these relics in the form of cards. You essentially create your deck of cards that your character will equip and that defines your build. There are 32 cards available for the knight character and you can equip up to 10 of them at a time. You can freely switch your cards even when curently in a dungeon.
At this stage of early access you only have the knight available, your character is stuck in a created path that you can't divert from, yet anemies occupy the whole place. No worries, it works well (although I had to get used to the auto-walk mechanic, where you click in a direction you want to go and your character walks untill he bumps into a cross-road, an enemy or you click behind him) and you can attack in all directions with a surprising ammount of range for a melee character, it feels like you have a bow equiped but honestly with the ammount of enemies you have to deal with in later levels, this only makes sense as you'd get swarmed and killed in no time without this range.
Admitedly, the game felt rather easy, I have yet to die a single time and I have finished the story and done a little of free-play, the first two levels were hardly a challange but once I got into hell it started to be a bit more interesting, there I got to finally see my character's ability when his HP reaches 0 (you gain some HP back and push enemies back, sort of a second-wind mechanic). The difficulty spike in the final area is pretty big and it felt like I jumped over a step before that. Once you enter free-play, enemies do much more damage, feels like a new game +, you keep all your loot and upgrades, but you can replay previous levels and unlock more difficulties for free-play, I can see how the high difficulties will be a big challange.
Bosses are well done, outside of the 3 main bosses, the random ones you encounter in dungeons have various phases that you have to beat in order to kill it. Sometimes you have to stand nearby the boss, sometimes you have to kill his summoned enemies and sometimes you just have to go trigger happy on him , I always feel excited when a boss pops-up and it's a shame they don't seem to appear as often in free-play (from what I can tell you get one at the end of the final dungeon in a level where as in the main mode you can sometimes encounter as many as 3 in a single dungeon). I believe they are randomly generated so sometimes you get a really weak one and sometimes you just wish it would die already. The main trio felt unique, I am going to spoil the first one where you have to destroy many pots to find a key but the pots are trapped with explosives, enemies and really no loot outside of junk, you can get a chain-reaction going there pretty easily as some pots spawn more pots with random properities so if you failed to kill that bomb that explodes into 3 more boms and these explode into 9 more bombs and so on, there's suddenly a swarm of enemies going after you. And that's the first main boss, or at least a path to it, good stuff. I felt that the final boss could have been more unique tho, it felt anticlimactic compared to the other two.
Overall I've had a great time and will most likely be returning to this game from time to time. Give it a shot if you're after a new hack & slash game, this one won't dissapoint you.

This game is a testament to why quality control needs to be better-utilized on steam, because this game is so, SO bad in every aspect that I can barely call it a game.
The controls:
Ground movement is the only thing that is the least bit functional. You move at a decent pace and can turn around on a dime.
Air movement, however, is about 90% of what this game does wrong. Pretend that every level is the ice level, but only while you're in the air. Also, you go insanely fast. I cannot even begin to comprehend how this got screwed up so badly. Landing on a 3-tile platform is a challenge with how little control you have in the air.
The dash function is meh, it works sometimes, sometimes you careen off in a random directions.
Now, the failure of a control scheme makes the game bad by itself, but it would at least be tolerable if the developers had realized how bad the controls were and designed levels with that in mind.
NOPE.
The entire last third of the final world, I freely admit to using speedhack on, because there is absolutely no way of getting the level of precision needed to clear most of those levels at normal speed; this comes down to the controls being flawed. The levels aren't *awful* on their own, though generally nothing to write home about, but they'd be a decent challenge even in a game with good controls, and they are basically impossible with this game's poor excuse for controls.
This is the closest a game has come to being "unplayable" for me without literally failing to boot up.
Oh, uh. The rest. The story: doesn't exist. Literally. The art style: Ehh, it's okay, the 3D models superimposed on the 2D landscape look a bit off. The music: Boring, grating chiptune crap.
In summary: There is absolutely no reason to buy this game. Hundreds of better platformers out there, this won't even entertain you if you're really bored. It'll only make you question why you were so stupid as to get this game in the first place. Thank the lord I got this as bundle fodder.

Thankfully, the CGI shots Valve gave off for the little Dota 2 bits were gorgeous to look at.
The film itself focuses on the life and times of multiple video game enthusiasts, trying to live the worldwide dream: Get payed to play video games. As inspiring as the premise sounds, the actual way the story presents itself is quite pitiful. It's just depressing how it really made me pity them when they threw their lives away, hoping video games would put them out of financial trouble. It's only worse when the movie itself says that there's no guarantee of even getting paid if you go terribly enough.
It's blatantly obvious how this movie draws inspiration from Indie Game: The Movie, yet it's such a shame how the movie failed to have me feel even slightly the same way as when I watched the latter. You might feel differently if you share as raw of a passion as the characters in Free To Play. It just didn't click for me.
The movie itself deserves your hour and a half, only because it's free. I don't see myself re-watching the movie in the near or far future, unlike with Indie Game: The Movie, a film I've seen literally countless times.

I get it, this is early access. I also get it, this is a game lots of people have been waiting for, for a long time and are exited. But there is simply way to many issues that are unrelated to the development / bugs and are related to design choices that make the game less fun... time and again.
First, the delay on every action... it feels like my character, from Engineer to knight all need to contemplate the combined works of shakespear before stabbing that goblin munching on your entrails. Every. Single. Time. This goes for triggering quest givers, stabbing dudes, running away, switching target and so forth... imagine playing on a latency of 500+ in a game, but by design.
This is compounded by the problems with the games AI, which, while never a strong point of the genre was never quite this braindead. Ai doesn't roam, doesn't call for help, doesn't flank or use counter abilities... it doesn't even reposition. This is even true for Bosses that can be defeated by the magic of "kite in circles".
Now, visually the game looks fine, and from a performance perspective, i have no problems with it. IT's not perfect by any means, and certainly, many games look pretties by a mile, but the aesthetic fits and melds well together and has no weird bugs in terms of clipping or the like.
Abilities are overal pretty cool with various effects and options that allow decent customization. While the upgrade system isn't my favorite, it does provide a nice incentive to "branch out" in the trees instead of just maxing one.
But, any goodwil on that front is lost to me by the bad Loot... And lets be fair, between cool explosions - you want to look awesome. And visually... you mostly do, but when you open your boss-taken loot and expect a cool Sword of summoning swords of flaming necromancy... you will find +3 DPS. or +3.5 Healing. Utterly bland.
So bad a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ai, bad loot and sub-par performance in terms of delays on actions make this one a game to hold of on. Maybe Early access will be good for it, but for now... pick up Diablo 3 or Grim dawn, they are infinitely better titles.

After several years, I finally got some money on my Steam account that I could use instead of just gifted and free games; I made a point of making this my first purchase. After a couple years of space since I found this game for free on Kongregate, this game has lost none of the charm and fun that it had, and I can honestly say that of all the games in my library, THIS is the one I'm most proud to have. The design is simple but not at all hard to look at, the sound design is good, the procedural generation works perfectly, the range of options for customizing your game is almost staggering, and it's super easy and fun to play. Even repetetive acts like mining, where you let the autopilot take over and just sit back while your ships and drones carve asteroids to bits, only taking over when it's time to head to a station and unload, then leave dock and do it all over again, come off as soothing rather than grinding, and serve as a good, long break between combat when you clear areas of enemies.
Of course, all this is dependant on what your settings are. If you want to risk enemies spawning in and making mining a risky business even after you've killed the local pirate captain, that's almost certainly possible. You don't even have to mine at all! The game is almost entirely freeform; Just you, a long term goal, and a ton of ways of reaching it.
So kick back, captain. Put on some tunes or a podcast or something, and relax as you make your fortunes.
And on a note outside of the game; The developer of this game is a motivated, passionate person whom the entire gaming industry should be looking at as an example. If everyone were as passionate and attentive to both detail and their audience's voices, we'd never have a bad game again.
Can't wait for the sequel.

First off, I've enjoyed the game, a lot. I would recommend it to anyone who was sorely disappointed with Devilian like I was, or if D3/PoE aren't open/multiplayer enough for you.
The game is early access at the moment, and had launch issues. Be honest though, how often do MMO's not have launch issues -_-? A lot of players were having lag and connection issues, but they have been largely resolved. With the upcoming NA server I expect them to be completely resolved.
There are bugs, as with all games. Most are minor. I never encountered a bug that hindered my progress... except for 1 quest! Grrrr! There are some translation errors in skill descriptions, which isn't a big deal IMO. The team is always on top of the bugs and quickly comes up with a workaround or quick solution for the community while they work to fix the issue internally.
The graphics are good. By good, I mean they are pleasant to look at. They aren't cutting edge, but they aren't bad.
The itemization and progression is enjoyable for me. The drops are random as hell and I love it. You can have a bow drop with +hammer mastery on it. If it wasn't like this, I would be geared in a few dungeon runs. I come out of the level 28 hard mode with over 50 blue items each run. There are ways to customize and fine tune your equipment to your exact specs. I have geared myself at the level 40 cap at the time of this edit and it has been an incredibly satisfying experience, I have all of my desired stats and am quite satisfied with the control I had over customizing my equipment.
The game has item enhancement. The standard +1, +2, +3, and so on. There are no items to aid in the enhancement process, and you get plenty of the enhancement materials from salvaging bad equipment.(I mention this for monetization and p2w reasons. No buying your way to +15 or +20 in this game.) The team has stated and shown that they are against providing pay to win features and have removed controversial items already.
Skills. There are a lot. Far more than you can utilize at once. There are a lot of possibilities for viable builds. I'm so excited that there is solid potential for a lot of build diversity. Much better than D3 or PoE. For example, in my build I'm using the generic whirlwind skill for mob clearing, and I switch to a nuke for bosses. The cool thing is that when I whirlwind through a pack of mobs, I have a chance on hit to summon minions. I can summon quite a few. ;)
Sound? The skill effects are nice. I don't know about the background music or ambience as I listen to music while playing.
Story and quests? I only read them when I got stuck. There are hidden quests and goodies to be found on the maps. People who explore the entire map and spend some time killing mobs to get specific drops will be rewarded. There are also a number of books throughout the maps that have hints to things. After having rushed through the quests and content to the current cap on my first character, I'm really looking forward to taking my time and exploring everything and trying to find all the secrets on my next character.
Monetization. As a mainly free player, I'm quite comfortable with their plan so far. They provide an alternate currency for the cash shop which can be acquired in-game on a daily basis.
I absolutely love the community. It is amazing. To prove this isn't all talk you can check my profile and see that for all my games I've played, this is the first review I've ever written, and I've even made two guides for this game already.
Ugh, it's late and I'm having a hard time thinking of anything else(At the time of this edit I'm a little more clear :P). If something comes to mind I'll update this later. I would and will be recommending this to my friends. If anyone tried the game during the technical tests or the first 2 days of launch and quit because of lag issues. I strongly urge you to give the game another chance. It may be rough around the edges right now, but it is a true gem in the process of being polished.

A re-make of the classic turn based X-COM/UFO series originally developed by MicroProse in the mid 90s. It has received a modern make over which many will construe as a dumbing down of the game - many components of the original game have been removed, presumably for the benefit of new players though the core strategical element of the game still comes through.
Once completed, you have the option of turning on several mods that bring back some of classic mechanics such as random stats on new soldiers and variable damage.
The game tends to be very punishing in the early game but once you get past the rookie stage and get a solid group of upgraded soldiers with fancy weapons it becomes increasingly easy, even the bigger and tougher aliens don't pose much of a threat when you have fully upgraded snipers!
For the insane there is the impossible difficulty which is extremely harsh and not recommended at all for new players no matter how good you think you are. Classic difficulty presents a good balance of challenge where you can get away with small mistakes/bad RNG but too many and you will be punished.
An easy way to wile away a few hours/days, especially as the game is pretty much always in the big holiday sales.

So this game came out not too long ago and is still in development, but I will give my feedback as well as point out ups and downs of this game. Let's begin with positive aspects.
-Although the game doesn't have many servers up or many people playing it right now, it does have smooth and pretty flawless networking in general. I experienced almost no lag or network bugs while playing on German servers.
-The game has 3 game modes to choose from, and although the maps aren't yet to the highest quality it is still fun to play, especially the recently added zombie mode.
-The game has a wide customization of weapons, although few weapons feel unbalanced to this point still, such as AK12 or flasbangs.
-Visually the game looks alright. Weapon models, animations and voice acting in the game are very well done. However the map design doesn't yet match the same quality, as some maps still feel unfinished, hopefully will be updated in the future.
Now I will point out few factors that are on the downside.
-The optimization. My PC isn't top notch, so I normally play on low settings. The game struggled to run at solid 60 FPS for me on low settings at 1280x720, especially on larger maps. Unlike GTA 5 or H1Z1 which I run on same settings presets at 60-80FPS. But if you have a good gaming PC than u will have no problem playing it.
-Although the game has a well made parkour system for hopping over obstacles, the game lacks a very simple yet demanded feature - plain jumping. Yes, you can't straight up jump in this game for some reason.
-The game has some unbalanced weapons as well as just some rare bugs, but I am sure this will be fixed in the near future.
Overall - the game is fun to play with friends, but due to not many people playing the game as of now - I don't play the game often, as sometimes the servers are empty. Hopefully eventually more people will play the game and the developers will improve the things I pointed out.

This is a one of the greatest puzzle games I have played, precisely because it's not a puzzle game in the traditional sense.
Most puzzle games, especially those in first-person, require you to solve the puzzle, and then execute the solution. So even after the level is "solved", you can still have difficulty performing the solution. For an example of this, check out Quantum Conundrum.
In this game, the game itself is the puzzle. Once you figure out the solution to an obsticle, it's done, you figured it out. No failing 6 times in a row because you didn't get your timing right.
So yeah, easily one of the best puzzle games out there, and while short, is worth your money.

Killing Floor 2 is a game I enjoy quite a lot, if my total hours played wasn't a dead giveaway. I will readily admit this game has had it's ups and downs within the community, most who own this will remember the whole MT debacle that plauged the discussion boards of Steam. Now that this game has left Early Access, I am going to write my opinion on this as someone who had this prior to the Incinerate N' Detonate update.
Likes: I enjoy the fact that this game has time put into the animation department, I will always hold Killing Floor (2009) as a game with medicore animation. That was changed in KF 2 since Tripwire used motion capture (Mo-Cap) for the zeds, players, and the weapons. This is most noteworthy in Zed-Time with guns and it shows, since the firing the guns during Zed-Time will have parts of the gun (I.E the barrel and magazine) wiggling and flexing.
Another like is the fact the community made maps are stellar, such as KF_Rig. This also goes to the part who are part of the Curated Workshop for Zedconomy items. Seeing as I have stuck with this game throughout the EA period, I must have an opinion on the whole MT issue, and I'll get to that later, for now, more likes.
The last like I shall list is the fact the Zeds look better than they did in KF 2009, and that is a huge plus, since I also played KF 2009 for some time. This is most notable with the comparison of the Scrake, Fleshpound, and Patriarch from both games. They all look like they bulked up and have gained new moves to boot.
Dislikes:
Now for my cynical side to come into this. I should explain my love for this game is more based on my love for KF 2009. They are both games that appeal to my niche of wave based co-op shooters and have good communities. Yet like all things, if you think something is flawless, you haven't looked hard enough at it.
First on my list is rather anemic, since I don't play co-op, would be a few instances of Zeds appearing when I close and open doors in certain spots. This is quite a problem when I'm fighting a boss and running from him, only to be grabbed and turned into a punching bag. This is quite small, yet small problems can lead to bigger issues in certain structures.
Second would be the questionable actions of Tripwire during part of EA. This I will just boil down to MTs while cute, are still something I won't understand much. Though it is explained that the sales on items will help with development of new content. It can also be with certain perks, see posts in the discussion board on the Firebug since I don't play that perk much anymore.
Lastly, would be the slow rate of updates and content being released to the public. I get that game development and updates take time and that perfection take time. Yet I would want the frequency of WWAUT post to increase in slightly. This mostly comes from me wanting the new T4 weapon for the Berserker and that new Gorefast to come into the Killing Floor.
To conclude, I think this is a game that is perfect for people who want something to play with a group of friends, strangers, or by yourself while listening to podcasts. Seeing as I don't exactly write reviews all that often, and there are people who do this far better than I do and with far better reviewing technique, take my opinion with a very small grain of salt.

text:
This game is for many, a part of their child/teenhood. That's not the case for me though, as I grew up with the PC so I got to expierence more "unique" games that others wouldn't have. So this review will be judged a little differently from mosts.
To kick this thing off, this game has a very good atmosphere. They really tried to hit that 80's theme and they definitely suceeded. Every aspect, the guns, vehicles, music, and even the architecture is about 90% accurate. That's really impressive and you can tell Rockstar did their research. But what about the actual game part itself?
It's pretty solid! The story can be very engaging and interesting to progress through. As part of GTA traditions, be perpared to meet a bunch of over the top characters. Most are really interesting and are humorusly on the verge of being 1 dimensional cliches.( That's the point though) Again, Rockstar really stuck to the 80's character types you would see in media during that time. The missions themselves are diverse and entertaining. I like how most combat focused missions give you options like sniping undetected or different angles to attack from. It's not much, but compared to GTA V's on rails missions, this was refreshing. They range from linear shootouts( Cannon Foddler, Phone Phem) to sprawling open ended sandboxes(Rub Out, Spill the Beans, Hog Tied). I also like how you can do certain story missions at your own pace. I held off doing an assassination mission that required me to go into a golfing club unarmed fight the target with his bodyguards. But since I held off that mission, I had a sniper available, so I didn't even have to enter the club and could simpily snipe the target from afar without having to fight. All the non combat missions are usually very mini gamey With timers or a some other gimmick to the mix. Races, bomb timers, etc. Some misssions are on the verge of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level design ( Demolition Man, Bombs Away,) However, they are ALL really short to complete.
This is when I realized the source of all it's flaws would be from: technical limitations. You can see it everywhere you go and do. From mission length, to graphics(which I don't really care about), to draw distances and so on. But it gets to the point where it affects the game. For example, cars explode for no reason if they are upside down. This makes chases or timed missions really tedious. But the thing that ticks me off the most is the WATER. You or any NPC cant swim, so you will die if you land into the water. Combine that with the sensitive as HELL motorcycles, and you will probably die in a timed mission due to a cop ramming your bike into a low wall and hurling into the water. Mods fix this of course, but that still doesnt mean its not bull.
If you can look past these limits, you can find a very decent crime game. It has interesting, varied missions and a great story that is a love letter to 80's crime. Actaully, this WHOLE game is a love letter to the 80's!

First of all, don’t mistake The Escapist with The Escapist
. The latter is a game about prison life while the first one is a tough platformer. Is it as brilliant as, say, Super Meat Boy or the Mario games, though  ? Read on and let’s find out.
There doesn’t seem to be much of a story here but the goal is to escape with as much loots as you can, hence the title. Sometimes you can take your time, other times you have to be a bit quicker.
Making the comparison to Super Mario isn’t entirely fair, because in no way is this a true side-scrolling platformer. As a matter of fact, The Escapist can best be compared to Sonic. So Sonic meets Super Meat Boy. Sounds promising, doesn’t it ? Well… no.
The game fails to properly incorporate all of the elements that made these games great in the first place. Meat Boy had excellent level designs and tight controls and Sonic ran at high-speeds, but also still had some excellent controls for a game back then. So yeah, it all comes back to controls.
Your character can run pretty fast and by clicking your mouse can bounce/roll (Sonic reference here) into a direction of your choice. So the best way to get to the top when you’re standing between two walls is to just use the mouse and bounce your way up. Arrows will appear when you hold the mouse button so that you know which way you’ll go. Unfortunately, the controls are very unreliable and imprecise. There have been tens of times that I knew exactly how to complete a level but the game failed to do what I had in mind; the character continued to run at high speeds, flew off into a different direction or simply didn’t respond to my mouse click. Selecting a path for bouncing also takes too long, and that’s not a good sign for a game that also partially focuses on speed.
The fact that you only have one life didn’t help either. This game would’ve been much, much better if it used a health system. I know the goal of the developers is to create a hardcore platformer here, but it just doesn’t work for this game. Especially in levels that scroll upwards, and you have to be both precise and quick. In combination with the slow planning of your bounces you’ll be replaying levels more often than you should.
Coins can be found in every level and collecting them allows you to buy stuff from the shop to make things easier for you. It will let you jump higher or give you even more speed, but keep in mind that if you die all loot found in the level you were playing in will be reset. Again, I think this was a poor choice. You want people to improve, but if there are people that can’t continue because of the game or the person him-/herself than you should give them a choice to improve themselves. The shop might just help with this and by resetting the coins every time you die they’ll eventually won’t be able to complete the game. Unless maybe they put a whole lot of time in it. It’s obviously an entirely different story if a character can’t be upgraded and is already at its best.
The level design is very, very bland and lacks charm and personality. So far I’ve only seen an industrial and underground design but I hope that there’s more to see than that. This could use a lot of work.
Now, the game is definitely not just about the graphics but they do help to immerse people into a game. And this doesn’t cut it. Not for me, anyway.
The music reminded me of old school platformers, again like Mario and Sonic, but mixed with some sort of heist theme. This is actually pretty good.
There are 48 levels in total and I managed to get to around level 20 or so. This took me about 70 minutes I think. I can imagine the levels will only get harder so I can only conclude that this will take at least a couple of hours extra before you’re able to finish it. I think it’s more than enough gameplay for a game like this.
In the end I’m sad to say that The Escapist isn’t the platformer I hoped it would be. I actually hope it will escape your attention because there are so many other games out there that do a better job at being an old-school platformer.
If you have too much money, or you just like to collect games then I can imagine you’ll (eventually) pick this up. But to anyone else; wait for a sale !

Really, it's pretty hard to get more Cyberpunk than Shadowrun. If you're into the cyberpunk aesthetic then this is definitely a game you should consider buying.
Shadowrun: Returns uses a hybrid of the 3e and 4e ruleset, so if you've played tabletop this is quite similar. It lacks a lot of interactions with armour that exist in PnP but a lot of that was eventually added into the second release, Dragonfall.
The basic gameplay consists of regular RPG staples such as trading, talking and combat. There's no looting system in place for corpses, so the only ones you'll loot have map triggers placed on them for that purpose.
The combat is an isometric turn-based strategy game that uses stats to generate probabilities for your units to hit. Think Final fantasy tactics or X-Com.
The UI is somewhat lacking, and sometimes the probability based gameplay can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The places where you can save are somewhat limited, so it's advised to save as often as you're able. Whether you pick up Thief: The Dark Project or Thief II: The Metal Age, look up a simple tweaking guide on Google to get the most out of the game. Definitely worth checking into.

Thief II is the gold standard upon which all stealth games/games with stealth mechanics are to be evaluated. The original Thief was treading into unknown territory and hedged its bets with more action/horror/Tomb Raiderish levels against mostly nonverbal inhuman foes. Thief II is straight up robbing human establishments against foes that you can always understand just how alerted to your presence they are. Light & shadow are integral to going undetected, but it's sound that you'll be relying upon more than sight.
You'll spend lots of time just standing still, just listening and watching, waiting to move. You're constantly under-supplied, and there's no point in hoarding inventory since it doesn't carry over between levels. Fighting won't end well. On Hard you're not even PERMITTED to kill. Escaping once detected isn't easy. Your maps are vague & incomplete. All that is what makes your victories that much more satisfying.
Modern AAA gaming will never permit this experience ever again.

Early Access Watcher Public Service Announcement
Game: Guardians of Ember
Update Version: December 13th Release
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Game Footage:
Originally released under the name Embergarde, this Diablo-esqe MMORPG has finally made it to Steam following three technical trial runs. The game currently features five classes, four races, Acts 1 and 2, housing and plenty of dungeons that can easily be soloed. The secondary class system is also available along with the crafting and guild systems. It is refreshing to see an early access game release with this amount of content out of the gate (granted it is primarily a localization effort), but every early access game is bound to have issues . Hopefully this PSA can shed some light on some of these issues that have unfortunately made it difficult to recommend at this time.
Latency is the Achilles' Heel right now and is going to very from person to person. The server location is outside of the United States (last I looked, it was in Asia) and with the increase in players the issues are only going to get worse. This is due to some unforeseen circumstances, but the end result has left the server riddled with spikes, hit detection delays, and movement stutter. It has also made combat suffer by means of input stalls.
Crashing is also a common occurrence that mainly struck during the random field events that spawn periodically. It also made an appearance in the first red dungeon the third blue dungeon and while exploring the slums of the main city. It starts off as a three to five second freeze and suddenly closes out completely. Considering how well my system was able to maintain a stable FPS (which I admit is rare for early access games), I have a hunch this might be due in part to the latency problems.
Combat itself feels rather lackluster, which falls back to the simple nature of the skill system. Left mouse, right mouse and buttons 1-4 have their own unique skills assigned to them and can be changed by unlocking different variations of the primary attack type using skill points. The problem is in the dull, sluggish execution of most of these attacks. Clicking the enemy can more often result in an attack shooting off into a different direction than the clicked target or even activate twice possibly due to the input stalls. Certain skills are also unreliable due to possible misconfigurations with their targeting style.
It doesn't help that the gear is mostly uninteresting stat alterations that result in gear having unaffiliated, useless traits for what should be apparent upgrades. Enemy types are also incredibly bland for the first ten zones with quests merrily placed along linear map layouts with little exploration on offer. It all feels incredibly unrefined and produces encounters that ultimately become short, encumbered AoE spams. This is also problematic when the hit range for enemies tends to be larger due to the latency delay, which makes it easier for melee to land hits from a greater distance
Movement through certain areas is hindered by visible pathing issues made worse by the fixed direction of the maps. While it is easier to move using WASD, the problem still occurs when maneuvering up stairs, along certain areas in dungeons and in between tight spaces such as barricades and object corners. Characters would often times run along the path, only to suddenly move in the opposite direction or get stuck momentarily before resuming their movement. This makes soloing dungeons much more difficult and at times feels tied to the previously mentioned latency issues.
Guardians of Ember feels like a free to play game at the end of the day, which is not a terrible notion. It provides a simple clicker based action RPG that is decent enough to be manageable, when it works. Level 30 is the current end point for the game and offers little content past it, which is expected given the last few acts are still being localized. There are random events that happen on the field, similar to the way Fates work in Final Fantasy 14, battleground style PvP and dueling to keep things interesting. It is just a shame the game's technical issues prove too much and make participating in most of these features frustrating. Hopefully when the server is fixed and the gameplay gets polished up the entertainment value will rise, but for now it might be best to avoid the Goblin conflict for other stronger campaigns.
This has been a EAW PSA
Additional Point Unrelated to Technical Problems
I will go ahead and claim this is the only part of this segment that contains a bias. An in-game store is functional and while the items are limited to the loot orbs granted by both versions of the game, it still feels out of place. The game was originally a free to play title, which might explain why this function is still active in its' pay to play state. The loot orbs can also be bought using coins gained from completing certain achievements and dailies (which are tied to the achievements), so there is at least an alternative to gaining the item. It is a minor gripe that might not concern everybody, but I felt it was necessary to mention it. Micro-transactions are going to be an issue regardless of what state a game is in, but for early access, the focus should be getting the game out the door.
Loot orbs also present an issue similar to other games that feature loot crates. These orbs award permanent mounts, pets, skill resets (that are crucial after level 25) and other one time use items such as the revive potions. These orbs are the only way to gain a lot of these items and the in-game substitute for mounts are limited time uses.

I was SOOOOOO excited about this sequel as a huge Batman fan who has watched in awe as game developer Rocksteady created two of the best super hero titles in the history of gaming.  Batman Arkham Asylum didn't just redefine the super hero game, it redefined the third person action adventure period.  And its sequel Arkham City elevated the Batman franchise to new heights, earning yet another well deserved Game of the Year accolade.  So how did they manage to fudge Arkham Knight so bad?  Well here's how, they lost sight of what was actually FUN about the character and the gameplay that they once labored so hard to perfect.
After an amazingly creative and engaging first person opening sequence you are thrust into the cowl of the scowling dark knight of Gotham and are quickly introduced to a new game feature - the Batmobile.  At first this thing seems SUPER cool, it sounds AMAZING, looks badass and spins massively gratifying doughnuts as plumes of deliciously rendered smoke bellow out around you.  But then... It turns into... A tank...  Oh...  Dear.  A TANK?!?!  This is BATMAN, he has a strict NO GUNS policy and absolutely refuses to use lethal force under any circumstances.  There is no threat in Gotham that would even warrant him owning a tank when the game starts so why the hell does it even exist?  You're let loose in Batman's transform-a-snack tank/ car and given forces of unmanned enemy drone tanks to destroy.  You're a crime fighter not a tank commander, it just feels stupid.  Not to mention that by drone battle three you're already bored to death of the repetitive nature of scrapping hordes of dumb drones with predictable, telegraphed attack patterns.
The game developer's reliance on the new Batmobile game mechanic continues into the Riddler missions.  The Riddler has built race tracks which Batman must complete in order to save a high profile hostage...  RACE  TRACKS?!?!  It's not a mind bending conundrum it's a dumb gamey race track which would be more at home in a Mario Kart title.  The in-game characterisation of the Riddler makes no sense in this context.  The Batmobile race tracks are all dumb and frustrating, feeling entirely out of place and under developed.
Perhaps 'under developed' is the best way to describe the entire game experience.  I was initially excited to realise that the game features numerous side missions where you go toe-to-toe with classic super villains such as Penguin and Two Face.  My excitement evaporated quickly however when I realised that every single super villain mission is just one simple sequence of events which must be repeated OVER AND OVER AGAIN until they are apprehended.  It's dull and repetitive beyond anything I was expecting; Rocksteady HAVE made great games before right?  What the hell happened here?
The main story itself plods along at a fairly uninspiring pace and does little to endear itself.  The main antagonist Scarecrow is no longer the creepy, darkly rasping menace he once was in Arkham Asylum.  Rocksteady have opted instead to make him a cookie cutter clone of Doctor Strange's performance in Arkham City.  His constant impassionate droning does nothing to instill any sense of threat or urgency.  Scarecrow is joined in crime by a militia commander, the titular 'Arkham Knight' whom leads a massed army of high-tech militia troops and armored drones into Gotham City.  It's this design decision that ultimately destroys the entire Batman experience.  Batman is the world's greatest detective NOT the world's greatest military commander, he fights crime on the streets of Gotham; he's a cop not a soldier.  It's a stupid story; the most technicaly advanced army the world has ever known launches a legitimate military invasion against a major US city and America provides NO MILITARY RETALIATION WHATSOEVER!?!?  The story tries to go big for the series' swan song and fumbles the ball almost immediately.
Rocksteady approached this project back to front, they designed a game and then tried to shoe-horn Batman into it instead of writing an engaging Batman adventure and trying to shoe-horn a game into THAT.  The game does have its merits however, the new tag-team style pairings in fight sequences are very Batman and hugely satisfying if oddly under used.  The Joker returns!  Mark Hamill's iconic voice performance as the clown prince of crime is a very welcome addition to the game even if previously killing him off WAS pure folly.  The Batmobile when it's not a tank is actually fun to get around in and the fully upraded ejector-seat launcher is outrageously satisfying to use.  It's just a shame that the counter intuitive control system makes the game more awkward than necessary to play and the new Wayne Tech upgrade tree is a sprawling over complicated mess.
My honest advice is steer clear of this game, it's the only game in the series I have no interest in ever playing again (and I completed the flawed Arkham Origins three times over).  If you're a newcomer I'd recommend buying Batman Arkham City and experiencing the height of developer Rocksteady's extraordinary prowess.  If you're a hardened fan however I'd recommend replaying Batman Arkham City and experiencing the height of developer Rocksteady's extraordinary prowess...  Again.
Oh, and the story ending of Arkham Knight sucks.  It sucks balls.  It sucks MAJOR balls.

South Park the Stick of Truth is a game I was really hyped for. A game made by one of my favorite developers, Obsidian, working on a South Park game. Which has been a television show that hasn't really had a good game up until this one.
The things Stick of Truth does that impress me the most are that it works as both an adaptation of South Park and as a game in it's own right. There was clearly a huge focus on authenticity, down to how the aesthetic near flawlessly mimics that of the show. It's clear Matt and Trey had a very noticeable hand in the game's development. All of the humor is spot-on with that of the television show. Where they not only try to satirize common video game cliches, but also take advantage of them to make a very competantly made rpg.
When I said it worked as a game as well I wasn't lying. The game is a turn based rpg, and this was an extremely smart decision on Obsidian's part. Because of the turn based nature to the combat you can have humerous moments like Al Gore putting your cleric to sleep with a powerpoint presentation. They also have small real-time elements where you press a button to block and attack at certain moments. It all works so well and it's phenominal to see such an attention to detail in a licensed game.
I'm extremely glad the game lived up to it's hype. There are very few flaws worth mentioning with Stick of Truth beyond maybe the lack of replayability. But it really is a game that appeals to fans of the television show and people who want a turn based RPG that succeeds in making you laugh.

A re-make of the classic turn based X-COM/UFO series originally developed by MicroProse in the mid 90s. It has received a modern make over which many will construe as a dumbing down of the game - many components of the original game have been removed, presumably for the benefit of new players though the core strategical element of the game still comes through.
Once completed, you have the option of turning on several mods that bring back some of classic mechanics such as random stats on new soldiers and variable damage.
The game tends to be very punishing in the early game but once you get past the rookie stage and get a solid group of upgraded soldiers with fancy weapons it becomes increasingly easy, even the bigger and tougher aliens don't pose much of a threat when you have fully upgraded snipers!
For the insane there is the impossible difficulty which is extremely harsh and not recommended at all for new players no matter how good you think you are. Classic difficulty presents a good balance of challenge where you can get away with small mistakes/bad RNG but too many and you will be punished.
An easy way to wile away a few hours/days, especially as the game is pretty much always in the big holiday sales.

I have mixed feelings here. On the one hand, the game is pretty stable. It's functionally playable. Nothing about it is inherantly bad. If this were 90's it would be an excellent edition to the gaming landscape. Trouble is this isn't the 90's.
I don't mean to imply the game is dated or anything but as it stands in the current market, it's not offering anything new. It's not even more of the same, it's less of the same. After two and half hours I realised I'd seen everything the game had to offer an hour ago and I was just going through the motions.
Back when games were scarce and you were constantly on the lookout for something, anything, that was new and you hadn't played before then this would be a fine distraction for a couple of days. These days you can easily find several better games in the same genre that are better and cost less. Even on sale I can't really recommend this because it's not worth the time invested you could be using playing something else.
I feel mean saying that.
I mean this is obviously an indie development and any indie dev deserves props for actually finishing and releasing a decently constucted game. But we are utterly awash in such things right now. I'm fine with the developer having the couple of dollars I paid for this but I can't recommend it. The time I spent on it I could have spent playing better things.
Better things like old classics such as space rangers or star control or freespace or freelancer or x3 or elite or eve or wing commander, or hardwar or tachyon or alliegance or decent etc. or I could have spent my time playing the current slew of new standout big name and indie titles like evochron or rebel galaxy or strike suit zero or god factory wingmen or endless sky or interstellar transport company or everspace or space run or spaz or rogue system or rodina and so on and so on.
Depending on how far you want to stretch the genre this list can go on forever and nearly everyone reading already has at least one title in mind I've missed. Starting to see the problem? Even on something like No mans sky my time was probably better spent.
The game isn't bad, it's between the good games and the bad games. It's a speedbump. A compentently designed distraction that delays you from getting to the good stuff.
It deserves no hate, but it merits little praise and it certainly doesn't deserve your time.

I bought this on sale for a paltry 4 bucks.  For the amount of time you can spend in the game, it was well worth it.  If you've ever enjoyed Eve Online but absolutely hated the "online" part of it (like I did), this could very well be what you've been looking for.
It emulates Eve almost perfectly, despite its obvious budget limitations.  It was created entirely by one person, which is a very impressive feat considering the effort that went into it.  As it was originally made to be run in a browser, you can easily run this application on a 10+ year old toaster, and it only takes up around 100MB.  (The special effects, or lack-thereof, are a testament to this.)
Due to the game's success and popularity however, the developer is apparently hard at work on a sequel that will be remade from the ground up as a new, stand-alone, not-made-for-a-browser application.  He's a very talented individual, and well worth following if you're a fan of this particular genre.  If he can bring this same level of care and effort to a non-browser game, I truly look forward to seeing what he can do without the graphical and engine restrictions.
If I had only one complaint, it would be the text size of the UI.  At 1080p on a large television, it's difficult to read anything, even after sliding the text scaling to max settings.  Despite this flaw, I find the UI intuitive enough to get around it fairly easily.
I look forward to sinking many more hours into this while multi-tasking other things at home.  :-)

Not the best RE game around, but not the worst by a long shot. The atmosphere and story are pretty good, feeling somewhere closer to RE4 than the later titles - The game being broken up into segments is strange especially because steam sales seem to only get applied to the first chapter (boo) and each chapter you finish ends with you being force fed the same unskippable credits (why?!).
Gameplay wise its proven to be fairly fun, if relatively easy. I havent played a RE title in years and pretty much rip through each segment with 1.3-1.4hrs play time , 70%+ accuracy and 3 or less retries (usually 0 with Barry). You basically go through with one pair of characters and then go through the same area (more or less) from a different or somewhat different path with another pair of characters so there is a lot of rehashing something like RE2 had.
The bazaar requirement to swap to your secondary character regularly to check for hidden items is different but tends to feel like it mostly serves to waste time and make the game feel larger than it really is.  Combined with the rating system, hidden blue medals to shoot and a 'upgrade bench' revelations 2 draws from pretty much every popular game around from The Last of Us to Deadspace 3 and everything in between. (Some enemies even look like they stepped out of a Silent Hill game)
Dispite its drawbacks and cheap presentation I do recommend Revelations 2, it at least tries to recapture the old Resident Evil feel but unfortunately refuses to abandon the action game feel that has progressively been the bigger focus of the series for a long time now. I did like how very few bullets I tend to have for a situation, haven't really felt a shortage of ammo sense the first, maybe second resident evil (though I haven't played the first revelations) so that was a pleasant suprise. ( I remember playing the original RE prior to auto aim being implimented, where sometimes it was better to juke a zombie or hunter than use precious bullets to gun it down or shooting a zombie dog to knock it down then knifing it the rest of the way.)

The gameplay is similar to other hack and slash games like D3, PoE, Grim Dawn, etc.  Guardians of Ember doesn’t really offer any combat features that are new or improved. The questing is your standard MMO style, where you run around complete tasks, fetching, killing, and clearing dungeons. You can group up with others, or play solo, but you must always be online and connected to their server.
The dungeons have normal and hard difficulties, so obtaining better loot is a good incentive to group up with others. Outside of the dungeons, there are no difficulty settings, so unless you lag, get stuck, or pull way too much, the game is pretty easy.
There is some story that is told with text dialog and cutscenes. I found they just weren’t interesting enough, and I wound up skipping them like I usually do in practically every MMO I’ve played.
The game has a dual class system, and you get to choose 2 of the 5 classes (a 6th class is still in development). You can change the secondary class, but I really wish that you could change your primary class as well. I don’t mind having to freshly level each class’s level, but after seeing the possible synergies of the other skill trees, I kind of regret the primary class that I picked.
When I first saw the skill system I thought it looked really awesome.
There is only partial controller support, and all of the keybindings are customizable except for these M1 and M2 controls cannot be changed from your primary and secondary skills.
Changing your stats/skills after certain levels can only be done using items randomly found in loot orbs. This bothers me. Here’s where the microtransactions come in: these loot orbs can be bought with real money or earned in limited quantity by completing daily objectives. The items you obtain from them are completely random, and I don’t like that being able to respec relies on random factors. This should be something that's available with the in game gold currency as well. The items you get from loot orbs are untradeable. Of the 25+ orbs I’ve opened, I’ve gotten mounts, a pet that auto-loots, loot/gold/xp boosts, instant resurrects, backpack expanders, and other cosmetics. So, while they don’t directly give any character stat advantages, they certainly do improve the game's quality of life.
I backed this game on IndieGoGo, and so far I’ve played over 12 hours of the live version, and about 15 more during the technical testing prior to release. To me, this game feels like it could have been a single player/co-op game, or maybe even a F2P game if they truly want to take the MMO route with microtransactions.
The game is in early access, so if you’re expecting a fully polished game, and perfectly stable servers, there are lot of other alternatives (D3, PoE, Grim Dawn, etc.) In the game’s current state, you can expect bugs, periodic lag, and some random crashes to desktop, but as far as early access and MMO launches go, I've seen much worse. Guardians of Ember has potential, and is worth keeping an eye on, but it’s going to take a lot more time and work to polish everything out. If you can get past the issues, and want to support the game’s development, then the game is off to a reasonable start.

Flashy and good presentation, but boring gameplay. The set of rules is actually very simplified: walls/objects here are not taken into account, as long as you have line of sight towards an enemy, bullets will travel towards your target. Everything gets assigned a defense value (by default 0), which is raised by being in half/full cover, and some equipment items. The more defense, the less likely for shots to hit. The thing is, some of the more difficult enemies have unnaturally high defense values, which can result in some of your soldiers with a SHOTGUN missing a CAR-SIZED target at FRIGGING POINT-BLANK. Which is ridiculous as hell.
Aliens spawning is a really tedious mechanic which results in initial engagements being extremely risky for your soldiers (on which the entire game hinges). Other gameplay mechanics such as aliens mind-controlling your squad are equally frustrating.
I really liked this game for the first 2/3 hours but it quickly got really repetitive and boring because everything goes through a RNG you can barely influence. It was still entertaining for me but I would not recommend it for this reason.
(not to mention some of the annoying bugs, one that notably ruined the ending cutscene as the last level's music kept playing over it)

Frankly the only reason i think this game is successful is because of what it accomplished.
Groundbreaking? Yes.
Fun? In my opinion, No.
Yes, this game is genesis on an engine which would spawn so many good games. However, if you take all of that away, the gameplay is frankly mediocre.
The combat is nothing special, what with a normal loadout system and normal types of guns.
The puzzles are frankly the dullest thing i have ever encountered in a game (other than the instructions to caravan in the beggining of new vegas). They rely on you interacting with normal items in the environment, and the only skill involved is the memorization of the items in the game and their uses. Not only are they time consuming, but the solution is usually something that when you find will leave you feeling stupid, not rewarded.
Completing a hard level in portal by shooting the repulsion gel through the portal? awesome!
Spending 20 minutes to find a valve (haha) in a dark corner of a sewer so you can FINALLY move on? yay... god im stupid.
A couple of other quick notes:
Playing a serious game in the graphics of the source engine makes me want to gag
Health packs are never right next to level start points, so if you start a saved game with barely any life, then good luck!
I can see why this game was so successful a long time ago... but if you are looking to get it in 2015 or later, i can tell you that you are not gonna be impressed.

I have a serious love/hate relationship with this game; all of the positives were amazing, but the negatives almost ruined the experience for me. Spoilers ahead.
Negatives:
- I don't know about anyone else but I actually enjoyed the boss fights and trippy psychadelic sequences in the other three games but they completely removed all of that making a lot of the potentially grandiose moments seem kinda dull or insignificant. It's also a huge missed opportunity because y'know Scarecrow is the main antagonist and that's his whole thing.
- Apparently Batman is now immune to Scarecrow's fear toxin because he recieves massive amounts of it and has no reaction for some reason. Like at the end he gets injected with 12 shots of the toxin and he just powers through it. Like no that's a neurotoxin and that's not how this works (Yes I know he was sort of the Joker who it doesn't affect but after "defeating" him in his mind, normal Batman gets hit with the drug). What about Asylum where a tiny bit sent him to a nightmare hellscape?
- I didn't mind the tank combat but it got tedious when you're forced into stealth missions with a tank. Example: Deathstroke's confrontation in Gotham's Times Square was about to be awesome until you roll up aaaaand there's a bunch of tanks.
- The Joker pretty much ruined everything for me. HE'S DEAD. The whole "Batman turning into the Joker" subplot had literally no effect on the rest of the game except to shoehorn in a character that everyone likes. The game would have been a thousand times better if they didn't use him as crappy fanservice. He was incredibly annoying showing up at every single plot point, talking over important and interesting dialogue and character moments and it broke any and all immersion in the game. He also totally stole and ruined the entire climax, especially considering that nothing ever became of his inclusion so why bother putting him in? Scarecrow was a great villain by himself.
- The final ending where Batman's identity gets revealed so in response he endangers a crowd of civilians by blowing up himself and Alfred for no real reason. I don't think this needs any comment.
Positives:
- Gotham looks and feels amazing. I love the pouring rain and bright neon look and each part of the huge city has its own distinct style to it.
- I'm probably a bit biased because I love Scarecrow but I thought he was a great villain. He was intimidating and creepy and his presence was felt all over Gotham. I especially love that he actually detonates his bomb and floods the city with  fear toxin. That moment felt very climactic and dire; I didn't think it would actually happen but I was pleasantly surprised.
- I loved the inclusion of the Batmobile. It was so much fun to finally drive around plowing over everything in sight. I also kinda liked the tank controls but they were a bit overused at times.
- Arkham Knight's character reveal and his becoming the Red Hood was done very well however I would have liked to see a bit more of him after his climactic confrontation.

This game still sustains the pass of time. The graphics don't look that outdated and have a certain charm to them. The gunplay still feels great, and it is important to look back at the great games that made history in the past.

GUYS, THE GAME WORKS!
Pros:
-It's fixed. The game is very functional and near glitchless at this point, though I couldn't get a consistent 60fps out of it. 30fps still looks fine, though. Performance may vary by system; won't list my full specs, but I am running it like this on a high-power gaming laptop, so it may be different if you're trying to run it on a worse/better system.
-WAY more new stuff than Origins, from mechanics to new gadgets and upgrades.
-The game looks great, with none of that pixelated texture bull from Origins.
-The new mechanics and gadgets are great to use.
-Predator encounters are a unique experience due to new environmental objects that can be used for takedowns and a thug group's enhanced ability to counter whatever Batman's been doing to them
-The Batmobile, despite its overuse, is still pretty enjoyable to use, especially when speeding through the streets of Gotham
-The good stuff it retains from the previous games is still good
Cons:
-What is up with the voices in Arkham Knight? They can be muffled, underacted, strangely acted - this wasn't a problem in City. I'm not sure if it was an intentional change in characters' voices or if the cast was off their game.
-Because of all your new options, some things can be mapped to the same button, which means you really need to watch how you press keys/buttons, particularly during predator encounters
-Batmobile is WAY overused, and drone battles can tend to have a lack of variety, not to mention they're not very Batman-like.
-Sidequests in general can be pretty long, and I don't just mean the Riddler quest
-The timing is off on some of your abilities, including reduced range for FreeFlow combat and the timing for aerial attacks
-The hotkeys can get obnoxious, especially with special combo moves. I get that E is for the Batmobile now, but why the Alt key?
-Some of the DLC doesn't add much to the game
-I'll admit, they never should have released it in the state it was in at launch
This one's been brutally ignored because of the launch disaster, and it doesn't deserve it. Don't let the list of cons fool you: I enjoyed Arkham Knight a lot, even more than Arkham Origins. Those brand new mechanics can be great to use, and the game looks great and does way more to be different than Origins did. There's plenty of new tricks to learn or work around, and that's what a sequel is meant to do, so Knight gets a definite plus in that regard. However, those cons can bog it down at times, and the DLC can be hit-or-miss. If you enjoyed the previous games, this one might be a good time for you, but there is a lot to keep in mind.

At a basic level, this game is a puzzle-platformer, however I would akin it more to an "Alice in Wonderland-esque" adventure game like Myst. If you've ever played Myst or its sequels you know the familiar feeling of being stuck at a dead-end. Being stuck in Antichamber isn't not knowing how to solve a puzzle, it's not knowing where the next puzzle is at all. There are several moments in the game where you will have exhausted all possible tricks, codes, doors, and rooms that you can think of and you resort to wandering aimlessly throughout the map clicking on everything hoping to find where the next puzzle element is. The obvious problem with this is that it's not fun. However, when you do know where the puzzles are, it is a joy to work out the difficult, often nonsensical answers and make progress. So, buy at your own risk.
