(Note: many comparisons to Hearthstone)
Summary: 8.5/10 (but 10/10 would play over Hearthstone again)
Pros:
-Excellent gameplay, with many mechanics and concepts which pushes the limit on what online, strategy card games   are capable of.
-Mechanics are not only fun, but functional as well. Serves to deepen the playing experience.
-Playing is smooth overall.
-Is a STRATEGY card game, as compared to Hearthstone. (RNGstone, Pavelstone)
-Comprehensive tutorial explains most of the mechanics well.
-All of the 7 classes, and almost all deck archetypes are viable.
-Solid PVE experience with a decent script and full voice-acting.
-Spell effects, card effects, and battle animations in general are vibrant and loaded with explosive colors.
-Well-structured ranking/reward system, and achievements; earn currency, packs and cosmetics as you play, not at the end of the month.
-Devs are generous, tons of free stuff.
-High probability of getting gold and legenary cards. (equivalent of epic and legendary in Hearthstone)
-Runs and loads smoothly, way faster than Hearthstone.
-Cutesy, anime-style art. (depends on preference)
Cons:
-Top decks are expensive if you are not lucky with drops. (can be somewhat remedied by re-rolling; google that)
-Single packs are expensive when compared to games like HS and MTG. (still cheaper than both those games overall)
-Clunky interface, way too many buttons, tabs and menus which clutter up the screen
-Poor liquefy-to-vials ratio, makes getting value out of trash cards hard. (HS equivalent of disenchanting and dust)
-1/15 games crash and do not reconnect which results in a loss.
-Art style may turn you off. (did the same for me until Kripp showcased the game on his stream)
-Backgrouns are very bland when compared to how vibrant the cards, and effects are.
Conclusion:
If you like strategy card games, then play this. If RNGstone makes you toss your keyboard and suffer from a salt overdose, then play this. Seriously, play this.

As someone who owns a GeForce 780 GPU, you can't play this game both screen-tearing free and at 30+ fps.
- If you enable vsync either in-game or from the NVidia Control Panel, the game's fps will drop to 30, maybe less; occasionally, if the scene is extremely simple (when looking at a wall, for example), you'll get 60 fps.
- If you disable vsync, the game will run at 60 fps, on most settings set to high, including anti-aliasing and anisotropic filtering. The benchmark will even run at ~90 fps. However, the screen will tear non-stop.
No combination of settings in the driver's control panel or the game's menu will allow you 60 fps tear-free experience, even after the game has supposedly been "fixed". This issue is so common, there's a pinned thread in Arkham Knight's discussion section that specifically mentions the fps drops.
I'll only recommend this game, if you have a G-Sync enabled monitor. Otherwise, the game is well presented.
Sorry that I can't comment on the situation with AMD GPUs.

If there's one thing I can say about The Last Revelation, it's that it surprised me greatly. I'd be lying if I said that my expectations weren't low for the fourth entry into the immortal Tomb Raider series. No Croft Manor? No Judith Gibbins as the voice actress for Lara? No inventory ring? No musical score by the awesome Nathan McCree? No locking Winston in the freezer? All these charming little things from the previous games that up and left with The Last Revelation had me thinking that I would be quite disappointed with Core Design's next foray into the adventures of Indiana Jane and the Breasts of Enormity. It's not often that I like being proven wrong, but I can happily say that The Last Revelation surpassed my expectations and proved why I can't keep myself away from this excellent series.
While it is sad to see the previously mentioned elements missing from this installment, the gameplay itself is still the stellar, straight-forward and damn fun formula players have grown accustomed to in the last three games. Lara returns with all her previous manouvres, and a few new ones to boot, including rope-swinging, shimmying around corners and pole-climbing. Nothing groundbreaking, but hey, if it ain't broke, don't fix it. The Last Revelation has seemingly taken a few pages from Resident Evil's book. There's a largely increased emphasis on puzzles and riddles, some of which are quite complex. This is a well thought out departure from Tomb Raiders 1-3, in which pretty much every puzzle boiled down to "find keys to open this door so you can open that door to get that key to pull this switch". You can also now combine certain items and vision-based items such as binoculars and scopes are frequently used. Some weapons also have multiple ammo types which is a lovely added touch.
The Last Revelation is also the most accessible game in the series since the first. I loved the slow but steady learning curve of the original release, and I found it irritating that in the second and third games, Core went kind of ballistic with the difficulty, throwing all kinds of cheap deaths here and there and ruining the pace accordingly. The Last Revelation is quite easy compared to its predecessors, but thankfully the challenge once again builds up as you get used to controlling Lara once again. Later on in the game, you gain access to hub-like levels and backtracking between areas adding some welcome open-world and exploration elements. Fans may be disappointed with the reduced difficulty though, and I find this understandable. Secrets are a cinch to find, and there's so many items jam-packed into Lara's tiny backback, I'm surprised she can even stand up, let alone monkey swing, drop-hang onto a crevice, crawl, 180, backflip mid-air, catch a rope, swing back and forth, jump pistols akimbo slaying infernal bats, sprint and dive-roll inbetween rotating circular blades.
The game is also fantastically long. The earlier entires opted for a smaller amount of levels, but these levels were insanely large and sometimes overly complex. This time, due to their reduced size and the addition of backtracking, combined with the ever-changing environments leads to a far less boring and cumbersome experience.
Apart from the first two levels in Cambodia, which serve as a tutorial, the entire game takes place in Egypt. The Tomb Raider series is well known for its varied locations, with Lara often globetrotting to retrieve her beloved artifacts, but even with only one major set-piece, the game never gets boring. The choice to have a single primary location for the setting helps keep the game more cohesive, and it makes the plot flow together much easier. Yes, the story is still not Pulitzer Prize worthy, but it's entertaining and far more involving than the previous games. It's great to have an antagonist who has some sort of depth and character.
Peter Connelly is no Nathan McCree, but he does a pretty swell job on the soundtrack. As long as we still have some form of the original theme, I'm content. Jonell Elliott also provides a great voice for Lara, although I did prefer her more mature tone that Judith Gibbins provided in previous installments. The Tomb Raider engine is showing its age at this point, but Core continues with its stellar level design and intelligent workarounds to ensure that levels remain unblocky, despite the engine's limitations. FMV sequences are heavily improved from past entires, but the animations are still kind of robotic.
What else can I say? I was so pleasantly surprised with The Last Revelation, and I think you will be too. Tomb Raider 2 and 3 felt more like expansion packs, but The Last Revelation is truly the sequel to the original masterpiece. Core has basically perfected their formula at this point, and I can only hope that Tomb Raider: Chronicles follows suit. It's definitely the best since the original, and I would even go as far to say that it surpasses it.

The excellent writing made this game. It set up the world and the atmosphere brilliantly. Dialogue was great and the characters felt real to me due to the writing and wonderful character potraits. I loved reading the splash screens. It built up the atmosphere fantastically. It was easy to become immersed is this world and fall a little in love with it. Story is everything in a RPG and Shadowrun Returns nailed it.
The plot was pretty good though it was disjointed at times. It was a lot of "go to Location A and do things then go to B and do more things" and repeat. The game suffered a lot from how linear it was. Dialogue options didn't really matter and maps were linear.
Character customization is pretty cool and very diverse. There are different races with different bonuses and a variety of classes and skills that for the most part you can mix and match. There's definitely a lot of viable builds you can run through the game with. It helps that the game is fairly easy on normal. I only ran with a support mage and a shotgunner because I'm a cheapskate and I had no difficulties killing everything in sight. The only times I needed more than two extra people was for the end. Consider turning up the difficulty if you want a challenge.
Core gameplay is solid. This is your classic squad based turnbased RPG in the same vein as XCOM. Combat is intuitive (although I didn't realize that overwatch was the blue icon until over halfway through the game but that's because I'm an idiot) as is the cover system. I wished that you had permanant squadmates, or at least some ability to interact with the hired runners. It's annoying not being able to even equip them.
This is personal preference but I loved the art style of this game. Colourful to give a definite more whimsical feel that I felt meshed really well with the cyberpunk theme. I adored the character portaits. They really captured the characters. And I actually liked that there was no voice acting. This left their voices up to me and like reading a good novel, let me develop them as I imagined them to be helped with the brilliant writing.
Despite its flaws, this is a good solid game. Unpolished but still good. I'd recommend this to anyone interested in RPGs if you don't mind turned based combat. It's a relatively short for an RPG, my playthrough took 12 hours but I enjoyed every minute of it. If you don't mind reading, like cyperpunk and fantasically immersive worlds definitely pick this up.

Here's a video I made taking a look at the start of this game.
After making that video I played through to the end of the game and my overall impression was positive even if the game tends towards being a bit repetitive, and not all that long.
In my video I said that I'd heard it was something of a roguelike or roguelite, but after having played it all the way through, I'd disagree with that categorisation.
In my opinion, it is more of an Action RPG, similar in concept to games like Diablo, Torchlight and Path of Exile.
Sure, it's a platformer, and it's all about guns instead of swords and magic, but the principles are the same.
The core gameplay involves murdering hordes of enemies and collecting loot, the majority of which is useless and only worth selling.
Occasionally you'll find a gun that's better than your current one, or you'll save up enough money to buy a larger backpack or energy shield.
These advancements will allow you to venture into higher level areas to fight tougher enemies and search for even better equipment.
Rinse and repeat until you get to the end.
Finishing the game on Normal difficulty unlocks Hardcore difficulty, but it isn't the perma-death kind of hardcore, just more of the same but with tougher enemies.
There isn't any kind of new game plus mode that I could find either.
I'd say this game is worth playing if you happen to get it cheap, but I wouldn't recommend buying it at full price.

I have somewhat mixed feelings towards this game, and that may be related to the fact that I purchased it as part of a bundle for a steal of a price.  While I had low expectations, I did find it to be a fairly enjoyable distraction for a few hours.
The randomly generated map managed to feel quite repetitive.  Enemy models stay the same throughout the game minus health/damage upgrades and a new color or outfit.  Additionally, while this may be personal preference, I found the art style unimpressive.
As far as gameplay, it largely consists of running, gunning, and jumping to dodge enemies, enemy gunfire, and oddly placed and numerous razor blades.  You collect guns (pistol, minigun, shotgun, bazooka) that progressively scale up stats (though given it's lack of depth, I would not compare this game to Borderlands as others have suggested).  Additionally you collect gems to sell or to use to refuel your shields.  Along the way, you find teleport gates to return to your base (to sell, recharge, and save).  Towards endgame, you may find yourself frequently teleporting back to base as a quick misstep into enemies can deplete nearly all your health.
Seeing the game's regular retail price is somewhat of a shock.  I definately couldn't recommend paying $10 for this game, and could really only suggest paying less than $5 for this IF this is the style of game you enjoy.  That said, for most gamers, I would not recommend this game.
TLDR: Minimal Content, Amateurish, Fun = 4/10

So I've played many a 2d sandbox cave-based game in my time, such as Steamworld Dig and more creative ones like Terraria and Starbound. I'm quite a fan and really like seeing new twists on the genre with things like Nom Nom Galaxy. I was looking forward to Platformines on a recent indie bundle, and I was unfortunately disappointed.
At its core, Platformines is a good start. Running and gunning, collecting gems and minerals and defeating baddies, then using collected shinies to buy upgrades. That's all fine and dandy, and it runs great to boot, but the actual presentation was less than perfect. The aiming mechanic, at least with the
controller, is abysmal, leading me to wonder why exactly I was shooting down when I was pointing up. The levels seem to be quite randomly rather than procedurally generated, with quick-access portals located right above giant drops (plus really easy-to-get fall damage).
The text and general UI, while maybe more of a technical thing, seems really unfinished, since there are occasional grammar issues and oddly scaled text. Plus single digit pop-ups always come across as two-digit like +$05 or -07, which seems a bit unnecessary. The store interface in particular seems really sketchy because of its UI, and that's not counting the distressing lack of a "sell all" button in a game that requires collecting and selling large quantities of resources.
So I'm not recommending this game mainly because it seems really unfinished. If you want a really simple pixely game with decidedly non-pixely music (classical is not retro!), then you may in fact like this game. However, anyone going for an in-depth, solidly built game had best look elsewhere.

It's Killing Floor, but much more polished in almost every possible way. I won't talk about the obvious graphics improvements, so let's get to things that matter.
Gameplay closely follows the original, but there's enough changes that it feels fresh. Most notably, the zeds got a lot more variety in their behaviors and attacks. They move more unpredictably, so getting headshots on everything isn't as easy anymore (thankfully the hitboxes are much better than in KF1 though). The melee system also got significantly upgraded with different directional attacks and parrying. You can also melee bash at any time now, which is handy for knocking zeds back to get out of a tight situation. Zeds can also get stumbled, knocked down, stunned or frozen, which adds a new layer of tactics to the combat. In addition to that, there are other new features that encourage teamplay: supports can now provide ammo to teammates, demolitionists can give out grenades, and medics can give teammates other buffs like damage resistance as opposed to just healing them. Healing darts can now lock onto your teammates, removing all the frustration around healing that plagued KF1. One of my favorite additions is probably the medic pistol, it's really cheap and only weighs 1kg so pretty much everyone can carry one to heal teammates.
Now to the downsides: there's still some balance issues, in particular firebug being too weak. The zed spawning system also doesn't feel quite right, sometimes they'll spawn right next to you instead of coming from predictable places outside of the map. There's a new PvP mode, but it feels unbalanced and not very fun to play compared to survival. Each perk also has only 4 or 5 weapons right now, and there's currently much fewer maps than in KF1. If you're worried about variety, you should wait for updates to add more content.
EDIT as of November 2017:
The game is getting a steady stream of updates and now has plenty of maps to choose from, not to mention the user-created ones on top of that. The weapon variety is also pretty good to the point where every perk has several viable loadouts. The PvP mode is still a barren wasteland that nobody enjoys playing, though there is some talk of a possible rework/rebalance coming in the future.

Reliving the days gone by.
For those who want to relive the old pixelated days of spelunking and exploring a
world with a new twist, Platformines is a great choice.
Platformines plays more like a classic rogue game with simple graphics, simple rules and addicting gameplay. In this world, you start as a named character derived from the clothing with which you’ve equipped your character. You explore the world with the hope of reviving your spaceship and escaping the planet. Unlike old games, the spaceship is made entirely of blocks and your mission is to find all the block-cannons that allow you to repair your ship by filling in the missing blocks. Thankfully there's a map, waypoint, and numerous portals which make this considerably easier. Unlike Binding of Issac, death doesn't remove you from the map which is both good and bad.
Gameplay
As with any rogue, you explore the world and get stronger as you go deeper (or in this case closer to the surface of the planet). The game differentiates the difficulty with colors, starting with a yellow core and moving outside into eventually red and some light yellow at the edge of the map.  As you get closer to the edge, the map gets harder to traverse (a lot more dead-ends in addition to more annoying bazooka enemies).
In addition, there are what I call dead spots on the map which are small, empty pockets that are impossible to enter since they don't connect to any main road. It can be bad if one of the required block-cannon pieces are in this. The map isn't completely random as there are common structures that appear throughout it.
There are random grey and red chests that contain guns, gems and gear.  The grey ones are unmarked and their loot is mediocre. Grey chest loot is useful but not rare. For example, a hat that gives you the double jump ability.  Red ones usually have better loot, are marked and usually placed in one of the few predefined "dungeons" which are small. The dungeon itself is rarely hard, but given how everything around it is randomly generated, it may require some effort to find the 'correct" entrance. Even then, not all enemies that are supposed to be inside are generated correctly.
Littered around the whole area are portals which allow one to easily jump back to base to sell their loot or deposit it in a safe. Upon death, you lose 5% of your current money and also keep, from experiments, the 20 most expensive items on you (not counting what you have equipped). The respawn is quick and the loot isn't too hard to retrieve as it is dropped where you died. I, however, did get a few gems stuck in blocks. In one case, I lost them as they landed on a spiked block moving left and right and the gems got stuck in the block above the spike. In other cases, it's possible for you to spawn into an enemy or group and take damage when you get out of a portal. I'd say this is a huge bug as you can't usually react quickly enough to kill everyone, leading to your death. More importantly, you lose 5% of your money and possibly gems, depending on what's below.
There's no true concept of levels or experience which is both good and bad. The RPG elements come down to you buying better gear(larger energy belt/back pack) and guns. Guns are dropped randomly from humans as well as robots… I guess all those machines have robot hands to fire them. However, the game does have a concept of unlocking guns as the first few "layers" usually only have pistol drops. You later unlock machine guns, shot guns and bazookas, although not necessarily in that order. Weapons are also randomly generated, like Borderlands, so there rarely are dupes.
Combat usually involves you shooting in one of four directions at enemies. It’s simple but there are a few notes to keep in mind. Ammo is infinite but reload time might not be trivial. The main character is powered by an energy bar which can be recharged by gems that can picked up. These gems come in different varieties and each instance is unique. Each item heals slightly more or less but items within the same bracket don’t deviate much. Your item cap is annoying early on and usually always is through all upgrades..
As I mentioned with layers above, each "layer" has a certain set of enemies, environmental hazards and loot. However, most all of the enemies are the same ones you've seen before but with different colors, different guns and more damage.  The patterns, once you get past a few layers, are mostly the same but their numbers and damage increase a lot once you get to the edge. Guns, in a similar fashion, drop based on their layer (in terms of damage) and so they "fit" with the layer. That being said, if you want the best weapons to use and sell early on, just keep going to the edge.
I leave enemies near the end of the review since there's not much to say. Most are generic and you'll see the same set of enemies, just with different colors which implies that they do more damage, depending on the layer. The only frustrating part is that you don't have an invulnerability window. If 10 enemies shoot at you and they connect, you will take damage from all of them. Other times, enemies spawn in a “dead-end” place and are unable to move or fight back. That being said, fall damage and crush damage is meaningless late game as it does <1% of your energy bar...
Overall, I like the old gameplay style and the new twist on it. That being said, there is a decent amount of grinding to get to the edge of the map by getting better guns. But compared to other games, it's not too bad.  However, it can get repetitive if you're not a huge fan of exploring or rogue.  Combat is ok and what I expected so nothing fancy. There are annoyances like being unable to get to the bottom of your inventory quickly so I'd say it's good but isn't polished. Because of this, I'd rate it at 7/10.
Graphics
Given the title and art, one shouldn't expect great things. The art is bland and in some places recycled with highlights for the layering. This mainly applies to some enemies, particularly the cannon ones but some later one as well. Mostly everything in the background environment (walls/floor), is a block or platform. This makes enemies and drops stand out a lot. I'd give it a 6/10 there.  If you're into old graphics, it's not a problem but could be for those who want something more.
Music
Probably the blandest section here, most of all the music is randomly selected and is mainly classical music (Mozart, Beethoven and the like) with highlights and modifications.  Its ok, but I'd recommend listening to your own music if you plan to replay it again in hard mode or related. 4/10
Replayability
This depends on the person. If you're ok with grinding/rogue then this has a lot of it, as maps and weapons are randomly generated. Otherwise, this might be a one-shot game. While there are a lot of places to explore and chests to open, the one thing I kind of hate is that the loot isn't scaled in chests, especially when you revisit to get all the red chests for example. I can see enemy loot not being scaled since their difficulty is defined by their layer and should be the same for a run. However, chests are random drops and since they usually require some effort to get to them, should have better loot. 6/10
Overall I'd say this game is made to scratch a certain itch. Like Binding of Issac it is generated from scratch and you're on it until you finish. The gameplay is dead simple and repetitive but there are those who might like it. I can't see myself going for the harder difficulty levels at the moment, but I might do it sometime later.

It's cute and funny. The art is great and the broken English is endearing. The 2nd or 3rd level after the tutorial the difficulty spikes and it becomes all but impossible.
The problem is that the game wants perfection while having random failure coded into it. You're given very little room for error (12 bullets for 10 targets, for example - oh but there's a sob story about a little baby squab starving so actually it's 10 bullets for 10 targets). You are a moving object (a pigeon) trying to hit moving objects (people), Your bullets (poos) are affected by wind, which blows either left or right (you're told which direction at least). The degree to which your bullets are affected by wind is based on the direction your pigeon is flying, and the poo's own weight - heavy poos fall faster and are pushed by wind less, while little poos fly all over the place.
The problem is that the weight of a poop is completely random and unknowable to the player, so ultimately whether a shot hit or misses comes down to luck. You can try to mitigate the RNG in various ways, like lining up your shots perfectly, or trying to aim for "clumps" of pedestrians in the hope a randomly heavy poop will hit someone you weren't aiming for, but ultimately it stopped being fun the 50th time I had to reload a level becuase a shot was randomly a different weight and went flying off in a direction I wasn't aiming.
If the game were more forgiving with ammo, or more consistent with firing, I'd have recommended it. As it is, I ragequit after about 25 minutes (steam didn't record my playtime for some reason?). It's worth a buck for the story and art alone, but the gameplay stops being fun very quickly.

Today marks the twentieth birthday of the
series, unanimously regarded as one of the most influential in the world of electronic entertainment, and if one looks past the countless lawsuits and negative media coverage the creations of Rockstar North have received, they are bound to discover one of, if not the best, crime-filled sandbox experiences. Each project from the studio is a worthwhile pick-up, nailing the atmosphere and the time era it revolves around down to a T, but the 2002's
is probably the most unique in that regard, captivating hearts of millions of gamers worldwide up to this date.
Having been released just shy of nine months after the ground-breaking
,
shares quite a lot of common elements with its predecessor, enough to make the veterans feel right at home and not too many for people to write it off as "the III clone". Gunplay is mostly the same, with the ability to carry one firearm per category at a time and relying on the awkward on-screen reticle when aiming, which at times does more harm than good in terms of accurate firing. Certain weapons, mainly assault and sniper rifles, alleviate this issue by allowing to "aim down the sights", which is basically firing in first person, but SMGs, pistols and the rest of the deadly arsenal this game provides got the short end of the stick.
A welcome addition in terms of vehicles is the motorcycles - something completely absent from
- as well as a vast expansion of different types of aircraft, including pilotable helicopters. Compared to the previos part, with its Cessna ripoff "Dodo" with clipped wings, it gives
the right to boast about its innovative content at the time of the release. Other noteworthy vehicles are based on the hits of the 80's, including Infernus (Lamborghini Countach), DeLuxe (DMC Delorean), Cheetah (Ferrari Testarossa F512) and many more.
The story in the game revolves around Tommy Vercetti, a loyal mob working for the Forelli family, who has been sent to the sun-soaked Vice City to carry out a drug deal that goes horribly wrong. In order to reclaim the money he has lost, Tommy reaches out to the criminal underworld of the city and establishes connections with many influential figures, from bikers and mafia bosses to corrupt architects and gang leaders.
is the first game in the series to feature a voiced protagonist, and the voice actor has done an amazing job, giving shape to the rugged criminal trying to appease his boss and make a name for himself in an unfamiliar environment, and the same can be said about the rest of the cast of the game - every character feels unique, even if they have clichee elements to them. Other than that, the story, while giving reasons for events happening in the game, is nothing to write home about - it is by no means a flop, but calling it a masterpiece would be a stretch as well.
Possibly the most captivating part of the game, the city, being a rip-off of 80's Miami, illustrates the carefree lifestyle mixed with shady drug business extremely well: every sunrise fills you with joy and every car you pass in a highway, radio blasting "Video Killed The Radio Star" at night, makes you push the pedal to the metal and never stop. Despite the rather small size of the city compared to other entries, it makes good use of its assets and brings out the best the game can offer, with diverse districts and lively landmarks filling Vice City and shaping it as the most atmospheric one of the series.
As is the case with any other 3D-era
entry, graphics aged poorly, with sloppy cubic models driving boxy cars and firing low-poly weapons a common sight. Of course, not much can be expected from a fifteen-year-old game, and thus this issue should not be a major concern to whoever decides whether to pick up the game or not.
Despite its shortcomings in terms of gameplay and graphics,
is a must-have for any fan of the series, no matter the degree of your affection for
games, as its special atmoshpere leaves a long-lasting feeling of content and adoration no other game can recreate.

I'd been looking for a decent puzzle game for a while when I picked this one up but none of them were really interesting me. This one breaks the mold, though. Actually, this one breaks pretty much every mold. What starts out as feeling like a series of completely random adjustments to real world physics actually starts to make some kind of weird sense. There definitely were some frustrating areas that took me a long time to get through, but it really isn't as random as it first appears. You'll need to be willing to try the stupidest of your ideas (the good ones probably won't work) and get ready for some serious thinking outside of the box. If you're into that, the game is well worth the time it takes to adjust. It isn't very long, though; I'd watch for it on sale if you're thinking of picking it up.

Put simply, Shadowrun Returns is a good game. A great cyberpunk setting. Well-crafted turn based strategic combat. Plenty of variety in how you can build your character.
However, it is let down somewhat by a storyline that devolves into a nonsensical, overdone
conclusion; a few issues with the engine (e.g. not being able to jack in to the matrix during a mission unless you're a decker, even if you have a decker in your team); and most of all, the lack of a 'team' element in the storyline. You hire mercenaries for each run and you do come across some returning characters, but their characters are not fleshed out at all and for a game with otherwise pretty good writing, they're pretty one-dimensional.
The good news, though, is that the sequel, Dragonfall, vastly improves in all these areas. There are a bunch of enhancements to the engine (including the ability for any team with a decker to use jack in points), and the storyline has a far more satisfying ending that allows you more choice in how you deal with the villains. Most of all though, in Dragonfall you have a team that follows you through the story. You learn more about them through the game, they level up as you do missions with them, and they have their own companion side quests. Even the NPCs are more well-rounded and have more depth, creating a much more immersive atmosphere overall. You can still choose to hire mercs if you prefer, but your team is always there to support you.
So, I would definitely recommend Shadowrun Returns if you enjoy turn-based tactical combat set in a futuristic, cyberpunk world.
You don't need to know anything from Returns to enjoy Dragonfall - they're set in the same universe but are completely separate storylines, set in different cities (Seattle and Berlin, respectively).
Shadowrun Returns isn't a bad game, but Dragonfall is unarguably a better one.

I think FTL is a very addictive game ♥ You start with a crew and a ship. You have a mission to survive and there are so many ways to fail, yet so many places to explore and unpredictable events to unravel.
What makes the game really fun is the decisions you make for your ship to survive and your strategy of micro-managing your crew, situations and resources in order to make it to your goal.
Depending on the roles you give to each crew member will also depend which skills and strengths they develop.
There are some interesting species to encounter and play as in FTL, from fireproof rockmen to telepathic slugs. The random name generation is quite amusing too.
As a roguelike game, this means there is no mercy if you die and your ship explodes. Failling means the end and you will need to start all over again. The feeling is bad, but the desire to play again is always there, just to see if luck is in your hands next time.
Also, you can unlock ships, in-game achivements and layouts if you do keep playing over again, depending on what you encounter and how far you get.
Sometimes when played for too long with the same ship and crew, it's easy to become attached to the crew members. RIP Charlie :(
I think those of you who ♥ sci-fi, challenging, strategic and resourceful survival games will really enjoy and play FTL over and over again. ♥

A word of warning: you will lose many hours into the night getting absorbed into this.  I've never played the original, so unfortunately I can't make comparisons with earlier games - but seeing this as a standalone, I've found this to be a very addictive (and challenging enough, even at normal difficulty) turn-based strategy game.
The pace of battle is taking cover and moving in slow, deliberated steps at a time while taking care not to expose your flanks in various environments, using the debris and buildings you have at disposal for your ingenuity.  If Game's Workshop were to make a Necromunda game for PC, I would look at this as a starting template.
Managing your base (a vague similarity to Evil Genius echos, but without boobytraps) is an extra factor to deal with when you're not on the battlefield.  Researching, upgrading, building ships to stave off UFO invasions and making decisions with consequences are many of things you need to budget for with your limited funding at disposal.
A (small) particular upside I like is that you can customise the look and names for your squad members - but it does make it harder to accept when you lose them in battle.
A  (small) downside is with the customisation - there isn't enough faces, races, hair, etc. to play around with.
Overall - you could probably play this game, one battle at a time and put it away and come back to it the next day (for all us full-timers out there, stuck at the grindstone), but chances are, you will lose sleep with that 'just one more battle and then I'm done'  kind of attitude.

I was tentative to buy Dying Light at first because *sigh* another zombie game.  But after reading a few reviews recommending the game I thought I'd give it a shot.  So glad that I did.
Dying Light has the atmospheric world that I've always wanted from a zombie game.  I haven't been this immersed in my game character since Far Cry 3.  I am so involved in the story and the emotions of the protagonist that I'll be playing with my jaw hanging....and that's no exaggeration.
The sounds in this game are top-♥♥♥♥ing-notch.  The soundtrack is astounding.  I haven't been in this much love for a soundtrack since Hotline Miami and FC: Blooddragon.  Aside from the music, though, the atmospheric sounds are perfect.  My first few hours of the game, before getting used to the different sounds, I would be turning 180's all the time whenever I heard the random grunts and groans that are ever-present.  Occasionally there will be these primordial screams that literally make your blood run cold and your hair to stand on end.  Even now, 15 hours in, I still feel that way when I hear those screams.  This game sounds so good, 100x better through headphones.
Graphics are spectacular.  Finally getting to use the most out of my gtx 780.  The draw distance and the depth of field filter really make the backgrounds seem realistic.  Character models are great, animations are great, framerate is great.
Combat is awesome.  The final detail that made me buy the game was hearing that the zombie ai is 100% random.  And it's awesome!  Before getting some of the badass weapons, combat is scary as hell.  They will dive, lunge, bash, punch, go for a bite, swing, twirl, etc, and there's no specific order.
My only complaints would have to be the scavenging aspect of the game.  While I enjoy how they did it, I would have liked it to be a little more developed.  Maybe having to scavenge through the houses (that are a little more randomized/unique) for food and medicine for the tower, or stuff like that.  Maybe more stuff like that happens later in the game, I'm only about 26% through.
Anyways, there is also multiplayer invasions, haven't played them yet but I'm guessing it's similar to dark souls invasions.  The good thing is they can be disabled for players that don't want to deal with them.  I haven't done anything with multiplayer yet so I can't really comment.

Also apparently it's just a browser game, because every time I hit F12 to take a screenshot (the default keybind in Steam) a Chrome debugger window pops up over the game.

One big problem with the game that I did not figure out until I googled it was how to switch characters while in the city. After coming out of a mission it locks you into two characters and you can't hold Y to switch. Until I researched it, I had no idea that I was supposed to first go to a blue vehicle/character machine to set the game to after you switch that way to then allow you to switch simply by holding Y. Yay!
Only Marvel super fans will want to sit and unlock all 100 chars, although needless to say, there is so much to do in this game that I have almost 30 hours in and still haven't unlocked all the characters. I haven't even finished story mode yet because I have spent so much time running around the city and unlocking things.
The combat, sound, music, effects, story, script, and graphics are all fitting of a Lego game. It looks and performs very smoothly. Of all the more challenging action and permadeath games I play, this is a nice casual game I can just relax and play without worrying about dying. Probably the most fun casual action game I've ever played. Worth it on sale but also at regular price if it is $20 or less.

Tomb Raider 4: The Last Revelation was the best TR game in my opinion. Why? Because it was a Tomb Raider game since the first one that was actuall about exploring tombs and fighting monsters (With a little appearence of bad guys). That said, let's go to the topics:
Graphics: Pretty good for a 1999 game, actually. Texture variation is not so present because ambient is also not. That's because you will be put in on closed spaces more than open ones. Pyramids, temples and hidden tombs will be more seen than anything else. But the presentation of these places are actually nice, it doesn't get repetitive and you always know when a place is new or not.
Gameplay: Picking up the style from the other TR games, it remained the same with a few additions. Lara can now jump into ropes, walk in them and best of all: DRIVE VEHICLES! That was a nice little adition, tough i din't find the vehicles gameplay so pleasurable for me. At least at a long time ago. For me, now isn't that bad. It's pretty ok.
Gunplay feels the same from other games and doging from enemies still feels impossible, tough, as in other games, exploring is the key too fill up with medkits and ammo. Not much problem here.
Puzzles are back and were the main focus of the game. You will waste more time on puzzles than killing enemies. They are complex, but not hard to do.
Remember when i said i couldn't remember if the secrets followed the same pattern as TR 5? Yeah, it follows. Global statistics for secrets, no statistics per stage. And this game is HUGE, it is a big flaw to make harder to find the secrets in this game. At least, you don't win anything by finding it all, besides new weapons/items on your gameplay. Exploration is the key, once again.
Soundtrack: More or less. Most of the time you will only hear ambient sounds. But when music plays, it always match with what's happening and feels like an epic adventure. Voice acting is quite decent and Lara's voice is sweet.
Story: Here was the big point of this game. The plot tried to explore a bit of Lara's past at the beggining and tried to connect to the actual story that was happening. It went pretty well and many things have been done. A lot of effort was put in the Seth and Horus backstory and as more as you explore, more content is revealed. The game goes roughly for a lot of time because of this. It all went you...Until the ending. The boss battle felt so empty for me and the ending itself was quite sad and a cliffhanger.
TR 4 was the best game of the franchishe for me and it was pleasurable to play. The focus on the adventure more than action served this game well for me and it made an unique experience.
If devs that are doing the new Tomb Raider were to see a game where they could see what they SHOULD do with the series style of play, it should be this one.

This is a fun little game, a cross between Steam World Dig, and Terraria. You start in the center of a Large Mine, when you create your world, the Mine is generated based on what you named it, so you can play the same map as your friends, though there's no multiplayer. As you move further from the center, where your base is, the enemies get harder and the loot get's better.
You get 4 different weapons: A Pistol, Shotgun, SMG, and Bazooka. You can either find upgrades for those categories, or buy them back at your base. There's various gems and ores you can find throughout the mine, which you can sell for money.
The objective is to find Block Cannons. You're trying to rebuild this huge bipedal Digging machine so you can get back home. It's made of different colored blocks, and each Block Cannon shoots a different colored block.
This is a pretty fun game, definitely worth it's price, though I can see it getting tedious in the late game, I'll be enjoying every step on my way to that point.

A CCG that is both compelling both visually and mechanically. Shadowverse has gradually taken up more time from me than Hearthstone has (I have many more hours on mobile). It plays very similarly to Hearthstone on the surface level (great for those coming from said game), but distinguishes itself through its evolve mechanic - enabling back and forth tempo swings that can make games feel much less one sided despite poor draws.
Each of the seven classes also have mostly unique mechanics such as Spellboost from Runecraft (each of your spells will power the rest in your hand) and Forestcraft (cards gain strength from the number of cards played on a single turn).
In terms of business model, it is fairly run of the mill with pricing that is similar to most other online CCG's, however it is quite generous in the free packs/content that is handed out - particularly early on.
Personally I like the art, however that is subjective. Mosty cards do have unique animations on summon and attacks and are all voiced (English VO is suprisingly good quality - there are methods to switch to the original JP voices however).
All in all if you enjoy this kind of art style there is no reason to not give Shadowverse a shot, and even if you don't, you may still find the gameplay compelling enough to get over the undoubtedly (albeit high quality) weeby art style.

DISCLAIMER: This is a repost from my blog at
. I don't write reviews. I write opinion and impressions pieces, meaning the detalization may vary from just general feelings about a game to indepth critique of particular game mechanics. Read if you're interested to know if I like a game or not (and for what reasons), which parts intrigue me and which parts push me away, but don't expect in-depth description of all gameplay and systems. Thank you.
The thing that inspired me to try out Antichamber was how psychedelic it seemed. Ironically enough, the same thing is what put me off from the game itself. I exited the game with a sour taste in my mouth and no real desire to come back to it.
It’s always hard to talk about how you don’t like a critically acclaimed game that has received a bunch of awards, especially when that’s an indie title created by one person over a course of four years. Some sort of stigma appears, and people ask how you could possibly not like it, or something like that. This reaction sort of always annoyed me.
However, usually I can argument clearly why I think something of a certain title, and reasonable people agree that it makes sense even if they don’t agree with the opinion. I don’t think I can give precise arguments for Antichamber though. Because it’s an unusual experience, and I found myself on more than one occasion saying to myself, ‘Oh, that’s clever!’ But in the end, I guess it’s just not my cup of tea.
I would say the motto of the game is, quoting The Matrix, ‘There is no spoon.’ Practically nothing is what it seems, and to progress forward you have to find a way to bend reality around you. But not before the spoon that doesn’t exist is going to metaphorically hit you in the head repeatedly. It’s intriguing at first. Enthralling, even. But eventually, it just gets tiring and frustrating.
I got to the point where I wanted there to just be a corridor that I could walk through without having to ‘teleport’ by moving close to a window, or backtracking to see that nothing is like it was before, or looking at a certain spot so the perspective would change. But after I fell down into a different chamber for the Nth time because the floor wasn’t actually the floor I thought it was, I couldn’t keep playing. I think one important thing missing for me was some atmospheric element beyond the gameplay mechanics, like GLaDOS from Portal for example (doesn’t necessarily have to be a voice-over character, but if you have played Portal, imagine going through the game without GLaDOS’ company, I think it would eventually become tiring too).
And just because I agree that ‘Nothing is true, and everything is permitted’ doesn’t mean that I’m willing to let the perceived notion of reality and truth be constantly snatched away from me. Still, I applaud the author, and it’s a game worth checking out so you could decide for yourself what you think about it.

Being new to the Shadowrun setting, I was concerned that my lack of background knowledge would take away from the experience.  I was definitely wrong, the story presented here is quite engaging and doesn't rely on elements of the setting too esoteric to decipher.
The game itself is an isometric turn-based strategy RPG with several diverse and interesting classes, loads of different items, spells, abilities and gear to utilize, and a decent variety of enemies to battle.  To be clear, if you are looking for a fast-paced, action-packed thrill ride, you may find XCOM: Enemy Unknown or something similar a little more to your liking.  This game is very, very story rich and you will find yourself reading a lot of text.  The text is definitely worth reading though, the story in the game is fantastic.  The characters are charming, in a gutter rat, "I like you, but I dont really trust you" kind of way.  The missions are interesting, diverse and have excellent pacing and escalation.
The combat is a classic turn-based strategy style that pits your group of 1-4 Shadowrunners against various enemies.  There are various classes to choose from, all of which offer a satisfying number of abilities, spells and equipment.  There are also strategically placed "jack-in" locations that provide access to "the matrix" that can be utlilized by a "Decker" in your group.  Sometimes entering the matrix is plot driven with necessary tasks to be completed to drive the story forward.  Other times entering the matrix is entirely optional, only offering chances to hack your way to a few extra bucks by collecting private information to sell, or to turn those pesky enemy turrets against their operators.  Deckers use an entirely different set of spells and abilities while jacked-in, and having played a decker as my main character, these instances made for a unique and enjoyable departure from the sometimes monotonous combat.
All in all, I definitely recommend Shadowrun Returns to any and all RPG fans looking for a story-rich RPG experience.

Risk of Rain continues a trend of indie games not paying enough attention to their controls and UX.
* Graphics are barely visible at 1080p.
* Prioritization of ability use over movement--If I turn around then shoot in the same game update, I don't turn around and shoot in the wrong direction.
* Abilities are tied to 4 buttons that have no relationship to how they're used. A dodge, for example, is mapped to "C" instead of the common double-tap left or right.
* Abilities use a numeric countdown. They do not flash when they're ready, nor is any indicator shown near the character.
* Abilities aren't strong enough to kill things quickly, and the spawn rate is high. This leads to clumps of enemies where abilities target them all differently, and if any gets close to you you take half your life bar in damage.
This is how the game designer wanted the game... "hard". But it's not hard so much as unpolished.
I wouldn't buy this game again.

To start off, the parkour is very well done.  Less restrictive and glitchy than Assassin's Creed.
-The gameplay is very similar to Dead Island, a little too similar.  You can see shared animations between the two games, which isn't necessarily a bad thing in this case.
-The shooter segments are pretty poorly done to be honest.  There aren't many guns, but they aren't very useful anyway.  Why are there different values and colors for guns that have identical stats and skins??? The animations are just as funky as Dead Island in terms of guns.  If there were suppressors, then maybe it would have a bit more depth.
-PLEASE OPTIMIZE YOUR GAME BEFORE RELEASE!!! I had to knock down the graphics to 720p and everything else on low just to get ~30-40 FPS.  This should not be happening on a GTX 760!! It's not the most powerful card, but it sure can handle a lot more than this game looks.  This is a PC!! 60 FPS is the minimum expectation on low settings with a reasonable rig! This isn't a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ console!!
*SPOILER ALERT*
- The story is meh at best.  I'm not sure if there was supposed to be a little romance between Crane and Jade.  Some cutscenes are illogical and out of place.  Cut his hand off, but let him live to extend the story?  Insert a far cry 3/4 hallucination level which honestly doesn't make much sense.  I don't think everyone infected traveled through a floating wonder world before they ate someone. It is also SUPER predictable. I was not surprised at any point. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be either.
-The voice acting is ok, could use a little more authenticity in their vocals.  Sometimes they don't show much emotion, as if they're reading someone else's script (that's pretty much what they do anyway).  Bioshock infinite is an example of voice acting done right.
- Some of the crafting doesn't make much sense.  I need a box of metal parts to bend a paper clip to use as a lockpick??  At least the lockpicking is familiar to Skyrim or Fallout 3 players and not the least bit glitchy.  The blueprints and upgrades are pretty standard, but at least it works like it should. It's a shame you can't make zombies fly with your great hammer of thor like you could in Dead Island.
-I think there is enough to recommend, just barely.  I wouldn't get addicted to it like I did with Skyrim.
-The missions are good with variety.
-I love the night segment since that actually made my♥♥♥♥♥pucker up.
-Why is there no manual saving option?  I understand the "sleep here to save your game", but I've BSOD'd twice and each time it happened I had already completed a few quests, which were not saved.  Why is there no save at the end of a quest???  Sure it could boost authenticity and immersion, but taking out that option just forces us to back track multiple times to make sure our progress was actually saved.  This is a major disappointment for me.  I don't like having to back track for something that should be in the menu.
Overall, the story sort of ruined it for me.  There isn't much immersion especially when compared to games like Metro Last Light. This game is not EVE Online.  The comparisons are hard not to make given the art direction and user experience of this game, but remember -- EVE Online is a massive undertaking by hundreds of people and tens of thousands of hours of effort, and this game is but a mere hint of a shadow of the things that are in that game.
That being said, this is a GREAT game for what it is, and it's reasonably priced even keeping its limited scope in mind.
It DOES have the feel of EVE Online in some respects.  The gameplay is very similar to your first few hours of cargo hauling or mining in EVE Online, but there it ends.   EVE gives you the complexity of a rich storyline, faction reputations, a complex and meaningful exploration option, and NPC pirates that make relatively smart decisions on their own - not to mention the multiplayer aspects of EVE that truly make that game great.
This game lacks all of those things, but what it does deliver on is rather enjoyable nonetheless.
This game would be like never getting past high-sec ferry missions and mining in EVE Online, but if that is what you are after (and sometimes I am) this is perfect.  While the complexity is not high and there are no other players to play with, sometimes that is the perfect thing.  There are no disgusting conversations in global chat.  There is no griefing.  You are free to be as slow and deliberate as you want to be.  The danger from moving into a new system is predictable and scales slowly, and once you clear a sector, you are pretty much completely safe there to mine as much as you like.  You don't have to fear walking away from the keyboard for a few minutes here and there.
I played EVE for years.  I'd often sit in 0.0 space, deep within my alliance's territory, and just mine the rocks.  It was soothing.  It was easy.  There was very little danger.  Then someone forgot to pay a bill and things went upside down quickly.  It was fantastic.  It was a worldwide event that affected hundreds of thousands of people, and I will never forget it, but the days when I can just sit back and accomplish things for my alliance while streaming netflix on the other monitor are over for me in EVE and have been for some time.
This game gives me the ability to do something very similar.  I do miss the alliance chat and the fact that every once in a while we'd get attacked by other thinking humans to spice things up - which is something that you do not get with Astrox - but this does fill a desire when I want to just relax and pretend to be a space miner.
If you are a recovering EVE carebear, or even an old-school EVE player who enjoyed more than just the multiplayer aspects of the game, then I would recommend this game highly.
If you are a recovering EVE rifter jockey who loves the thrill of the hunt, this game is not for you, but it's still a great game and it might even be worth checking out - it made me somewhat nostalgic for my early days in EVE.
This is one of those must own games.

- Graphics :
Yuck ! this game looks not very good. It actually looks like a 3DS game that's been upscaled to fit the current gen & PC gaming platforms. My theory is that it's a cancelled 3DS exclusive that got released on the other platform, because of how poorly the first Rev sold on 3DS. I've heard there were framerate issues which I only encountered once during the third episode and I'm guessing they patched it since, so....... yeah, the graphics are not very good, nothing to lose sleep over, though.
- Sound & Musics :
Musics are nice ; the beat from Resident Evil 6 Mercenaries is back for the Raid Mode, the boss themes are cool, and the ambience isn't that bad.
- Gameplay :
Interesting. This IS a modern style Resident Evil, which means more gunplay than in the older ones, but with some depth to it : they borrowed a lot from The Last of Us with the tool & items crafting, the abilities to sense enemies (one character only has it), the surviving aspect and some enemies provide interesting situations. The bestiary is kinda nice & varied so there's some fun to have here. The mechanics that borrowed from The Last of Us DO work here so .... I think it's safe to assume this game is actually good.
- Storytelling :
Claire is imprisonned into an island where a prison & a laboratory are found, ruled by some crazy megalomaniac blonde woman who happens to be the sister of another villain that's as blonde, megalomaniac and crazy as her.... later on, some older guy comes to the rescue and has to find said Claire & some other girl who happens to be her relative and... did I just write the story of Resident Evil Code Veronica or....?
Well, to be fair : Barry replaces Chris, he finds a scary little girl with scary powers (remember kids : in Japan, little girls are ALWAYS scary) ; his relative is Moira, a useless girl who litteraly does nothing but holds the flashlight while Claire is doing the rest of the work... I know that feel, Claire.
I may look like I'm deliberately making fun of this game bbuuuuut..... the story really isn't that clever, as always.
The ambience is cool, though.
- Length :
Well I put 40h into it to complete the main campaign once + the Raid Mode, so yeah. It's worth the 40€ I invested.
CONCLUSION :
Yep.
It's a nice Resident Evil game, I actually didn't hope it to be that entertaining, so this is a soft I'll easily recommend to you guys.

Mirror's Edge was the kind of proof-of-concept that, much like Portal, went far beyond just proving that it was a viable gameplay mechanic. Though the comparison to Portal makes Mirror's Edge seem lackluster by comparison, it is anything but a lackluster game. The DICE engine produces a kind of graphical fidelity that few games have rivaled since for this title, and the animations do something few games have ever accomplished: Mirror's Edge makes you forget you're controlling a floating camera attached to a mesh, and feel like you're in control of a human being. The music is fairly good, the story is okay, but the cutscenes inbetween levels are nothing short of atrocious. The cel-shaded art wouldn't look so disgusting if it weren't being juxtapositioned next to some of the best graphics the video game industry has ever produced.
Where Mirror's Edge stands out most is it's gameplay. The parkour mechanics are utterly flawless: from wall runs to dives to slides to wallclimbing, this game never wavers from perfection- except, sadly, in it's combat. Melee combat isn't necessarily bad- running, jumping, then kicking a cop in the face midair has a certain satisfaction to it, as does repeatedly punching an officer's testicles until they are surely removed from percievable existence. Even so, gunplay is so astoundingly horrendous that for some players, it kills the game. There are two easy steps to enjoy Mirror's Edge: don't play on easy mode, and don't pick up the guns.
For completionists: each level has time trials, variations, and three hidden collectibles.
The game is rather short (there's nine chapters plus a prologue, not including the time trials and whatnot), and so EA released some DLC levels- dissapointingly, they're ten dollars, and not available on PC. Yet, Mirror's Edge plays much better on PC, so you have to choose between better playability or more content.
Mirror's Edge is, overall, utterly magnificent-
Final Score:
9.25/10

I was surprised by how fun this simple-looking game really is.
In 4 words, it is a platforming/side-scrolling shooter, but surprisingly well done! Each level or world is randomly generated and in order to progress you must find 4 items. The graphics is crisp with an unique art style. The controls are responsive and there is a 5-6 multi-jump function, which can be VERY helpful! Unfortunately, this game also has a weird shooting mechanism, where your WASD movement keys are also used to control the direction of your aim. You can't use the mouse to aim. This can feel a little awkward and can get very annoying when you're trying to jump and shoot at the same time. The enemies are rather limited in terms of variety, and include humans, flying bats, floating blocks, and winged demon-things. Luckily, there is a ton of traps populating each world, which makes the platforming both chaotic and fun.
This game also has a currency system where you gain money from looting fallen enemies, opening treasure chests, or by selling items. You can then use that money to buy upgrades. There is also alot of items in the game and can be categorized into four groups: gems, hats, guns, and health. The gems are found throughout each world and can be sold for money or used to restore health. The hats and guns are found by looting dead enemies, opening chests, or buying from merchants. The health  upgrade items can only be bought from merchants, and will permanently increase your health.
In terms of weapons, there are only 4 types of guns, but with MANY variations in level of damage. This game also has  upgrades in terms of MANY collectable hats (that either increases the weapon damage and armor, or decreases weapon reload time). They are definitely useful and also look great!
Finally, this game has one very innovative feature that I haven't seen in other similar games. There is a fog-of-war effect where your visibility is limited when exploring a new area and it is also connected to how much health you have. So, the lower your health, the smaller your field of view!
In summary:
PROS:
Interesting fog of war feature
Randomly generated worlds
Good balance with alot of traps, difficult enemies, but also upgradeable perks
Many different types of collectable hats and guns
Tight controls
Nice graphics
Decent music and sound effects
CONS:
Weird aiming mech using WASD keys.
Limited variety of enemies (bats, humans with guns, not much more...)
Limited types of weapons (only pistol, shotgun, machinegun, rocket launcher)
Limited item perks (increase damage, increase armor, increase health, or shorten weapon reload time)
A fun, addictive game but lacks enough depth in terms of weapons variety (4 types of guns) and item selection (only hats, guns, gems, and a few health upgrades), and also has an awkward aiming system. If it had more variety in these areas with free mouse aiming, then I would definitely give it "10/10", "A must buy!", and "Has a ton of replay value". However, right now I would give it 8/10 and still recommend it to anyone who likes an affordably-priced platforming or side-scroller game.

I think FTL is a very addictive game ♥ You start with a crew and a ship. You have a mission to survive and there are so many ways to fail, yet so many places to explore and unpredictable events to unravel.
What makes the game really fun is the decisions you make for your ship to survive and your strategy of micro-managing your crew, situations and resources in order to make it to your goal.
Depending on the roles you give to each crew member will also depend which skills and strengths they develop.
There are some interesting species to encounter and play as in FTL, from fireproof rockmen to telepathic slugs. The random name generation is quite amusing too.
As a roguelike game, this means there is no mercy if you die and your ship explodes. Failling means the end and you will need to start all over again. The feeling is bad, but the desire to play again is always there, just to see if luck is in your hands next time.
Also, you can unlock ships, in-game achivements and layouts if you do keep playing over again, depending on what you encounter and how far you get.
Sometimes when played for too long with the same ship and crew, it's easy to become attached to the crew members. RIP Charlie :(
I think those of you who ♥ sci-fi, challenging, strategic and resourceful survival games will really enjoy and play FTL over and over again. ♥

Overall I do like the game if for nothing more than I love the setting. Cyberpunk is by far my favorite genre and it's terribly under represented in the gaming and mmo world. However I am very middle to the road on this game. It definitely sets the mood however that is about where it ends. The combat is a bit frustrating unless you take spells with +% to hit and +AP. Of course that should be somewhat of a no brainer but even in the near end game you see miss a lot with weak hits. If strategy is made harder by making RNG constantly want to screw you then Hairbrained doesn't know how to give strategic options well. Largely this is negated by taking cover and firing from cover to help mitigate damage you may take.
I played a mage my first run through and while I did feel powerful though I couldn't help but notice there is almost never any reason for using the decking skill. I really wanted it to be more integrated into the game and it's just not. NPC's get it done quite effectively while you mop up the meat world. There are options to bypass areas of the game through decking but it seems irrelevant to me as I previously mentioned combat is tedious but not difficult.
If you are looking for a cyberpunk/Shadowrun fix this will give you some but leave you wanting so much more. This game is so damn linear it is just ridiculous. There are nearly no side quests to speak of and it is terribly short. I just wish there had been more immersion into the game. I got it on sale for iirc $2.99 and while it was a deal at the price I still feel like my money would have been better spent elsewhere.
It is not a bad game but at the same time it could have been so much more. Yes that can be said of many titles but really Hairbrained dropped the ball here. The world is very small, not immersive and too linear. Three things in my mind that just make this game nowhere near what it should have been. I don't even see any reason I would want to replay it even though I want to make a decker but then I think.... why would I when the game wont change just the circumstances I beat it with and that by far makes me unable to reccomend this game.

XCOM: EU is a lightweight turn based strategy game with a bit of team development and technology progression. The opponents scale up to your team's technology level, so you never achieve any superiority. However, the game at normal difficulty is not too difficult, although bad decisions will cost you. The base development and technology progression are interesting, but the way the missions work, you can manipulate the progression by not achiving certain 'standing' goals. Once a 'standing' goal is completed, the storyline forces you into some fixed missions, and if you are unprepared, you will not make it.
The graphics are fairly well done, but some of the animations are clearly messed up. You will see your team sometimes shooting at an opponent with the projectiles coming out at 90 degree angles or the barrel of the gun pointed through solid objects. Sometimes a character will smash a window, even though the target is not on the other side of a window. But all of this is window dressing to the game itself. The game as a whole is worth playing. It's not spectacular or very deep, but it's not a total waste of time either.

As others have said, Dying Light is a game that is hard to recommend or not. It's not a terrible game but it's also not a great game. It has its cool and emotional moments but it also has its aggravating moments. The overall gameplay is okay, with the parkour being awesome at times and annoying at other times (usually when you end up with unexpected falls and lose a lot of time if your respawn point is too far back) and the combat being average at best. I do admit however that it's one of those things where you might not realize how useful and fun it can be until you play a game without it as an option.
Again, as others have said, Dying Light feels like a combination of Dead Island, Far Cry 3/4 (I haven't played four so I can't judge there) and Mirror's Edge. Some will see it as what Dead Island could have been. Others will see it as a game that tries to be too many types of games and ends up being a mediocre version of all of the above without excelling in anything.
Gameplay wise, it's an Open-World Zombie epidemic type of game. There is a main quest line you can follow as well as secondary quests that open up over time that you can play when you feel like. As others have noted, often the secondary quests end up feeling more (perhaps much more) interesting and/or emotional then the main quest.
You start with lousy melee weapons that don't do much damage and you can't take much damage, resulting in combat being risky and annoying enough that flight often feels like the reaction they intended for the player. While you do get guns later on, do more (and special via crafting) damage and become more damage reistant, the combat often (but not always!) doesn't feel all that fun. If anything, it can even feel like a chore at times (bear in mind, I'm saying *at times*). This may seem strange and it may have just been my personal experience however. The gameplay (especially at first) doesn't really seem designed for combat as the main course of action.
One feature the game lacks that gets annoying is the lack of fast travel. This means you're going to be doing a lot of running around, which can get very annoying and time consuming. Given that there are no vehicles (although I note that ground vehicles would probably be slower given the games Assassin's Creed attitude of getting around via rooftops) and you can end up in a situation where doing some quests (especially secondary ones) can become a chore and you may well end up avoiding some due to the distance you need to travel.
In short, it's all right game but it's nothing spectacular. While I do think it's worth at least a look (although be sure to bring plenty of patience) I might recommend it but only on a Steam sale. Because of this, while it does pain me to do so, I have to give this a not recommended even if only because I can't really recommend it and when deciding, I find myself favouring the not option, even if only very slightly.

I was hoping to unlock all the achievements before writing a review for this game, but I've lost my patience so easily, that I decided to delete everything and put an end to this whole thing.
Wow, I've gotta be careful, you might actually think that this is a bad game after reading such a brutal introduction, isn't? Well, it's actually a very fun game. It can get quite addicting too, if you're not careful enough. Playing cards, right?
Anyway, so what is this title about? The name pretty much summarizes everything. The only thing is that there's also this background story and objectives to be fulfilled, in order to try to keep the player more immersed in that realm. I didn't pay much attention to the story, to be quite honest. I just wanted to beat every level as fast as possible while I was playing.
Now for an overview: The graphics are ok, I only thought annoying the fact that the full screen resolution is so awful. The sound effects can get really annoying after some time. The music is ok, I actually loved one of the songs available. As for the gameplay mechanics, besides the premise of solitaire, there're also some RPG elements. The more combos you make, the more money you get. With that cash, you get to unlock certain power-ups that can help you a lot. You can also get to find some resources every now and then some eggs, but I'll have to get back to that in the next paragraph.
Ok, so there're also trading cards (which are always nice), and some achievements to unlock. And that's the part where this game kicks you in the nuts. Well, you can get more than 90% of the achievements just by playing the regular game, no big deal, right? Now, if you want to get every single one available, get ready for an endurance round. Remember the eggs from before? There're lots of them, and every now and then (really rare), you get to find one in the levels. After you find them, you can hatch them, and also evolve them through the experience points that you gather while playing it (it takes ages, just for the record). There's actually an update which actually allows you to purchase the eggs you couldn't find so far, but the prices (which are already expensive), rises exponentially. So, what do you do? You check the community guides, and what do you find? Everything is about those stupid eggs!
So, overall, how obnoxious could these devs be, to the point of basically pushing the players to their limits just for the sake of a couple achievements. This is simply ridiculous, you just don't do that, especially when you're planning to release a sequel.
Ok, now that the ranting is over, this is a fun game, really. Just be careful with the "Platinum" trap. It's surely not worth it. If you doubt what I'm saying, I read that there was this guy who had to play this thing for more than 225 hours just to find all the eggs. Have friggin' mercy...

Platformines is one of those games where I wish there was more nuance to the rating system than just "thumbs up or down."  This game is more sort-of in the middle of the two.    The basic gameplay and mechanics are solid and everything fits together really well.  Basically, you are in a randomly generated underground mine.  You run around killing enemies and finding resources, increase your money, buy upgrades and keep repeating the process.  The goal is to find all the pieces of a special gun you need to rebuild your spaceship.  Once you find all the pieces, you then go into a kind of sub-game within the game where you have to put together the engine like a puzzle.   The game can be a bit random at times, but for the most part it works.  You get better weapons slowly and you find different hats that give small bonuses to certain things and make you look goofy.
So far it's great, but the grey area that Platformines eventually wanders into concerns its length.   The worlds that are randomly generated are mind-bogglingly huge.  The scale doesn't truly hit you until you've picked up 4 or 5 engine pieces and at that point you might think "Damn..I might never finish this."   And therein lies the flaw....the game is simply too huge for the gameplay that supports it.  The difficulty also doesn't scale particularly well.  The further away from your base you get, the harder the world becomes, which makes sense.  But the only stat-based upgrade you can buy, your health upgrades, only go up to a certain point then mysteriously stop well before the game is even remotely close to being finished.   Better guns help a little bit with this, but the odds you will find random weapons that will vastly improve your survivability is a dice roll at best.   Don't get me wrong, this is a good, enjoyable game.  I just think it could really use an update where you can buy more upgrades and possibly have a better selection of hats that provide a greater variety of gameplay style options.

This is one of the few games I can say that I had to force my self to get through it to the end. Not to say the game is bad but it isn't great, and at times it's just flat out not fun. The main idea of the game is to go and get these launchers, in a very large, randomly generated mine, that place these missing pieces onto your robot drill in order to escape. It seems a simple task untill you realize how crazy difficult some sections of the mines can be in order to reach your destination. Through out the mines you'll find nuggets of treasure all over the place that range in value and increase in rarity as you stretch out deeper into the mines, which are used to transform into currency back at the base so you can buy storage and health increase upgrades as well as weapons. The collector kind of player will certainly feel at home with this feature of the game as there are pleanty of different treasures to collect. Alternatively you can use the treasures for health. Most of the best weapons you'll come across by killing off other enemies or found in a chest. Weapons come with increasing stats as you venture further into the mine so that you can stand against the tougher badies as you progress, almost in Borderlands style. Sometimes spike traps, or electrical platforms will be inconviniently in your way of teleporters that act as checkpoints, which would eat away at your life, hindering you're ability to progress smoothly. Or you might be faced off with an enemy whose just too mighty for you and will kill you in seconds, even with quick reflexes. This doesn't become a huge problem till the end game. Platforming in the game is solid and pricise thankfully. This game can offer a nice sum of game time of about 5 hours on anyones first run, but the game doesn't give you much reason to do it all again in the higher difficulties. Perhaps at a cheap price, this game is worth your time but don't go into it with high expectations.
