I find Shadowverse to be a very enjoyable alternative to Hearthstone, and I feel slight differences in gameplay are just enough to warrant a try. For being a pretty shameless clone of Hearthstone I am surprised at how decently polished it is.
Pros:
+Runs on any toaster, also can share accounts with mobile versions.
+Much easier to get packs and gold than Hearthstone.
+Nice art on the cards (although the art is recycled from the defunct Rage of Bahamut).
+So far no crass greed in their free-to-play model. Everything that can be bought with cash can also be bought with in-game currency.
+Loli necromancer
Neutral:
•The evolution mechanic, 5 cards in play at a time, and lower amount of life compared to Hearthstone makes it more agressive, in my opinion.
•Instead of a hero power for 2 mana like in Hearthstone, the characters have a sort of passive that are tied a little more into their card gimmicks.
Cons:
-Lack of cards at this point. Naturally, you'd expect them to release more in the future.
-Single player story mode really just serves as a quick way to get some gold and practice in early on. The voice acted scenes  are underwhelming and kind of lame.
-Player base isn't and probably will never be as large as Hearthstone, but on that note I'm surprised that Shadowverse has at least gotten a decent reception.
So give Shadowverse a try if you like Hearthstone and want a change of scenery.

The basic concept is simple: get squad members behind cover where damage is minimized, and then take aim. Each squad member gets two actions per turn, though some of your soldiers will earn ways of extending this basic number. When possible, you want to move from cover to cover, diminishing the enemies' chances of landing shots while flanking them to lessen the benefit of their own cover spots. In the early hours, your options are few. But the soldiers that survive the mission level up and gain access to new abilities that you assign back at base. Additionally, you spend funds on better weapons, upgraded armor, and other enhancements. Simple grunts become trustworthy killing machines and when your killing machines are fully leveled and decked out in your finest equipment, you'd best keep them alive.

The old X-COM regularly makes its appearance as the #1 Turn-Based Strategy Game of All Time. This game takes the old game, gives it 21st century graphics and streamlines everything that used to be tedious about the old game. It's awesome. One of the best games I know. It is unforgiving and sadistic, but overcoming the odds rewards you with a feeling that's like scarfing a piece of chocolate cake like your mother makes during the holidays and doing cocaine at the same time off of Scarlett Johanson's butt. This game will make you cry with desperation and then with triumph as you assimilate the aliens' technology for your own use. You'll miss a 99% shot and watch your squad get subsequently annihilated, but a few minutes later you make a 5% shot that breaks the back of your enemies. You will lose, you will lose, you will lose. You will cry out "♥♥♥♥ing X-COM!" But you keep coming back. And one day, you win. And you will cherish that moment better than the birth of your firstborn.
The only fault I can find in the game is the limited selection of battlefields. They're well-done, but after a dozen missions you will start recognizing the same areas appearing again and again. Also, there is no base-defense, and base building has been simplified as a part of the streamlining process, which is otherwise basically all good. That being said, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you love the old X-COM, you will love this game. I do and do. If you haven't played the old X-COM, find it. It's probably freeware by now. If you like it, come back here for an up-to-date, polished, and streamlined version.

I'll echo what others have said -- Astrox feels very much like a single-player offline version of EVE or at least what I remember of EVE from 10 years ago.
If you haven't played EVE, the trading part of Astrox could be described as similar to Taipan, Space Trader, and probably a hundred other games, while the combat is much closer to watching Galactic Civilizations II battles than it is to piloting a spaceship in something like Star Wars Galaxies' Jump to Lightspeed. There are some skills to learn and improve, component upgrades to figure out, and rare looted components, but not close to the depth of JtL's looting and reverse engineering. Graphics are simple but well done and controls are well-thought out.
In its current state, Astrox is probably the type of game I'll play occasionally when I have a couple hours to spare and don't want to get stressed out. After just 11 hours, it feels like I've seen the majority of the game already and that additional advancement will require a lot of grinding, but it's enjoyable and the price is right.

As others have said, Dying Light is a game that is hard to recommend or not. It's not a terrible game but it's also not a great game. It has its cool and emotional moments but it also has its aggravating moments. The overall gameplay is okay, with the parkour being awesome at times and annoying at other times (usually when you end up with unexpected falls and lose a lot of time if your respawn point is too far back) and the combat being average at best. I do admit however that it's one of those things where you might not realize how useful and fun it can be until you play a game without it as an option.
Again, as others have said, Dying Light feels like a combination of Dead Island, Far Cry 3/4 (I haven't played four so I can't judge there) and Mirror's Edge. Some will see it as what Dead Island could have been. Others will see it as a game that tries to be too many types of games and ends up being a mediocre version of all of the above without excelling in anything.
Gameplay wise, it's an Open-World Zombie epidemic type of game. There is a main quest line you can follow as well as secondary quests that open up over time that you can play when you feel like. As others have noted, often the secondary quests end up feeling more (perhaps much more) interesting and/or emotional then the main quest.
You start with lousy melee weapons that don't do much damage and you can't take much damage, resulting in combat being risky and annoying enough that flight often feels like the reaction they intended for the player. While you do get guns later on, do more (and special via crafting) damage and become more damage reistant, the combat often (but not always!) doesn't feel all that fun. If anything, it can even feel like a chore at times (bear in mind, I'm saying *at times*). This may seem strange and it may have just been my personal experience however. The gameplay (especially at first) doesn't really seem designed for combat as the main course of action.
One feature the game lacks that gets annoying is the lack of fast travel. This means you're going to be doing a lot of running around, which can get very annoying and time consuming. Given that there are no vehicles (although I note that ground vehicles would probably be slower given the games Assassin's Creed attitude of getting around via rooftops) and you can end up in a situation where doing some quests (especially secondary ones) can become a chore and you may well end up avoiding some due to the distance you need to travel.
In short, it's all right game but it's nothing spectacular. While I do think it's worth at least a look (although be sure to bring plenty of patience) I might recommend it but only on a Steam sale. Because of this, while it does pain me to do so, I have to give this a not recommended even if only because I can't really recommend it and when deciding, I find myself favouring the not option, even if only very slightly.

Here's the lowdown: This is a very well made co-op, class based, horde survival first person shooter. The visuals are superb. The performance is fluid. The gameplay is spot on. The sound is wonderful, from gun shots to the shattering of a zed skull as you put a high caliber bullet through it in slow motion. There are specific areas that still require attention post launch, but those are not serious enough to outweigh the many good things the game has going for it, and I believe they'll be taken care of soon.
Overall 9.5/10 from me.
Some additional details:
This is not just a remaster of Killing Floor. The two games are, in terms of pace especially, are quite different. Killing Floor 2 is much faster, both in terms of the FPS mechanics and perk leveling. There are 25 levels per perk instead of 6, and you will level up much faster. You choose one skill every five levels, and your starting loadout will never change based on your level alone. I do agree that the characters, while plentiful, are lackluster in comparison to the originals. They're not bad, but if you've known the first, you can tell there's a world of difference. Owners of Killing Floor get a couple of classic characters with their voice acting for free. Your voice menu will be much simpler this time around, with only eight orders/answers to choose from.
Microtransactions are the equivalent of CSGO or TF2, weapon skins and cosmetics with effect on any stats. You will get crates and sometimes loot for free after a game.
The things most negative reviews will bring up are legitimate issues, but to be honest, it's nitpicking. This is a great game, get it.

The Grand Theft Auto series has come a long way since its early days, that’s for sure. Starting with a top down perspective in the original games, and evolving into the mod-hating micro-transaction machine that is GTA 5, each title has proved an invaluable stepping stone towards those that have followed it. Throughout all the years, however, I feel there’s one that really kicked things into high gear, and remains perhaps the best game to come out of the franchise to date. Guessed which one it is yet? Well, you really should have done; it’s Vice City.
There’s a plethora of reasons this is the case, but let’s start with what is unarguably the game's defining characteristic; its setting. Vice City takes the idea of a sun-drenched sunshine state in the 80s, dials it up to eleven, and captures the end result perfectly. From the garishly bright Hawaiian shirts and pastel coloured buildings that dot the landscape, to the rollerblading pedestrians and cassette player save points, everything here oozes an 80s vibe. To a chosen few this is destined to be an intense blast of nostalgia, but even for those who aren’t so lucky to have been around in that era the overblown and exaggerated nature of everything still makes it an incredibly fun setting to experience.
It’s the soundtrack that seals the deal, however, and I honestly think it’s hard to argue against the fact that this is perhaps one of the greatest video game soundtracks ever created. There are endless classic songs on here, from so many bands – A Flock of Seagulls, Blondie, The Human League… The list goes on, with enough quality music blaring out the car radios that the desire to never stop driving is strong.  It’s not even just the music itself, either; the accompanying chat shows and adverts are easily the most memorable that the series has ever produced. It’s a true high point that the franchise has often tried to replicate, but quite possibly will never better.
Thankfully,there’s a actual fun games here to back up its amazing setting. One of my main criticisms about the direction GTA has gone in the past few years is that everything has become grim, realistic and downright miserable. Combine this with gameplay which feels as is every mission ends in some sort of cover-based shootout, and it's becoming increasingly hard to crack a smile while playing the modern games. Vice City, on the other hand, has no problem with being way more outlandish with its missions, and as a result they’re both more memorable and far more entertaining. Hanging out a chopper while shooting a minigun at people below? Piloting a toy helicopter to plant bombs? Chasing an army convoy while trying to steal their tank? All things you can do, and they all occur in pretty much the first half of the game. It’s great stuff.
There’s no shortage of joy to be found with just messing around, either. It’s true that there’s far less diversity in your options compared to the GTA of today – your means of flight here is pretty much limited to helicopters, for instance - but there’s still plenty of hijinks to get up to. Younger me has fond memories of throwing the fastest motorbike I could find off anything that remotely resembles a ramp, and in my recent play I’ve taken simply to making myself fireproof and throwing Molotov cocktails around as if they were sweets. I concur that better sandboxes have perhaps come and gone in recent years, but there’s certainly enough here to ensure that there’s rarely a dull moment.
Many elements of the game are showing their age, however.  How it looks is forgivable given its age (even if the sheer amount of graphical pop-up borders on the ridiculous at points), but there are other issues here that are not so easy to let slide. Controls are the big issue – even given two different control styles and a chance to remap buttons, there’s always some element to them that feels fiddly or irritating. Helicopters are impossible to fly with a mouse and keyboard, for example, or the weapon lock-on will happily direct your aim at someone fifty yards down the street - rather than at the guy right next to you that’s taking great delight in pumping you full of holes.
The inability to swim is also a massive source of irritation; dare to dip anything greater than a toe in the depths and you’re instantly dead. Hitting the drink is also way easier than you might expect – the whole game’s set on a island, for goodness sake, and there’s many a mission which forces you to brave the high seas. You’ll die via drowning more than any other means, and it’s instantly rage inducing every time.
Overall, though, Vice City stands up against to the almighty test of time, even if it has been an incredible 15 years since its initial release. It’s perhaps not as perfect as you remember it, but it’s still an amazing slice of overblown and over the top fun that continues to be worth playing to this day.

Shadowverse is a free-to-play gem that lets you be competitive quickly without having to throw your wallet at the screen.
I installed this game on a whim and it has been sucking up a good portion of my free time since. It's very similar to Hearthstone in gameplay, but there is enough to set it apart. It is a strong game that stands on its own and has a lot of fun gameplay to offer for no financial investment.
The basics: You have several different classes, each with their own unique characteristics. Forestcraft, for example, focuses on lettting you build up large amounts of cheap "fairy" cards that can be played in combination with other cards to overwhelm your opponent. Another example is Havencraft, which is based on playing "amulet" cards with powerful effects that trigger once a certain amount of rounds have passed. Each class offers unique gameplay and all are relatively easy to learn but take a bit of time to master.
The mechanics of the game are very similar to Hearthstone and other CCGs: you gain "play points" each round, and how many points you have determine which cards you can play (think mana from Hearthstone). It is different from Hearthstone in a few important ways:
-Gameplay is fast, and feels much faster-paced than Hearthstone. This is my opinion of course but when I went back to play HS after a few days of SV it felt painfully slow. The fact that the leaders (Heros) only have 20 health also adds to this. However, even with the faster pace there is a lot of room for strategic gameplay.
-Deckbuilding is easy and beginner-friendly. While there are some popular decks that require certain legendary cards to function, you can easy build a competitive deck for the lower ranks with just the cards that the game gives you. The game is extremely generous with free cards packs and there are many ways to earn them without spending a dime. They frequently have giveaways too, and recently gave away 5 packs to all players just because the company reached a certain amount of twitter followers. There is currently a promotion to easily earn packs just by playing in the "take two" arena (which is a ton of fun!). You can of course spend money and buy cards, but it's not really necessary. You will amass a big collection just by playing the game.
-The evolve mechanic is unique and allows for more strategic gameplay. Basically, you can have a card grow stronger and/or gain certain abilities by evolving it. Done at the right time this can be a complete gamechanger.
The PC version of the game is a port of the mobile game, but it still looks fantastic and plays very smoothly. You can link the PC and mobile versions if you like to play on both.
One final word of warning: this game is addictive. It's very easy to sink in hours and hours for "just one more round".
Bottom line: Fun, addictive, easy to jump into and learn but with lots of depth. Highly recommended.

As a meta-gamer, who only plays achievement games, I wanted to avoid this game by default.

I personally always wanted an Eve-like where I could just mine in peace. I wanted to gather when I wanted to, and go looking for a fight when I was bored or in the mood to lose a ship. Eve failed here, Astrox did not.
In my 6 hour session, I was able (with the settings I had configured) to advance to the second best mining ship and secure 10 sectors of the 100 for safe mining. I very much enjoyed the process and was never at any point overly stressed about combat, in game grinds, or anything really. I took my time and found everything obvious or well explained.

TL;DR: A great open world survival game with tons of stuff and zombie smashing to do with developers listening and patching accordingly. CO-OP works fine now and it's better optimized so to all the people having read the bad reviews take THIS into account. If you're into this kind of game, I highly recommend it. It's GREAT!
Now my review:
I never actually intended to buy this game, until my friends suggested it. And here I am 50 hours later I've been playing one of the few games that have hooked me in a LONG time.
It has a bit of Far Cry and Mirrors edge with a dash of Fallout in it.
The parkour and freerunning system is so smooth you never want to use roads/stairs/streets etc.
When night falls and you decide to stay outside safezones, you often find your self in FIGHT or FLIGHT situations.
Pros:
- You can bash a zombies skull in until your weapon breaks
- Great combat system with a lot of different meleeweapons (in the end game there are fewer though)
- Night time is extremely fun and exhilarating, and offers various challenges. (It has day and night cycle, which if you choose you can skip by staying in a safezone and sleep until the morning).
- Good weapon customization and crafting. You want a kitchen knife which electrifies zombies? Slap on a powercable some batteries and a conductor, tighten it with ductape and you're good to go. Real McGyver stuff right there. You want an old fashioned double-barrel shotgun to split zombies in half with? You get that too.
- A lot of sidequests, varying from interesting to down right awesome!
- Supersmooth parkour/freerunning system which makes escaping and/or exploring really fun
- At night stealth is really a good option, which makes it exciting
- You can bash a zombies skull in until your weapon breaks.
And much more!
Cons:
- Story was OK but nothing special, the ending was kind of dissapointing.
- When you're at max level you have a smaller selection of weapons which are viable.
- You can't just kill a zombie, you have to make sure it's dead by bashing it with your hammer until there's just a pulp left, or maybe that's just me.... (Not really a con, it's awesome).
I really do recommend this game, and I think you should buy it. If you like open world games with deep survival elements you will not be dissapointed. You can bash a zombies skull in until your weapon breaks. The main reason I bought the game, but hey.. I now know that it's one of the best I've played in a long time!
Thank you for reading. Good night, and GOOD LUCK!

Take the best parts of Far Cry 3, Mirror's Edge, and your favorite zombie apocalypse game. Add in 4-player co-op, and invasions a la Dark Souls 2, and you've got a recipe for a great time.  I had heard about this game briefly back when it was announced and was so burned out on the zombie thing by then, I didn't think to give it a second look. When it was released, I remembered what I had heard, and after reading that it had co-op and invasions, decided I had to have it.
I jumped into the story really not having any clue what the game was about, apart from zombies, and while it's not the most exciting, original, or believable thing, it was enough to draw me into the game and get me on a path to where I cared enough about the characters I met early on to keep going. It pretty much stayed that way throughout. - nothing that I was super enthralled in, but enough to keep me going.
The big thing throughout the game is the day/night cycle and the difference between the two. After the tutorial and first major quest, you'll understand what I mean.  I don't want to ruin the fun.
The parkour-esque aspect of the game felt as good, if not better, than Mirror's Edge. Running, jumping, sliding, climbing, grappling, it's all really fluid and feels really well. Your character gets tired when it makes sense and, while there are some questionably inhuman feats, most of what you're able to do is believable apart from maybe some of the grappling stuff.
The combat feels great. Early on it can be a bit weird as you get used to the combat stamina mechanic and learn how much you can dish out before you need to take a breather, but overall it is very smooth and oddly satisfying when you bust open, chop off, or stomp on someone's/something's head.  The gunplay isn't bad either, it's about what you'd expect from something like this. There aren't but a few gun options in the game, most of which are pretty uniform throughout. If there are upgrades or options to them, I haven't found them yet.  That said, guns aren't usually the best idea anyway, as the noise can attract some pretty unfriendly folks.
The multiplayer is really satisfying. Co-op takes the singleplayer experience to a new level. It lets you drop in/out of friends games, and vice versa, and let's you help each other advance the story, create friendly competitions, or just go on zombie squashing rampages together. Finished the main game and I have to say...

Super Hexagon is a minimalist game in both a mechanical and aesthetic sense. Every art asset in the game is nothing more than colorful simple geometry, and the object of the game is move a little triangle around a hexagon-shaped tunnel and avoid colliding point-first into the obstacles that speed down the tunnel. The controls are as simple as they can be; there's only two buttons that move you clockwise and counter-clockwise around the tunnel.
It's a very retro-style game to its core; simple in terms of its mechanics and visuals, but hard as nails. This game takes a fair bit of practice to actually do well in. With six difficulty levels (the latter three being "hyper modes" of the first three, and need to unlocked by surviving each difficulty for at least one minute), there will be many frustrations to be had trying to master the game. The game will also throw occasional curveballs at you with its obstacles, occasionally collapsing the tunnel into lesser-sided shapes such as a pentagon or a square. It will always revert back to a hexagon at some point, however.
The soundtrack only consist of three chiptune tracks. I'm fairly neutral towards chiptune soundtracks; I enjoy quite a few, but it's certainly not my preferred genre even in the realm of video game music. One of three tracks I can live without, but the other two are pretty fantastic. They certainly add to the retro-minimalist feel the game was aiming for, but they also punctuate the intensity and pace of the gameplay.
This game is a port from iOS, and I think this is where the biggest flaw of the game comes from. The game feels like it was designed to be played with a touch screen, and to make this work on the PC you move around by pressing two buttons. Since the buttons move your cursor at a set speed, the controls are straight-up less responsive than controlling it with your finger on a touch screen. Still, it works well enough that one could master the sensitivity of the controls and do just fine, but it does create an extra hurdle of frustration on the road to mastering what is already a pretty hard game.
Overall, I highly recommend Super Hexagon. I would probably recommend picking it up on mobile instead of PC if at all possible, but if you're like me and you don't have a smartphone, then this port is entirely servicable. Just expect to be very, very bad at it when you first dive in.

Shadowverse is a free-to-play gem that lets you be competitive quickly without having to throw your wallet at the screen.
I installed this game on a whim and it has been sucking up a good portion of my free time since. It's very similar to Hearthstone in gameplay, but there is enough to set it apart. It is a strong game that stands on its own and has a lot of fun gameplay to offer for no financial investment.
The basics: You have several different classes, each with their own unique characteristics. Forestcraft, for example, focuses on lettting you build up large amounts of cheap "fairy" cards that can be played in combination with other cards to overwhelm your opponent. Another example is Havencraft, which is based on playing "amulet" cards with powerful effects that trigger once a certain amount of rounds have passed. Each class offers unique gameplay and all are relatively easy to learn but take a bit of time to master.
The mechanics of the game are very similar to Hearthstone and other CCGs: you gain "play points" each round, and how many points you have determine which cards you can play (think mana from Hearthstone). It is different from Hearthstone in a few important ways:
-Gameplay is fast, and feels much faster-paced than Hearthstone. This is my opinion of course but when I went back to play HS after a few days of SV it felt painfully slow. The fact that the leaders (Heros) only have 20 health also adds to this. However, even with the faster pace there is a lot of room for strategic gameplay.
-Deckbuilding is easy and beginner-friendly. While there are some popular decks that require certain legendary cards to function, you can easy build a competitive deck for the lower ranks with just the cards that the game gives you. The game is extremely generous with free cards packs and there are many ways to earn them without spending a dime. They frequently have giveaways too, and recently gave away 5 packs to all players just because the company reached a certain amount of twitter followers. There is currently a promotion to easily earn packs just by playing in the "take two" arena (which is a ton of fun!). You can of course spend money and buy cards, but it's not really necessary. You will amass a big collection just by playing the game.
-The evolve mechanic is unique and allows for more strategic gameplay. Basically, you can have a card grow stronger and/or gain certain abilities by evolving it. Done at the right time this can be a complete gamechanger.

I struggled with this, Id probably give it a neutral rating if I could, and on sale Id definitely give it a go. Its simple, but solidly built puzzle game where you throw blocks in to a central square to fill it up.
Music is servicable, there is a story to it of sorts but with hilariously awful translation, graphically its fine, and it controls well enough.
It has a lot of levels, but they go past very rapidly. (Ive finished the game with all achievements and quite some idle time and apparently that was still only 2.5hours.) There are a few trickier ones but it never gets satisfyingly challenging. I wouldnt say it wasnt fun while it lasted, it just doesnt hold up for any length of time.
Really the major problem here is variety. It feels like the game has thrown damn near every configuration of blocks its possible to put in with a grid of this size, but they are all much the same thing. The blocks come in only 3 varieties that are all introduced fairly early on, and pink blocks rarely show up and are a little frustrating when they are used. I worked those levels out fast enough but it felt more like I was more guessing than using any skill. Meanwhile the level grid only really varies once with a small increase in size that makes levels less trivial to pass. (Ignoring the earlier increase of size from 2x2 to 3x3 because 2x2 is only really useful for a tutorial.)
It needs more mechanics, perhaps more different blocks, maybe some blocks on the grid that do things as you drop on to them, something to keep your interest.
Perhaps my expectations are rather high, but I have a lot of small games in this price range and I think there needs to be more here to be worth passing many of them over to get this.
(Also, and an annoyingly common theme with a lot of games these days. It appears to lack some basic menu functions like windowed mode.)

As a 15 year player of the table top game, I may have a slightly different standard to measure this by.
The Good:
+ A beautifully executed isometric game with stock art that feels true to the feel of the SR series
+ NPCs in the first two stock games feel as they should - some with little depth, others with great backstories
+ A development team lead by the man who created the game in the first place, committed to making it great again
+ A flexible system which allows players to create their own stories and publish them easily
+ A combat system that feels largely balanced
+ Simple controls, easy to learn
The Bad:
- The combat system seems to favour non-magic users to the point where combat mages/shaman don't feel useful
- Matrix combat can be frustrating with only one decker at times, and team designs rarely allow for two to go on any given run
- Probability based attacks that seem to go on long strings of misses against high percentage targets (i.e. 4 straight missed shots on 90% targets)
- Abstract system skills that at least in the first module, didn't allow NPCs within your own party to satisfy skill checks
- A lack of real use for some of the non-combative skills in the game
Overall:
SR:R is a fantastic game on the whole.  If you can get past some of the little system quirks that exist in the adventures, what you'll get is a story that feels true to the SR universe.  (At least the two stock campaigns, Dead Man's Switch and Dragonfall.)  If you want to create your own stories, this can be done, and that's a great thing.  Be prepared to lose a few hours in this place, chummer.

For 10 bucks I took a chance on this little space sim.  It's not the sexy feature rich game on the scale of EVE, and the comparisons to EVE can't be avoided, because it plays a lot like it.  But its damn fun for what it is.
You create your name, pick an avatar portrait, configure very modular difficulty/galaxy properties, press play.  The galaxy is randomly generated.  There is a short simple surprisingly useful tutorial that is skippable, and you're on your way.  You mine asteroids, kill pirates, run missions, upgrade your ship and components along way.  You're a prisoner in a section of space essentially slaving to make money for the Corporate Government that put you there.  It's  a lawless zone with rules.
They way you move from one sector to the next farming, killing, looting, questing each sector with harder pirates to kill, cheif among them being an officer pirate, or even a pirate base.  It feels also like a dungeon crawl in some ways.  Which inevitably makes it feel repetative, but that's where all games end up eventually.
But, more features are coming, and I expect this labor of love will see continued development.  I think the Dev understands what makes games like this fun.  I've already got more than my $10 worth at 22 hours, and I'm nowhere near bored with it.  The only problem I see in its future is that unlike EVE with the MMO player presence, a single player game requires believable AI, and meaningful interaction with it, as well as a very well paced and balanced progression.  He doesn't have everything quite fleshed out yet, like the leveling and skill point system seems a bit clumsy.  A lot of missions early on aren't worth the time, unless you up the mission rewards in the diff settings, but that makes the good missions way too rewarding.  Fuel system needs more thought IMHO.  Just little things that don't break the game at all, they just need some balance here, some polish there....
Bottom line. I hope people buy this game.  I'm glad I did.

Again, as others have said, Dying Light feels like a combination of Dead Island, Far Cry 3/4 (I haven't played four so I can't judge there) and Mirror's Edge. Some will see it as what Dead Island could have been. Others will see it as a game that tries to be too many types of games and ends up being a mediocre version of all of the above without excelling in anything.
Gameplay wise, it's an Open-World Zombie epidemic type of game. There is a main quest line you can follow as well as secondary quests that open up over time that you can play when you feel like. As others have noted, often the secondary quests end up feeling more (perhaps much more) interesting and/or emotional then the main quest.
You start with lousy melee weapons that don't do much damage and you can't take much damage, resulting in combat being risky and annoying enough that flight often feels like the reaction they intended for the player. While you do get guns later on, do more (and special via crafting) damage and become more damage reistant, the combat often (but not always!) doesn't feel all that fun. If anything, it can even feel like a chore at times (bear in mind, I'm saying *at times*). This may seem strange and it may have just been my personal experience however. The gameplay (especially at first) doesn't really seem designed for combat as the main course of action.
One feature the game lacks that gets annoying is the lack of fast travel. This means you're going to be doing a lot of running around, which can get very annoying and time consuming. Given that there are no vehicles (although I note that ground vehicles would probably be slower given the games Assassin's Creed attitude of getting around via rooftops) and you can end up in a situation where doing some quests (especially secondary ones) can become a chore and you may well end up avoiding some due to the distance you need to travel.
In short, it's all right game but it's nothing spectacular. While I do think it's worth at least a look (although be sure to bring plenty of patience) I might recommend it but only on a Steam sale. Because of this, while it does pain me to do so, I have to give this a not recommended even if only because I can't really recommend it and when deciding, I find myself favouring the not option, even if only very slightly.

Overall rating: 3/5, Recommended if you can get it on sale (picked it up for $0.99 in a Summer Sale)

Alright, it's reviewing time.
First, my favourite point in "rogue-likes", customisation. After a two runs through the game, I can't say there's much customisation. Most likely, you'll change your hat/wig three or four times per run, because there aren't many different hats, and some of them are way better than others, meaning once you've found them, you won't change anymore.
The gameplay itself was good (I really liked the "must get to next portal" feeling, adds a bit of tension), but if you're searching for a game in which you FEEL yourself improving, I wouldn't recommend it. You have 4 gun types, only the stats change (maning you won't get "the cool weapon that shoots firebeams", which would be really nice though), hats don't change your play style that much (2 more jumps, a bit of armor maybe, nothing game breaking).
Speaking of the gameplay, you have to get 9 items to repair your robot and finish the game. Actually, most of the time, you'll be rushing straight to those items, while searching for portals along the way, which you'll be using as "checkpoints", or to sell your items. Two possibilities : the key item is in an area with high-damage ennemies, in which case you'll get some money (by killing ennemies and finding gems, metals and chests) to upgrade your health bar and just tank through it, or it'll be in a "low-level area", in which case you'll tank through it right away.
Ennemy variety was also meh, I counted 7 diffent ennemies (little flying monster, big flying monster, small splitting flying monster, big splitting flying monster, turret, human with randomized gear, flying worm), with some color or model changes (for exemple, bats and "eyes" are actually the same).
If you're a leaderboard fan, and if you like playing the same game (with a mildly-randomized map) to improve your time, or your number of death, I'd say it's a great game.
If, like me, you're a rogue-like/adventure fan, you'll play it once, maybe twice, and that's it. At least it kept me entertained for a few hours.

"the next evolution in collectible card games!"
This does not compare to Magic: the Gathering's complexity with stack casting, loads of special rules, &c.  One can't really say this game is the "next evolution" in that respect.
This game doesn't have an outdated user interface or a load of bugs like certain Magic: the Gathering clients either.  Well, I suppose it could certainly be considered an evolution on those terms.
A step up from Hearthstone?  Sure, and not just for the interface.  The basic game design's a bit better; this game's "Evolution" mechanic and a lot of little things make things a bit more interesting.  Some other players have commented on a lack of RNG, and though there's always some RNG to be found in a CARD-DRAWING GAME for goodness sake, certainly there is less RNG built into the tactical options (like Hearthstone's Knife Juggler, none of that stuff here, just nice targeted stuff, and area-of-effect stuff so far that I've seen anyways).
"Shadowverse features AAA artwork and unique game mechanics that make it the most visually and tactically rich CCG on the market."
These days there's a lot of CCG type games online that have good artwork.  This game is a bit different in that I think the art is more integrated into the overall presentation.  Though I might not say it is "The most visually . . . rich", I certainly wouldn't say it's bad either, so that claim does stand up to some scrutiny.
"Tactically rich", though - well, you don't need to have the complexity of Magic: the Gathering to have tactical options; it could be said chess is more complex in terms of rules than go, but go is said to be far more complex in terms of the application of those rules what with one thing and another.  But I really don't feel the tactical options here are incredibly open; you do have seven classes, sure, but you can't really operate multiple class cards together in one deck (where with Magic: the Gathering you could combine even all five colors into a single deck gaining different possibilities and drawbacks).  While this is the case, balance is inevitably going to rely more on balancing those classes against one another, rather than generally developing increased interactivity between different cards, new cards, new playstyles, so this game is probably always going to be rather tactically limited compared to some other CCGs in my view.  (Though again, if comparing this to Hearthstone, I'd say this game is pretty good - but Hearthstone is NOT the only other CCG out there.)
• SUMMON 400+ cards, each lavishly illustrated with jaw-dropping fantasy art
Sure, more or less.
• STRATEGIZE with innovative mechanics that guarantee thrilling battles
Mm . . . given previous caveats, sure.
• MASTER seven character classes each with unique play styles and killer cards
Probably you will not "MASTER" seven character classes if by that you're thinking of playing all classes at their top possible level.  Sure, you can get a pretty good idea of the different styles, but ultimately better decks require better cards, and you'll probably be far better off trying to build a single strong class, and hoping it doesn't get nerfed, than building a bunch of sorta-kinda decks.
• BATTLE real-time opponents from around the world, or enjoy the fully voiced story mode
Yup.

Reason why this game is better than Hearthstone :
- Less RNG
Most cards don't have RNG. You don't have to face Yogg-Druid or The Hunter guy who have 100% chance to Spawn Huffer if he plays Animal Companion) or the Shaman guy who play Turn 1: Tunnel Trogg (he also could have Coin to play another Tunnel Trogg), Turn 2: Totem Golem, Turn 3: Feral Spirit. Which leads me to my next point:
- Less Tempo
Evo-Point >>>>> Hero Power. When you're falling behind against Hunter/Zoo/Shaman aggro, tempo, and you don't have AoE or draw a perfect answer against these kind of decks, you're screwed. The chance of coming back in hearthstone is really slim because top decks in hearthstone always playing on curve. The amount of overvalued cards makes Mid-range Druid or Zoolock never ever falls in top 5 decks. I think the problem lies in Blizzard who are clueless about balancing. They overnerfed cards (Warsong Commander, Blade Flurry.. ) or release utterly useless card (Purity). In Shadowverse, everyone got evo-point which help a lot when you are falling behind. (Evolution mechanic is a really good mechanic in this game to create tempo and board control). Cards are pretty much balance and play style is more diverse than Hearthstone. See how Molten Giant got nerfed and Handlock was disappeared from the ladder. But I'm pretty sure that Bloodcraft (which got similar play-style with Handlock) won't disappeared in Shadowverse.
- Less grinding.
In Hearthstone, you never able to create a Control Warrior deck (Control Warrior is one of the best deck in hearthstone) within 3 months. Packs are easier to buy and quest are more rewarding in Shadowverse. Hearthstone got 1 quest per day. Shadowverse got 3 quests per day. No need to say which one is more rewarding.

The game puts you in the shoes of a starship crew, the ship being about corvette sized, depending on what you compare it to. The game takes place in a completely procedurally generated (randomized) set of space sectors with several star systems that you need to cross while fleeing from an advancing enemy fleet. In doing that, you keep hitting a just insane amount of different random encounters. Hostile ships that need to be battled, spacefarers in need of different kinds of assistance... very diverse anyway. The possible ways of winning a spacefight are also quite interesting. Either you employ the classic and shoot your opponent up with LAYZ0RZ .... or missiles, or you could disable his life support system and suffocate the enemy crew or you can just send your people over there and slap those guys dead... tricky to do sometimes though since they tend to slap back.
Anyway, it's a really interesting and fun game to play and is really worth the price. Defnitely recommended.

Day and night: both have their strenghts and weaknesses. During the day, roam the streets and rooftops, searching for supplies. But come sunset, and only one word is paramount: SURVIVE. Either by sneaking around the transformed enemies, avoiding detection, or, when spotted, running like hell, your objective is to reach a safe zone, so that you may live to tell the tale. Better get ready of a few good deaths.
Last but not least, it's a compelling story of survival, and doing what's right in the midst of chaos. A few emotive elements (it was said that the main character has a problem with emotional attachment) make this game worth playing, while enjoying the story.
I like the motto of the game:
. It's not just a marketing line. Around those words, there's a way of life. So you better stick them in your mind.

Here are my thoughts on Resident Evil Revelations 2 in a hopefully short review. So the things I liked about RE:REV 2 are as follows: The voice acting is well done, with the voice actors generally matching the characters they portray. Most of the voice acting really matches the characters and their outlook on their predicament without seeming out of place and helps set the mood well. Sound design is also well done with gun sounds and the monster sounds. The character/monster models in the game are polished and I enjoyed the small little details available (really, kudos to the art department).  An I like how you can upgrade your characters abilities with BP (found by collecting items and certain actions during the campaign) while playing to help ease the difficulty in situations.
The story for RE:REV 2 is rather well done and keeps you guessing on what the villains true aim is up until a point (then reveals it prematurely in my opinion).The main campaign itself runs more like an interactive movie than a game where you play to find out the next part (interactive movie does not mean loads of QuickTime events). So for the most part except for some very abrupt levels and an almost ridiculously drawn out stages I thought the main campaign was sufficient. There are also additional game play options and DLC missions that I did not personally delve into because for me, the main campaign and raid mode was enough.
Raid mode for those not familiar with these games is where you select available character and play missions for achievements, gear, and levels. Briefly, raid mode is a grind you can find in many other games, regardless of how tedious this can be most of my playtime was devoted to raid mode. There is also an online portion to raid mode where you can search for a partner online to help with the above mentioned raid mode goals. Personally, I enjoyed some of the challenge in higher-level raids quite a bit and the interaction between
and your raid mode experience is a nice bonus.
Now what did I dislike about this game. I will first mention my gripes with the main campaign. The main campaign is cliché, there are explosions in which your characters barely escape while leaping into water, posing with big guns, one liners, slow-mo villain deaths and worse of all sequel baiting. All of these cliché situations really sucked out some of my satisfaction (not that it did not look cool). The second and final complaint with the main campaign is without having a spoiler is that there is a DLC to explain an event so the ending makes sense. I know my description is vague but like I said no spoilers. The problem with having a DLC necessary for THE GAME ENDING TO MAKE SENSE is that you should never ever EVER have to purchase additional content just for a complete story.
The last complaint I have encompasses raid mode and the main campaign, it is the grind. Want better character abilities during the story, grind for it, want to see in game art and models, grind for it, want to enjoy raid mode more, grind for it. Now for some players they are quite happy to grind away and enjoy it, I do not because repetitive game play eats away at my soul.
Now for the verdict, I am giving the game a thumbs up because regardless of my complaints, if you consider the price of $40 dollars that includes all the extra content, a pretty game relatively free of bugs, and the raid mode interaction with
it’s well worth the price. Though the Resident Evil franchise seems tired and played out to me, it is still a fun play through if only for the main campaign.

REvelations 2 is a game that came off as an awkward sequel to Resident Evil Revelations but ended up being a pleasant surprise. The game improve some mechanics of the previous game, although others where worsened.
Compared to the first game, you now have an inventory that needs to me managed properly so you won't end up with excess of items you may not need and lack of those you may need, much like the classic Resident Evil. Despite being more linear compared to the first game, it still encourages exploration and searching using Moira's flashlight or Natalia's ability to see certain things in the dark, which adds to the linearity making it a nice change of pace.
Unlike modern RE games enemies don't drop items, but you have to find them on a fashion similar to the GENESIS of REvelations 1. However, customization of weapons is lacking on this title, due to pieces being extremely rare, by end game you'll probably use all of them on your guns, unlike in the first REvelations. The health system is the same, but it indicate poorly since it only adds the bloody effect rather than both a bloody and a desaturation screen effect of the first game.
Claire's chapters 1 and 2 are a bit dull, 3 is good, it even includes a puzzle for extra stuff, although 4th is basically a escape from the auto destruction sequence we see on all the games so far. Barry's chapters on the other hand are far more interesting and add a sense of isolation from early RE games, since Natalia can only help pin pointing things and throwing bricks.
The plot gave me mixed feelings due to how the game ended, but the story tellign makes up to it, despite being nothing exceptional. And although Capcom wanted players to use play more on RAID mode, Story mode, despite being short compared to REvelations 1 has it's own share of replayability with hidden things to search for. I also recommend the extra chapters since they have their own interestign mechanics (one based on item gathering for progression without resulting in going to the start point when losing, and other based on pure stealth).
Final score based on my experience: 7.5/10 - Is not the creepy, scary RE classic fans want, but it's still nice for its setting and campaign.

Overall, I have three complaints about the game: 1) the collision detection on your cursor is imprecise, leading to situations where you die when you're "on" the line, even though you're to the correct side; 2) the randomness of everything means that you're not really getting better as much as you are hoping for a randomly generated pattern that is easy to navigate; and 3) the controls are not really as good as they should be for the twitchiness of the game.
On point number three, specifically using left or right to move isn't fast enough if you go the wrong way. You have the option, for instance, to go left or right around a hexagonal block to reach the open space, but that is a false choice because the speed of the collision blocks vs the speed of the cursor is such that you can only make it the shortest distance. That's a problem. Further, there's a vast imprecision about where your cursor ends leading quite often to problem number 1. Had there been some lead up to the difficulty the game starts at to give you a good feel for the cursor speed, that might be one thing, but there's not.
I have a hard time recommending the game. Its gameplay is shallow, and the controls aren't tight enough to allow for the difficulty curve it's asking for. The two best things going for the game are the quick replayability (no loading screens, etc.), and the excellent chiptune soundtrack.
One final note: there are no cards for the game, and that's severely disappointing considering how simple the game is.

A while back I had given this game a review. I love Lego's style, and I think it is enjoyable. Now, why I do not recommend this game. First off, it's just a puzzle game that attempts to also be an action game. The puzzles are repetitive and are far too fast paced. What I mean is, the puzzles are like as if they are just weak spots on a villian. They are uncreative. Every stage has a poorly built villian, with every stage also being about "beating up the baddies." With the combat, if it even is that, it's slow and again, nothing but weak spots or taking down an army of minions that do no damage, yet one shot and they are dead. It bores me. The only three modes areopen world, freeplay, and story. There are no multiplayer, arena/survival, or chasing modes. You only can use co-op, which I doubt on the PC is even relevant, which you either need two controllers or to share a keyboard. This game is first person adventure game in which you manuever around a series of chambers tryingto get to "The End," which always seems so close yet so far.  The game beings with chambers/rooms that are more mind-bending and riddle-based, relying on manipulation of your senes, namely what you see and your sense of direction.  Sometimes you'll hear sounds which can serve as clues.  There is no dialogue in the game except for the brief life lessons attached to small images scattered before and after many of the rooms and puzzles.  Some have found these to be a little patronizing, but I found them to very charming and they provided a narrative to an otherwise silent and minimalist game.  These bits of wisdom and the ability to appreciate them I think is crucial in the enjoyment of Antechamber as a game.  This collection of images and messages are added to the "antichamber" which acts as your base throughout the game and to where you can escape to at any point by clicking ESC.   This room gives you access to somewhat cryptic map of where you have traveled so far and allows you to quick travel to the puzzles so you do not have to waste time finding them again in the brain boggling realm.
The game quickly (or not so quickly, depending on your pacing), moves from a game that relies on manipulating your perceptions to a game that relies on more understandable puzzles (not necessarily easy to solve, but easier to see what your objective is).  This transformation happens when you find a gun that allows you to manipulate cubes in the world around you that you use to solve puzzles.  Of course, puzzles still test the limits of your imagination and your ability to think outside the box   These puzzles till test your ability to see things in different ways and give you more easily discernable objectives in which you have to cultivate novel ways to get to.  The game is still non-linear and puzzles can be solved in different ways or bypassed completely by taking another path.
Some have found the game frustrating in that it seems intent on forcing impractical and unthinkable solutions on the player, but the game is ultimately about learning.  In this mini-universe, you have to learn and find new skills, which is what many of the messages try to convey.  For this reason, I want to describe this as a sandbox game, not in that you can change the rules of the game as you see fit, but that you are in this sandbox, and you are given a certain set of tools and rules, and with those tools and rules you can do anything you want in trying to navigate your way through the dungeon crawl.  The game is definitely a learning experience and a lesson in keeping you rmind open to new ideas.

Stringing togheter lines, jumps and tricks would've been ideal, yet each objective can be reached by taking only one predetermined route, and that seems counter-intuitive. It is also a surprisingly brief experience, so you moneybag Johnnies know what to expect if you buy it during The Sale.

Faerie Solitaire is just that, standard solitaire built into Windows with a little fairy dust on top in the form of colorful wallpapers and unlockable abilities that make solving puzzles easier. Everything else is just baggage that sinks the entire experience: horrible forever-alarmed narrator, forgettable cliche of a story that has the player rescuing fairies over and over ad nauseum, and collectible purely-cosmetic pets that serve no purpose and are just busy-work tied to achievements, to keep people playing. Pets drop when completing stacks of cards, and may require hundreds of hours of gameplay to complete the collection due to the random nature of the drops. Completing game levels offers little more in terms of excitement and comes down to playing 9 games of solitaire per level, while accomplishing up to 3 objectives, like getting a certain score or finishing in a certain time frame. Achieving objectives early still forces the player to play through all 9 games, and failing objectives to replay all 9 games again. There is no way to lose, short of quiting and not getting to the end (guess what, you rescue the fairies and defeat evil), which brings me back to my original point - there is no game here, besides the basic solitaire that everyone can already play for free.
Apart from the annoying importance of getting a good start with your free packs this is quite possibly better than if not at least as good as Hearthstone

+Cygames are really commiting to improving the game after their previous blunders this past year.(2017)
-Classes are currently imbalanced (Dragoncraft and Shadowcraft dominate)
-Music gets annoying after a while.
-'Link to other service' quest that takes up a daily mission slot that can only be achieved if you have a mobile device or can run an emulator.
-They needlessly censored one of the class characters for English players.
+/-? Tons of waifus
Overall a decent CCG. I'd definitely recommend it if you liked Hearthstone or other similar CCG's.

At first i was very sceptical of this game, since it is a Digital Card Game and we all know how those turn out..
I thought i wouldn't want to invest into another one since I already play Hearthstone and have all the cards there, but i still tried it out since i saw a lot of people talking about it and urging others to at least try it.
And i must say i am SO GLAD that i tried it out, because i immediatly fell in love with it!
This is literally the only non-pay-to-win Card game out there, you can literally play this game as a F2P game without investing any money into it, but seeing how well made and polished it is, you will want to support it.
Firstly the developers are VERY generous with the free packs they give you ( I got around 40+ when i first started ) and one pack includes 8 cards. There are daily login bonuses and 3 daily missions, loads of achievement bonuses, level up bonuses etc, you can easily get the cards by just playing the game.
Secondly the game ACTUALLY has a Main Story which you can play with each of the characters ( of which there are 7 ), as you play the story mode you unlock yet more cards and Arena passes for free.
The game is very complicated, but the tutorial system with the Story mode does a great job of teaching you how each of the classes play, you should definetly play through the story mode before heading into arena or ranked play. ( The story mode is around 8 - 10 hours long, its pretty insane, also its fully voice acted ).
So to sum it up, you should absolutely play this game, even if you play HS or MTG, at least try it, i did and now i don't even care about HS.

There's not alot I can say that's positive about Shadowrun Returns, but alot of it is personal preference over the game itself.
So I'll start with those few positives.
Firstly, it's nice to see another Shadowrun game out in the world. The pen and paper was great, the first Shadowrun game I played on the SNES was addictive, and the genre itself is fantastic.
I love that the style of gameplay in Shadowrun Returns is the same as that first game I played on the SNES, it's Nostalgic. The character development has massive potential, the story (if flawed by what I find to be some silly mistakes in parts) is entertaining enough and very little of the pen and paper roleplay has been sacrificed to make the game, which, again, I love.
I do have a fair list of gripes, but I'll keep them to a minimum.
Firstly, and the most annoying one is that all the skills aren't really implemented in the game. Backgrounds that aren't used, classes that seem useless playing because there's no really enticing role or function for them to play that the game doesn't provide someone to do it for you anyway. They're two very big thumbs down for me.
Secondly, is how linear the game is. It's reminiscent of playing a platformer like Black Tiger. You go along in a line, and as you reach certain checkpoints you can upgrade your gear, and then you continue on your merry way. You can't even revisit areas. Once you hit leave, it's lost to the ages. Fallen out of existence. Well, until the game sends you back there, albeit an alternate version where nothing that was available before shall ever be available again. A linear roleplay is a bit of a time waster. Even as you progress through the game you don't really feel as though you've accomplished anything. Coupled with a number of false bluffs, after a while you just want it to be over so you can do something else.
Along that line as well, you only have the one campain or story to play. Even though it's been out for 18 months, I cannot find a single item in the workshop. Not even some DLC to introduce something different. Only a standalone expansion. There's a lack of side quests, minigames, etc that you would expect to see in a game of this genre. All these add to the linear feel of it.
Lastly there's the progression unlocks of upgrades. It's a pet hate of mine, but some of you might not mind it. Coupled with a lack of variety (especially where cyberware is concerned) it all just feels a bit bland and terribly disappointing.
A bit of a spoiler, but not really either, but you can't save charaters to play in the expansion. ISo if you're hoping to get this and play though it so you can contine on the story with the same character, that's not an option.
All in all I probably wouldn't recommend this game, but I haven't played through Dragonfall yet, so if you're looking at getting a shadowrun game I'd say get that instead as it has alot more additions or so the info says, or get a SNES emulator and play the 1993 title.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is a sequel, follow up from the first RE: Revelations, there are 4 episodes that are quite long, and provide good amount of playtime. Also the campaign has some replayability as well, since there's a skill tree that you're supposed to level up with many different skills. You won't get all of the skills unlocked on the 1st playthrough of course, but that encourages you to play through the campaign a 2nd time, with a harder difficulty of course, which provides a new challenge.
SADLY the campaign doesn't have an online CO-OP, but it does have a local coop. The campaign has always 2 characters, the other character will be controlled by an AI, if not played coop locally. Whilst you will be controlling the "main" character. Altough you can change between these 2 characters in a blink of an eye, and you can make some teamwork happen between these 2 characters because of this very easily.
If you really think that that's not enough of content for the price you're about to pay for this game... FORTUNATELY there's also a mode that I like really much, which is called the "Raid Mode" which can be played in CO-OP, and it's a blast! Here you also have many characters to play with, that have own unique skills on them, and you have to level up every single character individually, when you level up to a specific point, you will able to replace to an old skill slot or gain more skills slots and equip that skill to your active skill tree. Leveling up happens by completing missions where you have to eliminate a certain amount of enemies while you gather treasures and supplies to survive.
Gathering treasures is a very important part of Raid mode since when you open a treasure chest, you get an item. This item could a weapon, or a mod that you can make your weapons better with. These weapons and mods have a range of quality, there's a very basic weapons/mods or a very nice and epic weapons or mods that are a lot more powerful than the basic items.
You will end up finding yourself farming these weapons and mods at some point. (:
I really like this game, and it's a different approach than the other Resident Evil's and to be honest. But some of the hardcore fans might say this game sucks because it's not like the first Resident Evil games that were released, I'd say that variety is the spice of life.

BATTLE ARMOR DIVISION is an action platform/shooter that features a sci-fi storyline where a new global war rages within mankind.
Military forces rely upon modern technologies including the use of mechanical humanoid tanks, mechs, called BATTLE ARMOR.
The game as may easily guessed pays a lot of homage to great glories of this kind like A.S. LEYNOS and Valken, for example, as well some anime references.
Quick overview:
Gameplay>>>
16 missions within different environment and approach (like D-Day style missions) ensure variety, and the games plays quite different while in zeroG. Avoiding bullets, using the shields or approaching with a bit of attention using smoke grenades or chaffs for missiles while shooting/jumping/running is fun once you get good with the controls.
Graphics>>>
Detailed B.A. and vehicles and soldiers, it does its job since goes very well with this kind of games, one of the main reason for being a "gaming homage". Weakest part: the artworks and some animations for the bigger objects.
Musics&Effects>>>
Some tracks are nice and do the right atmosphere around the action, while some effects (glad the bad ones are all in the menus) are annoying.
Controls>>>
Aiming it's not so easily done. it requires some practice. The layout for the controls may not be liked by all so a change in the settings menu may be needed, but using a gamepad makes the game enjoyable.
After all is an homage to games that were born for use with a gamepad. Keep this in mind if you plan to play with a keyboard.
Within Steam you may find other similar games, and I have all of them, but this one has some really nice unique points in its gameplay that try to add a bit of "realistic" feel:

Having played the game about a year after its initial release (2012/version 1.1.0, looks like it was released in 2011), I felt it was...okay. Nothing too special, just in the realm of average. The graphics are rather plain but doable, the music's not too memorable except for the main theme, and the sound effects feel like they're ripped from some other source (just a feeling, but maybe you can make the connection).
Fast forward with a couple of patches later (looks like 5 patches were made after 1.1.0 according to my email account) and...it's even buggier than I remembered. You've probably already read about the controls. I had to test out the keyboard before I moved to my controller just to see what the fuss was all about, and it's a bit of a mess; it seems that every time I go to the Config Key screen, it's a guaranteed crash when you try to start playing the game, whether you go to Start, Continue, or Training. *** This guaranteed crash appears to be fixed in 1.3.5, released on August 20 ***
Even after configuring my keys, I can never get my Smoke Grenades or Anti-Ballistic Missile flares to work. I even reset it back to the default keys, which is already a strange layout:

And they still don't work. Smoke Grenades still seem useless to me (in v1.1.0, you only get 3 to use and they don't recharge in the level unlike the ABMs, and you can still jump forward + shield to advance just fine in this version), but ABMs to avoid enemy missiles is a key defense mechanism that is basically unavailable to keyboard users.
Switching to my controller, I noticed that the Smoke and ABMs are locked to the Right and Left D-Pad respectively and could not be changed at all. That means I'm forced to use the joysticks to move. Why is it like this in the later patches? In v1.1.0, although I wasn't able to remap the buttons at all and was forced to use the defaults, at least the Smoke and ABMs were mapped to the shoulder buttons.
Another bug I wanted to check was if the Time Spent carried over. After completing a mission, you get a results screen that ranks you based on your performance. One of these factors is how fast you completed the level. In v1.1.0, there was a bug where the Time Spent on one mission carried over to the next missions you played, and this didn't reset until you restarted the game. So in order to attempt getting an S Rank on a mission, you have to keep restarting the game. Is it still present in the latest patched version? Yup. Kinda annoying, especially if you're going for that unlock all illustrations achievement...
Your mech has a melee weapon, but unfortunately you can take damage by explosions that enemies produce when they die, making it unfavorable to use.
Enemy Battle Armor (BA) combat is still the same from when I've played. Basically, shield up, use your ABMs whenever you're locked on, and try to take the lower ground 'cause enemy BAs won't deliberately shoot your feet. Also, wait for them to jump into the air so you can dash under them and peg them in the back.
As for the rest of the game, if you can actually get through the buggy stuff, I don't think the experience you get from this game matches other similar titles already on Steam such as Gunhound and Gigantic Army. I can't note anything unique from B.A.D other than the weapons probably, which are somewhat balanced if I remember correctly. I've posted all 16 missions in the Video section of the Community Hub from v1.1.0 if you want to check them out.

Platformines has been one of my bigger surprises of 2014 so far. Launching in late March without much, or really close to any fanfare, I decided to install it one rainy Saturday afternoon and it was like finding a box of brightly colored toys in a dusty, spidery attic. A lot of the gameplay elements here are very familiar -- precision platforming, gobs of randomized loot, a never-ending cycle of weapon upgrades -- but it feels fresh, these elements were never combined in quite this way before.
It reminds me most of the lauded roguelike platformer Spelunky, except where Spelunky is all about survival, Platformines is more about exploration and aggression. There is a very large overworld to explore, and the further you move away from your base in the middle(ish) of the map in any direction, the more difficult the enemies are, enemies you can eliminate with one of four different types of gun. After finishing the game on the default difficultly level (5-6 hours) I uncovered about 25% of the map, so there's a lot of map here to explore if you're willing. There's also a fun, punk-pixel sense of style from outlandish costumes and hair-dos to five-eyed blob monsters to platforms filled with whirring blades of bloody death.
On the downside, the game is a tad on the short side, but for the price and the type of game, I'm really not sure a 10-20 hour epic would have worked. I would have liked to have seen more enemy and area variety, plus a better reward for finishing the game rather than "the same thing, only harder," but I certainly don't feel cheated in any way. This was a great little game from out of left field, and I'm going to be keeping an eye on Magiko to see what they come up with in the future.

If you’ve played any previous Lego titles, you should know the drill by now - they are family-friendly, humorous adventure games with a strong collection aspect worth hours of playtime. Though I would describe the Lego games as formulaic by this point, I don’t mean so in a bad way; they are more ‘reliable’ than ‘stale.’ As long as Lego Marvel Super Heroes capitalized on the successes of the previous games by Traveler’s Tales, then this title should have proven to be a solid choice.
Thankfully, that is exactly the case. It is very hard for me not to recommend a Lego game, but despite my glowing affection for the series, I would never place them in an overall top ten list at year’s end, unless they would do something which would really re-define the genre. There really is no need, though, as the Lego games generally move onward and upward making basic quality of life changes.
For this title in particular, the visuals have received a bump that I hope stays in place from now on. Smart lighting effects and motion blurs add to the production quality, but the superheroes’ minifigs are the most appealing change - for the first time in the series, they appear to be made of plastic, with a highly reflective finish, instead of the standard matte colors. A small update, admittedly, but one that really makes it feel as if you are playing with toys come to life.
The story is somewhat fuddled and long, but that’s typical from Lego games which create their own tales instead of drawing upon pre-existing material, such as the Harry Potter games. These Lego games are best played when the story mode is rushed through from one mission to the next, in order to unlock Free Play mode for each chapter, so that item collection can begin in earnest. The voice acting is top notch, with several sound-alikes to the Marvel studios movies that come pretty darn close to the real deal. As for the interface and the controls…that is where I will hedge my complaints.
Flying is very cumbersome in Lego Marvel Super Heroes - as the controls are mapped to two buttons (instead of to an analogue stick, which worked MUCH BETTER in Lego Batman 2: DC Super Heroes), I typically wind up pinballing my hero all over the map as I try to effectively get from point A to B. Mentioning the map brings me to the other major complaint of mine - the map overlay is horrible. Lego Lord of the Rings got this feature down just fine - dotted lines easily showed you your path, while missions and side quests had informative text to display where you were going. Not so in Lego Marvel Super Heroes - the map is zoomed in very closely to the details, and none of which are labeled. Where are the missions at, from a glance? What unlockable heroes are being displayed around my cursor? These were features that were working JUST FINE only one game iteration ago, and they now feel worthless.
Otherwise, I can’t really knock this game too much - the gameplay is still rock-solid, and these titles appeal to the random item collector that lives deep down in my psyche. For all of the games that exist on my to-do list right now, I still feel compelled to spend extra hours with Lego Marvel Super Heroes in an attempt to 100% complete it. That sentence alone should properly convey the overall quality of this game.
Recommended, at any price, and to gamers of all ages.

There are a lot of former Hearthstone players jumping ship to this game, and I can see why. To be fair, it is probably at least partially due to the game being new and therefore inherently more exciting to explore, however I would still recommend Shadoverse as the superior alternative. If you have not played HS before and have no idea what I am talking about, then disregard everything I said up to this point.
Short Version:
Pros
- interesting mechanics and card synergy
- wide variety of strategies and playstyles
- easy to pick up, both in terms of gameplay and getting cards for free
Cons
- personally not a fan of the flashy anime art (some could see this as a pro)
- like any card game, potential balancing issues can lead to salt (not too bad atm)
Long Version:
Shadoverse has great emphasis on synergy, as opposed to stand alone powerful cards that are considered 'safe' in any situation. Each hero/class has an inherent ability or theme associated with it that is complimented by cards that also follow a similar theme. For example, the Bloodcraft class has the Vengeance ability that activates added effects in your cards when you are at 10 hp or lower. There are also certain subthemes in each class that allow for even more strategies and win conditions to be developed.
One thing that can be difficult to get used to is the evolution mechanic. Each player starts with either two or three evolution points (first player gets 2 second gets 3) that can be spent in order to power up your followers. This almost always results in an instant stat gain and the ability to immediately attack any non-hero enemy, and sometimes enables an added special ability depending on who or what is being evolved. This allows for some interesting comeback plays, but also makes a certain game mode called 'Take Two' favor whoever has the most evolution points (so there are some potential balancing issues associated with evolution).
If you are worried about this game being freemium, then don't worry. The Shadoverse team is generous in giving cards out, enabling free to play scum (like me) to still be competitive. Anything that can be bought with real money can also be bought with in game currency (which is easily obtainable), including hero portrait reskins.
As far as art style goes, some may be initially turned off by the excessive levels of anime. For me the gameplay was more important so I got over it, but if you absolutely cannot stand that type of art style then you will have to stick to playing Urias (vampire Geralt) or save up for the Runecraft reskin Erasmus (Gandalf) and enable the "standard background" in multiplayer to relieve visual clutter.

Highschool Possession is a not so ordinary slice of life visual novel both developed and published by Dharker Studio. After a strange force causes Hikaru to suddenly switch bodies with two of his female classmates, he soon begins to realize that these young women he has had a crush on for some time are not quite as perfect as he once believed them to be and that they indeed have many problems just like the rest of us. While stuck in their bodies will he be able to help their personal situations or only succeed in making things much worse? Quite a precarious situation in this fish-out-of-water story yes? How you choose to proceed is entirely up to you in this wonderfully written and thought provoking V.N..
Visually I found this novel to be quite nice to peruse. It has a beautifully penned manga artstyle filled with bright and joyful colors that are very pleasing to the eye. Also, the sound while capable doesn't really come into play much in this particular title other than ambient noises such as the ringing of doorbells, opening and closing of doors, etc. which does do a great job of immersing you within the story I might add. To summmarize, the true highlight of Highschool Possession would be the story which is really interesting as well as quite entertaining and shouldn't that be the best quality of any visual novel that you take the time to read?
Highschool Possession was a fun read despite some rather dark and somewhat disturbing subject matter which I won't spoil by talking about it. The novel offers multiple decisions to choose as well as two romance options to explore. Also, the title has the typical amount of basic options that most V.N.'s offer in the settings menu for music/sound effects volume and text speed. There is a image gallery to unlock as the story plays out as well as Steam Achievements but sadly no Steam Trading Cards to collect. Highschool Possession is a very solid enjoyable title in this genre and I would RECOMMEND it to anyone even remotely interested in the visual novel genre.
