I'll tell you a story.
Once, I went to my grandma's house in March- the THIRD month of the year. It was also the THIRD. I arrived at my grandma's house at 3:33. She has THREE houses on her block. I went up to the door, which had THREE chips on it, and knocked THREE times. After THREE seconds, she said: "Be right there!"- it had THREE words in it. She came up to the door and took off THREE locks on her door. She invited me into the kitchen for cookies, while all of her THREE cats ran past me, one of which had THREE spots on him. She told me to sit down next to the table, which had THREE chairs. She handed me the platter with THREE cookies on it, and said that her THREE cats took THREE of the cookies THREE times. So we sat down for THREE minutes, and talked about THREE subjects: Major companies, Games, and Numbers. After that, we sat in my grandma's living room, and watched THREE different channels. After a while, she started to get thirsty, so I generously got up from one of the THREE sofas, went into the kitchen, and opened the fridge. I spilled THREE drinks, but I got more for my grandma. When I came back into the room, she was watching a commercial for a product that said: "If you don't get it in THREE days, it's free! Only $33.33!" I sat down and started reading a magazine for children- the THIRD issue. It was on how to add. 1+1-1+1+1=3. That didn't seem appropriate for a children's book, so I went on the computer in my grandma's bedroom, and found out the company had been in buisiness for only THREE years. Now it made sense. It was time for me to leave because I was going to a party with THREE of my friends. My grandma gave me THREE seashells as a present, which I thanked her THREE times for. So then I left out the door, walked to my car, and drove away.
So, what I'm trying to say is that I had a great time at my grandma's house.

is first of Dharker Studio's games that I've decided to try, since it's been sitting in my library for quite some time. Reviews are mixed here around in the community about this, due to the game's "mixed" quality altogether. I, personally, am not impressed though. Sure I wasn't expecting anything groundbreaking, but narrative depth, or at least originality is everything for me in a game and it is exactly what the game fails at. Even though it tries to deal with some common and serious emotional problems,
fails to present any sincerity about the issue.
Well... the story starts a bit generic, as we being the high school student Hikaru who has a crush divided between two ladies: Akiko and Kasumi. Akiko seems to be the good natured and ladylike of the duo, and Kasumi is the silent, submissive yet sporty one who also attends the Swimming Team alongside Hikaru. As we pass through the introductory scene, Hikaru gets a nasty headache and decides to lay down in his room. From there on, we wake up in our lady friends' bodies, switching between them as we wake up each morning. Apparently, we are in a coma and we decide to utilize this supernatural and never properly explained opportunity to learn more about our crushes. As the story progresses, we realize these golden girls do not live golden lives anyhow. Akiko is heavily depressed and enduring an abusive relationship, as Kasumi is constantly bullied at school while her self-confidence gets crippled before the bully. So, we try to better girls' lives by influencing their choices.
Here is the thing: the game can be played either with the NC-17 material or without it. But it's a lose-lose situation concerning this content. Without the adult material patch, there will be some implications within narrative about what happened, yet the plot is heavily undermined. It is more than obvious someone cut out a portion of the story. With the adult patch though... well, brace yourself for some amateur hentai pictures, which really don't fit for the tone of the game, at all.
The story openly discusses that these girls were emotionally abused, so sexualizing them this openly is more of a damage to their psyche and an insult to their character depth – if there is any to begin with. It also undermines the genuineness of their situation. One moment a girl comes into a heartbreaking confession, tears welling up - and the next second she gets feisty and gets ready to be nailed down by the now boyfriend protagonist. I mean, it's not the pornographic part that is disgusting - its target directly cheapens everything, as if artworks are not exaggerated fan service enough. Let us not lie to ourselves, we all are human and bear lust to a degree, so pornography, or at least well done pornography is okay. But when dealing emotional material in a VN - not lustful, EMOTIONAL - bringing in fan service or worse, p0rn, cheapens the context. If you wanna present sexuality, just present it and do it better. Just do no wrap it up with "we are trying to deal with depression here". That's plain lame.
Another side note: If you are familiar with anime/manga culture even the slighest bit, you'll realize that these girls are lamely altered physical copies of Rei and Asuka from
. School uniforms, hair colors and styles, even the fact that one of them is a swimmer are too much of a tell. They could have had original character design, at least.
Art? Not interesting. Music? 2-3 tracks repeating over and over again. Character expressions? Weird and limited. Game time? Really short. Plot? Nope, it is softcore hentai covered under "dealing with depression" flag. I sincerely cannot recommend this one to anyone, for any reason whatsoever. Especially not for 7 dollars. You can get many 1 dollar, or even free VNs with much more depth and sense of emotional community compared to this one. Even if you want some hentai for the spare time, you can do much better.

I have always been fascinated by seamless illogical spatial loops in video game maps, and Antichamber is a swirling labyrinth of insanity and madness. It reminded me of The Stanley Parable. You walk down a corridor and suddenly it's a different corridor. You turn around to get your bearings, and you see a totally unfamiliar area, completely different from the place you walked by only seconds ago. Repeat again and again and again. The level design is simply genius, because this feature works great with the minimalistic styling. As for the puzzles themselves, they are really clever and intrinsically rewarding, although some of them can be quite mind-bending, but it's always deeply satisfying when you manage to wrap your head around them. The only thing missing is a specific narrative, and it's a shame, because it seems like they found this amazing set of mechanics and then didn't really know what to do with it. 9/10

There are nits to pick, and standing in the shadow of the original is not an easy task, but this evolution of the franchise manages to simplify some of its more arcane elements while still delivering a solid experience.  This is undeniably a good thing, as it exposes more players to a genre many had thought to declare dead outside of a few niche, cult titles.  With more exposure, we can hope to see more demand, and with more demand we can hope to see more variety and complexity.
I personally miss some of the more arcane elements of the first two games.  For instance, with the exception of psychic potential, all units progess identically based on class.  I miss the unique character that your units used to develop, compared to the flat class and level structure this uses.  There are also no base defense missions.  You only have one base structure to manage.  The alien base assault missions are scripted story events rather than procedural content.
I still understand the need for those changes though.  And I respect and highly recomend this game for what it's done with and for both the franchise and the genre.

In my first playthrough I was a kind, devout, honest, brave person and I fell in love with a local girl. But the gods decreed that it was not my destiny to be with her. I therefore defied the gods and tried to hold on to love for as long as I could, yet ultimately the gods interfered and convinced her to leave me. Furious, I vowed to destroy the gods and their "destiny". I became a successful champion of a city-state, and with the help of my best friend-turn-general of the army I led my adopted city state past many hardships and adventures. Eventually all seemed successful, and on the eve of my friend and the princess's wedding night a chaos god attempted to destroy fate. I intervened, and in fact I tried to help the chaos god destroy fate, but the gods knew of my blasphemous nature (probably something to do with me telling them to go ♥♥♥♥ themselves whenever they tried to talk to me) and robbed me of my free will, forcing me to destroy the chaos god and protect fate. Afterwards, the gods deposited me back in the city state, where my best friend now hates my guts for my affronts to the gods, but hey I am rich and a hero, I only lost all which was precious to me.
In my second playthrough I was a merciless warrior that was full of devotion to the gods. I scared off that local girl who I had been involved with previously when I executed a prisoner in cold blood right in front of her. I once again became champion of the port city, but this time I had a rather heated affair with the princess. In many ways, this is one of my favorite products produced by Choice of Games in terms of setting and story.  Inspired by Greco-Roman mythology, the author creates a unique and excently detailed setting.   The supporting cast did not come across as flat and responded better to changes in the main character's personality than in some CoG products I've played.  I did two complete play-throughs, opting first for a very sincere and altruistic hero and then a proud and selfish war-loving type.
About 1/3 of the time, the very divergent ways my character acted and reacted brought about somewhat differing content.  The story itself was not really affected by my choices and that's a big flaw for a CYOA game.  The emergence of a mostly linear story detracts heavily from replayability.   But I did not feel rail-roaded into making specific choices as much as felt like different choices created more or less the same story with just a little window dressing changing from time to time.
That said, I truly enjoyed the story that unfolded, only wishing there had been more unique elements to it upon replay.  I consider "Champion of the Gods" worth the price that I paid for it ; I got it 25% of full cover as part of a bundle.

With four different characters used smartly across two interconnected campaigns, Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is a great survival-horror experience. Presented in episodic form, the story rolls forward and brings variety that ranges from stealth to escape sequences. The supporting characters are more than just companions; they are part of a team because the player can control them at any time. The campaign becomes a collaborative effort and the complementary skills bring diversity. Splitting the campaign in half allows for some experimentation, as levels change based on previous actions and key areas are revisited. Online play is supported through a RAID mode that provides arcade inspired content as you level up characters and fight creatures in small battle arenas. Both the online and campaign modes employ a fair combat system that minimizes rigidity while maintaining basic survival-horror mechanics. This is a game that makes it clear that teamwork is about characters with complementary skills, and fear is an excellent motivator.

If you’ve played any previous Lego titles, you should know the drill by now - they are family-friendly, humorous adventure games with a strong collection aspect worth hours of playtime. Though I would describe the Lego games as formulaic by this point, I don’t mean so in a bad way; they are more ‘reliable’ than ‘stale.’ As long as Lego Marvel Super Heroes capitalized on the successes of the previous games by Traveler’s Tales, then this title should have proven to be a solid choice.
Thankfully, that is exactly the case. It is very hard for me not to recommend a Lego game, but despite my glowing affection for the series, I would never place them in an overall top ten list at year’s end, unless they would do something which would really re-define the genre. There really is no need, though, as the Lego games generally move onward and upward making basic quality of life changes.
For this title in particular, the visuals have received a bump that I hope stays in place from now on. Smart lighting effects and motion blurs add to the production quality, but the superheroes’ minifigs are the most appealing change - for the first time in the series, they appear to be made of plastic, with a highly reflective finish, instead of the standard matte colors. A small update, admittedly, but one that really makes it feel as if you are playing with toys come to life.
The story is somewhat fuddled and long, but that’s typical from Lego games which create their own tales instead of drawing upon pre-existing material, such as the Harry Potter games. These Lego games are best played when the story mode is rushed through from one mission to the next, in order to unlock Free Play mode for each chapter, so that item collection can begin in earnest. The voice acting is top notch, with several sound-alikes to the Marvel studios movies that come pretty darn close to the real deal. As for the interface and the controls…that is where I will hedge my complaints.
Flying is very cumbersome in Lego Marvel Super Heroes - as the controls are mapped to two buttons (instead of to an analogue stick, which worked MUCH BETTER in Lego Batman 2: DC Super Heroes), I typically wind up pinballing my hero all over the map as I try to effectively get from point A to B. Mentioning the map brings me to the other major complaint of mine - the map overlay is horrible. Lego Lord of the Rings got this feature down just fine - dotted lines easily showed you your path, while missions and side quests had informative text to display where you were going. Not so in Lego Marvel Super Heroes - the map is zoomed in very closely to the details, and none of which are labeled. Where are the missions at, from a glance? What unlockable heroes are being displayed around my cursor? These were features that were working JUST FINE only one game iteration ago, and they now feel worthless.
Otherwise, I can’t really knock this game too much - the gameplay is still rock-solid, and these titles appeal to the random item collector that lives deep down in my psyche. For all of the games that exist on my to-do list right now, I still feel compelled to spend extra hours with Lego Marvel Super Heroes in an attempt to 100% complete it. That sentence alone should properly convey the overall quality of this game.
Recommended, at any price, and to gamers of all ages.

This game really kicked off the modern GTA series. A do-not-question-logic-story combined with cliche-loaded offensive humor, a protagonist with a personality, and a cool 1980's setup add up to a milestone in the series. The 80's vibe is supported by the choice of music played at radio stations; I was especially surprised when the first car I highjacked blasted Slayer out of my speakers.
Unlike its predecessor GTA III, Vice City has a reasonably designed map and largely feasible car driving physics. Graphics are slightly improved, over all they are more colorful, which does take some seriousness of the game - thumbs up for that.
However, Vice City still has has major flaws to ruin the game's experience. First, some car physics are still messed up: Bumping into cars or even boardwalks at high speeds may or may not cause you to lose control, which is annoying especially in later parts of the game when four or five star chasings happen. Second, boat physics are a nightmare. This is especially a major flaw that ruins the game after buying the boatyard. Third, cars' spawning and despawning behaviour are twisted. On the one hand, a car I exited two hours (real time) ago will stay at its place, while on the other hand, a car I took out for a mission (e.g. the second final mission where Mafia members stealing money from assets), disappears during the mission's introduction cutscene. Fourth, crosshair and bullets' actual path are not aligning (as they did not in GTA III), meaning you have to aim slightly to the left and downwards to actually hit your target.
On compatibility with modern operating systems: GTA Vice City works on Windows 10 after compatibility mode for Windows 98 has been enabled.
At least mouse and keyboard input will work flawlessly then, I cannot speak for game controller devices.
As I wrote in the beginning, this game is a flawed gem. There are many fun moments which make the game enjoyable, but all the flaws make up for them. I never rage-quitted a game so often as GTA Vice City because all of a sudden the game's physics behaved in a different way than they did before. I actually skipped some content due to this by leaving out the last remaining asset missions - I want to enjoy a game and not fight it. Replay value is zero.
So my final verdict: I hardly recommend the game to anyone except real fans of the series. When in doubt, thumbs up.

I'm a stickler for games that have that 16 bit feel, and this one definitely hits that nostalgic feeling.  However this game is really weird.  The start of the game is REALLY good, and I mean REALLY good, and it keeps on flowing... all the way until you get to the final 2-ish dungeons.  Then everything crumbles at the seams where there's lots of frame rate issues, confusing designs, and esp if you have ever played his games before, rather weak enemies.
I don't mean that in a bad way but when the enemies not only in the final but the BONUS dungeon are auto-killed from you being too strong there's a problem there.  Plus a bit of a problem is that the final dungeon (which has 2 parts), and the post-game dungeon (also 2 parts) both have the exact same soundtrack, and the same graphics assets.
Also in game there are 13 record keepers that keep track of certain things you do in game, each giving three rewards for reaching certain milestones (bronze, silver, and gold).  Some of these are fairly easy to do for example the gold for monsters defeated is around 3k enemies which you will EASILY hit in normal gameplay.  Others for example hitting a 30 overkill streak on a SINGLE enemy require very specific setups to obtain.  This has been the bane of my existence over the last several hours when doing this, because of how difficult he made some of these.  For example the gold for treasure chests requires you to not miss a single chest in the game (thankfully there are no one-time-only locations)
But overall this is a rather phenomenal game that I highly recommend except for when the entire game falls to pieces at the 90% mark.  Everythign up until then is fantastic but not as good as his other titles that are on steam.

This will be a very in-depth review so be prepped to be reading for a few minuites.
Story:
First thing I will start on is the story, the story is fairly good bringing together many iconic heros and enemies in a way that makes sense, there are quite a few laugh of loud moments with the usual lego parody and the voice acting is not bad.
Also, there are a bunch of semi hidden missions called "deadpool missions" that are given a bit of backstory by deadpool, each mission can be about things unrelated to story, from cleanup after a hero fight, to a kickass party at starks place, these extra missions are worth doing as they can unlock new characters, gold bricks and are the only way that I know of obtaining red bricks.
Note that to play these deadpool missions you will have to have the proper amount of gold bricks beforehand, you do not pay bricks, you simply must have your amount past a threshold. i.e A mission may require you to have gotten to 50/300 gold bricks before your allowed to play.
Characters:
The Character roster is the most impressive to date! A crazy amount that is made even better by the fact that each characters different skins count as different costumes and not different characters, by thta I mean that in prev lego games all the different Iron man suits would have counted as 6 different characters, while in this he still jsut counts as 1 character but with 6 different versions. However I think the system for selecting alternate costumes is ineficent, the characters different costumes/look are constantly rotaiting every second so you may be required to wait a few seconds to select a certian costume.
Also, the BIGGEST reason I think lego marvels character roster is the most impressive to date is thta for the most part, all the different characters are ACTUALLY different. Ofc some heros abilites are more unquie and recognizable that others, like thors hammer, sandmans heavy changeing atatcks or spidermans web slinging. They have even included characters that are useless gameplay wise just for backstory like mary jane and others.
However, when you have a game liek this some heros are OBJECTIVLY going to be better than others, example in story missions if you have a big fig hero you will ALWAYS play them in fights because they just tear everything apart and other heros in that same mission will only be played for utility purposes. And some heros have REALLY contrived and dumb utilities that have cleary been put there so that they are useful in some way, in a few story missions your forced to play logan so they he can use "claw switches" switches than need blades to use... wat.
Free Roam Hub:
Moving on, the free roam hub is extremely impressive and is one of the best free roam areas I have even played in a superhero game, not so much for detai lor things to do but just the general feel, when you fly you feel that you are going very fast, even more so that the superman returns game from a few years ago.
A HUGE improvement in lego marvel from the past games is that lego just works somuch better in this setting, lego against the dark dreary colours of middle earth of the dank city of gotham clashed heavily with the light hearted cherry vibe of lego, however within the bright artifical city of new york the natural fun feeling of lego is... kept intact?
Something strange is that even with the ability to fly at ???mph (fast) you still have a garage of cars and aircraft to collect to use... there is literally no reason to use these except for a few races to get gold bricks that require you to use a certian vehicle. I'm not saying this is bad though, while it is useless its a nice detail that adds more frills and another layer for us collectors.
An improvement upon past lego games is that you no longer need to beat the game to get access to all characters while in free roam, instead you can go to a vehicle call point and switch character from their, then past that point you can swtich characters by holding Y (if on controller) though one you beat game you don't need to use vehicle point once to get instant character select, you have it all the time. However, it still has the prob that there are sections in the free roam hub that require a certian character you won't unlock until near the end of the game, so bum rushing missions is still advised.
There are many side quests with some decent variety, some require you to fight off an ambush, chace a crook, find an item, escort someonem take control of someone etc. These usually reward you with gold bricks for unlocking special deadpool missions.
Gameplay:
The gameplay has changed a little in places, most notible is that the combat is way better than prev lego games, its still too simple I think but way better than before. If you defeat enemies quickly in sucsesion then it builds up combo to a max of 10, the higher the combo the more studs you get from beating enemies. (yes, eating enemies now give you studs :D a very good mechanic imo)
When attacking enemies with melee there is a chance that your character will pull of special finishers, quite a lot of characters seem to have a few, you will however get to a point where you will be liek "meh, seen it before, jsut kill him already" however the first few times you see spiderman grab a guy with his web and slam him of the ground like a mallet will make you say "thats pretty ♥♥♥♥in sweet"
The combat is split mainly into these attacks...
Ranged projectiles - explosive, energy, magic, bow, web, bullet (all pretty much act the same)
Laser - eletric, magic, fire (hold down to aim a constant laser of dmg)
melee - simple melee, some characters have different stances/fighting styles
melee weaponry - most melee users also have the ability to thorw their weapon and have it come back like a bommerang
and then there are a few special attacks that are hero specificm like hulk clap, ironman unibeam etc.
There are multiple instances where certina powers will be needed to progress in certian areas, I won't list them all as it would take too long, like I said earlier some are kinda contrived like claw switches and sheild switches, others make sense like grates and sneaking past cameras.
Though for once there are moments that you actually look forword too! There are points hwere sandman or mr fantastic will have to morph into a certian shape to get past a point and its always a different thing thta happens, or hacking a point with a smart character starts a (easy) minigame thats usually allways different.
There arestill many times where you will be required to build things to get things done, soemtimes this can be kinda dumb, where you have to build handles onto an object so a big fig can hold it, and some are really cool like ironman building a water cannon out of water tower that you jump into and use as a weapon.
Boss fights are... okay, better than normal lego games. There are still those that require you to do the same tihng multiple times and are more complicated than they need to be, but there are some decent ones liek the final boss, green goblin midway, sandman at start etc.
Controls: The controls are fine, controller support is nice and the character select has dropped that awful wheel LOTR had, also there is a way of quick changing to certian character using the front tirggers (on controller).
Flight controls are fine I found, though could be better as I sometimes found myself wanting to make a tight turn and would instead fly forword a little then turn around and cover way too much ground.
Rushed Verdict:
I must stop here so I will hurry, canisters arent worth collecting as all it gives is short crappy comics of story cutsenes, game needs bios to explain characters we might not know.
Though easily best lego game made, not perfect by any stretch, but shows huge improvements upon previous lego games with a large amount of content to keep you playing intesely for hours upon hours.

I'll tell you a story.
Once, I went to my grandma's house in March- the THIRD month of the year. It was also the THIRD. I arrived at my grandma's house at 3:33. She has THREE houses on her block. I went up to the door, which had THREE chips on it, and knocked THREE times. After THREE seconds, she said: "Be right there!"- it had THREE words in it. She came up to the door and took off THREE locks on her door. She invited me into the kitchen for cookies, while all of her THREE cats ran past me, one of which had THREE spots on him. She told me to sit down next to the table, which had THREE chairs. She handed me the platter with THREE cookies on it, and said that her THREE cats took THREE of the cookies THREE times. So we sat down for THREE minutes, and talked about THREE subjects: Major companies, Games, and Numbers. After that, we sat in my grandma's living room, and watched THREE different channels. After a while, she started to get thirsty, so I generously got up from one of the THREE sofas, went into the kitchen, and opened the fridge. I spilled THREE drinks, but I got more for my grandma. When I came back into the room, she was watching a commercial for a product that said: "If you don't get it in THREE days, it's free! Only $33.33!" I sat down and started reading a magazine for children- the THIRD issue. It was on how to add. 1+1-1+1+1=3. That didn't seem appropriate for a children's book, so I went on the computer in my grandma's bedroom, and found out the company had been in buisiness for only THREE years. Now it made sense. It was time for me to leave because I was going to a party with THREE of my friends. My grandma gave me THREE seashells as a present, which I thanked her THREE times for. So then I left out the door, walked to my car, and drove away.
So, what I'm trying to say is that I had a great time at my grandma's house.

The game also front loads you with tons of cards you can get in shop. It's like 30-40 boosters or something, each containing 8 cards. If you're lucky you can make at least one good deck to help you learn the game. The learning curve isn't that high though. If you've played Hearthstone, you'll catch understand the jist pretty swiftly. Most of the key words are the same just with different names.
At any rate, it's free like Hearthstone so you'll have a good time.

Taktisches Befehligen eines Raumschiffs auf einer geheimen Mission, Fähigkeiten der Crew zum Steuern der einzelnen Bereiche lassen sich verbessern, Alienrassen mit speziellen Perks lassen sich rekrutieren, Zufallsbegegnungen, jeder Spieldurchgang ist anders.
Auf dem schwereren Schwierigkeitsgrad fast nicht durchzuspielen!
Nach jetzt etwa 20 Runden echt eines meiner Lieblingsspiele geworden!
Kleines Update nach nun über 30 Stunden:
Immer noch ein ganz spezielles und klasse Spiel. Taktische Simulation einer Raumschiff-Crew und das fantastisch in Szene gesetzt mit minimalistischer Grafik, Story und Zufalls-Events erzählt in Textboxen (wohl der grüßte Kritikpunkt wenn man so will, denn diese klickt man häufig einfach nur weg).
Es gibt unterschiedliche Alienrassen (die meisten kann man auch anheuern, haben spezielle EIgenschaften/Fähigkeiten), feindliche Rebellen, Piraten, denen man auf der Reise begegnet, es gibt Händler wo man sein Schiff weiter aufrüsten, nicht benötigtes loswerden kann und vielleicht genau das findet was einem noch gerade fehlt, Quests gibt es auch diese muss man aber eben auch finden, genau so wie Schiffe in Not.
Bei den Events können bestimmte Optionen nur mit der richtigen Ausrüstung gewählt werden, was auch toll ist dies alles zu erlernen in etlichen Runden :)
Und genau diese bruacht man auch, denn Ziel ist am Ende das Rebellen Flagschiff, und das zu erreichen ist selbst auf normal immer wieder ein harter Brocken bedarf guter Planung, Geschick und auch einem Quentchen Glück.
Alles in allem total empfehlenswert, wer auf Spiele wie Rimworld oder PrisonArchtect steht nur eben ohne Basenbau, denn Schiff wählt man zu Beginn aus, und das in meist etwas schnelleren "Rogue like" Runden hat hier auf jeden Fall seinen Spaß.

While I did love the 4-dimensional level design - and seriously, this is some of the best level design ever - I felt that in the second half after you get all the guns to manipulate the blocks, it turns into every other block pushing puzzle game. The last part really doesn't deliver the same quality of level design as the first part and I really loved exploring the different rooms, but once you reach the exit stretch of the game that basically becomes irrelevant.
Still, I highly enjoyed the game overall, the puzzles can be a bit of a brain twister at times, especially since a couple of times the solution, even if you've guessed it, lacks a clear definite response for the player. And it really helps that the aesthetic is so minimalist, while it is striking and at times quite beautiful to look at, it also manages to not take away the mind of the player from the puzzles.
I think however that the game could've been better by actually having a plot. As it stands you're just trying to progress through the challenges you see not unlike Portal, but the difference there is that Portal actually told a story. Not just you being some lab-rat in a cage of an insane computer, it also uses its environments to flesh out the world this is taking place with scribbling on the walls and hints to what actually happened and how the weighted companion cubes are actually coffins for previous participants and scientists, etc. and there's nothing of that sort in Antichamber.
And finally, I think $20 is a bit much to ask for this game. I get that trying to create a 3D representation of what a 4 dimensional world looks like does require some brainpower and talent to realize, but I've beaten the game in 3.5 hours which isn't much. I'm not saying that the game should've been longer, not at all, it's quite a good length although I've read that on subsequent playthroughs, the game takes less than a half hour to complete so it doesn't have replay value. I've bought it at the Humble Bundle for $0.50 and for that it's a steal, but I can't recommend it to others for the full price. If you can get it for $10 at a sale, that would be a fair price in my estimation.

I rate the game Champion of the Gods 3/5. It's OK but generally not as good as Choice of Robots.
This is another text-based choose-your-own adventure style computer game/book/story with multiple endings and no way to turn back to the previous page (just like in Choice of Robots). On one hand being able to turn back to the previous page would be sort of like undoing a mistake you made previously and would be unrealistic. On the other hand, It gets frustrating to have to skim through the whole game over again just to find the page where you might want to make a different choice. Since you can re-play the game anyhow with knowledge of what you previously did (unlike real life), a "back button" would have been a good feature to have had in this kind of game. The absence of this feature does add replayability but more than that, it also adds unnecessary frustration.
This is a fantasy Choose Your Own Adventure style text/story based game apparently set in a world not extremely dissimilar to that old Clash of The Titans movie (or its remake), though honestly this game felt more like the original Clash of the Titans movie to me than the remake. The context of this game felt campy and silly throughout but that did not diminish its charm. The decisions were well implemented and their are several nifty endings. There is some allegorical meanings and messages to be had as well as more direct messages about the effects of being a moral or immoral or anarchistic hero. Mostly however, this story simply espouses that one should be true to themselves and to others regardless of any other considerations.
Unfortunately, though this story has a great number of choices (one on almost every page) the results of those choices are far more limited than in the one other game of this kind I have played (Choice of Robots). Usually when faced with a problem in this game, you do not have the choice to ignore it or avoid it. The game mostly takes note of what kind of person your character is becoming according to how defiantly or loyally you respond but all choices tend to lead to 'yes.' You cannot totally avoid your character's destiny and each play through will see you fighting the same set of enemies and coming upon the same obstacles again and again (also unlike much of Choice of Robots). Perhaps the most freedom you have is in who you try to seduce and whether or not you alienate different side characters. And, unfortunately, while you can choose to be gay, straight or bi there are no detailed sex scenes to be found in this game. For the most part there is no highly detailed ANYTHING to be found in this game.
Indeed, as in Choice of Robots, the entire game feels like an outline of a story rather than an actual short story or book. The descriptions are bare-boned and concise with an amazing lack of visceral detail. I think I've read newspaper articles which seemed to come alive in my imagination more than the scenes in this game. For the most part, if something in this game is supposed to be beautiful then it is simply described as being "beautiful." Though there may be a lot of words in this game, the vocabulary and usage is all extremely basic.
However, the fact that there are multiple endings to this story (and which of those endings you get is dependent on your precise choices throughout) is to be highly commended despite the fact that this structure is the entire point of reading through this game at all. Having a good multiple ending structure dependent on each major choice you make is still better than what most games do for their audiences. In this day and age, the fact that it is perfectly normal for a game to have just one potential ending (if you don't die) is just stupid. Mediocre writing and the general lack of features (and the absence of cool 3D graphics) aside, there are a lot of fairly big-budget, high-end graphics games out there which could learn a lot from Champion of The God's good, and fairly replayable plot structure.

I understand Co-Op doesn't necessarily translate into "Multi-player." You can 'co-operate' with the AI. But, that's sort of a given. The term implies a union of two or more players working together. This game allows you to control two characters to work together, but it’s more impairing than imperative. It’s a nuisance to shuffle between individual characters a mere few feet from each other, instead of just being able to shout commands other than ‘stay here’ and ‘follow me’ which is a futile effort because the enemies you try to sneak-kill are still going to spot your partner and alert every enemy in the tristate area for a shoot out no matter what you do. Maybe if there were more puzzles in the game that required the divided attention of two people acting separately it would make sense, but you have a total of two or three instances where such action is called for. Additionally, you shouldn't have to lazily retrace your steps with slightly mapped alterations of forcing Natalia through a crawl space to unlock a door for Barry from a chapter where you just finished playing as Claire & Moira.
I'll admit the graphics are top-notch, the cinematics rendered especially beautifully, and the chemistry between the voice actors feels natural as if they really do care for each other. But the visuals and dialogue do not make up for the subpar gameplay. Of all the Resident Evil games, this was perhaps the most linear. Just something to consider if you're interested in adding this to your collection. My advice: pass, or wait for it to come on sale.

I had never heard of Shadowrun before this game but, it being on sale as well as the fact that I love a good solid RPG (additionally, I'd been considering picking this up for a while), I did buy it. I expected it to be somewhat interesting or even hold my attention for a little while but I didn't expect to play the game for three days in a row because I liked it so much. That's how long it took me to beat, 3 days. While I regularly finish RPGs faster than is intended by developers (including doing many of the optional things that many games have) this is a very short period of time for a game with a solid story like this. Since it's short and since it's good, it is a game that makes you want more. You want more of the turn-based battles, you want more of the story. You want to take your created character and keep them going through more stories and more quests and you want to know what happens to you afterward. In short, I don't think there was a thing I didn't really like about this game excepting only it's shortness which is something I can easily overlook.
It's been a long time since I picked up a game on a whim to be pleasantly surprised upon playing it and I recommend it to anyone looking for an RPG that is engrossing but won't take up too much time as well as anyone just looking for a good RPG.

TLDR: Game bad, no like old game, Raid good fun with friend if have one. It only worth it on discount.
That being said let's look at the other aspects of the game.
Champagne:
Combat: About the same as any other resident evil, it grows as you progress but ultimately becomes a game of annoyance with slow reaction times and twitchy bullet sponge enemies.
Weapons; You start out with your standards and it’s best to keep with them any gun you find will likely do less damage and hold frwer rounds, I honestly dont know why they bothered adding any extra weapons in the campaign I didn't swap one of my originals out the entire playthrough.
Environment; I enjoyed the look of most of the maps the designers really did a good job this time around. the only thing I disliked was how the colors didn't change much from inside to outside. it was all a vague brown red with black.
Sound; I think the soundtrack and sound effects were spot on, even at times i jumped a bit when enemies entered or chased me because something about the sound actually put me on edge this time around which is something that hasn't happened in a long time for a Resident Evil ( looking at you Nemesis).

First time I launched this game, I couldn't stop playing for 3 hours straight. Basically, if you like platformers, rogue-likes (minus permadeath) and exploration, you just can't regret purchasing this jewel.
It's both hard and easy to describe it: you're locked in a kind of transe, quite unable to say "okay, I'm done for today". You're never really done because the game makes it very hard to stop playing: everything is smooth and lightning-fast (no loading times, no complicated GUI; you can warp back to your base, sell your loot and be back exploring the mines within a 10 second time window), so you never really find a down time that allows you to exit the game.
In Normal mode, death is not overly punitive (haven't played higher difficulty modes yet, took time to post recommendation :p), but just enough to make you wish you weren't dead, so you just basically dive back into it to get your loot back and farm some more. It has this strange "Metroid meets Rogue" feeling that will make you play over and over.
The Metroid feeling is present both in the visuals and the tight platforming controls (which are excellent by the way, it's pretty scarce to see a dev get it right, and it's especially important in this game where basically everything wants you dead), and this strange loneliness/suffocating feeling when you're exploring the mines and can't find a portal to warp back to your  base and get some heal.
Kudos for the 5-jumps feature, which I was skeptical about at first, but I gotta admit, mastering it gives an incredible feeling, again, quite similar to Metroid's Space Jump.

Ohnoes! The Robodig is destroyed and you must fix it! Or something! So let's just shoot the story and go for a little platforming and shooting and loot collecting... in a mine!
Platformines is a nice package indeed, combining features from several genres to create a fun game that does nothing really new but still feels fresh.
You start by creating a male or female character from a couple of visual options, and are then brought into a randomly generated mine (where your ship, the Robodog, totally crashed). Your job is to explore the mine and relocate several building blocks to restore the ship- and to do so you need to fight masses of enemies, collect coins and loot, upgrade your equipment and be an all-round badass.
You also get to listen to a chiptune rendition of "Hall of the Mountain King."
Platforming is nice and precise even with a keyboard, though a pad is clearly better. From the get-go you have quintuple jumps, and there is almost no momentum, so you'll quickly put Mario to shame by staying airborne and shooting things easily. Vanity items you collect can give you even more jumps and also change armour rating, weapon damage, and other attributes.
Shooting feels old-school and satisfying. You can equip up to four weapons (pistol, shotgun, machine gun and launcher) and just like the Borderlands games every weapon is procedurally generated, so you'll often find something surprising. There's no ammo limit either; while weapons have magazines and reload times you always have "infinite bullets".
And there's more equipment, most notably energy belts that increase the amount of damage you can take but also larger backpacks: You'll collect gems on your way to sell in your homebase OR, and this is interesting, to replenish your shield belts. Do you dare to try and secure that teleporter over there and chash in on the gems, or would you rather play it save and spend them to make it further down the mine?
All in all, this really feels like an over the top "roguelike" without permadeath. Your home base is a safe haven where you can store loot, shop a little, and save your progess. The mine is constantly repopulated with enemies so if you need to grind for money you'll soon have some "easy places" to get some cash. It's NOT a metroidvania game- from the get-go you're able to explore as you see fit, only limited by your firepower and skill.
And is it fun? That's the most important question after all! And yes, it is. It's a fun little platform shooter with charming retro graphics and a lot of replayability. It's not OUTSTANDING and it doesn't really do anything new, but it's a nice mix of genres that'll keep fans of simple arcade games entertained for a good while!

For this reason I thought long and hard on whether it is fair for me to give a negative review to Faerie Solitaire, considering that the core gameplay - the solitaire - is solid. The art direction is just abysmal, the colour palette, the ugly faces of the faeries, all of it was continuously driving me up the wall. The story is annoying, the voice acting is annoying. The pet system does
, it feels like it was slapped on as faux-content. The base building system is okay but you run out of upgrades quickly and then there is nothing to do with money. The last two achievements require so much grinding it would put some Korean MMOs to shame.
I suspect there is a target demographic out there that loves this sort of combination (otherwise it wouldn't have 91% positive reviews at the time of writing), but I have found myself too far removed from it to be able to give a thumbs up.

Do you like loot + platforming + randomised levels? Look no further. With elements of Steamworld Dig (randomised mines, collect minerals of ever-increasing value the deeper you go, locate portals for quick returns in trickier parts of the map) this offers plenty of replayability, even though the shooting and platforming elements start to get a little repetitive over what seems to be a single enormous level. Similar to the level creation in Cargo Commander, you give your new level a name and the game randomises it based on that name...somehow.
The deeper you go into the mines, the more chance you have of scoring better guns, although the loot system is a little disappointing. There aren't randomised gun effects, only % stats (higher damage, firing rate, etc) and there are precious few different hats you can wear to give you extra stuff, like 2 additional jumps (yes, you can jump 5, 6 or even 7 times in the air).
Jumping feels a little floaty, and your gun has the annoying tendancy to point upwards when you're jumping up to a higher platform, meaning you inadvertently fire vertically rather than horizontally like you were expecting. However once you get used to how your character moves, you'll be zipping around levels in no time (an XBox 360 controller is recommended).
Your character can only see a limited distance around him/her, and when you get damaged this cone of vision starts to shrink, meaning you can get into some really nasty spots with extremely limited vision - you may find this a welcome addition or an annoyance.
Still, those quibbles aside, Platformines offers a ton of platforming content and that addictive, often elusive "just one more play until I get to the next portal/find a better gun/grab that sparkly bit of ore over there" feel. Here's hoping the developers add more randomised loot and abilities in a future patch. There's certainly no reason to try the demo first and see if you like it.

At first glance, looks cute, about an hour in poking around.. It was a pain to setup the controller because, for whatever reason, "controller support" just means xbox. (have already beaten normal mode in < 3 hours, see edit towards end.)
If you have a non xbox controller, then dig  your xpadder/joy2key or whatever else and fight with it.
For heaven's sake, devs.. Why do you keep making controller supported games that DO NOT support simple basic Windows-recognized controller keymapping? Come on. :/
After playing a bit, well.. You'll be disappointed by weapon variety. There's four, that's it. They're randomized, sure,  but unless you find the difference of 10 damage from one pistol to another to be "unique" and "fun" then you won't be amazed by that. There's also some gear, but all I've found so far are hats and wigs, which occupy the same 'slot,' and seem to only be slightly randomized. Most of this gear also seems to be stuff available at character creation, as well. You pick a hat/hair/etc., and I haven't really seen anything separate from what was available at creation, so there's no real excitement to loot or progression, except the randomized slow increase on weapon stats. Not at all interesting or fun.
The AI on enemies also seems very basic.. They can see you through walls and will just shoot randomly while pacing back and forth. You also start to see repeats in the world organization pretty quickly, I'm already starting to recognize configurations of rooms and such. :(
It's a cute game, but there's just not a heck of a lot of bulk to it, especially for $10 compared to others in that same range. Needs many more weapons, more effects and random properties, etc.
As best I can tell there's a big randomized map, the game randomizes the location of some 'block guns' into locations that arbitrarily harder. There's no real metroidvania progression or anything to get from one to another, just pure stats - you'll be one shotted if you don't get better weapons and farm money for higher energy. You collect the guns, shoot some blocks near where you start, win; rinse repeat on higher difficulties. It has a good look overall, I just feel like this game needs more depth.. More varities and variations on weapons, not just four with slightly different attacks. Contra had more weapons!  The 'equipment' also seems pretty slim. Unless you really wanna pound out each difficulty for the arbitrary increase in difficulty you probably won't get but a handful of hours from it, and it rings in steep at $10 for other games with much mor depth and playtime.
Edit: Well.. Less than three hours and I beat normal mode. No real incentive to play the harder difficulties, I imagine it's just the same but arbitrarily harder. :(
I also understand the nature of input types and dealing with it, it's just frustrating to have to fiddle 3rd party programs just because my controller (which is all but a clone of an xbox contrller anyway, just nicer and with better battery life/bluetooth) doesn't jive with how they set it up. PC games are ideal for their flexibility- you don't have to have a specific keyboard or mouse or peripheral, and particularly considering it's fully recognized, buttons and axes and all, in Windows itself, a little support would be great from more games.
As for PLatformines, well, if you have a total hard-on for leaderboards and intensely repetitive gameplay then more power to ya. It's a cute game - the music is all kinda cute but also just chip-tune-y remixes of well known songs (sugar plum fairies, stuff like that.) As I said above: There's four weapons, they do not get in any way more interesting, there's no randomness or random abilities or special effects except for their damage/reload times; they remain largely the same, just higher damage and some variation reload time and such. The only reason to even bother to kill enemies is to upgrade your belt (health) and perhaps get a better helmet (knight is good since you don't have to kill anything, just get the defense and run.) It's a cute game all in all, but it just feels beyond flat. Sorry devs, good effort, but I definitely feel like I just wasted $10 for a mere couple hours of fun.

This is one of those where I wouldn't press thumb up or down and would opt for a hand making a jiggly gesture instead if I was given the chance. Steam doesn't offer that, so after some debate I decided to just go with the thumb up.

☆☆☆☆☆☆★★★★
4/10 – Below average
As shown above, my biggest gripes with the game land on the text presentation and the plot (but I'll return to that later), but all in all this isn't an awful game. It's short enough and the skip option works flawlessly so you can easily get all the endings. Despite there being multiple endings, there isn't much difference in the main story even with different choices, but again, this is a short game.
The art style of the game isn't pleasing to me personally but I suppose it isn't entirely unsightly. The backgrounds are decent even if occasionally it's obvious they didn't pay that much attention to what they were using with dialogue (for example, main character talks about how the water reflects off the ceiling at an outside pool). Music is simple and repetitive, but not distracting.
There are H-scenes in this, and I did download the restoration patch (if for no other reason then because I'm always against censorship like this) but I must say that this game didn't even “need” the H-scenes. There was nothing you absolutely needed to see, and much like the forced romance endings, they even felt jarring in couple places.
Finally, some words about the plot itself:
Akiko thrives academically and is a pleasant person to be around, while the shy Kasumi is a great swimmer and also very pleasant. Our main character, Hikaru, is friends with both of them even if he often ponders how such perfect girls would even look at his way. Hikaru has the hots for both of them but when one day he wakes up in the body of Akiko, he starts to learn that they aren't as perfect as he had always envisioned them to be.
The story follows as Hikaru finds himself possessing Akiko's body for a day and then in Kasumi's the next, and then back to Akiko. He does his best to get both girls through their routines without causing trouble for them, and somehow he isn't immediately trying to locate his own body or wondering what's going on with it. Instead Hikaru marvels at the perfection of the girls' bodies, and then gets exceedingly confused as he learns that they both have quite serious troubles in their lives. It becomes clear very fast that Hikaru must not have been very good friends with either of the girls as he wasn't even aware of the fact that Akiko and Kasumi were friends with each other.
Once the story actually kicked off to focus on Akiko and Kasumi's respective troubles, I was surprised over how much more serious the plot turned out to be than I had expected this game to be. It might not have been perfectly written but it was enough to keep you interested and some shortcuts are excusable since the game itself is rather short. To me the main problems came from the choices feeling greatly insignificant, even doing “everything right” somehow landed me in a bad ending on my first playthrough.
But the thing is, the game's good endings have Hikaru end up dating either Akiko or Kasumi, but that feels completely out of place for the game's setting. You only have little time to see Hikaru interact with both girls, the rest of the time he is for all intents and purposes missing from their lives. He learns a lot about both girls during his possessions and aims to help them in their problems, but I fail to see how that results in Hikaru ending up dating one or the other. Had this not tried to be romance game and acted like Hikaru staying single was a bad ending, then the game would've felt more solid.

A thrilling roguelike action platformer with multiple classes to play as, and a unique way to handle the game’s difficulty.
14-16 hours (Main game), 1-2 hours (Single run)
Platformer / Action / Roguelike
8/10
Controller recommended.

is a strong action platform, it has some roguelike elements that give it some interesting qualities, as well as some unique quirks too.
The game features 12 different classes to play as, though you only begin with one, the Commando. While it’s not my favourite class to play as, it’s thankfully a good one to begin the game with. The other classes are unlocked by completing various tasks in the game.
Each class has its own unique attacks and qualities. You have 4 attacks or abilities with each class, 3 of which require a cooldown period before they can be used again, the duration of which varies by character and attack. The final attack is just a basic attack that can be used as often as you like with no cool down (essentially it’s your basic attack). The cooldown on some attacks and abilities gives the combat an interesting twist, as you can’t just use any attack at any time. This means that sometimes you must think before using an attack so you don’t screw yourself over in case you need it
after, or to prioritize the order of your attacks so that the one with the longer cooldown is used first.
For the Commando you have a basic shot, a shotgun attack that pierces through enemies, a rapid shooting attack in both directions, and finally a dodge roll. My favourite class to play is the Huntress, as she’s the best for kiting (running back and forth while shooting, and causing enemies to follow you in a way that groups them together); she auto-targets when firing, and one of her attacks even hits multiple enemies too.
The game features a total of 7 levels per play-through, with most levels having 2 different stages to play, and each stage having more than one possible layout. Being a roguelike, the randomized elements don’t end there; scattered throughout each level are various chests and shrines that give you items to augment your character. The pickup items are randomized through each play-through and their effects range from improving your attack by increasing damage, attack speed, or adding an electrical shock that targets enemies near the enemy you hit. Other augmentations improve your health regeneration abilities, increase your movement speed, or even give you a use item of some sort (with varying cooldown rates). One must purchase chests to be able to get the item inside; as the difficulty level increases, so does the price of the chest, in general, the more expensive the chest (relative to the others on the level), the better the item. Money is earned simply by killing enemies.
One of the unique aspects of the game is the way the difficulty scales. For every 5 minutes you spend during a play-through, the game’s difficulty goes up one level. There’s a bar in the upper right corner showing you both the time and difficulty level, such as Easy, Hard, Nightmare, Impossible, etc. After 10 levels the text will cease to change, though the difficulty level still increments every 5 minutes. For each level of difficulty increase, more enemies will spawn, they’ll have more health and do more damage, and tougher enemies will also spawn. Eventually the difficulty will increment to the point where bosses will spawn along with the normal enemies. This forces one to balance how much time they spend farming on a level before progressing to the next one, as they risk increasing the difficulty at a rate disproportionate to the reward.  The game itself has some difficult, but it’s not terribly high. However the combat system does have some unique quarks (as discussed earlier), and combined with the difficulty scaling, it does take some getting used to.
The game took me somewhere in the neighborhood of 14 hours before I completed my first successful run. Each run will only take about 60-120 minutes to play all the way through (obviously less if you die early).
If you play with a keyboard then the controls default to moving with the arrow keys, jumping with space, and using zxcv to attack or use abilities. I found this set up awkward, and while remapping the attacks to qwer did make things easier, I still greatly preferred playing with a controller. A friend of mine mentioned that this control set up was similar to DOTA 2 or other MOBAs, though I haven’t ever played any, so I can’t comment. However, I mention it just in case those used to that sort of game find the keyboard controls more functional than I did.
The game has some UI issues, for one I can’t scroll through the menus with the arrow keys, I instead need to use the mouse. It’s a minor thing that should be added, and it’s quite an annoyance at times. Furthermore, the game does offer controller support, but it must be toggled on/off in the sub-menu for the game controller setup. Toggling this on will also disable the keyboard controls in-game until it’s toggled off again. This is counter-intuitive in two ways, both in that the controller needs to be turned on, and in that it renders the keyboard unusable until it’s turned off again. Finally, and the biggest one for me personally, is you are not able to use the Steam overlay to take screenshots or upload them to Steam. This meant I had to use ctrl print screen to take pictures, pause the game, paste them in a Word doc, and then eventually upload them to Imgur.
So in the end,
is a very strong action platformer, with roguelike elements to help spice the game up; its combat system and difficulty scaling help keep it interesting, while the different classes help extend its longevity.
GG Valve.

This....is a game that is beautiful art.   In that, I mean that while it has almost nil replayability (you'll need to give yourself time to forget what you learned between playthroughs), it beautifully executes in concept.   The "eureka" moment, where fun is had through learning how to play, mastering a skill, and then suddenly seeing how to build on that skill is what this game is about.
This is not a shooter.  You will get one tool; a "gun" that allows you to drag, collect, deploy, and otherwise manipulate colored blocks.   This is a tool that upgrades over time so you can manipulate new colors.   You have to be a quick thinker, and willing to take time to understand puzzles and identify red herrings.   There are few opportunities to exploit the level design, and no such tricks are shortcuts beyond simply recovering from your own mistakes.
Like Serena, this is a game worth playing for the fascination factor, but unlike Serena, the suspense comes from sterile white walls and an environment that rarely reacts how you expect.   There are no jumpscares; the only real enemy is the deadly Black Energy that seems to absorb all light, and a hallway that every time you find yourself in it you realize you just screwed up and have to retrace steps.   Great game.
If I had to pick one negative thing, it would be that because level design is so key to the game itself, mastery in one playthrough is mastery of all playthroughs.   It will never get harder and the map will never change.   Still, worth the cash for the time you do get out of it.

Dying Light is a zombie fighting survival game.
-The Day/Night cycle is very well done and help build the atmosphere of the game as zombies scale to your level, so unless you join a friend who is just starting out, fighting is always a challenge no matter what time of the day.
-There's always a place to explore and scavenge, seriously like holy cow there's so much to find and look for I don't think you understand how much was put into the maps.
-Graphics aren't mindblowingly awesome but are gritty enough to really make you feel you are in a war-torn zombieland.
-The game doesn't shove crafting in your face. Like really all you need to craft early on is about 20 med packs, and you really don't need to do anything else. As a guy who really despises games who throw in crafting just to make it a selling point, it was reasuring to see that it wasn't a main focous of the development.
-Bashing heads dead or alive is so satisfying, really just seeing these litte buggers collapse to a well placed dome swing is just so rewarding in of itself.
-Mod suport!
-Night time is absolutely horrifying. During my time in the game I've never wanted to land once on the ground due to fear of what lurks below.
-Horrendously unoptimized. I've got a decent machine that can at least run these current gen types of games at high graphic levels, but all graphical features are either off or set on low.
-Freerunning isn't 100% ready, so you'll either be making jumps you didn't want or fall to your death multiple times.
-The game itself feels like it needed another month to squash out these bugs, though to their credit the dev team has been patching the game every 3 or so days, so at least they've been taking care of their baby (unlike most AAA games released these days).
-The main story really isn't something to sing praises, plot holes galore, uninteresting, tries to force emotion by taking lives of characters that aren't really estableshed, and the main villain acts like he's so deep and understands that humans are scum bla bla bla. All in all it takes maybe 4 hours if you power through missions like crazy.
7.5/10 if you like the number system. All in all just straight up fun zombie survival game that feels like it had lots of love put into it, something that you don't see in games of this caliber these days. Has bugs, but the developers have been patching this game to bring it to the high standards they've set themselves since release.

Shadowrun Returns
Shadowrun Returns is an isometric RPG with tactical combat, set in the world of Shadowrun, a pen and paper RPG. You don't need to know a whole lot about it going in; I certainly didn't, though I've looked into it a lot more since.
The basics are that its the year 2054 and magic returned to the world. Along with magic are the standard fantasy races and such; there are elves, dwarves, orks, and trolls. These "metahumans", as they are called, live alongside regular humans in a cyberpunk dystopia. Several megacorporations have gained extraterritoriality, and in many places the corporation has replaced the state as the enactors of law and society.
You are a shadowrunner. In essence, a kind of mercenary who conducts various operations either for or against the corporations, as well as some other things.
Gameplay
Its an isometric RPG. You have your main character, and you will generally have 1-3 other shadowrunners working with you. Some are plot NPCs that will work with you for free, while others are professionals that require payment up front before going with you on a mission. There are a wide variety of shadowrunners for hire, of different classes and specialties, with some that are more better equipped or more potentially versatile commanding a higher price. It is therefore relatively easy to get teammates that complement your particular player character. While you can give them consumable items, you can't change any of their equipment; they're professionals, and their gear is theirs.
Character creation is not terribly detailed. You choose your gender and race, which determines what sort of portraits you'll have available. There are about twenty or so portraits per race/gender combination, though they usually come in "groups" of two or three. The ones in these groups are very similar and generally have a few different features, like tattoos, a different hairstyle, or some augmentation. This also sets the default appearance of your character model, though you are free to change your skin color, hair style, and hair color if you so choose. After that, you can choose your class, which determines where most of your starting points go; you will also recieve a few extra to invest as you wish. The options are Street Samurai, Mage, Decker, Shaman, Rigger, and Adept. However, any class can learn any ability, so the starting classes are really just pre-built characters; you can also choose to make a custom class, which starts everything at zero and gives you the points that all the other classes had pre-invested.
Most of the game revolves around a central hub (a bar), from which you get sent to various places to do your shadowrunning. Its not open-world, but there are plenty of NPCs that just sit there and make the world feel bigger than it really is. Background characters with their own motives and problems that exist solely to give the setting more depth.
Combat is tactical, on an isometric grid like the rest of the game. Its somewhat like XCOM's combat: you have two "action points", which you can spend to move around, use items, or attack. There's a much wider variety of weapons available though. There are several tiers of pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, SMGs, and melee weapons, as well as consumables like grenades. In addition, there are also spells, both offensive and defensive. There's a cover system much like XCOM's, though at times what qualifies as cover is a bit odd. There isn't a ton of combat in the early game, but it gets more common as you go.
There is a downside though. Not all skills and weapons are equally useful. "Decking", the ability to jack into and fight in the cyberspace realm called the Matrix, is not terribly useful. There are a handful of points where it unlocks a little bit of extra dialogue, but there aren't very many opportunities to jack in. There is a point in the story where you do need to, but if you lack the ability to, another character will go in and you'll control him. There's another point later on as well, but a decker is provided for you at a very low price. Most of the time they'll end up being fairly useless in your party. Melee weapons are also in general fairly terrible. Don't bring a knife to a gun and/or magic fight.
I'd also suggest turning the difficulty up. Particularly late game, you'll have gained so many points that you'll destroy enemies.
Graphics/Audio
The environments are really nice and the character portraits are quite well-drawn. In addition, the music is actually pretty solid. Dunno what else I can note here.
Story
Shadowrun Returns is a bit different from the standard game in the story aspect. In effect, when you buy Shadowrun Returns, you are buying a platform for a campaign. There is a campaign included, Dead Man's Switch, but the game supports the modding and design of your own campaigns, which can be distributed on the Steam Workshop. The Dragonfall DLC is an entirely separate campaign.
Dead Man's Switch is about a dozen hours long and is fairly solid. It is quite well written, with interesting characters and many flavorful dialogue options. It is, however, extremely linear. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but something to note if that's important to you. Though there's generally several different dialogue options in any interaction, they will all ultimately have the same effect. You're on a railroad, just one that gives you some opportunity to flesh out your character's personality through dialogue. There also aren't a whole lot of real sidequests; besides a few "pick up item X during story mission Y for money Z", there's also one real, optional sidequest later on.
The plot itself is relatively straightforward: an old friend of yours has died. Before that happened, he set up a contingency that would send you a message in the event of his death (a dead man's switch). In this message, he offers you a large sum of money in exchange for dealing with his killer, whether via lethal methods or through getting them thrown in jail. As you are currently very much down on your luck, you go on a mission to find those responsible and bring them to justice (whether street or legal). Its nothing really special, and rather predictable.
However, I stress that the dialogue is actually really well written, with relatively interesting characters, and its certainly an enjoyable experience. The world is full of minor NPCs that don't really do anything but make the world feel bigger than it is. Its not something that you really need to know much about the source material for, but I can't help but feel there were several references, particularly near the end, that I missed because of my lack of knowledge about the setting.
There's a DLC campaign, Dragonfall, which is supposed to be even better than Dead Man's Switch. I will likely be purchasing it when it drops in price during a sale. In addition, there's also several major campaigns available on the Workshop, some of which are also really well written and very highly recieved. I'm currently trying out some and am enjoying them.
In short, Shadowrun Returns is solidly written, has a nice artstyle, good but flawed combat mechanics, and hours and hours of additional content available freely. It may not be very long, but its not very expensive (particularly on sale), and all the workshop campaigns more than make up for it. Being a fan of the setting will likely make you enjoy it even more, but it is by no means a requirement.

Great game. The system requirements are over exaggerated though, because my Gtx 560 ti 2gb phantom runs the game on ultra graphics settings with an average of 45 fps. And also, no matter what graphics settings or resolution I set it to, the game still performs exactly the same as it did before. The only thing that impacts framerate is view distance. I played it with medium view distance at first, but I set it to the lowest later on, because it barely impacts the graphics at all. The framerate actually depends where you are and what you are looking at, and what time of day or night it is. Near the ocean the framerate averages at around 60, but in dense foliage it can drop as low as 30 fps. Sunset and night time totally kills the framerate though. When the sun starts to set, the game runs mostly at 20 fps, and also at night time. When entering a cutscene the game freezes for about 3-5 seconds, no matter what time of day it is. Same happens sometimes when a zombie grapples you, and when a zombie spits acid on you. The only complaint I actually got about this game is that it is poorly optimized, it runs like Gta IV, except it also has lag spikes. Yes, I get the same framerate with Gta IV. Except in Gta IV when it becomes daytime the framerate goes to 20, and at night time it goes to 40. In dying light it is the other way around. But I still recommend this game, because it is really awesome, and fun. You can break literally any bone in the zombies's bodies, because they have fully modelled skeletons, and every bone you break affects the zombies realistically. The parkour and the controls are also great, and the graphics looks gorgeous as well. I haven't gotten far in the story yet, only at 12% so far, so I don't know how good the story is yet. So far it is ok. The game copies far cry with the radio towers you must climb and activate, and the zip line down after you activated the tower. It is basically Mirror's Edge + Dead Island + Far Cry 4 all combined into one great game. Also, I got this game for free. But really, the only bad thing about the game in my opinion so far is the performance. Otherwise, it's a great game!

Often, cultures and belief systems associate particularly with specific numbers. 3, 7, 12, and 13 are numbers of particular importance in the Catholic faith for instance. The mechanic of evolving your followers got me really pumped, since I have never seen that on a online ccg before. It's a free game wich adds to the things that are good about it, and with the rerolls (google it) you can have a really nice deck right out of the bat.
I've played 80+ hours and I can proudly (or not) say that I have a good knowledge of the current meta. No games are perfect so I will say that the metagame has a lot to improve yet. In the most part because almost every player that plays a certain deck will 95% of the time use the same boring strategy. I'm a simple kind of player, so I don't much care for gimmicks, I like a more straightfoward strategy, just hiting the enemy player until his dead. And I'm not saying a ccg can't have gimmicks, but the ones on shadowverse are so overused that sometimes can be a little tiring. The game gets really dull and 8 out of 10 times you can figure the opponent's strategy before the match even starts. I'm always trying to find different ways to play my class, to improve and to have fun, creating combos and strategies, testing new cards, but at the same time following the meta a little. To summarize,  I really hope that in the future the meta can get a little bit more mixed and that the players can come out with different and awesome ways to play.
So far I'm having a good time, so should you if you're a fan of Card Games. I strongly recommend this game for anyone that's a fan of ccg and anime.
