I feel I've come to love documentaries about gaming, and Free to Play only solidifies this love.
*Spoilers (if you don't follow the competitive Dota scene at all)*
In this film, we get to personally know three top players of DotA 2. As we follow their journey through the first International, we root for them. We experience sadness, frustration, and victory with them. As I listened to the stories of Fear and hyhy, a looming feeling of dread came over me as I remembered the outcome of The International 2011. By the middle of the movie I was hoping I didn't have to see their disappointment. Unfortunately, we can't change the past. Ultimately what this documentary does is allow us to know their stories and learn there's a side to competitive e-sports beyond watching our favorite teams and players dominate.
Let's be honest, when you tell someone of an older generation that you want to make money playing computer games, the response is more than likely always going to be the same. "That's stupid, get a real job, get a different dream, etc." Many of us never get to experience the hardship and the reward that comes with making that dream come true. Free to Play brings out all the difficulty of playing competitive e-sports while also having to balance a life outside of that. However, this documentary also shows the changing scene of e-sports. Where in 2011, mostly China and Korea seemed to be the most ethusiastic about e-sports, now other countries around the world are pushing e-sports more than ever before. It gives a sense of hope to know that the world is changing to be more accepting.

Free to Play turned out to be everything, except what I was expecting it to be. It sure is a documentary about the Dota 2 International tournament which had a prize pool of 1.6 million dollars, 1 million being to the number one team. Free to Play isn't an after movie of the tournament, it is a documentary which tells you, and shows you, the lifes and the obstacles that top Dota 2 players face and have faced. Being one of the best at something doesn't mean you're happy. Is it worth giving up your studies to persue your dream and go against everything that your family teached you, should you embrace the opportunity to try to prove yourself not only to those that keep telling you that what you're doing is wrong but to show everyone that you really are the best at something? Free to Play, was surprisingly pleasant for me to watch, considering I barely play Dota 2, thing is, for me it was more of a documentary that shows you the financial, moral, social and life difficulties that esports players face nowadays. I truely hope that the next generation, our kids or even the kids of our kids, will take video games to a whole new level, to make it the most successful and enjoyable entertainment in the whole world.
Free to Play, shows you what people don't know about each of these top Dota 2 players, hyhy, Fear and Dendi. It is truely something worth watching even if you have never played Dota 2 or Dota on your life. One last thing, which is really bugging me is the title they chose for this, Free to Play, I guess it isn't just because Dota 2 is a free to play game, I guess they chose it because each one of us is free to play.

----A 3D Real Engine ran puzzler, that left me short of words at the end. An indie game I passed by and played a couple years after its release, that has some pretty clever puzzles, from the simple movement of blocks, to the outright mass replication of the same few blocks to (in my case) an entire floor of the same block set you started with. Mind you I missed some puzzles more than likely, and the mystery of the pink roaming block is yet to be cleared as of this review, but what I did from a standard start-to-finish playthrough of this gem, I can safely say theres plenty to do that I've yet to see myself. You get pretty much thrown into the world, with no real spoken start, just signs that can be used as proverbs for life, or big hints for the games. Even the silly little cartoon drawings in them made me chuckle from time to time, while others made me reflect on life.
----The controls itself, were pretty direct, and the menu was thrown into the nexus room, not saying that it was a messy move, mind you, it in fact was quite the opposite. The Esc menu itself was actually something you returned to often, whether you wanted to or not. It in of itself, was a nexus that almost acted like a brick wall, but at the same time, an indicator for where you are in progress. Sensitive and precise, you can easily snag a block from across the room and place it elsewhere, which it requires you to do exactly that in some puzzles. Even when you gain new abilities though a differently colored "Matter Gun" (as I like to call it), it gives you a lesson on the basics, and leaves you to notice the rest on your own. The controls are quite simple and limited to your three mouse buttons (left and right click, and mouse wheel click) and the standard WASD to move. Those familiar with FPS games in terms of controls, won't feel too alien to the game, at the same time, anyone can just simply pick it up.
----The gameplay, is puzzles, puzzles puzzles puzzles. Not that its bad as well, in fact its quite nice, since the puzzles aren't simple after a while, and involve some true out-of-the-box thinking. I can't say too much about the puzzles without spoiling too much, but your worse enemy is your eyes. Theres also no bugs that I've found, only the occasional graphics flicker in very miniscule zones, which is very ignorable, and likely due to my GPU. Also your ESC menu is a damn room with a map to warp from place to place on. So the puzzles won't be so draggish if you have to repeat them for some form of progress.
----The music is sort of there, not that I'm complaining about its subtlty, since its all atmospheric sounds and music. From a meadow to a swamp, you pretty much get placed in a rather clear state of mind, and in my opinion, a good clear mind for some of these puzzles.
----The graphics are simple, and yet clever in reason. Even the graphics will make you wonder if its part of the solution. Hint hint.
----The difficulty is wholy dependent on you, this could be the easiest game you will ever play, or the hardest one you will even attempt. With the game throwing you for loops, sending you into "Dead-ends" or just outright dumping you somewhere else entirely, new or familiar. Things change around you, causing you to miss things, or notice them outright. It keeps you on your toes, and tries to fool you into thinking some parts are pointless, while others may get you somewhere.
----All in all, the game is a fantastic grab, even if I got it on Humble bundle, and did this review after it was done and over. Its still worth a purchase and some time. Though personally, for the purest experience, don't use any guides, considering it can easily reduce the effect of the game. I don't want to review this game on a numbered scale, because that stuff is so askewed lately for game reviews, so if you're into puzzle games, or just into something to sink your time into between breaks of other games, hell even just to play it, I say its highly recommended.

Polyball is a fun little early access title that brings back great memories of playing the Super Monkey Ball games as a kid. I still go back to playing those games often (with SMB 2 being my favorite!) through the excellent Dolphin Gamecube emulator, so as a result I’ve become pretty familiar with what makes SMB such a great title. The controls, the physics, level design and charm all add up to create a phenomenal gaming experience. Polyball was obviously inspired by Super Monkey Ball, but
Super Monkey Ball. It doesn't try to be and instead tries to be its own thing.
As a result, we get a great platformer that breaks free from the classic gameplay elements of its inspiration. For one, you can jump (which was a concept implemented in the underrated Super Monkey Ball: Banana Blitz but not found in the classic SMB games), and the level design is completely based around this. There are plenty of platforming challenges sprinkled throughout the levels, but the game's medal system still encourages you to race to the finish. The levels are also much bigger than that of Super Monkey Ball's, and can sometimes take upwards of 2 minutes to complete. While this might annoy some players who enjoy going for good times on the leaderboards, I was personally fine with this decision. The levels are fun as well, and similar to the SMB games they are fun to replay over and over again.
The physics aren't perfect, but are generally really tight and make for fun gameplay. The devs can obviously refine the physics over the course of development so I’m sure they’ll improve. The controls are also tight and responsive, which is absolutely key for a game like this. If the controls weren't good then the game wouldn’t be fun to play and thus be completely ruined. Lastly, SMB's charm is replaced by a striking art style and minimalistic design principles. I personally love this and find that it makes the game even more enjoyable. All in all, Polyball is shaping out to be a great game and I'd say this is one to keep your eye on if you were are looking for a game similar to Super Monkey Ball. I’ve enjoyed my time with it and look forward to the updates down the road.

In its current state, I cannot recommend this game unless you are the most casual of players, and even then it's very overpriced.
The gameplay its self is okay, but there's a plethora of UI issues and technical grievances:
* First of all, this game has no business being 2.3 gigabytes in size. That's just disgusting.
* You must access the main menu to switch to a level that is not the next one after what you're currently playing.
* You press R to restart a level in the middle of it... but R to go to the next level if you're on the "Level Finished" screen. You must use the mouse to restart in that case. R cannot be rebound. This usually causes me to accidentally switch levels, and switching back is a 15 second process or so.
* There's a large delay at the end of a level before it shows you your split. This is terrible for people grinding IL's, which the game seems to be aimed at.
* Menu navigation is very slow, especially going to the main menu. This wouldn't matter much if we could change levels without going to the main menu.
* The timer for the level starts without player authorization, which makes restarting a frantic rush to position the camera exactly where you want it.
* Restarting a level in the middle of it results in an even faster count down to the timer starting that can often end while I'm still moving the camera. Why not just wait for movement input?
Overall this game feels more like a cashgrab that was thrown together over a couple of weekends than anything else.
Edit: about the game disk space thing, since a lot of people don't seem to get it. 2.3 gigs is a pretty decent space to make a pretty big game, especially for a game that may or may not have been done without the use of any real textures. 2.3, for a game like this, is absolutely massive.

Ok, serious time, champion of the gods is by no means a bad game, its just not up to usual standard. By that I mean, it does not COMPARE to choice of robots, in my opinion, the best of the "choice of" games so far. The usual formula is here, your actions effect stats and how the story plays out, but not even close to the extent choice of robots did. It has one storyline and you have no choice but to follow it, want to rebel against the gods entirely? Refuse to follow their commands whatsoever? Sorry cupcake, you're being forced to. The story itsef isn't...bad, its just limited by how little your actions seem to affect the story.
Alright, I'm gonna give you an example, late in the game you come to a point where your character sees...and you get three options to what type of person they are, but no matter what you choose they are completely enamoured with you from the moment you meet, and the choice does absolutely nothing but affect what clothes she/he may wear and that is it, that's what you get. This character is by all means, the central love interest, but he/she has absolutely zero personality, no offence choice of, but you've managed to make a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥on beanpole" character IN A TEXT ADVENTURE. The story is incredibly linear even down to the fine detail, early on you get a choice of what powers you have, but from that point on the only interest in combat sections (of which there are less than 7) is trying to figure out what stats these decions go by, you picked speed? Find the option that includes any of the following words: Quickly, swift, evade etc. Oh and another thing, THERE IS NO FAIL STATE. You are physically incapable of losing this game, choice of robots made me value my characters life because I knew if they died I would have to start over, no matter how badly you may fail you just spring back up and keep moving.
Yes, ok, it involved me when I played it, but half of that was assuming there were other directions to go in, I was expecting the ability to be the villain, to have another hero replace me and have a climactic final battle that didn't rely on stats but your own personal intelligence, but nope, its all just stat registering and more stat registering. The game made me value some of the characters, but then I realised in the act of writing this that I only valued their lives because those steamy lines of text were about all that was keeping me going...as well as that sweet sweet achievment.
It's an ok game, its by no means an open game, I say it's far inferior to some of Choice of's other games, like choice of robots, by that first, then buy this, if you still feel like it. You aren't getting out of here without a recommendation champion of the gods, but only just.

Risk of Rain has to be tied for the best rouge-like game I've played. I say tied (the other being Spelunky) since the only elments I could see being improved upon in the game are very minor elements of UI polishing. There are a couple glaring bugs in the main menu design that get in the way, but that's more or less nitpicking and they don't impact the main gameplay ever.
The art design, music, feel of the characters and bosses all add up to a special and frantic experience that, even on its lowest difficulity, goes out of control in a good way towards the end. There's elements of a story told in a sort of Dark Souls-style through the collectable monster logs that makes for a mysterious and brooding atmosphere that is very cool.
There's such a wide variety of powerups to collect that, at first glance, feels like a roll of the dice if you're going to do well on a particular playthrough or not. Yet there's an impressive amount of strategy hidden away via Artefacts you can collect. Unlocking those and turning select ones on allow you to control the pace of the game a lot better and add a lot of depth to choosing which items you want to roll with down the line.
When I found out this game was deveopled more or less as a pet project by two guys, I was astounded. This is a game that feels foundational, that feels like it should be part of something bigger. I feel like I should be wanting a Risk of Rain 2 or something, but that seems unlikely. Luckily, there's enough content in this very indie game that can keep you going for a very long time.

This game is a black hole. It is a slow-paced game, yet the turns move by quick (or even slower if you want it to).
As a history buff, and a fan of similar games such as age of empires and Axis and allies, this game enthralls me. The attention to detail, the voice acting, and everything else set in this ambience operates to make an excellent experience for the gamer.
After a few hours of play, I've found that my strategy is quite a bit worse than I had thought; I have some rust to dust off, things to learn. Even on the second-easiest diff I'm being outpaced. Not a complaint, in fact, the opposite: a game as complex and realistic as this will tend to be more challenging for the uninitiated. Starting out, I found that it is possible to play a peaceful playthrough, and there are always barbarians to fight. But the game forces you to take risks and grow in order to win. Takeaway: you need a specific gameplan and need to stick with it to have success.
5/5, would highly recommend! Stick with it, and if you're any fan of strategy and/or history at all, this will be a LEGENDARY game for you.

The game's good. Very addictive, bloody fun slicing and smashing up zombies.  The main character is yet another generic white dude, and the villain is a generic sociopath. There's a consistent and somewhat interesting narrative. The story isn't great, but isn't terrible.  There's a good line of engaging story missions, although there are fewer of them in the second half (the story completion percentage goes from 50% to 75% in like 2 missions once you get to Old Town.)  Looting empty buildings that all look like ghastly crime scenes, decapitating zombies, and running across rooftops through a dead city makes for surprisingly compelling gameplay.  Exploders are cheap AF though.  You end up with a pretty big arsenal to cause all kinds of destruction, but you will still get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you fairly often.  The day/night cycle, in which powerful zombies come out at night to chase you, and especially the dense sound design create a really tense atmosphere; volatiles aren't all that powerful once you get some good weapons, but you will still want to avoid them.  You'll also want to avoid some of the abitrarily timed challenges, but if you're a completionist you'll try them over and over anyway, angrily.

Overall I believe this game is one of the more solid games that Capcom has actualy made in a long long time for the Resident Evil series. Even with the graphics being toned down on this game, it never pulls away from anything the game brings. The music, ambiance, and the sounds the mosters all together create that erie tone that I feel like has been long gone in the series. The level layouts are a bit drawn out I feel like, but they bring back some of the puzzles you used to see in the older games to try and counterbalance it all.
Raid Mode is an RPG/Shooter style of Mercenaries, you basically go through stages and shoot down monsters , trying to get that perfect as you level up in Raid Mode. Whats nice about this is that you can swap between characters with relative easy and still use the same weapons.
Overall, I would say this a great game to buy and get in to, even if you aren't big on the Resident Evil series or the Horror Genre at all. It's definitely something worth looking in to getting.

Set in a near future "utopia," Mirror's Edge follows the story of Faith (a runner: a securer and deliverer of "questionable" goods) as she uncovers a conspiracy and fights the authoritarian system of her city. Played from the first-person perspective, this action game focuses on environment navigating through parkour (a form of urban athleticism , melee fighting, and the option of firearms (using basic real world guns). While the story is a little lacking and is on the short side, it has very enjoyable gameplay (which can be a little frustrating at times due to the player perspective) and a beautiful cityscape to traverse. A unique take on first-person games.

Ah yes... Mirror's Edge is, without a doubt, one of my favourite games, ever. I'll glady recommend it to anyone looking for a new, visually spectacular, experience. I keep telling my friends this is one of the few games that they should've played at least once in their life. Unfortunately, no one ever listens. I don't mind though, because let's face it - it's their loss. And while there's definitely room for improvement, what's there is already very solid and lays the groundwork for a possible sequel, minus the story.
About the story: Mirror's Edge puts you in the shoes of Faith, who has to clear the name of her sister after being wrongfully accused of murdering someone. Doesn't sound all that exciting ? Well, I might agree with you there. However, it's the way the game is played that makes it fresh and interesting. You see, the game is played from a first person perspective. But instead of shooting your way out (which is optional, but not recommended, for maximum enjoyment) you'll be running. Parkour style. In other words: free running.
You'll be running through offices, on rooftops and many other places in order to get to where you want to go, all the while fighting off the police. This is all shown in one of the most beautifully realized environments I've ever laid eyes on (those office interiors ! *drool*). It's truly stunning.
Like I mentioned before, the game does have some flaws. First of all, it's short. Many people will complete it in a hour or 4-5. Not terribly long, but not terribly short also. It keeps the experience fun. I personally would've liked it if it was at least twice as long, but it's nothing a sequel can't fix. Besides, the time trials will keep you occupied for days, maybe even weeks. One other thing that can definitely be improved for a possible sequel is the number of routes you can take to get to your destination. Mirror's Edge gives you the illusion of an open world, but in fact there's only one way to get to your objective. Agreed, this way it keeps you focused on the story, but it certainly would've been nice.
Not much else I can say, really. This game is the reason why I play games. Play it yourself, and you just might agree with me. Maybe not today, but one day, I'm sure of it.

When you play a maze-type game where finding the goal is the purpose of the game, you expect certain conventions to hold, and rely on some tried-and-true principles to guide you.
This game doesn't follow those conventions.  Things may change when they are or aren't being observed, spaces connect in ways they could not in three-dimensional space, and your tools may have undocumented features you may need to move on.  Each new tool can be approached from several ways and add new options to picking up and placing blocks to make it past the obstacles.
There are some consistent patterns to find which will help you, and you can reason your way past many obstacles with some creative thinking.  This game is best played without foreknowledge of the puzzles, as the joy of the game is in the discovery, whether you aim to explore every corner, or race to the final destination.
There are some developer areas which are very tricky to reach, but these areas are optional.

I am making a new review to reflect my opinions on the game now that it has left Early Access, as requested by the devs, since previously I was disappointed by the beta releases. I will be quoting remarks I made in my old review to see if any of my views have improved, worsened, or remain unchanged.
Overall, right now I can say Polyball is still an underwhelming presence in the rolling ball series of computer games.
One thing I want to note is how... disappointed I am with the lack of improvement/changes in the official level selection. I was told by the devs in the past that certain worlds (like the Volcano world) would be getting gigantic overhauls, and yet all this time later most of those levels have remained the same. You can't just say those things and not follow up on that, and now that the game is out of Early Access the devs just don't seem to care anymore, and as I customer I can't say I care any more about their product in return.
• "The ball control is also very stiff and has trouble responding at times, especially during platforming segments."
This still remains true for the most part. I can feel a slight improvement in the turning, but it is not polished. There is no comfortable middle ground when it comes to cornering around sharp curves. If you slightly turn the ball it barely turns, but once you hold the turning for a long enough time it turns almost too sharply and there's no stopping it, causing me to careen off an edge. A lot. Even on platforms that aren't terribly thin it is still easy I feel to accidentally roll off into pits.
• "the camera slips around every which way as if it has ice physics programmed into it, making re-orienting yourself in the right direction nauseating and confusing."
Now I will acknowledge that camera control is a lot more steady and stable now, this was a much appreciated improvement.
• "I do like the idea of racing through vast, open environments at top speed while zooming through smooth slopes and ramps"
I still very much agree with this past remark. The levels where you're racing down huge slopes at fast speeds is a gratifying experience, but there's not enough of these levels.
The lighting in the volcano sector is better, however, but that's the only significant change I have taken note of in this entire release. I also have complaints about how nonexistent the lava effects are in this game; it's just all white, nothing else. I was assured by a dev that was the intended design, and it's supposed to be glowing, bright lava, but no matter how I look at it, it's just a plain white texture, absolute nothing.
I also never covered this before, but there are no out of bounds triggers for almost all of these levels. Except for the ones where you drown in lava, there is no real way to go out of bounds here, and because of it I find myself falling off of the main track and just rolling underneath the levels. This is the lack of polish really begins to show because while down here I see a lot of unconnected platforms and tons of clipping cameras views, it's not a pretty sight.
Additionally I absolutely HATE that there are no checkpoints. A lot of these levels are surprisingly long, and because of how easy it is to get off track and/or fall off platforms, this means going all the way back to the beginning. There's also occasional levels where for one reason or another there are projectiles or hazards that instantly kill you if you make direct contact with it. Not cool.
• "In between all of the slick, speedy levels are what I refer to as "TIGHTROPE" levels, a term coined after MarbleBlast Gold's infamous level of the same name."
There are still quite a few frustrating tightrope levels in the game, though I think to a lesser extent than in the beta, but these are still blemishes of level design that do not belong in this kind of game. I will take note that slowing your ball down is noticeably easier, so they aren't quite as bad as they used to be.
There are also still quite a bit of very generic levels that feature plain, polygonal platforms and a multitude of singlular jumps. It's disgustingly basic design and it should NOT be in what is now a finished product.
There were a decent amount of improvements made from the beta, but other than those points, my experience has remained unchanged. I do still like the ball customization, and the music for each world is really cool, and there's even a workshop now so that adds a little bit of incentive for me to come back to it. But honestly this is still a very subpar game, and I am disappointed at how little has changed overall. When I got this game in Early Access last year I expected significant improvements and changes over the course of development, but given how fearful the devs are of change now I am not happy with the now finished product. This is not a title worth getting.

I can hear the Devs:  "Let's just make an environment and let physics dictate the game play, it'll be easy!"  I think they bit off more than they can chew.
The trailer to this game looks like a blast, however, I'm having a hard time finding that kind of fun in the game itself.  You start off with a hand full of levels that are just move forward to win, then suddenly you're on a track where if you fall off you might as well just reset because you are going to find the world's edge before you find the proper goal.  Odd that it's not insta death like the other levels.
Try racing, okay.  Hold down the go button and run in a circle for 3 laps.  The winner will be decided by whoever pressed the go button first.  Finding shortcuts would be a plus, but apparently the dev thought that should be against the rules and put up invisible walls and death pits everywhere.  There's no real real reward for playing "well", but there is capital punishment for making a mistake.
Battle mode.  Players actually swing at each other with weapons?  That's hilarious, but not at all practical.
In summary, there are promising features in this game, but they are a long way off from being properly implemented.  There are many many levels and lots of content to this game, but I played for 2 hours and didn't find anything that actually felt polished.  The majority of it felt like it was barely functioning.  Given that they're asking $16 for this it's pretty disappointing.
If the devs actually had 2 or 3 levels nearly polished for fun gameplay, and cranked the price down to match the content available, I'd be writing a positive review here.

Like all of the LEGO games, it is a fantastic game hampered by a few really bad bugs. TT Games continues their trend of focusing more on exploring the world map than completing levels. In LEGO Marvel, you can complete the fifteen levels right away and save all of the exploration until after. This actually works in the game's favor as it makes the world seem huge. The levels make up a coherent story that takes place after the end of the Avengers movie, but is not related to anything in Phase 2. As can be expected, the story is a goofy parody of the movie version of the characters.
The levels follow the same pattern of previous games - go through with a certain set of characters for the story and then return later with any character you want to collect treasures and find secrets. There's also a set of 11 smaller levels that can be accessed when you have a certain number of bricks. These are smaller levels that can be completed in a few minutes. Besides the levels, there's well over 100 bricks found in the city. These are found by solving puzzles, winning races, helping citizens, etc.
Unfortunately, the game isn't without flaws. Finding all of the city bricks gets repetitive, especially the tasks involving fetching something for a NPC. This is made worse by the fact that you just follow the arrows to find it and then return. Unfortunately, if it wasn't for the arrows, you'd never find the stuff because it's a random item/person in New York City. There's basically no thought required for completing the tasks. The platforming puzzles are better since you actually have to try, and they are usually rigged so you can just fly to the brick and grab it. Flight controls continue to be obnoxious, though it is better than in LEGO Batman 2. It’s bad enough that the air-races are not worth the effort.
There are some pretty bad bugs as well, though not on the level of the game-ruining bugs of the first LEGO Harry Potter game. Sometimes, the races will not give you your brick after you complete them, but they will still flag it as finished.
Ok, you actually can get the brick, but sometimes it takes a while for the system to reset the flag. It doesn’t happen a lot, so you won’t be locked out of any areas, but you may have trouble getting 100%.
Overall, it’s still a really fun game and worth it, despite the bugs.

There are so many characters to choose from, I'd say double than any other Lego game I've played.  The open world in this game is amazing, and there is so much to do even after the story levels have been completed.  The voice acting is decent, and the Lego humor is still there.  The fact that there are so many different characters allows for a lot of unique types of interactions, whereas in previous games you might only have different items to carry (like Indiana Jones, where everybody is a mortal human).
There are a few flaws, most of which boil down to the game being pretty buggy compared to past Lego games and other games in general.  It probably has to do with Lego/Traveler's Tales not being used to handling such expansive games, but I've gotten physically trapped in places, and other glitches and freezes that force me to have to repeat the level or find some way to kill myself and hope I respawn elsewhere.  If you've played many Lego games in the past, I will add that minikits are not very complicated to find.  They usually just involve using some character who wasn't originally available on the first play through to do something (coughmagnetocough).  I remember that finding minikits in older games (the first and second Star Wars) actually was very difficult, or at least took multiple playthroughs, although there's a chance that was because I was just dumber back then.  Just thought I'd mention that.
- Huge Open world +positive
- Large selection of characters, 100+, +positive
- Long levels, cool campaign +positive
- Pretty buggy -negative
Conclusion:  If you liked past Lego games, this is a no brainer, especially when it's on sale.  If you've never played a Lego game, this one is as good as any to try, although I might recommend a smaller scale game like the Star Wars ones or Indiana Jones ones.  If you can't handle bugs in your game, then I guess I'd stay away.  This is definitely not the best video game ever made, but I have had a lot of fun with it.  Emphasis on fun.  I'd also recommend the co-op, it's more fun with someone else.
Bonus: I bought both DLCs on the cheap (like <=$1.50 for both), and they're not really essential to the game.  Both DLCs give you like 15 characters total maybe, and while some of them are cool (Thanos, Rick Jones), most are redundant (Dark Phoenix, The Warriors four) and dumb (Jane Foster mostly/only).  Get them when they're cheap, but it'll be more of a "eh why not" purchase.

As Civ games go, this is a well-designed and visually pleasing game which is potentially truly great in strategic terms. Having said this, however, Civ V has one major flaw: while it
sometimes be very enjoyable, the game is sadly often made either unwinnable or
easy-to-win due to the often-imbalanced (sometimes extremely so) random initial spawns (in terms of either amounts, locations, or both) of six critically important resources: Horses, Iron, Coal, Oil, Aluminium* and Uranium. This frequently occurring problem is then exacerbated because these resources are not visible until the player (or AI) researches the tech required to utilise the resources in question, meaning that long-term games which look promising, and may have taken many hours to develop, may either have to be abandoned, or may end up being far too easy to win and thus very unsatisfying.
Negative rating given with
regret, since I am normally a huge fan of the CIV franchise.

So much has been said about Civ V (and indeed the whole Civ franchise) that, to be honest, anything I might attempt in the way of an "overall" review - short of writing a really, really in-depth spiel, which I don't have time to write just at the moment! - would be pretty redundant. Another day, I'll get round to the really, really in-depth waffle - but for now, here's a somewhat in-depth waffle, but about just ONE aspect of the game - and, for me, it's an absolutely crucial one.
And so: here's my solitary, but significant, whinge about an otherwise excellent game - only one point, but a real game-breaker for me. While Civ V is everything that the previous Civs were, and more, and while it's graphically lovely, great fun to play, very well-balanced, impressively rich in content and complexity, and, in short, ALMOST everything a turn-based strategy game should be, it has (for me) one critical flaw, which always ends up frustrating me to the point of screaming into the nearest pillow while scuttling back to trusty old Civ II - yes, with its terrible Advisers and all! (Actually, I rather like them, but this is meant to be a review of Civ V, not Civ II... :D)
Civ V's fatal flaw, in my view, is the way in which resources are initially spawned and distributed - combined with the fact that you
get to discover where the resources are until you research the necessary tech required to use that particular resource, so you can't just glance at the map at the beginning, see that you're in a dreadful location resource-wise, and start over again without wasting any time and effort. This doesn't matter too much for "optional" or "desirable" resources, but - and here's what drives me mad - it can happen, according to the game's random spawn, that you may find you have very little, or even NONE, of the six CRITICAL resources, all of which are absolute game-winners or game-breakers, depending on whether or not you have them, and/or how much you have of them. These resources are Horses, Iron, Coal, Oil, Aluminium* and Uranium - with Horses, Iron and Uranium being insanely important.
BUT, as I say, you can't see any of these resources on the map until you reach the right tech level. Without these resources (especially the Big Three), or with only tiny amounts, and (as often happens) with the rest located on the wrong side of one or more other nations' territory, you'll lose  sooner or later - definitely. May as well just re-start.
And no, this isn't hasty pessimism - it's endless attempts, via various methods (trading, warring, trying to sneak around the edges of whatever nation does
want me to reach those lovely resources... or all three at once!), followed by simply giving up, after too many promising games ground to a dead halt at the point where I realised I didn't have any (or enough) of X or Y essential resource.
For example: trying to survive the early game with no Horsemen, the mid-game with no Iron or Coal, or the end-game with no Aluminium or Uranium is simply impossible, unless you play in Idiot Mode, which of course is no fun (and sometimes even then!). And, of course, the AI - especially once it realises (and it does!) what a huge advantage it has gained by owning these critical resources - will
trade anything for them, no matter HOW much you offer in return, and especially if YOU have none at all of whatever you're trying to bribe, cajole or threaten out of them. In my experience, the AI nations would (and often do, if I can muster the armies!) rather die than hand over so much as a single pony, or a small cupful of iron filings. As for trading Uranium, well... hahaha. Ha.
In short, and while, of course, not EVERY game ends up with the player suffering from a crucial lack of essential resources, this insanely annoying random resource spawn problem can mean going through hours (or, if you like to micro-manage as much as I do, WEEKS!) of game-play, setting up all kinds of lovely trade routes, road networks, mighty cities, military strategies, diplomatic agreements and so on, generally having a great time... BEFORE realising that you'll get no further, thanks to a poor resource spawn shooting all your plans down in flames.
Of course, it's not ALWAYS the case that the game's critical resources are unevenly distributed: that's the nature of "random", after all! *SOME* games are enjoyably equal matches, all things considered and give or take a Horse here or an Atomic Bomb there - but I found that at least 75% of the games I started would end up, sooner or later, failing due to either the player or the AI lacking crucial resources. Some might think that it would be a stroke of good fortune if it were the AI whose resource-lottery luck was awful, but in my opinion, when this happens, it's actually ALSO pretty non-fun: for me, at least, easily wiping out helpless adversaries simply because your resources dice-roll was better than theirs is oddly unsatisfying. Not so much "turn-based strategy" as "turn-based luck"... :(
Anyway. After many, many failed attempts, I am now more or less an ex-Civ V player, although I do still give it a whirl, in the hope of striking a nice, evenly balanced resource spawn (I know, I never learn!). I *love* the Civ franchise, and I REALLY wanted to enjoy Civ V, with all the general improvements it has over Civ II - and, to be fair, I've already gained a lot of enjoyment just appreciating the in-game mechanics and the wonderful amount of work that went into the game... until, near enough every time, I inevitably hit a lack of X or Y resource, and realised that The End Was Nigh.
In conclusion, then, it's for this reason, and this alone, that I can't honestly recommend Civ V (much though I wish I could), and it's also why I very rarely play it now... of course, that doesn't mean I'm Civ-less (can't imagine that!): yes, I'm back with good old Civ II - which, for all its AI faults, at least doesn't feature anything as critically game-breaking as the Dreaded Resource Spawn of Doom!

Dying Light, developed by Techland which developed Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide brings the player into a new world with new mechanics and a new strain of virus. Many people bashed Dead Island since there were so many faster paced zombie games like L4D, COD Zombies, Zombie Mall, etc - but don't let those reviews discourage you from this game.
The main benefits of this game amonst also with Dead Island is that they're the only true free form roam games for zombies that there is with the exception of DayZ which is a completely different article. If you want an idea of DayZ, go ahead and read my article on Arma 3. Dying Light not only delivers a large map and highly detailed cities, but it gives you a wide variety of weapons and modifications. If you've played Dead Island, you'll notice some differences:
-Weapons only have a set amount of repairs so you can repair them only 1-5 times depending the weapon and quality
-Adding modifications no longer lower your weapon durability
-There is a secondary type of weapon modification which add bonuses to durability, handling (rate of durability), damage, and etc. Some of these modifications are rare though, very rare, and weapons can only use a specific number per weapon
-You only have one character to play as
-There are many more crafting options, but they don't play as much of a part as they did in Dead Island games
-Day and Night cycle (when not locked by a current main quest part)
-No more "Butchers" and the equivalent of Butchers are now replaced by the Volatiles (or as I call Night Stalkers) that only come out at night, and no more pointy arms lol...
-Guns are much much more powerful in this game and actually create an impact BUT there are no sniper rifles, and gun rating varieties are limited
-You get a freaking Grappling Hook... like.... what more be said... That's freaking awesome, holy crap batman
-And the start of the game is muchhhh slower than the standard Dead Island game... It may take you 20 hits to kill your first walker, and the beginning is much more difficult
-Finally, that I can recall from the top of my head, the city is more alive: Zombies are more alive, they react to the player and react to sounds that players AND ZOMBIES make, they adapt to your flash light (not Night Stalkers though... they must have zero light perception since they never take notice of it), but you will also find many NPC's in the game that are randomly generated that you can help for bonus money or mods as well as survivor experience
As I have mentioned in a comment though as for coop gameplay:
"Some things to look for when you play this game is... Play by yourself and the game is fine.. but if you play with other people try to find friends that ALLOW you to actually experience the game. Too many people out there do nothing but rush every destination, every quest, everything... To actually get the worth out of this game you have to just experience it.. Roam around, search, try fighting some groups of zombies, chase down air drops and MOST importantly....... Play the game at your own pace... I beat the game in around 45-50 hours, some people beat the game in less than 10 hours and that is NOT the way to play a Dead Island/Dying Light game."

Wow.
The reviewers were very, very wrong.
So, i'll just go through a few things first.
1. The story is not ABSOLUTE GARBAGE. Sure it's generic, but some characters scan be likable, it's logical(to an extent) and it fills its position well.
2. It doesn't get boring. The brilliant mechanics here make it a joy to play. Don't take my word for it, look at the people with 30+ hours barely after release.
3. I love the human combat. If you use(abuse) the dodge mechanic, it makes the melee fights interesting versus the skull crunching of zombies.
Anyway, a few thoughts of mine on the game were that albeit the map looking awfully small, the verticality, claustrophobia, terrifying night mode, and imminent danger while on the ground leaves it constantly new, as you're moving too frantically to really pay much attention.
The parkour is absolutely fantastic, with a well worked out skill tree that has very fair progression. It's fluid, fun, and quick, compensating for the hordes of versatile undead.
Speaking of the zombies, I love them. Unlike most gorefest games, these zombies are rarely easy to kill. They're resilient and persistent, making sure that you always second guess that escape plan.
Nighttime is absolutely brilliant, the startling shift of atmosphere and gameplay is jarring and great. The volatiles are terrifying, and I have never enjoyed such a chase as the ones in this game. With the freerunning here the pursuits are pulse pounding and fun. Never have I loved the eerie violet glow of UV lighting more.
Multiplayer is fun, the night hunter is terrifying. The invasion idea is great. Playing as the zombie is fantastic as well.
Weapons are good, I hate the speed at which they break, but it adds a sense of conservation and urgency that's important. Upgrades are interesting, guns are rare enough and dangerous enough to nearly be useless, and the melee produce such a satisfying *crunch* that I rarely use guns anyway.
Soundwork is great when it isnt the voicing. Lots of groans, pops, crunches, etc make it feel real.
Harran is a great setting for this. Really.
KICKING
Overall, the story's failings are made up for in excess by incredibly addictive gameplay. I may not have played much yet, but I have had more fun than in any game from last year in it's entirety.
EDIT: Quick tip: there ARE bugs. Right now i'm stuck where I need to open an elevator, but the doors stay shut without allowing me the command. Watch out for bugfixing updates and wait it out for that if that's your thing.

Shadowverse. This is Japan's #1 card game. So of coarse, its full of anime goodness. The guys and girls are overly sexualized and full of color and  the detailed artwork is absolutly astounding. AND ITS FREE! So with a card game pretty simular to this genre of Magic; the gathering or Hearthstone you pretty much have an idea were it is headed. Choose a leader of Arisa-forestcraft, Erika-swordcraft,Isabelle-runecraft,Rowen-dragoncraft,Luna-shadowcraft,Urias-bloodcraft and Eris-heavencraft. Each leader and craft has a specific playing style and theme. Some cards are specific to that craft. Your leader does have its own set of voice lines and animations for the game. Some of them pretty cool. With your chosen leader and craft there is a story mode. A set story and facing an AI to advance the story and gain rewards of Rupies ( in game currancy) or card tickets to get booster packs of more cards. You learn how to play the game, ( like what a ward,fanfare,ambush,storm and amulet cards are and how to play that specific craft ) The story line keeps you going and the rewards are great. I think I got 20+ booster packs to start the game with and make my own deck. The real diffrence in this game is the evolution ability. During the game you can 2 or 3 times, evolve a card. This beefs up its stats and sometimes even gives abilities. Its becomes a love/hate relationship. Great for when you do it, bad when the other player uses it. The evolved card does some cool animations and changes with some pretty neat artwork to represent the evolution upgrade. Other than story mode you can face the AI or other players in a ranked or unranked games. Rewards are handed out accordingly and you can lv up your leader to gain even more rewards.MORE AND MORE. They are rather generous with the rewards. Also there is a arena mode  where you make a deck and see how many times you can win for....rewards! Deck creation is available or you can auto make decks if you havnt got the right ''formula'' down, but know you have good cards. A profile hub can be created with the right flair and profile name and picture to show your personality. You can even show your contries flag to ''represent'' There is a viewing cards part too, witch is fun to go through and see the incredible artwork. And to think of it maybe this game should be rated for mature....

Resident Evil Revelations 2 was actually a good game. The story is quite interesting, the atmosphere is defenitely creepy (Though feels like Silent Hill), not to mention some enemies are scary looking. The gameplay is fantastic, you will enjoy going through the story from start to finish, conserving ammo is back for you will reach those moments when you are quite low on it, and melee is quite useless so don't try to rely on that.
Claire's and Moira's campaign was pretty good for the most part, though I was not a big fan of Moira not using a gun, she only uses a crowbar that is useless, therefore shes pretty useless as a teammate and when you play as her aswell. She is only good for locating goodies with her flashlight, and opening barricaded doors.
Oh yea, prepare to hear the word "F .u. c. k" in every sentence that Moira speaks, this game has ALOT of Swearing from any other Resident Evil game.
Barry is Back!, Barry & Natalias campaign is okay, although not as good as Claires & Moiras but it still held its ground. Barry is now older, and hes character model seems like something you would see from "The Last of Us". He still has his magnum and hes a pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥guy, that being said he comes to the Island to rescue hes daughter Moira and meets Natalia the little girl on the way, and they grow a strong bond.---
--> Natalia is a little girl, so it makes sense she cannot use guns. But she is very helpfull with her ability to detect enemies through walls, I would even say shes more reliable then Moira for Natalia can atleast pick up bricks and throw them from a distance to do some serious damage.
The only con I have is that if you switch from the character with a gun to the non-gun user, the AI that controls the gun weilding Claire or Barry will not use their weapon. There is a trait you can unlock so your AI partner (Claire or Barry) can use their guns on their own, that being said their extremely redudent for they basically refuse to shoot enemies and their slow as hell to do so, not to mention they do little to no damage to enemies.
Overall I really enjoyed Resident Evil Revelations 2, and I would definetely recommend it. Though the story is not as long as previous games (Story is about 10-12 hours), it packs alot of entertainment for new and old RE Players.

With (most) of the performance issues fixed, this game finally gets to show its grunt; And my god, is it a masterpiece.
This game is the sequel Arkham City deserved. Origins was great, but it did not bother to step up from City (it was a stop-gap release, after all). Arkham Knight, on the other hand, offers a very fresh take on the Arkham formula.
The Arkham series has been established for its state of the art combat system, offering an easy to learn, but harder to master freeflow combat that packs a very satisfying punch to it. Arkham Knight takes the "seamlessness" up a notch, whereby once you get into a flow, the combat feels nearly rhythmic (and in a very very delightful way). Your punches are more powerful than ever, and you never have to break your flow anymore (unlike the previous games, whereby stuff like combat takedown requires you to break from your combos in order to execute. This is definitely one of my favourite parts). Not to mention, enemy variety has been buffed, with the medic offering a new take on what weapons to use on who (and requires quick thinking in large enemy numbers). My favourite addition (or improvement from origins) has to be the dual team fights. If you thought combat couldn't get any better, this will prove you wrong soooo bad. I do not wish to spoil any one of the first time you get to fight with
. Overall, Knight pretty much perfects the formula, and I can't see them improving it any further, which is great, since it sends off the series in an unmatchable note.
While the mechanics of predator mode have been left relatively untouched (with the exception of a lot more booby trapping and hacking introduced through gadets), they environments in which these challenges take place have been revamped entirely. The maps have been dramatically improved, and are more fitting to the respective themes of the areas they're situated in. They feel much less formulaic, which means you need to work on your strategy each time, and that alone improves them so much.
Now, I understand there is a lot of hate towards the Batmobiles' implementation in this game, but I do not see why it is so profound, considering it is the best implementation that matches the style of gameplay in the Arkham series. Many of us wanted the Batmobile so bad, but only a few of us understand how difficult it would be to implement it in the context of the Arkham games. I feel that Rocksteady has done their best to include the Batmobile in the games, offering a very slick driving experience and a thrilling (albeit frustrating) combat mode. It was either they make a batmobile that made sense in the context of the Arkham games, or not implement it at all; And I am glad they chose to implement it, as it is very fun. Driving the mobile through the streets of Gotham was so satisfying, to the point that I prefer it to gliding around the City (even though that was one of my favorite parts of Arkham City).

, the technical side of things are extremely impressive, and definitely put this game up as one of the most impressive titles I have ever had the privilege to play on my gaming PC. The character models are very detailed in comparison to the previous games (Catwoman and Scarecrow are two shining examples of improved character models) and the whole cast seems much more lifelike with the very well done animations and expressions. The map this time around is also very very well designed, with Gotham City feeling extremely satisfying to manuever around and explore. Whichever angle you see it, whether in the sky while gliding, or on the roads in your batmobile, you can abosrb the insanely dense feel this map provides, and I love it! Good to see this generation of gaming put to very good use. You are getting a very good treat just watching the main story events unfold, as the cinematography is just top notch. Even if the story doesn't live up to Arkham City, it definitely is an experience to sit through with the well designed cutscenes. This game is a masterpiece, and ends the Arkham Series on the high note it truly deserves. This series will be remembered fondly in the future, and I see myself replaying this multiple times. If you have the system to experience this (including a very nice audio and monitor setup), you will love this game.

Fun variation on Tri Peaks solitaire.  If all you're into is playing cards, you will enjoy this game.  The art style was bright and colorful, which I loved.  The story was decent until the ending.  The developers clearly intended to make a sequel as they ended the story without any resolution, which was disappointing.  The concept of collecting eggs and hatching them using gathered resources is great, but the execution falls flat.
The egg drop rate is too high overall as often after hatching/raising an egg you will have several other eggs already waiting in your inventory.  I don't think I ever ran out of the resources to hatch eggs either, making them rather useless.  I never had the opportunity to plan out what egg to hatch based on resources because I always had more than enough.  The rarest eggs do take longer to drop but they are manageable.  I think I had all but one egg hatched by the time I finished the story.  That dreaded last egg though.  Apparently it purposefully has a very low drop rate and I have given up on trying to get it after playing through the story twice, doing all the challenges, and countless free plays.  It leaves a bad taste that after getting all of the other eggs with ease, the last is designed to be next to impossible to get.  If you have to force people to continue playing your game by holding one last achievement over their head, then you are too insecure about your game.   It turns the game into a grind.  I don't start up the game thinking "Yay I can relax and play some solitaire for fun", but rather "Maybe this is the time I'll finally get lucky". I think this was a poor design decision that drains the fun.
If you are considering buying this game for the easy achievements, don't.  The last egg takes forever to drop and you will become very frustrated waiting for it.  If you are looking at this game because you like solitaire, go for it.

Shadowverse. This is Japan's #1 card game. So of coarse, its full of anime goodness. The guys and girls are overly sexualized and full of color and  the detailed artwork is absolutly astounding. AND ITS FREE! So with a card game pretty simular to this genre of Magic; the gathering or Hearthstone you pretty much have an idea were it is headed. Choose a leader of Arisa-forestcraft, Erika-swordcraft,Isabelle-runecraft,Rowen-dragoncraft,Luna-shadowcraft,Urias-bloodcraft and Eris-heavencraft. Each leader and craft has a specific playing style and theme. Some cards are specific to that craft. Your leader does have its own set of voice lines and animations for the game. Some of them pretty cool. With your chosen leader and craft there is a story mode. A set story and facing an AI to advance the story and gain rewards of Rupies ( in game currancy) or card tickets to get booster packs of more cards. You learn how to play the game, ( like what a ward,fanfare,ambush,storm and amulet cards are and how to play that specific craft ) The story line keeps you going and the rewards are great. I think I got 20+ booster packs to start the game with and make my own deck. The real diffrence in this game is the evolution ability. During the game you can 2 or 3 times, evolve a card. This beefs up its stats and sometimes even gives abilities. Its becomes a love/hate relationship. Great for when you do it, bad when the other player uses it. The evolved card does some cool animations and changes with some pretty neat artwork to represent the evolution upgrade. Other than story mode you can face the AI or other players in a ranked or unranked games. Rewards are handed out accordingly and you can lv up your leader to gain even more rewards.MORE AND MORE. They are rather generous with the rewards. Also there is a arena mode  where you make a deck and see how many times you can win for....rewards! Deck creation is available or you can auto make decks if you havnt got the right ''formula'' down, but know you have good cards. A profile hub can be created with the right flair and profile name and picture to show your personality. You can even show your contries flag to ''represent'' There is a viewing cards part too, witch is fun to go through and see the incredible artwork. And to think of it maybe this game should be rated for mature....

GTA Vice City is, and will always be, one of the most memorable GTA games. From the voice acting, the setting and the general   #~Ａ Ｅ Ｓ Ｔ Ｈ Ｅ Ｔ Ｉ Ｃ~#   of the game, this game is just down right amazing.
You play as Tommy Vercetti, a recently released from prison mobster from Liberty City sent down to Florida to make some money for the mafia and set Tommy up with a new job. However fate has different ideas for Tommy and one drug deal gone wrong sets this entire movie esq story into motion. A brilliant mob tale set against a neon drenched 1980s Miami parody helps create one of the most wonderful experiences in gaming history.
The game uses the same engine as GTA 3 which did have its issues but they seemed to have been ironed out in Vice City making the experience much more enjoyable. You have access to cars, bikes, boats, helicopters and planes this time around and an arsenal of weapons to help you shred through gangsters and drug barons raging from a chainsaw to a M60 heavy machine gun or even a katana. Unlike later instalments of the GTA series this game doesn't allow character customisation nearly at all, but there are some preset outfits that, in my opinion, are designed well and help create some interesting scenes. For instance you can dress up in a boiler suit and a hockey mask, used in a bank heist, while having a meeting with a real estate mogul.
The missions in this game are awesome, tonnes of variety and there are only a few missions that can be a bit tricky, for example "Checkpoint Charlie" as well as the task for the Cherry Poppers "Ice Cream Factory", but they are few and far between. There are missions involving shoot outs, car chases, blowing up drug factories, gather stars to shoot a porno and being hypnotised by a voodoo lady, it's a long story. Anyway, what I am saying is there is an amazing amount of variety. Furthermore, there are lots of side missions including, assassinations, running a taxi firm, and becoming a vigilante; this game has hours upon hours of game play available.
If you come across any technical difficulties in the game, they can almost all be fixed, from my experience, by turning on the frame limiter for a brief period of time. I don't know why that causes some missions to bug out, mainly missions involving boats, like the previously mentioned "Checkpoint Charlie", as well as a mission with a sea plane and how having the frame limiter off stops the plane from taking off.
The games pace is okay and slows down a little bit towards the end when you have to start acquiring assets and buildings to grow your empire across the city, but that all leads to a satisfying. With voice acting from people like Ray Liotta, Burt Reynolds, Dennis Hopper, Tom Sizemore, they really help convey their characters feelings and thoughts through only their voice that really helps carry the player through the game, making them want to keep playing.
Although this game is old, it still holds up. No i'm not wearing any nostalgia glasses, I genuinely believe this is still a good game over 15 years later.
Pros:
- Great Voice Acting
- Wonderful Setting
- Fun And Enjoyable Missions
- An Amazing Story
- Tonnes Of Features And Content
Cons:
N/A
To conclude, GTA Vice City is a game worth having in your library, and worth the time and effort to play through; from well thought out missions to the setting of the game GTA Vice City is a masterpiece of a game.

Wow.
The reviewers were very, very wrong.
So, i'll just go through a few things first.
1. The story is not ABSOLUTE GARBAGE. Sure it's generic, but some characters scan be likable, it's logical(to an extent) and it fills its position well.
2. It doesn't get boring. The brilliant mechanics here make it a joy to play. Don't take my word for it, look at the people with 30+ hours barely after release.
3. I love the human combat. If you use(abuse) the dodge mechanic, it makes the melee fights interesting versus the skull crunching of zombies.
Anyway, a few thoughts of mine on the game were that albeit the map looking awfully small, the verticality, claustrophobia, terrifying night mode, and imminent danger while on the ground leaves it constantly new, as you're moving too frantically to really pay much attention.
The parkour is absolutely fantastic, with a well worked out skill tree that has very fair progression. It's fluid, fun, and quick, compensating for the hordes of versatile undead.
Speaking of the zombies, I love them. Unlike most gorefest games, these zombies are rarely easy to kill. They're resilient and persistent, making sure that you always second guess that escape plan.
Nighttime is absolutely brilliant, the startling shift of atmosphere and gameplay is jarring and great. The volatiles are terrifying, and I have never enjoyed such a chase as the ones in this game. With the freerunning here the pursuits are pulse pounding and fun. Never have I loved the eerie violet glow of UV lighting more.
Multiplayer is fun, the night hunter is terrifying. The invasion idea is great. Playing as the zombie is fantastic as well.
Weapons are good, I hate the speed at which they break, but it adds a sense of conservation and urgency that's important. Upgrades are interesting, guns are rare enough and dangerous enough to nearly be useless, and the melee produce such a satisfying *crunch* that I rarely use guns anyway.
Soundwork is great when it isnt the voicing. Lots of groans, pops, crunches, etc make it feel real.
Harran is a great setting for this. Really.
KICKING
Overall, the story's failings are made up for in excess by incredibly addictive gameplay. I may not have played much yet, but I have had more fun than in any game from last year in it's entirety.
EDIT: Quick tip: there ARE bugs. Right now i'm stuck where I need to open an elevator, but the doors stay shut without allowing me the command. Watch out for bugfixing updates and wait it out for that if that's your thing.

The sequel to Killing Floor improves the game in many ways, and adds to it. From the improved classes and leveling systems, for the graphics and AI; everything has been improved.
I'll start with the good:
-Graphics have been brought up to date with todays standards, with really good gore and physics.
-AI and difficulty has been improved. In the original game increases in difficulty was simply enemies had more health and dealt more damage, although this remains the same, enemies now have added mechanics that make them more difficult, from blocking headshots, to increased speed and additional abilities. Hopefully additional abilities and mechanics will be added in future.
-Classes have also been changed, with some new classes added. Although the range of weapons remains similar for each class as in the original, the way the classes level up has been improved, with added perks that you can choose to change the playstyle of each class from match to match.
And now the cons:
-Map pool isnt that great in my opinion. Although this is very subjective, i think there isnt a great deal of variation in maps for the game. Although the maps that are there are very good (with one or two exceptions) there just arent enough of them in my opinion, especially big maps like Mountain pass and Farm from the original. The maps for the game right now are all either too small or too claustrophobic. Some people may like this, while some wont.
-Number of weapons. There simply arent enough of them to choose from, and each class (as far as i'm aware from the classes i play) falls into the trap of "these guns are the best, don't use anything else", and not all of them are the most expensive weapons, for example, for the support class (uses mostly shotguns) the sawn-off shotgun and AA12 is the mandatory load out.
-Load times. Not sure if this is just me or a wide spread problem, but loading the game takes far longer than it should, hopefully this will be fixed soon, otherwise its a minor inconvenience.
Possible suggestions for improvement:
-Weapon customisation. Although the game needs more weapons for each class, it'd be a nice addition if you could customise your weapons. Currently there are weapon skins, but i think additional options, such as different sights and attachments would be a nice addition.
-More bosses. Right now there are two different bosses, and i think it'd be nice to have a few more to add to the pool, provided they were different.
Overall, i would definately recommend this game, especially if you have a bunch of friends to play it with. If you played the original, or enjoy co-op horde based FPS then this is for you.

Calling 'Antichamber' a game either says too much or says too little. Yes, you can succeed in 'Antichamber,' sometimes on accident; there are puzzles to solve, and there is a goal. But the goal doesn't really matter; 'Antichamber' is definitely about the things you see on the journey rather than the destination or even the journey itself. The puzzles should be maddening, but they're not. There is a soothing, peaceful detachment to the game, as you wander around the impossible, intricate maze. The mechanic of the space around you warping based on your perception doesn't get old, though there are times when you just really, really want to get past a door - and have absolutely no idea how to do so.
It's definitely not for everyone, but it's worth a look for no other reason than just to see it. Clever, strange, and created by accident (the origin of 'Antichamber' was a mistake by its creator while building an entirely different sort of game).

I wanted Marble Blast Ultra with some things to make it its own. It's not that, but it's decently fun. The physics are good and the aesthetics/music are very well done.
That said, the level design is bad. Real bad. The first world is legitimately great, with sprawling levels that have just enough linearity to have purpose and just enough space to foster exploration. People are complaining about the second world a lot, and they're correct, but the problem doesn't really go away.
Yes, the bloom in the second world is such that you can't see platforms. And thus far, it is definitely the worst world I've seen (though I've only seen three so far). However, world three has many of the same problems. Platforms that are tiny, a wonky camera and environments that stifle progress,
An example: An early level in world three (er, two in the game) has you navigating tiny platforms along a cliffside. The platforms are so small that even a slightly mistimed jump means you're rolling into a pit (that doesn't kill you). Even worse, the cliffside juts out from the side in many areas. This means that on some platforms, if you jump straight up, you'll get knocked to the side and off the platform. It's either an oversight or an attempt to make the game longer. It's just bad.
I am making this a positive review because despite everything it is still somewhat fun. The devs are pretty active and I believe them when they say Workshop support is coming. When that drops, the game may become a must buy for user-created levels.
Verdict: If you want a simple rolling physics game with some quirks and no originality, pick this game up, play it for a week and forget about it until Workshop comes along.

In a world of AAA titles with breathtaking graphics, I suppose it's strange to some that people still buy and play these dinosaurs... But much like a how a book can pull you in, this story can be so engrossing that you look past the archaic nature of it and enjoy it for the sum of it's parts.
Because I've played some of their previous titles and trust in this developer to deliver quality text games, I jumped on this when I saw it on sale for 2.99. It did not disappoint.
You play the role of a mortal that gradually becomes aware of their growing power, and of a greater destiny. But this power does not come freely, and the responsibilities that come with embracing it ( or are thrust upon you, depending on your character ) lead to many challenges.
The game borrows here and there from Greek culture, mythology, and folklore to set up a world to tell the story you want to read. You can play the part of the brave warrior, a reluctant hero, a cruel tyrant, etc. The story itself will generally go in the same vague direction every time, but enough of the details change that if you can get absorbed in your character and the various outcomes, you will enjoy it.
The only things that bothered me were that sometimes the choices didn't make it clear which stat an action drew upon. For instance, during a battle scene, I thought throwing a spear might rely upon dexterity and quickness, and chose it because I thought it fit my character. Nope! Turns out it's more strength than anything else. There's a few moments like that, but you can figure out the lion's share of the choices.
All in all, I had fun with it. It took me just over 5 hours from start to finish, but I feel I got my money's worth, and I've yet to start my second run. The ending hints at more games to come in the series, and I sure hope so. I want my chance to break even with the Gods for all the guff they've given me.

Such as thorn-covered cards, which you need to uncover by getting rid of another pile first, or frozen cards that you need to melt with a 'fireblast' card in some other pile, which you need to get rid of first. Also, there are unlockable power-ups of sorts. In its core, though, it still is a pretty simple solitaire-like game, so it does get repetitive and boring pretty fast. Unless you are into that sort of games, of course.
I do recommend the game, as it has a pretty original feeling to it, it's made pretty well (despite looking pretty amateurish here and there — such as the pets, I'd say), and even has an adventure mode with a voice-acted story. Besides, despite it starting to feel repetitive to me, I still kept playing it for some reason, haha.

is a isometric tactical RPG. In a dystopian future, where dormant elf, orc and troll genes reemerged in the population, where immortal dragons run mega-corporations that control the world, mercenaries run the shadows to do everyone else’s dirty work with the use of guns, magic and technologies. They call themselves Shadowrunners. This review takes into account the free
released later after the game.
: The first module, called Dead Man’s Switch, is a nice although straightforward introduction to players who aren’t familiar with the game and explores the Seattle setting. The second module, called Dragonfall, offers a lot more character development and additional flexibility and options to complete any given quest, all while exploring the anarchy-governed flux-state of Berlin. The game backgrounds are gorgeous hand-drawn stills, added with the techno-trance music gives the game an eerie atmosphere, each building and object seemingly having a story of its own to tell, while the music adjust to combat scenes before slowing down once you’re back from it. The game progression is straightforward, the skills are broken down into skill trees with a clear view of what you get from raising any attributes or skill. There is no set character class, although you have pre-generated archetypes you can start from.

: The story is somewhat linear, most of all in Dead Man’s Switch, where choice will change the dialog but not the outcome of the story. General graphics aren’t on par with the AAA industry, so anyone looking for graphical realism will be sorely disappointed. There is no voice acting, so get ready to read a lot if you want to have any hopes of feeling involved in the story. The two modules which happen at the same time, aren’t related to each other, so there is no progression from one to the other, and are both somewhat quick to play through.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
Let’s judge the game for what it is: a crowdfunded indie game (the success story that put Kickstarter on the map for many people) meant to be used as an engine for the modding community, community that has been very active at creating new stories, new equipment, new world object for other modders, and is using the engine in new and creative ways. As you play, you can feel the richness of the game’s tabletop RPG heritage, and you just wish you could learn more about that world. It is fun, it is well worth the money and time, and it’s definitively a game I recommend!
