As Civ games go, this is a well-designed and visually pleasing game which is potentially truly great in strategic terms. Having said this, however, Civ V has one major flaw: while it
sometimes be very enjoyable, the game is sadly often made either unwinnable or
easy-to-win due to the often-imbalanced (sometimes extremely so) random initial spawns (in terms of either amounts, locations, or both) of six critically important resources: Horses, Iron, Coal, Oil, Aluminium* and Uranium. This frequently occurring problem is then exacerbated because these resources are not visible until the player (or AI) researches the tech required to utilise the resources in question, meaning that long-term games which look promising, and may have taken many hours to develop, may either have to be abandoned, or may end up being far too easy to win and thus very unsatisfying.
Negative rating given with
regret, since I am normally a huge fan of the CIV franchise.

So much has been said about Civ V (and indeed the whole Civ franchise) that, to be honest, anything I might attempt in the way of an "overall" review - short of writing a really, really in-depth spiel, which I don't have time to write just at the moment! - would be pretty redundant. Another day, I'll get round to the really, really in-depth waffle - but for now, here's a somewhat in-depth waffle, but about just ONE aspect of the game - and, for me, it's an absolutely crucial one.
And so: here's my solitary, but significant, whinge about an otherwise excellent game - only one point, but a real game-breaker for me. While Civ V is everything that the previous Civs were, and more, and while it's graphically lovely, great fun to play, very well-balanced, impressively rich in content and complexity, and, in short, ALMOST everything a turn-based strategy game should be, it has (for me) one critical flaw, which always ends up frustrating me to the point of screaming into the nearest pillow while scuttling back to trusty old Civ II - yes, with its terrible Advisers and all! (Actually, I rather like them, but this is meant to be a review of Civ V, not Civ II... :D)
Civ V's fatal flaw, in my view, is the way in which resources are initially spawned and distributed - combined with the fact that you
get to discover where the resources are until you research the necessary tech required to use that particular resource, so you can't just glance at the map at the beginning, see that you're in a dreadful location resource-wise, and start over again without wasting any time and effort. This doesn't matter too much for "optional" or "desirable" resources, but - and here's what drives me mad - it can happen, according to the game's random spawn, that you may find you have very little, or even NONE, of the six CRITICAL resources, all of which are absolute game-winners or game-breakers, depending on whether or not you have them, and/or how much you have of them. These resources are Horses, Iron, Coal, Oil, Aluminium* and Uranium - with Horses, Iron and Uranium being insanely important.
BUT, as I say, you can't see any of these resources on the map until you reach the right tech level. Without these resources (especially the Big Three), or with only tiny amounts, and (as often happens) with the rest located on the wrong side of one or more other nations' territory, you'll lose  sooner or later - definitely. May as well just re-start.
And no, this isn't hasty pessimism - it's endless attempts, via various methods (trading, warring, trying to sneak around the edges of whatever nation does
want me to reach those lovely resources... or all three at once!), followed by simply giving up, after too many promising games ground to a dead halt at the point where I realised I didn't have any (or enough) of X or Y essential resource.
For example: trying to survive the early game with no Horsemen, the mid-game with no Iron or Coal, or the end-game with no Aluminium or Uranium is simply impossible, unless you play in Idiot Mode, which of course is no fun (and sometimes even then!). And, of course, the AI - especially once it realises (and it does!) what a huge advantage it has gained by owning these critical resources - will
trade anything for them, no matter HOW much you offer in return, and especially if YOU have none at all of whatever you're trying to bribe, cajole or threaten out of them. In my experience, the AI nations would (and often do, if I can muster the armies!) rather die than hand over so much as a single pony, or a small cupful of iron filings. As for trading Uranium, well... hahaha. Ha.
In short, and while, of course, not EVERY game ends up with the player suffering from a crucial lack of essential resources, this insanely annoying random resource spawn problem can mean going through hours (or, if you like to micro-manage as much as I do, WEEKS!) of game-play, setting up all kinds of lovely trade routes, road networks, mighty cities, military strategies, diplomatic agreements and so on, generally having a great time... BEFORE realising that you'll get no further, thanks to a poor resource spawn shooting all your plans down in flames.
Of course, it's not ALWAYS the case that the game's critical resources are unevenly distributed: that's the nature of "random", after all! *SOME* games are enjoyably equal matches, all things considered and give or take a Horse here or an Atomic Bomb there - but I found that at least 75% of the games I started would end up, sooner or later, failing due to either the player or the AI lacking crucial resources. Some might think that it would be a stroke of good fortune if it were the AI whose resource-lottery luck was awful, but in my opinion, when this happens, it's actually ALSO pretty non-fun: for me, at least, easily wiping out helpless adversaries simply because your resources dice-roll was better than theirs is oddly unsatisfying. Not so much "turn-based strategy" as "turn-based luck"... :(
Anyway. After many, many failed attempts, I am now more or less an ex-Civ V player, although I do still give it a whirl, in the hope of striking a nice, evenly balanced resource spawn (I know, I never learn!). I *love* the Civ franchise, and I REALLY wanted to enjoy Civ V, with all the general improvements it has over Civ II - and, to be fair, I've already gained a lot of enjoyment just appreciating the in-game mechanics and the wonderful amount of work that went into the game... until, near enough every time, I inevitably hit a lack of X or Y resource, and realised that The End Was Nigh.
In conclusion, then, it's for this reason, and this alone, that I can't honestly recommend Civ V (much though I wish I could), and it's also why I very rarely play it now... of course, that doesn't mean I'm Civ-less (can't imagine that!): yes, I'm back with good old Civ II - which, for all its AI faults, at least doesn't feature anything as critically game-breaking as the Dreaded Resource Spawn of Doom!

Mildly entertaining, Shadowrun Returns, will keep you occupied throughout the game's brief plot.  The game seems to capture the feel of Shadowrun with the lingo, environment, and graphic content.  However, the turn-based game system and weak AI seriously detract from the challenge of the game.  There was no battle that I couldn't win due to obvious strategic placement of characters and there are fairly large flaws that allow you to exploit the game's design to ensure you win if you are only a bit more patient.  At no point did I feel challenged or uncertain of what my options or solution paths were.  The game's brief story is very railroaded which is disappointing because (I believe) everything is there to make a quality story complete with multiple paths and multi-finality.  It just seems like they rushed to get this game out once they had a somewhat functional system and put together a demo story.  I would give it a 2/5 stars for anyone who traditionally likes the Shadowrun feel or most Future Sci-Fi RPGs.   It's good to kill time, but nothing to write home about.

As you may or may not know, I spent years of my life playing every kind of tower defense game. Kingdom Rush, Incursion, Bloons, Cursed Treasure, Gemcraft, Protector..
I hope you know these series, 'cos they're the most beautiful games ever made!! Although unfortunately they're only available on Flash websites (but maybe they're also on smartphones or other devices, I don't know them).

Graphics of course are top down, but they're crap and the game is insanely slow and bugged.

Apart from the Trump/Mexican setting (I don't know if it's interesting to someone, for an European like me we really  don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about Trump and the U.S.A. in general, not in a harsh way don't get me wrong, it's just that Europe is already extremely complicated with all of our problems and most Europeans don't really care about Americas or other continents), which is poorly rendered, you don't have to "create your strategy" as the game store says.

Take a look at the screenshots in the game store page, 'cos that's everything you will get. Completely unrecommended, especially compared to free games which can keep you playing for months like the Gemcraft or the Cursed Treasure series or even series like Incursion in which you are forced to put (like in this game) the towers in pre-fixed places. Revelations 2 feels like several steps in the right direction, back towards the original Resident Evils. It takes contol elements from the later titles in the franchise and incorporates them with the older survival horror atmosphere, and has managed to blend the two concepts very well. On the harder difficulties there will be points where you have to weigh the value of running over expending ammo and possibly running out when you need it most. You're given a third choice though, through your partner: utilizing their abilities to stun your targets and follow up with a physical attack ala Resident Evil 5 and 6. The story is, to me, well written with strong characters, and it's refreshing to see Barry Burton in a leading role. This game has easily pushed him into one of my favorite characters in the franchise. If you've come for the story, I don't think you'll be disappointed. It feels like a true Resident Evil.

Steam graciously provided a refund and I continued about my way. Well, thankfully, either via patches, or h/w, I am able to play it quite easily at about medium//low settings, at 1920x1080 with the following h/w specs:
i3-2120 3.3ghz
12 gig ddr3 ram
Nvidia GTX 750 ti 2gig
I've played all the previous versions (on the previous h/w components), and currently, it plays almost on par as my previous experiences. I am about 80% through the main story, with a good chunk of the side missions concurrently running. The story takes place right after Arkham City, and it's jammed packed with a lot. Thankfully, there are a few lulls in the main storyline line to run the sidemissions (I've never liked the game concept of putting an emergency orientated main story line on pause to run side quest puzzles...seems like they'd always make the main plot such a priority, why would someone take time out to move some cows around, or something.)
One thing I've never liked about the Rocksteady/Montreal games is that everything takes place in a single night. Just the gameplay alone is going to take me a full day, if not more. How am I supposed to equate my sitting on a roof top, trying to figure out what to do next, a dozen times over, to equal out to a single night?! I continue to bend my own narrative, I guess.
So far, the only thing that really, truly bugged me about this game is the Riddler/Batmobile runs. If I have to die several times during a run, just to figure out the 'map,' it kills the immersion a bit. Puzzles are fine. Puzzles at 60 mph are a PITA. Maybe the Arkham Knight finale...I mean, how many times am I going to let the guy go before I beat his♥♥♥♥♥
Past that? The game rocks. The Batmobile battles? Awesome. The chase? Still awesome. The on foot navigation through the city? Always awesome. A bigger, more active city? Still awesome! (though I really liked Origin's Xmas theme...)
End result...you liked the previous games and have my hardware, or better? You can get in on this now and should be fine.

Intro
TL;DR: Polyball is a marble rolling game in a low-poly artstyle with many features where features and exploration are strong, but the gameplay itself is not as deep as others like Marble Blast. Got this game as a key from the developer. Since I have not completed all the game, I also must inform that I've only completed worlds 0-2 (3). This review will be updated as I play more.
Gameplay: Best: 7.5, Worst: 4, Innovation: 2
[Mechanics]
Solid but not special. Unlike other games in the genre like Marble Blast, there are very few special mechanics, let alone unique mechanics in this game. If you are looking for a game in this genre that's new and unique, you won't get it here. The mechanics besides basic jumping and moving, as far as I've played: instant death, "balance" platforms, booster pads, jump pads.
[Design]
The game's design can be split into the couple worlds it has right now as well as misc. design. Overall, it's fluctuating but overall okay.:
[World 1... Um, Zero]
Known as the "Great Forest" in game. And in my opinion, it is great... as it's the biggest highlight of the game as far as I played. As the game has no unique mechanics to really surprise the player with, this world appears to be a start towards trying to take advantage of another thing, exploration. The levels are pretty big, yet for some reason, most are still linear. However, it's still solid.
[World 2... Wait, One]
Known as the "Volcano" in game... but is more like "Bright Glowing Pizza Land". This is probably the lowest moment of the game, since most levels have the platforms (brown) blend in with the walls (almost the same shade of brown) and also at an angle where you can't exactly see the shape of the next platform! The linearity of the levels get even stronger with this one.
[World 3... Er, Two]
Known as the "Desert" in game... but is more like "Slowly Shrinking Chopstick Land". The game seems to push away from exploration and go with simple platforming which is fine, but seems misguided since it is of course, simple. There is nothing too bad about this section.
[World 4... Actually, Three]
Known as the "Space" in game... I've only played around 4 levels. Only problem is the fact that along with the camera jitter, there are so many models on screen it will frameskip a lot.
[Miscellaneous]
The camera has "mouse acceleration" and if you have a bad framerate or even just a few skips, you will find yourself making 360's for no reason on a frameskip if you're looking around. That screwed me over a couple of times.
[Features]
Each level has 3 main notable things about them: "shards" (100 points, and you can use them to buy cosmetics in the shop), goal time, and hidden trophies. The game has a lot of customization available to you, including a lot of choices for marble shape/color bought with "shards" found in the levels (graphically annoying when you hit them softly and it still resembles a shard that has not been taken yet). Level selection is completely linear besides the extra levels.
Graphics: Best: 7, Worst: 3, Innovation: 0
[Game]
It's a low-poly artstyle which has been done before, and it's done well here too... besides the "glowing pizza" zone that I referred to earlier. Nothing too special, though.
[UI]
Decent. There are some particularly annoying elements, however, like not being able to know if you passed a par time or score, as well as not showing if you got the trophy of that area. It would also benefit from customization options.
+ Decent otherwise
- Bad second chapter
Story: 5, Innovation: 0
This game has a "story mode", but there's not really a story. It's more of an excuse to have different backdrops/looks for each level. Not much to say here.
Sound: 7.5, Innovation: 0
There are no sound clashes and the music is pretty good and it fits. I especially like the effects when you are going too slow.
Replayability: 7.5, Innovation: 3
There is a lot of replayability in the game as with the other games in this genre. You do get to see world bests and their marble-ghost.
Overall: 7
Positives
+ Unique world exploration
+ Good amount of features
+ Speedrun-friendly
Negatives
- Gameplay depth is shallow
- Price is high if you aren't going for replayability
I recommend this game to
- Speedrunners who want more levels
- People who would like a small amount of exploration elements
I don't recommend this game to
- People looking for something new and unique
Misc
+ Devs respond to community

Even in Early Access, Polyball is still a really fun ball-rolling game! The main focus is the Marble Blast gameplay, and it's solidly executed. The controls felt tight, whether you choose keyboard or controller. Because of how unique the gameplay is, the controls take some getting used to, but it's satisfying to blast through a stage once you have the hang of it. Another great addition are the leaderboards. After every stage there is a list of times, and it really increases the replayability when you try to get your name among the top 10. The developers are actively asking players for input, so you can expect for this game to have more levels, more customizations, and hopefully more modes. As it is, I highly recommend giving this game a shot if you're familiar with other ball-rolling games.

On the same day that I express a disinterest in FaeVerse Alchemy (by the same devs) because of content, I will also express an enjoyment for this game. It's Solitaire, but a tweaked version of it that is really easy to pick up. Additional mechanics are slowly introduced as the game progresses, so the learning curve is pretty gradual.
I'm not too keen on the management bit of levelling up dropped eggs that can be hatched, which
have to be evolved with the right materials. I feel like the aspect is there for people who like playing a game with some quest-like structure, but it's so unobtrusive that I've been playing this game for a couple of hours straight and have completely forgotten about my pets. You know, the more I play, pardon the phrasing, "Choice of Games" games, the more I grow accustomed to them, expecting to see more or less the same, just in different setting. This game was a very pleasant exception to me.
There were moments when I thought "damn, I wish the author thought about including this or that". But just playing a bit further revealed that the author actually thought about this too. It was one of the rare games, where by the end of it I actually felt like it's a complete story, finished just the way I wanted it to end.
The stats are non-intrusive and absolutely logical. I have never felt the urge to redo something just to fix my stats a bit, like I did in some of the games.
The choices and consequences are there and of the two playthroughs I've had, I didn't find a single choice that wouldn't at least change a scene or two, which is great - the replayability is definitely there.
And one last thing I simply MUST mention. The game is finished. With the current trend of many great games (CYOA, I mean, of course) being "Part 1, wait for another game to see what's coming!", it's a breath of fresh air. The pacing is great. The length is perfect. The endings are satisfying. And yet if author wanted to, he could still write a continuation to that story, I bet. That's how you do these games. Amazing.
So, overall, this is one of, if not the best Choice of Games adventures I've been through. Definitely recommend it to anyone interested in the genre and/or setting.

How do you poke fun at an entire industry, like the video game industry, that already tends towards being self-deprecating?  I don't know.  The makers of The Stick of Truth largely don't either.
Make no mistake, the game has funny moments.  But most of the game's humor is not "funny - ha ha."  It's "funny - I recognize this from the show!  That makes me part of something!"  You see all your old favorite characters doing all the things they did in real episodes.  Sometimes there's a twist on it, sometimes there isn't.  If you thought it was funny when you saw it on TV, you'll think it's kind of, sort of funny playing that scene again here.  Yippie, I guess?
The overarching plot is original, though.  To the extent there's any belly laughs to be had here, they're in the original jokes and plot points.
Game play is in the style of a classic RPG.  You and your sidekicks fight bad guys in turn based battles.  You gain levels, and you equip weapons, armor and accessories.  But something about the implementation feels wrong here.  The whole idea behind levels and experience is to manage the player's progression - it keeps you out of areas they're not ready for, and encourages you to leave areas they've effectively leveled out of.  But in this game, the enemies level up right along side the player.  If you thought a baddie was too tough at level 5, when you come back 2 levels later, he's now level 7 too and basically just as tough as he was before.  I wonder why I bothered to fight those 20 elves when I could have just avoided them, gotten to the boss battle and done pretty much as well as I did with all that time and experience invested into the game.
Upgrading your equipment makes a difference, but it doesn't feel like an accomplishment.  It just feels like a grind.  Finally being able to equip the level 13 sword doesn't make me feel more powerful. It just makes me feel level 13.   I can't find the energy to care that much.
On the whole it's not a bad game, and it's a solid adaptation from the show.  It's the South Park game that South Park fans were waiting for, but that doesn't make it great.  It's just OK.  Ok is enough.

I Know this is a text-adventure game, but it's still too lazy on the front-end side. As a designer, here are my notes to improve that feedback;
- I think the typography is really weak. The dialogues, story and any other text-based information uses the same style. I think the emotions, the story and the dialogues should be used with different typographic presentation. (for example; dialogues should be bigger and more contrast in color, whereas the story could be a bit smaller.) I believe this will in general reduce the stress for the pages that have TOO MUCH TEXT.
- Also, i think background music / ambient sounds would be very effective for the game. When in battle, a more dramatic music, or when in a Town Hall or somewhere near danger, a bit stressful music. Also when your attempt fails or works. I mean there are tons of opportunities of aural feedbacks.
- Yes i still know it's a text-adventure game, but subtle visual elements would enhance the gameplay feedback still.
For example some background image when your environment changes, or again, when you success or fail. Or when one of your stat increases - decreases, or you have a new gift etc. I'll talk about that in the GUI section.
The game also has GUI in the "stats" section. Which contains your characters summary, her stats, attributes, gifts etc. These are visual elements, but for some reason they are poorly presented, and even hidden from the game. Text is visual, and i think representing those Attributes, Gifts, Items etc. in-game as a Graphical User Interface would be much more powerful. (Blizzard's spell icons is a nice example)
Those elements i just mentioned are used in the game called Cypher, it looks like a REALLY nice text-based game. I just think being a text-adventure game does not compensate the lack of visuals still. I'm having fun, but i sometimes get bored when it's a huge chunk of text with no visual polishes in it.
I recommend it though.

hello this game is Hearthstone but better. there's almost no annoying RNG cards like "summon a random x-cost minion" or Discover, and the cards that do have a random effect are just ones that draw a card or not really useful. the games are also much quicker too, like around 5 minutes each at tops, and i'm pretty sure drawing your whole deck is an instant loss so there's no painfully tedious fatigue battles either. the evolution mechanic, which is sort of the Main Thing of the game, is much more interesting than the dinky hero powers of Hearthstone. you can use an evo point on a follower the same turn you play it to slam a threat out of the way, wait until the next turn and use it to go for face, or utilize one of the many followers that have an additional ability upon evolution. it's basically Inspire if it were limited to 2/3 uses per game and most of the effects were actually Good.
the arena is also much more expedient, lasting only 5 rounds and the rewards break even at around 3/4 wins, which is not difficult to achieve in my opinion. it's very easy to do arena infinitely and build up the standard card set to a respectable level, which is what i did and thusly i have never spent money on this game at all and do not plan to as i do not feel like it is necessary. there's also login bonuses and frequent card / pack giveaways, as well as many in-game achievements that reward the in-game currency. you can even buy character skins with the in-game currency, wow!
there's also a story mode for each of the seven characters. it's bad and rowen is a jerk and i have no idea why he's the face of the ENG App icon. but you'll want to do them all to get the rewards and they all serve as a nice tutorial to get used to each class's specific gimmick.
last and most importantly there's memes. there's a ding-dong, and a really funny egg, and you can gasp 3 times as an elf and have a good grand old time.
in conclusion this game is good and Hearthstone is bad and even badder in comparisonation. i've been playing this for like half a year every day and am still not tired of it somehow. on the other hand Hearthstone puts me to sleep and i hate it. that's the end of my review. thank you

Wow.
The reviewers were very, very wrong.
So, i'll just go through a few things first.
1. The story is not ABSOLUTE GARBAGE. Sure it's generic, but some characters scan be likable, it's logical(to an extent) and it fills its position well.
2. It doesn't get boring. The brilliant mechanics here make it a joy to play. Don't take my word for it, look at the people with 30+ hours barely after release.
3. I love the human combat. If you use(abuse) the dodge mechanic, it makes the melee fights interesting versus the skull crunching of zombies.
Anyway, a few thoughts of mine on the game were that albeit the map looking awfully small, the verticality, claustrophobia, terrifying night mode, and imminent danger while on the ground leaves it constantly new, as you're moving too frantically to really pay much attention.
The parkour is absolutely fantastic, with a well worked out skill tree that has very fair progression. It's fluid, fun, and quick, compensating for the hordes of versatile undead.
Speaking of the zombies, I love them. Unlike most gorefest games, these zombies are rarely easy to kill. They're resilient and persistent, making sure that you always second guess that escape plan.
Nighttime is absolutely brilliant, the startling shift of atmosphere and gameplay is jarring and great. The volatiles are terrifying, and I have never enjoyed such a chase as the ones in this game. With the freerunning here the pursuits are pulse pounding and fun. Never have I loved the eerie violet glow of UV lighting more.
Multiplayer is fun, the night hunter is terrifying. The invasion idea is great. Playing as the zombie is fantastic as well.
Weapons are good, I hate the speed at which they break, but it adds a sense of conservation and urgency that's important. Upgrades are interesting, guns are rare enough and dangerous enough to nearly be useless, and the melee produce such a satisfying *crunch* that I rarely use guns anyway.
Soundwork is great when it isnt the voicing. Lots of groans, pops, crunches, etc make it feel real.
Harran is a great setting for this. Really.
KICKING
Overall, the story's failings are made up for in excess by incredibly addictive gameplay. I may not have played much yet, but I have had more fun than in any game from last year in it's entirety.
EDIT: Quick tip: there ARE bugs. Right now i'm stuck where I need to open an elevator, but the doors stay shut without allowing me the command. Watch out for bugfixing updates and wait it out for that if that's your thing.
It's like Hearthstone but with better artwork and voice acting. Also, the evolution aspect of the game makes it much more exciting.. This is a fantastic game and this is a fantastic review. Rate up.

Batman Arkham Knight is the final game in the Arkham trilogy. It has a new large map with upgraded graphics and the batmobile.
The Plot
I will be talking about events which happened in previous Arkham Games so im going to write this in a way thats assuming you've played them. The main story is probably the best out of the Arkham games. It is no longer set in mainland Gotham but on the islands on the edge of Gotham. Scarecrow is the main villian and he just threatened the entire population of Gotham with his fear toxin. Everyone is evacuated and coincedentally, the story is set on Hallowe'en. The only people left behind are those who enjoy violence and terror. Scarecrow has hired a whole Militia run by an engima known as "The Arkham Knight". Very liitle is known about him and he has a very strong grudge against Batman. There are also other people who are interested in taking down the Bat. This includes Two-Face, Penguin, Riddler and more. Playing as Batman(Obviously) you must takedown Scarecrow and the Knight. In Arkham City, when Joker dies, Batman becomes guilt ridden and believes he is responsible for his death. Joker always said that Batman was his equal, that he had the mind of a killer like him, that they are both the way they are becuase of "Them". This is Batman biggest fear: Turning into Joker. Due to this, Joker hops into dialogue frequently, talking to Bruce. This is a great feature, I was worried there wasn't going to be anymore Mark Hamill. It has alot of side missions with alot of available DLCs. However, in order to unlock the games full ending you must complete EVERY sidemission which means you have to complete EVERY RIddler challenge. After over 100hrs, i still have not gotten everything as it is too long and boring. In Arkham City I actually enjoyed collecting the Trophies because the tasks were actually interesting.
Gameplay
The gameplay is great, as you can tell by my playtime. It keeps the same freeflow combat as before and the AI(Enemies) has been improved. The counters are no longer delayed and the combat flows so much better. There are new combo takedowns and new enemies. These enemies include medics who can revive neutralized opponents, and Martial Artisits who have very complex move patterns. The biggest upgrade is the Batmobile. You're going to end up having a love/hate relationship with the Batmobile. Let me first explain what it does. It has a 60mm cannon and a machine gun. It also has a missile barrage, an emp shock and a virus to stop drones. The new UI includes new WayneTech upgardes for the batmobile which will enhance it in combat. The batmobile is very entertaing at the start of the game but then it gets overused. The game forces you to use it and it becomes a very tedious chore.
Performance
At its launch.... Im sure you know about those days. But now most bugs have been patched and the game runs perfectly. It really eats away at your RAM so I suggest using a memory cleaner if you have below 8GB RAM. The graphics are really good, no jagged edges or bad lighting and smooth animations, so... You're going to need a good GPU. I'd say 2GB minimum which will only support lowest settings. 4GB for 30-50fps on High settings and for optimal performance use a 6GB GPU which will get you 90 fps or even 120(You can change the Max Fps in Bmsetting.ini file. The directory is ProgramfilesX86/Steam/steamapps/common/BatmanArkhamKnight/Bmgame/) You're also going to need a good CPU, Id say and Intel core i5 2500 3.3Ghz or an AMD equivalent. Match this criteria and you're good to go.
Overall
It has a great dark story, unique combat and beautiful visuals. A great way to finish the Arkham series which has a bitter-sweet ending. Get it on sale and savour every moment of gameplay. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys a great story or a Die-Hard Batman fan.

Mirror's Edge is very different from most 'FPS' games because it pretty much loses the 'shooter' part and becomes 'first person parkour'. This is a very interesting concept at first but after playing through this game I've come to realise the concept doesn't work too well. The problem I had with this game is that it seems to contradict itself. The game is supposed to be fluent with the free-running in first person view  which should keep you immersed... But this didn't really happen with me. I would have my moments but I would end up in a room or some small area where I just got stuck for ages, so I would be in one place for a while trying to figure out what to do and/or even having to pull up a walkthrough, even worse there was a point where I'd keep dying because I couldn't figure it out and I ended up having to retry this small area too many times to count. The problem is that you can't really see all around you because you're just staring at walls (and sometimes the textures weren't too nice to look at) and the parkour is pretty much down to you, it's not automatic like in the 'Assassin's Creed' games, so the actual parkour becomes a puzzle and as a result you're likely to get stuck somewhere. The story wasn't anything special and it was a bit confusing to follow, also being chased by the 'blues' got pretty repetitive. Finally, of course the graphics are very, very beautiful except for close up textures, which I mentioned earlier. I recommend buying this game but I wouldn't suggest buying this at full price.

I heard a lot of mixed reviews for this game, and I have to say I was quite pleasantly surprised. It's not a perfect game, but it's a very enjoyable take on the genre, with enough innovation to feel fresh.
PROS:
- the biggest pro is the writing; the story is excellent noir-ish cyberpunk fare, and the dialogue is very well written
- combat (especially late game combat) can be thrilling
- the environments are attractive
- there are some small and pleasing genre innovations (for example, hiring a party on a mission-to-mission basis, inventory/stash management is well done, the stat/levelling system is very versatile and effective)
- the hacking system can lead to some really great combat encounters with fighting happening simultaneously in the real world and the matrix, and consequences of each fight has limited spillover on to the other
CONS:
- the game is quite short with very little outside the main story path; I did every side mission and finished in under 9 hours
- the combat music is repetitive
- not enough weapons,  some balance issues,  some stats/classes basically worthless
- the environments felt dead; few people in the environment, even fewer that will talk to you, and zero incentive to explore (not really any scavenging)
- some of the lategame setpiece fights are too long and repetitive
- the game was too easy overall (played on normal)
anyway, I hear Dragonfall is better, so I'll be getting that too, but if this is on sale or something and Dragonfall isn't, it's still worth your money.

For a game from 2008, damn it still looks good. This game is atmospheric and terrifying. The close quarters claustrophobic and dim lit rooms tied with terrifyingly disgusting and difficult aliens makes this game gritty and unnerving while still being so enjoyable. Dead Space throws you into tight cramped and dark rooms that give almost an anxiety of what lies beyond the corners, and the game throws you the curveball of limited ammunition and tough enemies that makes you hope for ammo and money. Dead Space has a feel that many games fail to achieve, and that is vulnerability. As you play as Isaac, theres this vulnerability to you that questions your safety in every room until closer to the endgame, and it almost makes you question areas you considered safe. Even with a long 10-14 hour story, the necromorphs never really get old or stale, and in fact get increasingly more difficult and grotesque the more you play, keeping you just on the edge of your seat the whole time. The story to Dead Space is also quite good, in fact, it kept me hooked from start to finish. Overall this game is a pretty good horror classic that I would recommend.

Dead Space is one of the only games I've immediately replayed upon completion. I remember the first time I experienced this game back in 2008 on my 360, and I am amazed at how well it holds up. Great atmosphere, gorgeous art direction (beautiful in the way it depicts a greasy mining ship!), excellent voice acting, varied and disgusting enemies, and incredibly satisfying combat. I find the game a tad too easy, but fortunately you can play Hard mode the first time through and that gives a decent enough challenge. If you are a fan of scifi horror in the vein of The Thing/Event Horizon/Alien then you would definitely enjoy Dead Space. Be aware that you will need a fan made patch for mouse aiming if you don't plan on using a controller (X360 controller works beautifully), and a program to cap the framerate at 60 (I recommend free Rivatuner). Physics are absolutely broken if you don't cap the framerate, otherwise I encountered no issues in my playthrough on a gtx1080 and 6700k with Win10

How do you poke fun at an entire industry, like the video game industry, that already tends towards being self-deprecating?  I don't know.  The makers of The Stick of Truth largely don't either.
Make no mistake, the game has funny moments.  But most of the game's humor is not "funny - ha ha."  It's "funny - I recognize this from the show!  That makes me part of something!"  You see all your old favorite characters doing all the things they did in real episodes.  Sometimes there's a twist on it, sometimes there isn't.  If you thought it was funny when you saw it on TV, you'll think it's kind of, sort of funny playing that scene again here.  Yippie, I guess?
The overarching plot is original, though.  To the extent there's any belly laughs to be had here, they're in the original jokes and plot points.
Game play is in the style of a classic RPG.  You and your sidekicks fight bad guys in turn based battles.  You gain levels, and you equip weapons, armor and accessories.  But something about the implementation feels wrong here.  The whole idea behind levels and experience is to manage the player's progression - it keeps you out of areas they're not ready for, and encourages you to leave areas they've effectively leveled out of.  But in this game, the enemies level up right along side the player.  If you thought a baddie was too tough at level 5, when you come back 2 levels later, he's now level 7 too and basically just as tough as he was before.  I wonder why I bothered to fight those 20 elves when I could have just avoided them, gotten to the boss battle and done pretty much as well as I did with all that time and experience invested into the game.
Upgrading your equipment makes a difference, but it doesn't feel like an accomplishment.  It just feels like a grind.  Finally being able to equip the level 13 sword doesn't make me feel more powerful. It just makes me feel level 13.   I can't find the energy to care that much.
On the whole it's not a bad game, and it's a solid adaptation from the show.  It's the South Park game that South Park fans were waiting for, but that doesn't make it great.  It's just OK.  Ok is enough.

FTL: Faster than Light is honestly like no other game I've played before. You control a spaceship and its crew, flying through space while trying to evade the rebel fleet chasing you across the galaxy with random encounters over every horizon. You'll find bandits, settlers, ship wrecks, rogue AI ships, as well as the occasional merchant station. Your ultimate goal is to gather enough weapons and scrap through exploration to outfit your ship with enough weapons and upgrades to win the final battle, or valiantly die trying. Its roguelike nature ensures you will die many times before you successfully beat the game, but it's such an enjoyable game that you'll want to keep coming back till you beat it. There's also ships to unlock that have vastly different layouts, with different crews and weapon systems, that add a lot of replayability. Finally, the soundtrack is perfectly matched for the game, enhancing just about every moment of the game with its wonderful themes and melodies that really complete the whole experience.
This game has earned an automatic purchase from me for any DLC or expansion they make in the future, no matter what price. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a well rounded, finely polished game at a great price that is truly worth every penny.

Captain's Log, Stardate -309538.54318873666
We have just departed the Federation base and the crew is optimistic about our chances, despite the fact that we have literally the entire Rebel fleet just a few light years behind us. We're passing an asteroid field and have decided to investigate it for resources that may aid in our journey. Captain out.
And so begins your journey in FTL, where you, a lone ship, needs to cross to the far side of the galaxy to deliver important schematics regarding a superweapon the Rebels have constructed, and which you'll face in combat in the final sector. Sound familiar? It should, because FTL is a game meant to evoke memories of all those times you imagined being a starship captain, and placing you in control of everything from the crew's roles to where power is being allocated.
In the grand tradition of Baldur's Gate, the game also features real-time-with-pause, which you'll need to use when everything starts exploding, catching on fire or being boarded by a killer robot. There's a bevy of ships to unlock (many of which bear an uncanny resemblence to famous sci-fi vessels like the SSV Normandy), each of which also has a variant that plays in very different ways, and since the game itself isn't very long, it's been designed for tremendous replay value. And you will get a LOT of that, since it's also punishingly hard, yet generally fair in how it kills you
Of course, sometimes the RNG is merciless and you're dead within the first few minutes, but there's something about this game which makes you just want to click New Game again and go for it once more.

This game sets itself apart from other CCGs by being fast(er). This is because of the evolve mechanic wherein you can evolve your followers making them stronger and/or giving them special abilities. Another reason why this game is fast, is because you can't interrupt enemy attacks or spells. So there is little incentive to save orbs (mana) (with a few exceptions).  Followers usually die within 2 rounds and you have little health compared to the strongest followers. That isn't to say there aren't slow matches. You can drag out the game if your deck supports it.
The only downside I have found so far are the rewards after the free stuff dries up. You only have 3 daily quests, which give only a little gold (unless you get a good quest). That wouldn't be a problem in itself if the arena rewards weren't also kinda bad. A card pack costs 100 gold. It costs 150 gold to participate in arena. You always get 1 card pack even when you lose. But even if you win 4 out of 5 (which is decent), the reward is only 120 gold extra. Subtract the 50 gold from the extra entrance fee, leaves you with only 70 gold reward. Other CCGs I've played gave better rewards.
+ Evolve mechanic
+ A lot of free stuff for beginners (+20 card packs and plenty gold)
+ Different classes have different play styles
+ Card art work
+ Japanese voices
- Arena rewards are kinda bad
- Limited daily quests and rewards
= Unsure about the meta of certain cards, like Path to Purgatory and Prince of Darkness

The instructions take care to note that the suit of the cards don't matter, so why did the designers bother giving the cards suits at all? BUT I'm going to anyway: The crying fairies got old fast. I'd like to see them... y'know, do something. They're magical flying glowy things; I have to imagine they're capable of more than crying at the protagonist.
But, I digress. The game's fun enough, although maybe not $10's worth of fun. If you catch it when it's at least half off, I do recommend giving it a go. I got this game with serious reservations due to some of the negative publicity around it but for the first time in a long time I was pleasantly surprised with this one.  A triple AAA title that is worth the moniker triple AAA for something other than just its price.
However, what I can say is this.  I am having a damn good time playing this game but what gets in the way is the field of view.  There is a field of view slider so its a good port or crossover but it could still do with being wider..  Its not as bad as some console cross over games but its still pretty limited and it really stop a good game being a very good game.
For once, the game, though multi platform seems to have had some effort put into the PC.  The graphics are good and within the limitations of the style (looks a bit next gen console) have some additional eye candy which really does enhance the visuals a bit in the enhanced edition.  The world looks far more "alive" than many similar games with wind and other effects playing a real part through foliage etc.   So looks wise, it is good depending on your experience and expectations.
The gameplay itself is very entertaining. This is dead island done right.  I hesitate to put that due to the really negative connotations of dead island but take the concept, make it beautiful, make it work and take more of the console induced limitations out of a game like this and this is it.
Actually, the game is less cartoonish than other games in this genre and the environment more immersive than say Dead Island ever was. The characters are not so annoying that you want to kick them to death before the zombies even realise that dinner can run and the plot is not intrusive if you want to play it like a bit of a sandbox.
The environment is large enough to  be engaging, with a fair amount of real estate to explore which these days, is unusually good for a game like this.  It has pretty basic character development but overall its quite satisfying.
The way the game progresses you start off thinking, hmmm, this is a bit weak but quickly, learn that with the night comes your wake up call. One of the outstanding aspects of this game is the balance.  You think your owning it, get complacent and get dead.
The combat is fun and diverse enough to hold my interest, the use of environment and the way you navigate the environment also stands out.  Missions are relatively diverse and the storyline and subquests engaging and seem to contribute to the overall narrative.
I left the best until last.  The best thing about all this is that it comes with a Field Of View slider.  OMG. At last, a company that worked out that nothing screams, terrible console port like using the terrible field of view consoles have to use to cover their hardwares weaknesses which to many PC games feels really strange and actually cause real nausea.  At last!. I would recommend it for that alone but fortunately, this game has a lot more going for it. I am putting a thumbs up but would make it 2 thumbs if I had the choice.

Dying Light is fast, furious and fun. It takes the best parts of all the big AAA games. It has the parkour of MIrror's Edge. It re-uses melee combat from Dead Island, though I think it's improved.  It has the lock picking from Skyrim. It has the upgrade/perk system from Far Cry 3, and also the sandbox of that game. It very much reminds me of Shadows of Mordor in how it was constructed (another fantastic game), putting together a bunch of awesome systems that feel natural combined.
The game systems work well, even if the story doesn't. Character progression is noticeable and significant. You go from a jerk who can parkour okay, to a killing machine that can parkour like Faith. It makes a difference when you start running night missions and need to move like the wind to avoid Volitiles, this game's version of the predator. The night time ones are like the vampires from I Am Legend. Night time is scary stuff as the vampire volitiles chase you like bats out of hell.
Melee combat starts difficult at best, but once you get a decent weapon and a few upgrades, it starts clicking. By the time you have a flame thrower sword or an electric baton, it's the zombie wrecking hour. Even so, a dozen or so zombies can wreck you if they trap you in a corner so there's always that threat. Some might find it annoying, but the real threat of zombies is that they slow you down or grab you when you're fighting something tougher. Everything is about learning. You start a total noob and turn into a zombie slaughtering machine, somewhat because of the game systems, but also because you realize how to fight them properly. I liked that because the character you play is in that exact same situation. Slicing heads is second nature later in the game with a saber or a hatchet.
The story is mediocre. Random white American guy goes to a random non-Euro-Centric city to get files from some rogue operative (read: McGuffin), but ends up becoming the savior of the people. It's very Far Cry 3, though I think less racist in its actual delivery (read: no magical people of color stereotypes), which is an improvement if nothing else. I mostly skip the cutscenes and dialogs anyway, as they aren't as interesting as they think they are. I mostly want to run around like crazy beating zombies over the head. The NPCs are forgetable, except for the pretty agent you work with named Jade. I rather like her, but again, every other character looks the same or doesn't matter. The story suggests you're best friends with some of them, but there's no real way to know that. I spent 99% of my time sleeping in a safe house across town to avoid night time enemies, only going back the Tower, the city's big safehouse with the majority of survivors, once in a while to collect more quests and buy a few new rare weapons.
While I think it's not great, the story doesn't detract from the fun, of which this game is all about.
TL;DR: Jump on zombie heads, and then cut people in half. Run around like Jason Bourne. Awesome. 9/10.

Oh my, Risk of Rain, possibly one of all time favorite games
I'll break it down into 5 categories; Characters, Story, Gameplay, Sound Design, and overall uniqueness
Characters:
All of the playable characters have their own strengths, weaknesses and "personallities." No character feels like a carbon copy of another even though some have some similatities, which is good, you can easily swap from one to another with little to no effort or feeling stuck, all of the character abilites and attacks are unqiue so no two characters play exactly the same
Story:
Honestly not too much going for this category, but honestly that's what makes the story of this game good, you simply know a little of the backstories of the character and what happened before the game began. Not the greatest aspect of the game but it is still interesting
Gameplay;
As a 2-D platform shooter with an infinitely scaling difficulty, RoR doesn't seem like too complex a game, but when you add in the runes and the randomness of the portals, boss spawns, and items that you can get, no two runs are the same, you always feel like something new and unique is happening, easily the games best feature. The controller support is also amazingly good as a side note.
Sound Design:
The music in this game is wonderful, from the opening theme to the final bosses theme the sounds keeps you engaged and intranced with what is happening on-screen and is in no way immursion breaking, which is a huge plus
Overall Uniqueness:
This game is insanely unique, with a cast of many playable character to a few silly and dumb looking enemies, and a wonderfully designed final boss. This game can keep you going on for hours and hours, literally, my longest run was nearly four and a half hours long, and the only reason I stopped was because I realized I had other things to do.
TL;DR: A masterpiece of a game and easily on par with some other great roguelikes, the characters are all unique and fun, and the music is top-notch, while the enemies are all interesting, story is lacking, but makes up for it in gameplay and replayability. I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys rougelikes or 2-D platformers/shooters

So, really XCom is the leader in this sort of game, but Shadowrun compensates by adding some decent story and RPG elements. I had a good time with it, and apparently the sequel buffs out some of the quirks. There's a few oddities. The inventory management and party system is non-standard, but you're a grown person - you'll figure it out. The art is great, and you want a closer look at it. I only wish the game didn't keep trying to force you to zoom out. A few other weird issues manifest, especially in the early game when you and the game are still getting to know each other. I get the impression of a solid foundation having been laid but then parts of the structure being abruptly canceled and quickly made to achieve a base level of functionality. You can specialize in a weapon but then there's only 3 weapons of that class you can ever buy sort of stuff. Probably a result of the tabletop system being implemented literally without followthrough in the game proper
A few other areas assume a familiarity with the tabletop system and aren't explained especially well in the game, but they weren't gamebreakers for a 13-hour long RPG. You might make a bad decision and sort of de-optimize your build, but it's not a huge hassle. The game isn't very unforgiving. I played through on hard mode and only failed once in an early mission. For example, cybernetic upgrades aren't really explained very well in the game, and I purchased some cool robo-legs, and then later discovered that I was kind of stuck with them and there would never be any significant upgrades. I get the impression that the tabletop actually has lots more depth that they just sort of ran out of time to implement, and that these shortcomings (Just add more items to the shopping cart) could be easily addressed in fan made levels or whatnot.

FTL: Faster than Light is honestly like no other game I've played before. You control a spaceship and its crew, flying through space while trying to evade the rebel fleet chasing you across the galaxy with random encounters over every horizon. You'll find bandits, settlers, ship wrecks, rogue AI ships, as well as the occasional merchant station. Your ultimate goal is to gather enough weapons and scrap through exploration to outfit your ship with enough weapons and upgrades to win the final battle, or valiantly die trying. Its roguelike nature ensures you will die many times before you successfully beat the game, but it's such an enjoyable game that you'll want to keep coming back till you beat it. There's also ships to unlock that have vastly different layouts, with different crews and weapon systems, that add a lot of replayability. Finally, the soundtrack is perfectly matched for the game, enhancing just about every moment of the game with its wonderful themes and melodies that really complete the whole experience.
This game has earned an automatic purchase from me for any DLC or expansion they make in the future, no matter what price. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a well rounded, finely polished game at a great price that is truly worth every penny.

Polyball is one of only 3 early access games I own. I haven’t purchased them consciously, they were just parts of bundles that contained other games I was genuinely interested in. But Polyball immediately caught my eye in its particular bundle because of its charming art style, so I figured I’d give it a shot, even though I expected that it would still be somewhat unfinished.
This is incidentally the reason why I usually don’t buy or play early access games: I pay for an unfinished product that I get to play in an objectively worse condition than the actual release build. The other reason for not buying early is, obviously, that a final release build is far from guaranteed, as we’ve seen with a couple of abandoned games now, and the slew of early access titles who seem to stay in early access for years to come.
But enough ranting about the business model, you’re here to know if the game in its current state is any good. As the developer claims, Polyball is a rather simple ball rolling game in the vein of other classic ball rolling games, such as Super Monkey Ball. The objective in each level is to find the end goal while overcoming a variety of obstacles, and that’s basically it. You can also collect shards, which are used to customize your ball in a variety of cosmetic ways. But there are no micro-transactions to unlock this stuff, which is nice. But in the end, the game tracks your time, and gathering all the shards seems like it’d only increase your time spent in the level. This is only exacerbated by the fact that apparently there’s a trophy hidden in all the levels and I barely managed to find one, so there is a bit of a mixed message going on.
Like I mentioned above, the art style is what drew me into it at first, and throughout the game, the environments you get to play in really manage to create a sense of atmosphere. This is obviously helped by the wide variety of levels that are already accessible in this early access version, with promises of more on the way. The music underlines the general aesthetic as well, going for a lot of synthwave, which fits the general visual tone of the game quite nicely.
If there’s one thing I can criticize, it’s the controls. They’re not awful, but at times they seem a tad unresponsive. Given that you can also change your trajectory mid-air, you are allowed a lot of control over your sphere, however the jump mechanic needs some work in my estimation. The biggest problem I see with it is the fact that you can only jump when the ball is in contact with the ground on the bottom part of the ball. So say your ball is perched between two ledges on the left and right side, you can’t jump, because the bottom part of the ball isn’t touching anything. The same thing goes for certain very steep sections where you can do nothing but watch as your ball loses momentum and slides back down again. This was particularly infuriating in one of the levels where around 70% of the time I lacked momentum to clear that particular wall and couldn’t continue with the level because of that.
In addition to that, I feel that the tolerance between what counts as touching and not touching is exceptionally slim. Visually it could appear that the ball is touching the ground, but the physics calculation in the game actually tells you it isn’t, which is why at times the ball seems to completely ignore your input and refuses to jump. If I may be so bold as to suggest a fix for this, I’d say make the collision box slightly bigger than the ball to allow for some margin of error on behalf of the player. It can get quite frustrating after a while if it seems like you’re losing control of the ball for no apparent reason.
Other than that, I’d say definitely had fun playing this game, even though again, it is still in a somewhat unfinished state. The developer claims that the game will feature a bunch more levels upon release, as well as local multiplayer, and the game will be Steam Workshop enabled, which could benefit the longevity of the title. But even in the state it’s in, it’s a nice little title. The only thing I’m a bit dubious about is the price. $15 for a game about rolling around a ball seems like quite a lot to me. If you’re the competitive type and you want to see your name on the leaderboards, you’ll invest plenty of time into the game to justify the investment. But if you’re like me and you just want a bit of challenge without going crazy over shaving off a few more milliseconds, in its current state, you can expect around 4 hours of entertainment. If that’s good enough for you, go for it, it’s one of the very few titles I’d say deserves to be in early access because it’s in a playable and almost finished state and from the looks of it, all the mechanics are in place, so only a few levels and the multiplayer portion are still missing.

Captain's Log, Stardate -309538.54318873666
We have just departed the Federation base and the crew is optimistic about our chances, despite the fact that we have literally the entire Rebel fleet just a few light years behind us. We're passing an asteroid field and have decided to investigate it for resources that may aid in our journey. Captain out.
And so begins your journey in FTL, where you, a lone ship, needs to cross to the far side of the galaxy to deliver important schematics regarding a superweapon the Rebels have constructed, and which you'll face in combat in the final sector. Sound familiar? It should, because FTL is a game meant to evoke memories of all those times you imagined being a starship captain, and placing you in control of everything from the crew's roles to where power is being allocated.
In the grand tradition of Baldur's Gate, the game also features real-time-with-pause, which you'll need to use when everything starts exploding, catching on fire or being boarded by a killer robot. There's a bevy of ships to unlock (many of which bear an uncanny resemblence to famous sci-fi vessels like the SSV Normandy), each of which also has a variant that plays in very different ways, and since the game itself isn't very long, it's been designed for tremendous replay value. And you will get a LOT of that, since it's also punishingly hard, yet generally fair in how it kills you
Of course, sometimes the RNG is merciless and you're dead within the first few minutes, but there's something about this game which makes you just want to click New Game again and go for it once more.

You can't go wrong with solitaire. Faerie Solitaire is the game that everyone has played at some point in their life plus a story, rpg elements such as exp and upgrades, and some pleasant background noise.
.Game play.
Your objective is to count. You have a deck of cards from which you draw one card and then you try and place it on a card on the game board before you that either precedes it or follows it--i.e, if you have a 6, you can place it on a 5 or 7. It's very simple and very satisfying if you can get a good count running. Some boards have a gimick such as ice that can be removed if you clear the cards in front of a 'fireball' spell and thorns that can be removed if you clear the row of cards over their roots.
Besides that, you sometimes find eggs if you clear the rows of cards on the board and you can equip the pets inside of them so that they passively gain experience while you play. The pets evolve using ingredients you can find the same way you find their eggs, but their only function is for vanity (and achievements).
.Story/Premise.
You're trying to save the Faerie Land and you progress through each area by playing solitaire. It doesn't make much sense, but... Magic!
.Art style/graphics.
It's colourful and cartoony. The illustrations on the cards and for the pets are cute and the animations for the spells you cast or the combo meter are neat.
.Soundtrack.
It's peaceful. Suitable for a card game.
.Bottom line.
There's not much else to say. Faerie Solitaire is a nice way to pass the time. Definitely worth a look.

If you enjoyed Civ 4 or any strategy game ever then you'll enjoy Civ 5. It feels much more polished than previous games in the series, with elements like religion and espionage (in the BNW expansion) playing a much more balanced role. This is largely due to the imbalance of playable civs, you'll end up seing the computer civs behaving the same way time and time again. This is despite the vast number of civs in the base game and DLCs. Additionally, many of the playable civs' bonus features are simply not worthwhile meaning you end up choosing from the same few each time.
That said, I've played the game for many hours now and enjoyed every minute. Definitely worth picking up the game and all DLCs next time they're on sale!

An entertaining Solitaire game, with quite simple, but engaging gameplay; and a nice story about faeries. This game is good for some relaxing during an afternoon; even though it's simple, there's still some challenge to it. The aesthethic is really nice, featuring some nice backgrounds for each of the different levels, all following a fantasy theme.
The game offers several modes; an adventure mode, in which you play through 40 levels, following the story of a kid who encountered faeries, and all the dangers he encountered during his journey to save them which, although might sound unnecessary for a solitaire game, adds a nice backstory. There's also a quickplay mode, in which you can replay any previously finished level, and a challenge mode, with some more difficult levels. Each level consists of 9 hands, and, while it's not necessary to collect all cards in each hand, there's still different objectives to complete in order to beat a level.
The game also includes a "Faerie Land"; think of it as an upgrade/collectibles shop, where you can get several different upgrades spending money you earn during the game, and also a hatchery for all the different pets you may encounter while you play. It is a nice addition to the game, giving it a bit more of depth.
As far as soundtracks go, it consists of several relaxing songs that play during each level, providing a calm environment while you play.
All things said, I think this is a recommendable solitaire game, for when you want some casual, relaxing fun.

Short Report: Shadowverse [First Impressions]
Still have to climb the ranked ladder so take this review with some grains of salt.
At this point (with my number of hours in Story Mode and Take Two), I'd say Shadowverse is a pretty solid CCG and I'd actually put it up beside the giant Hearthstone as a testament to how good it is.
I actually plan on switching over to it since I think at this point it'd be a better investment as it's still growing and there's not much expansions to blow cash on yet.
When you start, you're pretty much given like 20-30 free card packs to start so you already have a mini-collection growing. With the giveaways, promos, and maintenances they do, that collection will pretty much just keep on getting bigger. They have the usual daily deal for pack buying like most JP gacha games (around 50% off for "rolling a gacha" once every day), so there's that as well.
The gameplay itself is typical for a mobile CCG, but the classes, card effects, and the Evolve mechanic make it a pretty unique and fun experience. There's not a lot of RNG as well, so it's mostly reliant on skill and proper deckbuilding (and always, the luck of the draw which can't really be removed). There's 7 classes and each class has an entire single-player campaign to go through which in the end rewards a free Arena ticket, so that's pretty sweet.
The other thing to talk about would be their version of the Arena or multiplayer draft. Instead of the usual HS "pick 1 from 3" system, it's a literal Take Two - you choose between two pairs. It's nice since you actually have to think whether you're going to take the one with a really good and a really bad one or one with both decent cards. Take Two also doesn't kick you out after 3 losses, so you have a set 5 games and even then you get a free pack for going 0-5.
Keeping this short, Shadowverse is a free-to-play CCG that's already big in Japan but is slowly growing in the West and bringing a lot of promise. Hopefully it keeps growing positively since it's really damn fun.
First Impressions Score: 8/10

A good buffer for my opinion is this review:
.
1) Platforming: Yahtzee is just bad at this; he always brushes it off, but the facts stand. He’s in denial.
Practice. You have a very good idea of where your legs are and if you don't just look down then slowly look up to judge the distance. I got accustomed pretty quickly. You’ll die now and then but easy mess-ups are platforming tropes. It's similar to getting a sense of when you should move in a sport in real life. You know where things are, but you have to visualize and time it right to get a good picture.
There are minor collision issues. It isn't perfect, but if gameplay and story could be compared, gameplay is way ahead and kind of fun.
2) Story:
Yahtzee is right. The protagonist spends more time than she ought to pulling off a more convincing version of Metroid: Other M's monotone, bland monologues. It's something you except to see in an anime with their weird concept of how monologues and storytelling go together. I guess Swedish developers fall into the same trap.
The twists toward the end are also obvious and a bit perplexing due your character's reactions. Luckily by the time you're over it the game ends.
3) Presentation:
Yahtzee sums it up well again. The visuals are a nice change of pace. I was playing with default settings at a lower resolution so I can't talk about the graphics themselves without speculating.
You'll mostly find yourself paying attention to the brightly colored parts of the environment which act as indicators that you can interact (mostly through parkour) with them. They went too far with the brightness, straining eyes. The cut scenes are done in an anime sort of style; it's nice. It’s weird when you still see a yellow crane in the animations when you'd assume in reality they're normal colors. On the other side of things is the weird. Too clean.  And why does the game end in normal game graphics when all of the most important parts of the story are delivered in cut scenes?
I liked the little scrolling texts you see that make references. Overall, PWETTY.
4) The Other Gameplay:
I actually SOMEWHAT liked that half of the game that was set in close spaces. It changed the mechanics. I do agree it asked for more open spaces so the small environments disappoint. I liked how the game rushed you. There is succinct satisfaction in knowing you pulled off a difficult parkour move in the middle of a chase, whether being chased or doing the chasing. It happens too often however thus validating what people complained about: The game demands you rush far too often. It's not as bad as it could be though.
A lot of fighting moves are unnecessary. It often takes longer to take an enemy down with normal punches than to do a simple counter and steal their gun. This can get difficult with enemies who blunt you faster but it never gets frustrating due to an unnecessary “Matrix” feature. There's nothing unique about the forced fights. Shooting a small wave of enemies is just too typical. Pretty standard boggled down mechanics from games like COD right down to the red flash when you get hurt and very minor physical effects as you near death or unconscious.
Verdict:
More of an indie game even for 2008. At a price of $5 it's moderately reasonable. Once you beat it you can play on hard and collect bags you might have missed. There's time trails too but you need an EA account to play online and keep track of your scores. If you decide to, get it on sale at a very low price preferably around that $5 mark. You'll have 5-10 or so hours of time to mess around. It's an original and decent fun-filled IP if nothing else. Don't take my score as meaning it's a terrible game. Think of it like this: Regardless of its positive reception and experimentation in gameplay, aesthetics, and gender (not a guy!) it's a disappointing experience rather than a terrible, unexpected one.
5/10

Resident Evil 4 is one of my favorite games, and I think Dead Space succeeds as another game in the same style. One of the things I enjoyed most about Dead Space was how it integrates the HUD into the visuals of the game. Your inventory and map screens appear as holographic screens in front of your guy Isaac, which he, and the player, look at. The video calls Isaac has with other characters also appear as holograms that he looks at, and they look fantastic. Your health bar is represented by blue lights on the back of his suit. These lights are given in-universe justification -- so workers could easily see whether someone was in a critical state after an accident. Other characters have these suits as well, and they even look different because there are obviously different styles of suits. Having the information of the HUD be within the game world, rather than onscreen, makes the game more immersive. The graphics and art design have some strong elements. The cutscenes are done in-game, showing off the game’s graphics. The design of the ship fits the atmosphere, with it’s dark, claustrophobic halls. The space scenes are pretty, and remind you that you’re on a spaceship. And when you step into space, you only hear what Isaac would be able to hear – his increasingly ragged breathing inside his helmet. You’re using weapons that are actually tools, and you can see how your plasma cutter, for example, would work as a tool. It feels like a missed opportunity that you don’t use these weapons as tools (except as killing tools).
In addition to the unique take on the HUD, you have the combat mechanic of shooting limbs off rather than traditional torso and head shots. This helps the game have its own identity, and the enemy and weapon design make this mechanic work where it wouldn’t in other shooters. Unfortunately, they didn’t go too far with this, and some of the weapons and enemies don’t really use this mechanic. The assault rifle and the swarm enemy, as examples. Then you have stasis, which isn’t revolutionary but helps mitigate the speed difference of Isaac and his enemies. It’s limited by a meter, though, which forces you to choose the best time and place to use it.
Isaac is in a heavy suit, and the controls are appropriately slow and clunky, which increases the tension because you can’t deal with enemies quickly. This also leads to frustration with some of the enemy designs. One is the “sonic” enemies, which test your reaction speed to frantically aim and stasis as quickly as you can. Then there are the scorpion enemies which are very hard to de-limb and surprisingly fast. You also have a miniboss that shows up multiple times: the armored tank enemy. His charge attack has to be anticipated because of Isaac’s slow movement. And once you dodge it, you slowly turn around to find the guy clomping up to you to charge again.
A downside of the game is that the horror elements fall flat. The game is very tense, but certain aspects that were meant to be scary ended up deflating some of that tension. Jump scares are heavily relied on, to the point where it becomes predictable. The player becomes desensitized to the monsters bursting into the room in every section of the game. You also have someone singing Twinkle Twinkle Little Star in a spooky way, and traumatized survivors sitting there laughing. I didn’t find these parts effective. The most effective horror was near the beginning of the game when you didn’t know what you were going to see next. And that cult was creepy, with the followers wrapping their heads and stabbing a hole through their face in order to allow themselves to become necromorphs.
Instead of cutscenes, the story is told through characters having audio or video calls with Isaac. This means you don’t have to wait for a cutscene. You can continue through the game and simply listen to the call. You do have to sit through a cutscene when you start a game, where all you can control is the camera. There is also one when you walk into the final boss. The problem with this one is that you have to watch it every time you start the boss fight. I had to watch it over and over. Once you beat the game on Hard, you unlock the hardest mode: Impossible. There were parts near the end of Impossible where necromorphs come from all around you, and I almost gave up on beating it. I almost gave up on the final boss, too. It has a part where you have to shoot certain areas while your aim is constantly shifting. There are other sections like this in the game and they are really frustrating, since the aiming isn’t very precise during them. The beginning of the run was tense because ammo was scarce, but by the end, I was rolling in it. I want to point out how silly it is to call the mode “Impossible” when it is not only totally possible, but not even extremely challenging.
A problem with the PC port is that it feels like it was designed for consoles and ported as an afterthought. Controlling with mouse and keyboard works, but the mouse sensitivity and camera movement felt off to me. Playing with a controller worked well. I revisit Dead Space sometimes, and I always have a blast when I do.
