Man, I really REALLY wanted to like this game...
A big part of that is because I think the world of Shadowrun is an awesome setting for a game, I mean I've never played the tabletop game but I've heard loads about it (primarily from watching Counter Monkey) and I think the idea of mixing a Gibson-esque Cyberpunk setting with elements of more traditional western fantasy (Orks, Elves, Dragons, what have you) is a really cool concept. I'm one of those people who could never really get into games/movies/books about western medievil fantasy settings, they just always seemed kinda boring by design, seen one seen 'em all y'know? Skyrim is one of the only games with that sort of Tolkien-esque world that was able to hold my attention, and that was only because the Nordic stuff was able to overshadow it and make for a more interesting world (Snowy peaks > green fields, just sayin').
But Cyberpunk? I ♥♥♥♥ing LOVE cyberpunk!
I love the idea of speculating about  a darker future, how technology has changed us for better or for worse, the ethics and practicalities of cybernetics and artificial intelligence, it's just got so much more meat to it. And when you take all that AND THEN add magic and elves and♥♥♥♥♥♥ You've got the potential for some really interesting ideas and stories, and I'd absolutely love to see a game do this setting justice... but this is just not it.
First, I'd like to disclaim this by clarifying that I am not entirely versed in the Shadowrun lore, I don't know how true to the books this game is, so I won't judge it one way or another in that respect. I will however say that had I not known anything at all about Shadowrun prior to playing this game I don't think I'd have gotten much from it. Things like the Sixth World and the Great Awakening are referenced but nobody ever explicitly explains what they are or how the dynamics of this world work. Why did magic come back? Where did it go? Where did all the elves, orks, and trolls come from? Who are S.T.A.R.S? What's a Doc-Wagon? None of these things are addressed, and while I understand that this is a game made for and by longtime Shadowrun fans, and as such there's going to be references that only long-time fans will necessarily understand, I get that, but It's not a good sign when I feel like I need to crack a players guide for the tabletop game just to understand what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on, and that's how I felt while playing much of this game.
Also, the writing in this game, or atleast the base campaign, is very... eh.
I Mean it wasn't bad, it all makes sense, there were no glaring plot-holes or laughably bad exposition, but that's just the thing, it's very... okay. It's not what I'd call bad, but save a few stand out-moments it wasn't all that exceptional either. The idea of building a story around your dead friend hiring you to solve his murder from beyond the grave is an interesting idea but I've seen it done before, and far better. Also, while I definitely think that a noir-style crime drama would be the perfect framework to explore the world of Shadowrun, I just don't feel like the story presented lived up to the setting's potential. But again, this only refers to the Dead Man's Switch base campaign, I understand that many fan-made campaigns acted as a far better realizations of the Shadowrun setting, but I don't really think it's fair to include user-made content in a review like this.
I think one of the major things that kills this game for me is the fact that it tries to be a throwback to old-school CRPGs, but it's completely linear, and doesn't give you the kind of freedom one would come to expect from a CRPG. There are very few optional missions or objectives to speak of, and while there are multiple ways to complete many of the objectives, much of the time it feels less like a choice, and more like a calculation (I recall one situation where a dialog choice asked me if I wanted to pay this guy 100 creds for what he knows or 50 creds. No speech check, no skills or disciplines involved, flat question of "would you like to pay more money or less for the same information?"). The Dialogue trees in general just feel pretty cut and dry to me, very "nice response/jerk response/witty response," much of the time, and it just comes off as boring to me. I do however think that going text only instead of recording some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥voice acting was definitely the right thing to do, in my mind CRPGs have always been about replicating the experience of reading a good book in the context of an interactive environment, and when a game like this adds unnecessary voice acting it sometimes kills the experience, at least for me, and since quite a bit of the actual written dialogue is pretty damn good despite the plot in which it takes place, I am glad they went this route.
The turn-based combat is actually one aspect of this game that I thought was pretty good, I mean it's pretty much XCOM light but that's okay, it functions very well and doesn't feel out of place in the setting or genera. I do feel like melee weapons were made somewhat under-powered, which is disappointing to me as I decided to play a Street Samurai specializing in melee and shotguns. Also, this game seems to have some kind of percentage skewing problem in which you seemed to miss "70% chance" shots 80% of the time, but that might have just been my rotten luck. Other then that the combat seems to work just fine for what it is.
Another aspect of this game that I found a very mixed bag is the aesthetic, the backgrounds for one thing look fantastic, they're all hand-drawn in the classic CRPG style, and they do the seemingly impossible task of making the aesthetic of a grimy, neon soaked, cyberpunk world look beautiful (all-be-it with a little too much blue-saturation for my tastes). The in-game models on the other hand... not so much. I understand, this game was kick-started, they were on a budget, and as someone who doesn't have a very beefy PC I am rather grateful that they didn't emphasize graphical fidelity and turn the game into a performance hog, but that said, I do think they could have put a little more polish into making the in-game models match the backgrounds a little better, as it stands they just kinda clash and it creates a very odd contrast, it just doesn't look very good.
I have other criticisms I'd like to level at this game, the character customization was a little lacking for my tastes (especially the outfit choices), some of the character portraits look better then others, and cyberware is drastically underplayed (which is one of my favorite aspects of the cyberpunk setting, so that's especially disappointing to me), but at this point I'm nearing the level of nit-picking so I think it's about time to wrap this up. I feel like a total jerk right now, because this is a kickstarted game I'm talking about here, it's a miracle this game was even made at all, and as a budding Shadowrun fan myself I am glad that it exists and is introducing the setting to other people. However at the end of the day the mark of a good game is whether or not I feel truly engaged in it, feel self-driven in playing and enjoying it, and look forward to playing it some more as soon as I power it down, and Shdaowrun Returns just didn't do it for me.
I have been informed that Dragonfall fixed many of the problems I had with Returns however, so I do intend to give that a go when I can, and I really hope that turns out to be true because Shadowrun deserves a game to truly do it justice, and this just ain't it.

This game is an interesting one- very much worth the value. It's premise is simple: move a triangle around a central axis so as to not hit any walls that are approaching the center of the screen. Musically, this game is amazing. It's soundtrack may be short, but each song is perfectly crafted to fit the segment of the game you are on.

On the whole, Kudos to the developer who made this game.

Dead Space blends horror themes and mechanics with more action-oriented third person shooting. Expect to deal with scarce supplies, enemies popping out of the walls and ceiling, dim and flickering lights, and lots of blood. Blood is just... everywhere.
As Isaac Clarke, a silent mechanic/soldier, you will fight off numerous alien-infested crewmembers while unraveling the mystery of their origins aboard the Ishimura. The game runs a bit overlong, with some middle levels that could be cut or combined, but starts and finishes strong. The plot is engaging, reminiscent of the System/Bioshock games in linearity and non-roleplay nature. Levels typically feature an overaching objective and a series of sub-objectives, sometimes requiring lite puzzle solving, almost always featuring at least one combat arena with numerous enemies. The player is rewarded for thorough exploration, with many items hidden in corners of rooms.
There are enough mechanics brought via new monsters and weapons to keep the game interesting through its length. Stand outs include the zero gravity jumping (one of my favorite movement mechanics in any game I've played) and the inventory seen as an in-world projection. The only obnoxious mechanic, I felt, involves a certain giant tentacle and the way it affects Isaac's aim.
The combat is not always enjoyable, as some enemies seem to have inconsistent hitboxes and some weapons are not particularly effective until heavily upgraded (if at all). There are some fine setpieces with combat, however, and overall I found myself enjoying the hard difficulty (curse that difficulty bug that hit me later in the game!). In contrast to many FPS, enemies typically have weak points at their limb connections, and many enemies are only killed by severing a limb or two. Slowing a clump of 2-3 mobs and blasting them into pieces is particularly enjoyable.
Excellent sound design. The eerie sounds heard throughout my exploration of the Ishimura often had me spinning around to make sure something wasn't behind me. Visually the game is from 2008, with middling world textures and fairly nice player model. Keeping Isaac's helmet on was a good choice.
Recommendation? If you like Third Person Shooters and Horror themes and don't mind aging visuals, certainly.

Input lag prevents completion of the hexagonest stage.
To reduce input lag, I have to turn off the V-sync option and accept screen tearing.
What does input lag do to me in this game?
-Distorts what I feel I'm doing, making prediction impossible. The triangle won't move or stop on time.
**As soon as I turned off V-sync, I completed the hyper hexagon and hyper hexagoner stages, getting 97 seconds and 99 seconds. My previous records were just over 30 seconds.
What does screen tearing do?
-Makes recognition of the coming path more difficult. Coupled with the blur effect found only in the hexagonest stage, I have to play by "luck" until I'm able to ignore the screen tearing. A few tens of retries allows me to play without much distraction.
I enjoy the game, but I don't recommend it.
Edit/Follow-up:
I beat the hexagonest stage. The biggest issue was getting used to what meant collision and what didn't. If I let the triangle sit still, I can have half of it blocking the incoming bars and be fine. If I'm moving and have only two thirds of the triangle in the appropriate section, it's game over. If I try my luck and ram the triangle into the side of the white bars, it's a 50/50 chance of death. Screen tearing increases chance of death if I rely on what I see.
Most evident in the hyper hexagonest stage, the movement speed of the triangle is determined by rotation of the screen. When moving upstream in hyper hexagonest, the triangle has half of its original movement speed. Combined with delayed input and shifts of the plane, this may account for the times I felt the path stood still in easier stages. It's absolutely necessary to understand this to get the last achievement. I'm just not good enough yet.

I finally began to play Half-life 2 after it sat in my steam library for around 2 years. I finally decided to start playing because I was intrigued. I wanted to see what made this game so highly acclaimed. So much of my game time was spent trying to find the answer to a single question:
"Why is Half-life 2 so great?"
For a majority of the game I struggled to find the answer. It wasn't that I didn't like the game, it was just I couldn't understand why it was considered to be so amazing. I considered the possibility that the game may have had a different charm back in 2004 when it was released, but the more I played, the more I realized there was much more to the greatness of this game. Onward I struggled with this question and continued to ask myself about what elements made this game so heralded.
Was it because of the beloved source engine?
Was it because of the quirky and stereotypical FPS story?
Was it because of the amazing powers of the gravity gun?
Was it because of how well the graphics held up to this day?
Was it because of the unique characters?
Was it because of the excellent shooting mechanics?
Or was it because of the absence of any cutscenes in the game?
No, all of these things were good, but they weren't the elements that made Half-life 2 great.
The more I searched, the more I realized I was overlooking the one single determining factor in the ability of a game to please its audience. Enjoyment. So I asked myself the question: "Is Half-life 2 fun?" In asking this I realized that what Half-life 2 does so well is the fundamental goal of all games.
This is to provide its audience with enjoyment. Half-life 2 does this as well as any game I've ever played. Throughout the game there was never a dull moment. And while all of the elements of this game I mentioned before are great, the game truly excells at making sure you have a good time.

FTL: Faster than Light is honestly like no other game I've played before. You control a spaceship and its crew, flying through space while trying to evade the rebel fleet chasing you across the galaxy with random encounters over every horizon. You'll find bandits, settlers, ship wrecks, rogue AI ships, as well as the occasional merchant station. Your ultimate goal is to gather enough weapons and scrap through exploration to outfit your ship with enough weapons and upgrades to win the final battle, or valiantly die trying. Its roguelike nature ensures you will die many times before you successfully beat the game, but it's such an enjoyable game that you'll want to keep coming back till you beat it. There's also ships to unlock that have vastly different layouts, with different crews and weapon systems, that add a lot of replayability. Finally, the soundtrack is perfectly matched for the game, enhancing just about every moment of the game with its wonderful themes and melodies that really complete the whole experience.
This game has earned an automatic purchase from me for any DLC or expansion they make in the future, no matter what price. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a well rounded, finely polished game at a great price that is truly worth every penny.

Super Hexagon is NOT A RHYTHM GAME. It is very much a fast-paced action game, and an excellent one at that. However, if you're thinking of giving Super Hexagon a try, you need to get this through your head. Super Hexagon does an excellent job of looking like a rhythm game, and it could have been--but it isn't one. Here are some important facts you need to know:
-The patterns you need to avoid occur in a randomly selected order. There is no memorizing the stages; you must react to everything in real time, and that video trailer is actual footage that's not sped up in any way. Warning: this game is HARD.
-Rather than memorizing the stage, you must memorize individual patterns, learn to recognize them quickly, and react to those patterns with the proper input, while also identifying and preparing for the next pattern. If you like fast-paced action games, you will have a lot of fun with Super Hexagon. If you prefer rhythm games, you will most likely get frustrated.
-The rhythm of the music has nothing to do with what's happening on screen. The hexagon "beats" to the music, but that's about it. Sometimes the rhythm of movements you make will match the music, but that's an occasional coincidence.
-However, the music is incredibly good, and to the extent that music can match the "mood" of moving polygons, it totally does. The music is enjoyable, but somehow, even though it's not a rhythm game, nothing beats playing while listening.
-There are no "step" controls. You might think that pressing the arrow key once will move the triangle perfectly from one side of the hexagon to the next, but you'd be wrong. The longer you hold the arrow key, the farther you'll move. You will have to master manually holding the arrow key for the correct amount of time, every time, and on faster stages, the timing changes.
-This makes the game many, many times harder than you'd think. However, it never crosses the line of being unfair. As long as you aren't having any input lag, every failure is going to be purely because of a mistake you made. The collision of the triangle and the obstacles are also much more forgiving around the edges, kind of like a bullet hell. Seriously though, turn off vsync.
-If you played the original "Hexagon" for some reason, moving into the sides of obstacles no longer kills you, only crushing.
In short: Super Hexagon is another excellent game by Terry Cavanagh.
Just don't go into it with the wrong expectations.

Because there are no checkpoints, and the levels are forced to be unlocked in a sequential order, you may be stuck repeating the same level (from the very beginning!) fifty times in a row before you're able to move on to the next. I guess that counts as replay value? I know that I had to play the level where I'd roll across an incredibly narrow path surrounded by LAVA maybe two dozen times. And why is the camera completely controllable in the y-axis? The computer controlled camera is crappy enough to warrant turning it off completely and just using the second stick on a controller to move the camera around, but under what circumstances do I need to see the ball from UNDERNEATH the track? The camera stick has complete control here, but that's not helpful in real life. What would be nice would be if pushing R3 would "right" the camera to point in the same vector as the ball's velocity. An arrow pointing to the destination would be nice, or at least, pointing to the next crystal-thing. Pushing any buttons on a standard gamepad makes a distracting cursor appear on the screen - I couldn't see how it'd even be possible to play ANY game like this without a gamepad for analogue input. Polyball is a momentum-based precision platformer with a focus on "Goin Fast". The game is beautifully minimalist in design, controls, and visuals. I play using a controller, and the movement feels extremely tight and satisfying, especially when going near top speed. You are given the controls of movement (acceleration), and a single jump. With limited controls, the mechanics don't run especially deep, but mastering the momentum control required for later levels, or to compete for top times, can present a worthy challenge for even experienced players of momentum platformers. Fans of these games will also appreciate the quick restart button for endless resets in the quest for the perfect IL run. With online leaderboards, you can race against anyone's "ghost" and see how they complete the level. There is also talk of a replay system, but nothing solid as of yet. It should also be mentioned that the developers are extremely responsive on the forums, so many of the early-access kinks are being smoothed quickly.
Since it is early access there is a fairly small selection of maps (sectors) to choose from - 30 in total. These levels progress from easy/beginner to some considerably difficult maps towards the later levels (with some crossing the line into "tedious"). I personally feel as though there are more difficult maps that require precise movement than necessary. I would like to see more levels in the easy-to-medium category that allow for a focus on optimization, rather than not dying. There are currently a few packs of unreleased maps which will be coming out soon, so hopefully this comment will no longer be relevant at that time.
Overall I would definitely reccomend this game to anyone on the fence, or anyone that is interested in the genre.

Re-review (Ignoring DC)
Pros -
1. Great to see Barry back, the little girl he is partnered with is a great new character.
The two characters work well together, a kind old man and a baby faced girl. Compared to Clair with her terrible romance plotline, and Moira complaining constantly, these two characters are a joy to be around and probably the best characters and interaction the franchise has seen.There levels themselves, particularly in the fourth chapter, are far superior.
2. Runs well
On a mid end Machine this runs a silky smooth 60fps for me while also looking decent.
3. Fairly long game
Depending how you play, if you play easy or normal you will shoot through it. On survival (recommended) it is a much longer, more meaningful and enjoyable game that involves concerning ammo and thinking now and again exactly how to approach situations.
Ignoring raid mod, the single player can run 20+ hours, higher with replay's as the game features various mods and collectibles.
4. High replability (skills/collectibles)
Upon finishing the game, mods such as invisible enemies, time challenge as well as a bunch of unlocks can be done, extended the game length a fair bit.
Cons
1. Checkpoint system designed by man with brain damage
You know those upgrade benches in Dead Space? Imagine it saved, just before you collected an upgrade 5 feet away, just before you actually added and modified upgrades. Imagine a cutscene two seconds afterwards, that needs tapped over as well.
Imagine that over and over and over and over, because someone didn't have the common sense to put the checkpoint  afterwards.
Possibly the most badly designed checkpoint system ever implemented, it's that bad.
2. Odd difficulty spikes
On survival is decent, but not impossible. Yet it seems to randomly jump from easy, to a very hard with no sense of flow. Some bosses (drill) are outright broken.
3. A bad story
Feels almost non existent for most ofthe game. Some characters are basically "fill space here".
4. Partner AI is stupid
At time the player will be required to dodge or move, while you do it, the AI will quite happily stand there regardless of using the "follow me command". The exploding zombies are by far the worst problem.
Overall: I prefer the first Revelations, it had a more interesting setting, was better designed and although stupid, had enough story to keep me engaged.  This isn't a bad game by any means, it's actually one of the better entries in recent years. But, problems exist, be aware of that, esp if you plan on playing survival mode. It probably would have ended up a better game if it was purely Barry and Natalie, as these are the overwelmingly the single players strong points.
For me personally, the checkpoint system is by far the most infuriating, even on the most basic level, did not a single person developing the game say "this doesn't make much sense?. Apparently not.
Playing this game makes me feel like a single 40 year old woman with an office job, but it's fun and simple if you just want to pass the time.
All I can say is that this game is incredible. It is very rare to find a game that balances plot and good 'ol shoot 'em up fun. Just remember: gravity gun+rotary saw blade=a whole lot of fun.

A very cute and simple game, but there are a lot of things that needs to be improved on.
For starters, it's practically a gamble to guess which blocks you could actually stand on - and that could REALLY risk you your game. Apparently you can step on flowers but not trees. Okay.
Secondly, the controls are a bit odd, making the game unnecessarily tough. It's not uncommon for you to lose because you fail to jump on a cloud (because you REALLY have to aim for it's top) and end up landing on spikes. Also ended up getting stuck on flowers a few times.
Third, lives are practically useless - you restart from the beginning if you die anyway. they serve no purpose whatsoever other than to save you time from going back to the menu and selecting the level again.
Fourth, There are very, very little help for new players in the beginning. Yes, the game shows you which key to press when you open the game - but that screen barely lasts for like a second. I had to restart the game like three times to read it to figure out which key I have to press to shoot (it's the down arrow key by the way, which is highly unusual). In fact, I didn't even know I could shoot until about ten minutes into the game, which was when I realized the monster placements are far too ridiculous for there not to be a way for players to kill them.
Fifth, the game lacks a 'tutorial' level for new players to get used to the game. The very first level, it ruthlessly throws you into a full-on game where you have to collect literally 70 lemon blocks or whatever it's called (barely read what the guy in the beginning said since it's one big, clumped wall of text with no punctuation whatsoever).
Overall, the game is cute and it definitely has some potential, and I would recommend it to people if what I wrote above got fixed - but otherwise I wouldn't really bother with it. I really dig the music though. Super fun and bright.

Pure masterpiece. Just have a look at some of these:

Firstly, we got a new boss:
Dr. Hans Volter -- Lower HP than Patty, but deals more damage. Once his HP drops under 75%, 50% and 25% he will enter a hunting phase. Then he gains a shield which is able to take some ammount of damage. If the shield is destroyed - he get's back to his previous state, but if it's not - he will drain HP from a player he caught.
We got 4 types of clots:
Alpha Clot -- Regular clot, just as in KF1. He can still grab you and stuff.
Cyst -- Depressed clot. Very slow, low damage and he misses his attacks pretty often.
Slasher -- Agressive variant of Alpha Clot. Deals more damage, has hight attack rate and moves a bit faster.

ALSO, on Suicidal and Hell on Earth, zeds gain new abilities. For example:

Husk -- Can use his fire-ball cannon as flame thrower if you get too close to him. Also, on all difficiuties, Husk can perform a suicide move which deals a lot of damage.

Every perk has their unique melee weapon and granades.

Commando -- HE grenade, which is... HE grenade.
Support -- Frag grenade, which is... Frag grenade.
Medic -- Medical grenade, which both deals damage to zeds over time and heals teammates.
Firebug -- Molotov, which is... Molotov.
Demolist -- HE grenade, which is... HE grenade.
Sharpshooter -- Freezing grenade, which freezes zeds.
SWAT -- Mentioned Flashbang.
Survivalist -- He has a choice between Medical grenades, HE and Molotovs.

Mirror's Edge is a one-of-a-kind game with it's own expirience when you play it. Get involved into some action and fast-paced parcour on roofs, inside buildings and on the streets! All that comes in addition with a bright style of graphics and a handfull of other, very fitiing, colours.
To begin with, the mechanics and the idea are a very neat thing, and it keeps you occupied for the time you play the story, as you get to use the variety of interactions, like wallrunning, pipe climbing, walljumping, disarming, sliding, etc. in a totally random order, depending on the levels.
The con at that part is, that the level design forces you to take a passage, the game is rather linear when it comes to that. There sometimes are several possibilites to get around though, still they end with the same result/position to be in.
The idea behind collecting secrets to unlock artwork/extras is a neat idea, still, I do believe that it does not really improve the fact, that the replayability is kind of low, as you barely get to see something new when you play for a second time.
The multiplayer, if you can call it like that, is more like a racer. No cool disarming, no avoiding or dodging of gunfire. You race other people, with the hope to win. Nothing else to say at that point.
In total, I can recommend Mirror's Edge at the price it is at. It is worth buying and enjoying, as it is a different expirience.

It will redownload the Japanese version once it finishes go to the folder where steam resides.  It is generally in Program Files if you didn't change its default path C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/teamapps/common/Shadowverse/Shadowverse_Data/StreamingAssets copy the v and m folders to desktop.  Change the language of Shadowverse back to English and replace the v and m folders.  You are set for Japanese voices with English words.

As a fan of the original X-COM: UFO Defense, I eagerly anticipated playing Enemy Unknown. Enemy Unknown has proven to be an intensely enjoyable yet often frustrating game, one which I continue to enjoy, an be frustrated by nearly a year after first playing it. The Enemy Within DLC has added new levels of enjoyment and a lot of reduction in frustration to the game.
Pros include excellent graphics, clever game mechanics, a decent story, creative missions, top quality voice acting (mostly) and a rich experience in combat tactics and (minor) global strategy.
Cons include unbelievable (and ridiculous) random number generation, apparently illogical restrictions and some scripted elements that could be better appreciated if they were more random so as to improve replay value.
In summary, the game is mostly about the balance between choices and restrictions, and can easily frustrate perfectionists and more casual players alike, but it is beautifully executed and definitely rewarding to play through to the end. I highly recommend it, especially when coupled with the Enemy Within expansion.

Interesting take on an old classic.  The graphics have been dutifully updated and the responsibility of "reporting" to a higher Council leads to an interesting take on where to send your troops.  The cutscenes are fun and develop the background story.    Character movement and combat is easy and the cover system allows you to make tactical decisions far more easily than the old game.
But the game has clearly lost the older game's warmth and tension (admittedly, this may be nostalgia speaking).  The repetitive nature of putting characters into "Overwatch" becomes tiring (why no "perma-watch?") and the constant changing of hotkey assignments depending on situation(s) is completly annoying.  You develop no attachment to your characters (except the cutscene characters) other than from their skill development, and you're also artificially constrained by who can do what.  Character roles are pre-assigned via random player drop. You can't "grow" one character into a sniper, for example.  They're a sniper based on some random pre-determined roll. Super Hexagon is NOT A RHYTHM GAME. It is very much a fast-paced action game, and an excellent one at that. However, if you're thinking of giving Super Hexagon a try, you need to get this through your head. Super Hexagon does an excellent job of looking like a rhythm game, and it could have been--but it isn't one. Here are some important facts you need to know:
-The patterns you need to avoid occur in a randomly selected order. There is no memorizing the stages; you must react to everything in real time, and that video trailer is actual footage that's not sped up in any way. Warning: this game is HARD.
-Rather than memorizing the stage, you must memorize individual patterns, learn to recognize them quickly, and react to those patterns with the proper input, while also identifying and preparing for the next pattern. If you like fast-paced action games, you will have a lot of fun with Super Hexagon. If you prefer rhythm games, you will most likely get frustrated.
-The rhythm of the music has nothing to do with what's happening on screen. The hexagon "beats" to the music, but that's about it. Sometimes the rhythm of movements you make will match the music, but that's an occasional coincidence.
-However, the music is incredibly good, and to the extent that music can match the "mood" of moving polygons, it totally does. The music is enjoyable, but somehow, even though it's not a rhythm game, nothing beats playing while listening.
-There are no "step" controls. You might think that pressing the arrow key once will move the triangle perfectly from one side of the hexagon to the next, but you'd be wrong. The longer you hold the arrow key, the farther you'll move. You will have to master manually holding the arrow key for the correct amount of time, every time, and on faster stages, the timing changes.
-This makes the game many, many times harder than you'd think. However, it never crosses the line of being unfair. As long as you aren't having any input lag, every failure is going to be purely because of a mistake you made. The collision of the triangle and the obstacles are also much more forgiving around the edges, kind of like a bullet hell. Seriously though, turn off vsync.
-If you played the original "Hexagon" for some reason, moving into the sides of obstacles no longer kills you, only crushing.
In short: Super Hexagon is another excellent game by Terry Cavanagh.
Just don't go into it with the wrong expectations.

Played this a few months ago. This is a "classic" styled (mostly) combat oriented turned based RPG, set in the Shadowrun universe. It got me engaged for about 15 or 20 hours, which might be rather short for some, but to me, it was perfect: Before, Shadowrun was unknown to me, and the game served as an excellent introduction. It felt like a combination of 90s sci-fi and typical fanatasy lore including magic, dwarves, orcs and elves,... and I liked it very much.
The game, with the intriguing Shadowurn world, succeeds in creating great environments, characters, dialogue and above all, atmosphere. Combat reminded me somewhat of XCom: Enemy Unknown, but is less difficult, but still challinging and engaging (which is actually a plus compared to XCom imho).
Suffering from avataritis (I f*cking love creating custom appearances), the limited customisations options (and limited choise of matching portraits) where a little disappointing, but easily forgiven.
The thing that worried me most, was that there are no extensive cut scenens, voiced dialogues etc: The game (made possible by Kickstarter) relies heavily on text for that, including descriptions of what's going on. Infected by the internet era, it takes me some effort to focus on written text on my screen and actually attentivly read the damn thing. However, after I forced myself to do that, I was damn hard surprised how well that worked: Writing is overall great and adds incredible richness to the game, that I couldn't suspect before.
In Short: Great combat oriented suprising and engaging "little" RPG that due to its rather shorter lenght is a perfect in-between game. After my play-trough, I immediately orderd the Dragonfall DLC (now standalone and further improved), which is said to be "richer" in content and combat, and which I will play soon now and have great expectations of.
PS: I disagree with some claiming that melee is useless in the game. I had a well balanced chi casting melee specialised female Orc, and in combanation with the right team, it worked great. Played game on Hard.

I had never known what a 'Rogue-like' was before I picked up this game; I just loved the idea of being a starship commander. Not just some lone shmuck flying a fighter or a transport ship between systems; an actual captain, with a real ship with compartments, corridors and subsystems and a real crew to obey my orders. As soon as I realized that this game could let me do that, I grabbed it.
FTL is a challenging game, all the more so by the fact that you get only one life - when you die, you're dead - that's what a 'Rogue-like' game is. As in real life, failure means the destruction of your ship and crew. That's ok - the game is designed for multiple play-throughs, and a full game takes only a couple of hours to finish. As you must always stay one step ahead of the onrushing enemy, you can never unlock everything during a single play session, and a large number of unlockable ships provides incentive to keep playing again and again.
Combat is frenetic and nail-biting, as you must manage everything seemingly at once. You must keep an eye on your hull integrity, move your crewmen from room to room in order to repair damage and keep key systems online, even repel boarders who will otherwise wreak havoc on your ship. All the while you have to try to blow the other guy out of space! A wide variety of different enemy ships and armaments means that the same tactics will rarely work twice.
On top of everything, there is a multi-layered RPG system in place. Keep crewmen at one duty post and they will gain skill in that discipline, increasing your effectiveness. Scrap collected after each encounter must be used wisely - do you spend it all to upgrade your ship, or keep some in the hopes of finding a shop and buying new weapons? Keep in mind that you also need it to buy ammo, fuel, and repair your hull! There's never enough resources to upgrade everything to the max - you must choose carefully and decide what to focus on.

Finally... Capcom finally figured out what makes Resident evil well.... Resident evil. It only took like 2 major series games for them to really figure it out. After finishing up the last extra episode, I think its time to finally write a review. Be warned, I have not played Raid Mode yet so I will not be judging the game on that mode, just the main campaign and extra episodes.
Pros:
- Other characters that are not Chris... Oh my lord, Capcom finally realized they had other characters in the series o.o
- Very solid Gameplay, feels exactly like the old games in the past without it living TOO much in its past.
- Graphics
- Good atmosphere mixed with the gameplay
- Extra episodes offer different style of gameplay from the main campaign
- Partner Character actually feels really good, and teamwork is actually noticeable this time compared to the previous 2 games.
Cons:
- Story is ok but i think it could be better
- Controls are clunky and a bit unintuitive for keyboard & mouse users
- Graphics (both a pro/con)
- Still missing the charm of previous games but it does pay some homage back to them
- Lack of Big Boss Fights (Only saw 2, rest are mini-boss types)
Long Review Here (Shorter down below):
Gameplay:
Gameplay in this game is actually solid surprisingly. I honestly did not think Capcom would be able to recover after the disasterous gameplay of Resident Evil 6 but they managed to. Basically, take the great Resident evil 1/2/3 gameplay and mix it with Resident evil 4/5/6 gameplay. You got the scarce ammo (1/2/3) around that needs to be found, encouraging actual exploration of the area since enemies DO NOT drop ammo this time. This brings back the tense and scary atmosphere of the previous games. Several times throughout, i actually ran pretty low on ammo but their is enough to be able to get through all the episodes. Once I started to notice this, I couldn't help but crack a smile towards Capcom for returning back to this type of gameplay. Gameplay that defined the Resident Evil series, finally! This game, since its a third-person over the shoulder (4/5/6), employs a lot more stealth sections and stealth kills which are more crucial in Barry's Campaign and "The Struggle" campaign than anything else. Stealth is required for "Little Miss" episode as it employs a very Silent-Hill type atmosphere with the fog and enemy filled environments. It was actually a nice change to actually having to search the environment for weapons and ammo like you did in the past. This game also employs skill upgrades and weapon customization through parts found like in the 1st Revelations. You can also craft different types of healing items and different explosives that can aid you throughout the game. You will not find them through normal means and it employs that risk/reward value. Sacrifice a crucial healing herb to get some tourniques for bleeding? Or for disinfectants for gunk on the screen? Overall, their is soo much gameplay styles here through stealth, crafting, scavenging, and using different weaponry that it just feels so nice to have options once again in Resident Evil. What is a downfall though in gameplay is the fact the game is strictly linear for the most part with very little to no puzzles. Despite the previous classics where they imployed a large amount of puzzles and different paths to get to the same destination, sadly, revelations 2 lacks this. You essentially go from point A to point B while scavenging once in a while for supplies, not much else. At least in the classics, the linearity was broken up by offering different ways to get different cutscenes. 4/5/6 were mostly strictly linear games no matter what. Capcom has yet to break from this, but with the mass improvements to gameplay, I hope they will overcome this barrier soon.
Story (SPOILERS!):
Finally!!! A GAME WITHOUT CHRIS REDFIELD FOR ONCE, OR LEON KENNEDY! Oh its a joyous day when Capcom realizes they have other characters in the series. Especially a fan favorite Barry Burton who makes a great comeback in this game. What sucks though, is the fact that Capcom had to give a reason to bring Barry back which in this case... is his daughter missing for 6 months. Great, lovely. Claire Redfield does make a return though and its great to see her again in her usual badass form. While I think the story CAN stand on its own 2-feet, what I don't understand is the fact they leave a fair amount of plotholes. Like the chopper suddenly malfunctioning because Alex can remotely do that somehow just so we can kill off another annoying character? Even the T-Phobos virus is presented poorly. God forbid that every Resident Evil Game does not have to introduce a new virus every single time unless its a spinoff.  We have like what? 10 different Viruses now at this point? Apparently, all the major characters excluding Barry have been infected with the T-Phobos virus that triggers on fear... Game logic, won't argue against it. However, they forget to bring this to a closure after the game. After like the first 2 episodes, its kinda just dropped and forgotten, I mean, they leave the island WITH  the virus INSIDE THEM WITHOUT THEM CARING... WHY? Did they just suddenly forget about it? Guess they are screwed in the feeling fear department. Also, why did Alex Wesker even bother to kidnap the TerraSave people if she is just gonna kill herself and use one of her past victims anyway? What was the point of subjecting them to it? OH FOR GAME CONVENIENCE!! Oh whatever, at least Barry makes a comeback WITH HIS ALMIGHTY MAGNUM! I WILL THANK CAPCOM FOREVER FOR THIS! Even his closing line was done at the right time perfectly. I guess I can forgive the subpar story because Barry!! Nah jk.. Still a great character though.
Atmosphere:
The atmosphere is actually pretty good in the horror department. Their is a lot of dread and fear induced with the tight gameplay mechanics, even though the controls suck on the M&KB. The enemies actually have good field of view and not flawed where they can just randomly see you through that the random solid wall. This really adds to the tension and atmosphere because you can actually save ammo if you can succesfully pull off a stealth kill or fail and be in for a tough fight depending on who you are fighting. What also apparently happens is that the enemies killed in Claire's Campaign will also affect Barry's campaign so you'll see different things depending what how you kill the enemies. Personally, i never really saw this in action but just the feeling of it being there can really add especially when traveling 6 months into the future with the island, basically in ruins and disrepair. You can really see the effects and changes over the 6 months with the different enemies and all the ruined structures around. You will generally feel very creeped out as you realize that the island was the result of actual experimentation. Even the notes you read can creep you out. Well Done Capcom!
Graphics:
The graphics aren't the biggest things this game has to offer but at least they don't suck. In fact, a lot of the areas do look generally nice and the environments are well done. Not much else to say though.
Short Review:
If you been putting off Resident evil since 4, haven't played since then and been wondering whether its time to jump back in with revelations 2, I can safely say Yes! Its time to return to the series. Capcom has done well to learn from their mistakes with the past couple games by offering players the a better Resident Evil experience. Scarce ammo, clusterphobic areas, exploration, good gameplay. What is missing though is puzzles and actual item finding (crank/valve handles) from the previous games. However, if you can survive without those puzzles and those loving charms of the past games, this is a nice gem to add to your resident evil collection.

Faerie Solitaire is an interesting take on Relaxed Spider 'Patience'.
You can't really lose, so you can play as quickly as you'd like, though in order to advance to the next world you do need to complete some basic objectives.
Each world consists of 9 "hands" where the cards are laid out in front of you with seemingly random layouts and various annoyances between you and clearing all cards from the field for a perfect score, yielding bonus points. This leads to some interesting gameplay but is still very much luck based.
It's gotten really tiresome doing essentially the same thing every hand, so far across the 6 worlds and 279 hands out of the 8 worlds and 360 total hands in the story mode, I have completed. All of the gameplay elements are introduced fairly early, within the first 18-27 hands played.
I thought taking a break for a month or so would freshen up my perspective, but this game is really uninspired for the kind of engagement that I'm personally looking for in a game though that hasn't stopped me from recommending it though if you expect to have to think hard about solving puzzles and are looking for a challenge this is not the game for you.
Overall it's not awful if you can enjoy a card game for its surface value and it has a well crafted story and decent voice acting, the gameplay sounds are not that bad but are very generic. While the soundtrack is forgettable it does add proper mood to the games story.
Definitely not a game for achievement hunters as it could take you anywhere from 40 hours to easily over 200 to unlock all of them.

Polyball captures the gameplay reminiscent of Super Monkey Ball quite well, and goes a step further by adding a jump mechanic which opens up a whole new avenue for interesting levels and challenges to give the player.
Graphics:
The game is gorgeous and has a nice minimalistic aesthetic going on about it. The world is made up of low-poly objects and solid colors with shading. It all comes together nicely to create a surprisingly pleasing atmosphere.
There is a large amount of customization options for your ball that you can unlock with collectibles in the game, which change the ball's model, material, speed trail, and even a full chroma scale to pick your ball's colors from. These changes are purely aesthetic mind you, they have no bearing over actual gameplay.
Sound:
The music is pretty good in my opinion, ranging from high energy drum beats to chill electronic-style music. It fits in with the visual aesthetic quite well.
Gameplay:
I fully 100% recommend you play this game with a controller, you need access to a full stick to control the ball well.
There are only two controls that affect your character, the ball. The left stick moves the ball around and the A button (on a 360 pad) jumps. The jump is what really separates this game from being a monkey ball clone gameplay wise, as now more interesting obstacles show up such as levels requiring precision platforming, or having to jump from one ramp to another at high speeds over a bottomless pit. It is hard to get used to but once you get a good grasp on how the movement works you can get to pretty high speeds and get a very nice sense of momentum, but this is reliant on your skill. There are also your fair share of high speed downhill slides that don't need jumping as well.
Overall, this game takes an old idea and makes it fresh along with the great art direction. A fair warning though: this game gets very hard very fast. Be prepared to restart levels over and over again and get frustrated. However, the sense of satisfaction from beating a hard level drives you forward right into the next one.

I think this is probably my favorite LEGO game of all the LEGO games I've played. The missions themselves are fun and do a great job of utilizing the various characters in the marvel universe, but the real star of the game for me is the overworld. You get a gigantic (by LEGO game standards) overworld that consists of Manhattan with the helicarrier hovering overhead. The addition of flight means you can seamlessly fly from street level up to the helicarrier and the city is a playground by itself with lots of activity including traffic that you can charge through with a tank (or the hulk) sending bricks flying. Side missions abound with lots of hidden secrets to find.
My only gripes are the bugs (thankfully none of them were game-breaking) and the character creator doesn't let you choose the powers for the minifigure, they are attached to different parts so to get the power combination I want usually results in a very strange looking character.
Overall though this is an excellent game for LEGO or Marvel enthusiasts. Highly recommended.

I played Civ and Civ2 a long time ago. It is nice to see in Civ5 that it is possible to evolve the franchise without losing most of the ideas that made you love the original games.
We still have Civilopaedia, which is a nice way to learn a bit of history. We still have the wonders, and now they improve lots of stuff. We still have to think 5 turns ahead, because one wrong move may leave your army and cities too vulnerable. We still have the Spaceship and the Conqueror finales, and now have another 3 ways to win the game.
The different finales, together with the huge amount of playable civs makes the game challenging for many replays. I finished about 20 games and still have lots of achievements to get.
It is also nice that it is possible to run the game even in slow PCs, albeit there is a big loss of visual quality. But still, the fun of this turn-based game compensates.
In the Brave New World DLC, there is a major overhaul, because of the inclusion of tourism. I suggest you get the complete edition, so there is no problem when trying to play online. Totally recommended game.

As a fan of the original X-COM: UFO Defense, I eagerly anticipated playing Enemy Unknown. Enemy Unknown has proven to be an intensely enjoyable yet often frustrating game, one which I continue to enjoy, an be frustrated by nearly a year after first playing it. The Enemy Within DLC has added new levels of enjoyment and a lot of reduction in frustration to the game.
Pros include excellent graphics, clever game mechanics, a decent story, creative missions, top quality voice acting (mostly) and a rich experience in combat tactics and (minor) global strategy.
Cons include unbelievable (and ridiculous) random number generation, apparently illogical restrictions and some scripted elements that could be better appreciated if they were more random so as to improve replay value.
In summary, the game is mostly about the balance between choices and restrictions, and can easily frustrate perfectionists and more casual players alike, but it is beautifully executed and definitely rewarding to play through to the end. I highly recommend it, especially when coupled with the Enemy Within expansion.

Interesting take on an old classic.  The graphics have been dutifully updated and the responsibility of "reporting" to a higher Council leads to an interesting take on where to send your troops.  The cutscenes are fun and develop the background story.    Character movement and combat is easy and the cover system allows you to make tactical decisions far more easily than the old game.
But the game has clearly lost the older game's warmth and tension (admittedly, this may be nostalgia speaking).  The repetitive nature of putting characters into "Overwatch" becomes tiring (why no "perma-watch?") and the constant changing of hotkey assignments depending on situation(s) is completly annoying.  You develop no attachment to your characters (except the cutscene characters) other than from their skill development, and you're also artificially constrained by who can do what.  Character roles are pre-assigned via random player drop. You can't "grow" one character into a sniper, for example.  They're a sniper based on some random pre-determined roll. There are other issues which led me to feel playing the end-game was more tedious than the climax of an evolutionary game.

AntiChamber is one of those rare few games that really caught my attention. I brought the humble bundle that had this involved and thought: "Meh, free game, i'll give it a shot.". But low and behold, this game was so much more than I had anticipated.
Some people I know have said this is just another artsy fartsy game, but although it does have a refined style, it really works with the elements involved in the game itself. And regardless, this game hasn't just focused on looking stylised, the puzzles are interesting and enjoyable, give a real feeling of satisfaction once figured out and also has some puzzles which an individual can appreciate for being clever.
The sense of progression in this game is also rewarding due to some specific occurances as you venture through the game which change the way puzzles work, making the game suddenly seem fresh and this also allows progress to new areas obviously. I won't mention what since I don't want to spoil anything even if it is trivial.
The game itself is also charming due to its style but also something which I personally love, the messages which are relevant to the puzzles you come across. Little "Life" messages you could say, are relevant to the current puzzles in your face, examples being "Sometimes you have to take some steps back to advance." which is as you can imagine relevant to a specific puzzle in the game. This little imaginitive and quirky layout of hints really gives the game extra character.
Overall this game was one of the most encapturing games I have played in quite some time, and I feel it is also very unique to most other puzzle games. Sure I paid a cheap price for this, but I would have happily paid more if I had known the quality of this game. Don't be afraid to give it a go, you might find the change of game type refreshing!

TL;DR
Like many people have said before me but this game is is what Dead Island should have been, with parkour, fun zombie killing and fluid gameplay. It still suffers from some of the annoying things dead island did though.
7.5/10
+great co-op
+satisfying zombie murder
+excellent free running
+Mostly good characters (Gazi was an embarassment)
-Weapon breakdown is too rapid
-Singleplayer lacks because of co-op focus
-weapon effects have no real meaning (?)
WEAPONS
They still have this weapon degrading mechanic which is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Your weapons gets worn down with every hit but at an amazingly high rate. In the beginning you will be picking up every weapon you can get since every weapon has a durability of about 3-5 zombies before repair is needed. And repairs are limited so you can never really get attached to a weapon since it will later on break for the last time and then be useless. It is however easy to find weapons and you can get perks which prolongs the life of your weapon so in the long run it's more tedious than game breaking. Also you can add different effects to your weapons like electricity, fire and poison(why would you need to poison zombies?) but almost none of them seem to really have a big effect on the weapons stats. I mean sure the zombies get lit on fire or spaz out if you hit them with electricity but mostly they just keep on attacking with the effect ticks away minimal health. I would have liked to have had more diversity in effects not just better versions of the same four things and also that had more impact on the weapons damage output and handling.
PARKOUR
The freerunning is great. It is incredibly fun and fluid to get from point A to point B by jumping from rooftop to rooftop and avoiding zombies or straight out using them to climb. I really have no negatives on this part except maybe that it sometimes doesn't really goes exactly where you thought it would but rather climbs another obstacle.
CHARACTERS
I haven't finished the game but so far I must say that most of the characters are really good. And the voice acting on the main characters are most often really good. The player Kyle Crane is voiced by Roger Craig Smith and you can really relate to him and what he says. The animation is really nice too in the cutscenes.
ZOMBIES
The zombies are really fun and they work great. The special zombies don't really do it for me since there is little to no strategy to really take some of them down. For instance the giant guys with clubs you basically just have to kite since none of your special moves works on them and the spitters's spit is like homing missiles and will follow you if you move so the only real strategy is to go straight for them, take the attacks in the face and just bash it. Maybe it's just my personal preferences but still I feel they could have been made better. The day and night cycle is really good and when night falls you are really scared for your life. The sound of the nightmares are haunting and you really creep around trying your damnedest to not be seen while still hauling as much♥♥♥♥♥as possible.
CO-OP
This is one of the best co-op experineces I've had. I think it is mostly because of the seamless transition from single to multiplayer. Plus there is no restriction on being close to each other or taking care of each other. You can basically do your own thing but together. Sadly though I would not really recommend playing this game singleplayer since a lot of missions and encounters are so obviously made with co-op in mind. It makes the game insanely difficult to play solo at times and I feel sorry for all the people who don't have a buddy to play with. Still that should not stop you if you like getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you over and over again.
So ultimately I would say this is a pretty good game even though it might have needed some tweaks but all in all me and my friend have really fun playing this.

I'm going to compare Shadowverse directly to Hearthstone since that's probably where most of the interested players are coming from. Warning: This is pretty long
Things SV does better:
1. MUCH more variety than Shamanstone. We all know that Hearthstone is at an extremely low point right now- that's why competitors like TESL, GWENT, and SV are doing so well. All the classes in SV play differently and they all require different tactics to beat. Yeah, there's still the generic Zerg and Ramp class, but SV focuses a lot more on control and combo decks; Going aggro against Urias will get you slaughtered as he's able to push out stronger minions at lower health. But at the same time, going full on control against Isabelle may not go so well since she gets stronger the more spells she casts. You'll have to find a nice medium to do well.
Something I really like is how you'll sometimes have to do something for the first part of the game, and then adopt a completely different strategy late game since that's when certain decks are at their strongest. I'm a particular fan of Luna's playstyle where certain cards grant her a secondary resource (shadow) that'll be immediately spent if you play certain other cards. The fact that it's immediate is nice since it makes you plan multiple turns ahead: yeah, you could drop a minion on an empty board this turn, but you'll automatically burn through the shadows needed to perform combos later on. In which case, the best decision is to pass the turn- something that is VERY rarely optimal in Hearthstone
2. You don't have to play on curve every turn. Since your cards can have different effects based on which turn you play them on (like in my last example with Luna for example) as well as the order you play them on your turn, always playing on curve is not a smart decision. Curvestone players have the lesson of always needing to play on curve beaten into us; if you're stuck between two options in Curvestone, the best choice is almost always to just match the number of mana you have to the numer on the top left corner of the card. This Curvestone playstyle removes a lot of the thinking behind the game, which turns into a match of who can play more minions. A thinking card game like SV is a refreshing breath of air.
3.  waifus
4. The animation is gorgeous. Some cards in SV are animated, which is basically the Hearthstone equilivant of golden cards. Most of the golden animations in Hearthstone are pretty meh, with the exception being the dragons and a couple of legendaries. But every animated card I've seen in SV has been absolutely beautiful: the colors all pop out and the transition from background to foreground is done seemlessly.
5. The story isn't exactly deep, but I was surprised by how much I found myself caring for the characters. Everyone has their own personality, hopes, and fears and if you dig past the bright colors and chirpy emotes and sound effects, it's actually pretty dark. A little girl having delusions of her dead parents and copes with their deaths by trying to kill everyone she meets? A man accidentally kills his friend and puts himself through self exile to protect his loved ones? A women tries in vain to resurrect her dead fiance after he's murdered by their mutual friend?
The addition of a minion henchmen who reveal people's darkest fears and another who tempts the characters by promising them their heart's desires adds a surprising amount of depth to the characters of a free anime-esque card game
6.  Evolution lets you regain tempo really rapidly if you're starting to fall behind. You can smack a single opponent minion for massive amounts of damage in one turn, which in turn forces you to plan your moves ahead of time
7. The BM is actually hilliarious in SV. If you play AI, they'll sometimes sarcastically emote how they'll ever deal with your minions, before dropping a board wipe. Or they'll emote a BM right before smacking your face for lethal. It's actually pretty funny and the way that automute works in SV is also better than HS. In Saltstone, you're muted for a certain amount of time depending on how often you're emoting. Whereas in Shadowverse, you're only limited to the number of emotes per turn.
8. Smaller board size. You can only have a total of 5 cards on the board and this includes minions, artifacts (like from TESL and MTG. Hearthstone doesn't have it), and effects that are only activated after a certain number of turns out in play (think something like a reverse overload: you pay X mana now and Y turns later, Z happens). This means you to spend more time deciding which cards to play to optimize your board.
9. ARENA MODE IS FREEEE!! Kind of.
Things HS does better than SV:
1. Better menu UI. It's obvious where everything in HS is and how to access them. It took me 5 whole minutes just to learn how to open my cardpacks.
2. HS doesn't censor your decknames. Why is this a thing in SV?? How am I going to offend someone with my deckname that no one else can even see???
Conclusion: If you're sick of Hearthstone, it's worth checking Shadowverse out. The story is surprisingly good, it's more control oriented, actually requires thinking, and most importantly, it's free! If you're not a fan of SV's artstyle (perfectly understandable), I suggest checking out TESL.

It's been a long run for South Park: The Stick of Truth as development initially began in 2009, after South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone approached Obsidian about making a role-playing game designed to look exactly like the television series, which in the final product they managed to do flawlessly as The Stick of Truth feels like an entire season of the long running TV show, and a good one too. You assume the role of the new kid in town as you try to make friends and become a part of the fantasy role playing game that everyone in South Park seems to be a part of, either by standing behind Cartman's human race or Kyle's elves, fighting against each other to hold the Stick of Truth. Throughout this 12-16 hours journey you will meet iconic South Park characters, make new friends and gather allies to join your cause, so by the end of the game everyone in South Park will have a role to play in your game. What differentiates this experience from your normal South Park episode is its length and the opportunities that come with that to tell a longer, richer story without having to rely on previous episodes of the show to introduce you to some of the scenery in which the action will take place; of course, fans of the series will instantly recognize locations from the show, as all of the kids' houses as well as community buildings which often appear in the show are all here, but this game finally defines a map of where those buildings are located throughout town, and that gives great opportunities for exploration, even for old fans of the TV show. Among those iconic buildings and locations, The Stick of Truth comes with some new ones as well, and combining those in a map of South Park that feels authentic and logical creates an amazing playground for you and your buddies, giving great opportunities for side-quests, which the games comes no short of. While The Stick of Truth has a lot to offer for long-time fans of the show as the game is filled with references and even the smallest thing will bring back some memories to fans, the game manages to offer an amazing and hilarious experience even for those who haven't caught up with the TV show for the last couple of seasons, as it relies on basic humour, jokes and parodies of hit TV shows such as Breaking Bad or video games like Skyrim to make you laugh on every occasion. Aside from the fart jokes and all the hilarious lines it's pleasing to see how the world looks through a child's imagination, even when as an adult things are way different and Red Bulls are not magic potions, but since this is a South Park experience, even with that moment of revelation, be ready for things to quickly escalate into madness involving aliens, nazi zombies and Taco Bell.
The Stick of Truth at its core is a turn based RPG, allowing you and one of the multiple buddies which you will unlock along the way to form a party and adventure together, helping you out in combat, as well as keeping you company and occasionally make you laugh with an unexpected joke. Even though it keeps a simplistic look and basic controls to allow everyone to jump into the action, The Stick of Truth's turn based RPG elements leave plenty of room for strategy if you're willing to give the game a try on a harder difficulty level and face a real challenge. As you start your adventure, you can choose between four character classes: Fighter, Mage, Thief and Jew, and even if each comes with a set of unique skills, they make little difference in battle as there are no class specific items, meaning that a Mage can pickup a sword and use it just as well as a Fighter. Each character can perform two actions each turn,first giving you the option to restore HP or Mana using a potion, remove debuffs or use the character's special skill and then allowing you to perform a secondary action, attacking your enemies by using a skill, magic attack, or normal ranged/melee attack. There are plenty of options to choose from and The Stick of Truth's higher difficulty levels will challenge you to come up with the best strategies in order to succeed, but even with all those elements, The Stick of Truth manages to keep it simple for players who only want a South Park experience without the headache of a turn based RPG, making this title accessible to anyone who wants a taste. The greatest part about the game's combat system is that it's not overused to the point where it becomes boring and repetitive, leaving plenty of room for exploration, item gathering and non-combat sidequests throughout the story, often giving you a break between battles, and allowing you to gather more loot and better equipment to satisfy your needs, sending you on different paths to acquire the things you might need to progress further, and by the time you'll encounter the next series of battles, you'll already have new spells and items to play with, making it interesting once again. Since this game is the first time you get to fully explore the town, there are plenty of locations to visit and characters to find, the game often giving you sidequests to encourage you to explore more and find out what else there is to see and even giving you more tools as the story progresses to access previously unreachable areas such as small cracks in the walls which you can only enter using the Gnome Dust in order to shrink or high rooftops which can be accessed using the Alien Probe.
The Stick of Truth does not only feel like an episode of the show, but it looks like one as well, keeping the HUD elements to a minimum and only showing up when necessary, making the experience indistinguishable from the TV show outside of combat, and making it just as fun to watch as it is to play. Everything from the characters to the scenery and the iconic locations look authentic and add to the South Park experience you've always wanted to have. The menus are the only thing that could use a bit more work, as they can be disorienting and hard to browse at times, but that is only a minor issue as you will rarely have to use the menu as the game hardly breaks that atmospheric feeling of a South Park episode.
This thing sounds like the real deal, as all the voice actors from the shows are here to voice their respective characters, in beautiful high definition recordings that will make you laugh with each joke a character tells using his iconic accent and voice. Numerous songs already known from the TV show are present in here as well, used in the funniest ways possible and combined with some great sound effects also taken from the show, they help recreate an authentic South Park feel; after all, there is nothing like walking into a store and Cartman's "Kyle's Mom is a ♥♥♥♥♥" starts playing on the radio.
It can take you up to 15 hours to complete the campaign if you're willing to complete all the side quests and collect everything, unfortunately there is not much replay value after that as the character classes make no difference in combat, and there are no twists that might change the outcome of anything. The campaign is also the only thing the game has to offer, but if you're digging the turn based RPG elements, you might want to give it a second try on a higher difficulty level, unless you did that on the first try.
The Stick of Truth is like an entire season of South Park, keeping the humor, and its unique setting and adding some RPG mechanics that make it just as interesting to play as it is to watch, but even without giving much attention to its gameplay, the Stick of Truth is definitely a season of South Park worth watching

I just finished my first playthrough of XCOM: Enemy Unknown and I can whole-heartily recommend this game. It manages to do justice to the original 1994 classic, while offering the player a genuine 21st century gaming experience. On the whole, the game plays smoothly and the storyline is engaging and well-implemented.
If I had to mention two minor gripes, they would be these:
- Why is Dr. Vahlen not voiced by an actual German, or at least someone who properly speaks the language? The accent is convincing enough, but the few times that the character actually speaks German, it's very jarring to hear her mangle the words of her supposedly native tongue.
- The tension in philosophy between doctors Vahlen and Shen is a good addition to the story, one pushing for ever more discovery and victory at all cost, the other always arguing caution and reflecting on the implications on the human species as a greater whole. Good stuff, except we're not actually allowed to choose one path over the other. It would have been interesting to see an alternative path to victory, without experimenting with PSI.
But as I said, these are minor issues within an otherwise excellent game. I'm certainly looking forward to playing Enemy Within.

Takes everything you except from similar games of this genre such as Blizzard's HEARTHSTONE such as powerful Hero decks that play uniquely to one-another and fun card voice lines, then vary a few game mechanics such as freely Evolving the cards mid-battle to change their effects and triggers, and provide additional content in areas such as rich voice acting in a Single-Player story that you don't have to pay for to unlock and awards you to explore, and you get Shadowverse.
Simple and easy to get into, tons of variety in strategies to learn, multiple heroes with different battle mechanics- as well as Alternative Heroes (Skins+Voice Packs) for more variety that you can obtain swiftly with the IN-GAME CURRENCY from simply winning matches or in bulk by completing difficult challenges such defeating an AI on the Max difficulty or Completing a characters story.
At the moment, you are rewarded about 40 Card packs for joining (from 2 different reward piles for more range), and you get another 1 a week and as you progress in the Story (excluding what you manually purchase with your In-game Currency or Real Money), so your starter deck as your preferred Hero will never be the same as someone else's even if you're both new players to keep you on your toes for differences in tactics. You even get special rewards and cards dedicated to your chosen Hero when you progress with them in the story, so you get to learn how they work, unlock special combos/units for them, and take in an indulging  and increasingly challenging story all at once before you even decided to head online.
That said, like the rest, you can pay real money for more cards, so some players can find better strategies earlier than others, but this is currently commonplace in this genre and industry.
With the large range you're given even before you head online, how easy it is to obtain cards, the frequently updating card list, and the games built-in "randomise deck" mode to give you some good variations in strategies, it's great for beginners to the genre, and those who've spent many hours of games like it.
Definitely give it a try.

A fun turn-/squad-based strategy game - or something like that. Although it gets a lot of its content from the first UFO game, I don't consider it to be in the same genre. With vanilla options XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a game of chess, each soldier class is like a kind of piece on the board and two soldiers with the same class have (almost) the same gear and purpose on the battlefield. Even so it is fun to play - and I don't enjoy chess. The "almost" previously was due to the fact that you can select armour, weapon, pistol and one pocket item for each soldier - so you can have slightly different soldiers. No inventory management means you can't carry soldiers/captives, can't pickup, throw, give or drop stuff.
Luckily some of the sterility of this game can be reduced with the second wave options, which unlock after defeating the game once (I believe). Two things though even second wave options can't fix: the fore-mentioned missing inventory management and static maps: There is a limited amount of different maps and with only the original you will most likely run into the same map atleast twice on your first playthrough. The number of maps can be increased by getting Enemy Within as well.
The thing that's missing completely though is the "emergent story" aspect for which the first UFO game was known for. A soldier with a regular rifle can't pick up the shiny laser rifle from a downed buddy or throw/give grenade/medkit to other soldiers. If the soldier who was critically wounded and needs medical attention was the only one carrying a medkit, nobody can help him and will continue to bleed out. This makes no sense, but once you accept it as part of the (chess) rules, it is okay (for this game).

TL:DR: I recommend Dead Space. Just don't expect System Shock 2 or Resident Evil 4 out of it.
+Great sound and visual design. With every weapon having the right amount of punch and the characters and aliens having really interesting visual design. Combine that with a really immersive HUD and lighting to hide the game limitations and shortcomings and you have a game that aged quite well.
+More than a dozen unique aliens. Each more visually and mechanically different than the last.
+The cutting and stasis mechanic give an interesting spin on the combat.
+Great scares. But that's mostly because of jumpscares and spawing enemies behind you.
+Most fun when your thinking on your feet and when getting surrounded by lots of aliens.
+Zero Gravity. These are the best moments of the game. Where your allowed to lead the combat by zoofing back and forth from different positions.
-Dead Space lacks any kind of subtlety or build up. With your ship crashing and almost your entire crew getting killed within the first five minutes of the game. Because of this, the story of the game stays incredibly akward and doesn't really lose that akwardness until chapter four or five.
-At the later chapters it sometimes blurs the line between what is fun and challenging and what is just f*cking bullsh*t and really made me wish for something with i-frames.
-Don't you worry if you are going to forget how to kill enemies quickly. The game will jam it down your throat five times in
a row in less than two minutes in the the most straigth forward and unimmersive way possible.
-Audio logs. They just don't work in this game. At best they're not all that greatly performed. At worst they are just f*cking stupid.
-The characters are unintresting and bland. And didn't make me feel anything at all
-Inventory magement may as well not even exist. Because after upgrading your suit to level 2 (less than two hours into the game) you have enough inventory space for the rest of the game.
Even if inventory space would stay the same throughout the rest of the game.
resources are so limited and weapons have a seperate inventory space, ammo was either inside my weapon or inside the enemy.
-It runs quite often out of idea. With mini bosses and the play dead trick getting repeated again and again without any interesting new spin.
