So. Aliens have invaded and the fate of the world is in your hands. Invaded is a strong word. They're doing all sorts of diabolical things all around the planet, like abducting people and terrorizing cities. Invasion doesn't seem to be part of their plans. Yet. DUN DUN DUN!!!!
Anyway, you're in charge of XCOM, a super duper team of soldiers, engineers, and scientists. You capture alien stuff, research it, and build it to use against your enemy in turn based squad combat. As a fan of the original, I have been waiting for them to get this game right for decades. This one is close. You get some pretty good turn based squad combat, and some pretty good research and material management. I'm having a lot of fun playing it.
That being said, let me tear apart this game for a  bit. In the original, you could put your base anywhere. Except in the ocean.   (unless you bought that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game) In this one, you have six predetermined locations. You are also limited to four troops for your squad. While you can change that number by doing a little training, you still cant go above six. In the older version, you could take as many dudes/chicks as you could stuff into a skyranger. Hell, you didn't even have to give em guns. Then, you would throw human suffering at the aliens until you were victorious.
But yes. If you're a fan of the old, I think you'll like the new. Give it a shot when it goes on sale, or when the price drops. It isn't worth $40, but its a great game for $10 or $20.

Faerie Solitaire is a far better game than it has any right to be. As someone who's never dabbled much into solitaire, I figured I would spend an hour looking at this and chuckle at the whole thing. Weirdly, even though the story is a wonderful schlockfest of campy tropes and no connection to the actual gameplay or goals whatsoever, I couldn't stop playing.
Solitaire is a simple and admittedly boring game, one that is meant to pass time when there is nothing else to do and no one to play with. With only the lightest added perks such as monster collecting, light goals to reach, interesting card set ups and the removal of having to match specific suits, FS turns the whole trite affair into an exciting and wildly engaging affair that I couldn't put down for the next 3 days. I found it best served with some podcasts in the background so as not to feel like I was wasting my life away, but there is an amazing amount of content her from such a simple concept.
After it got its hooks in me, every hand I practically twitched when I didn't clear the boardfor fear of missing out on a new monster egg for my collection that might've been hidden behind those last two cards. The impressive difficulty curve the game presents is also kind of amazing, which is not something I was expecting at all. Fascinatingly complex set ups can lead to a surprising amount of forethought and tactical card plays that can make or break a run. Of course, like all games that surround the old 52, there is no garuntee you'll be able to clear the board, but Faerie offers a variety of unlockable tools that make the prospect more and more plausible. One tool in particular can save a hand for total defeat, in which if you can't make a move in 5 turns, you can zap a card and make it your base. It adds an extra layer to an already complex layer of moves, and once I got into the grove I could rip through hands at unbelievable speed. It's hard to describe just how rewarding this game can be without playing it yourself.
Of course, there are flaws. Plenty of them. The art used to differentiate the cards are not very appealing, the soundtrack can become grating, and the voice-acted story is cheesy and oh so teeth-grindingly bad. Somehow, though, this doesn't detract, but somehow amplifies the glory of this weird little game. While I wasn't neccessarily chomping at the bit to hear the next chapter in the riveting saga, there is a genuine aloof passion to the whole story that I can't help but admire. There is tons of great art in the game that just didn't seem to get used on the cards, but they do help stimulate recognition, to the point where I stopped paying attention to the numbers all together. This is not to say the art is bad; quite the contrary, but that goblin they put on the king cards really begged for a punch in the face. Of course for the soundtrack, you can always turn the music off and put something more to your taste on.
Not exactly a game I expected to like, and definitely not a game I'd come to love. Faerie Solitaire is the sort of guilty pleasure I never thought I wanted. I can't recomend this lovely pile of cheese enough.

One of my favorite games ever made, and definitely my favorite GTA up to this point for one very, very simple reason: the atmosphere.
In this game, you're in the 80's, in Vice City, and cocaine is rampant. The world is nearing the end of the Cold War, and everything has a pumped up, American spirit radiating from it in this time period... probably due to the cocaine.
Driving around, running dozens of people over while being chased by the cops as Flock of Seagulls' "I Ran" is playing in the background is one of the many simple joys in this game. This game's charm is bursting out the seams during every cutscene, the main characters are a nice homage to Miami Vice, and the plot is just about the same. This is pure 80's bliss from the legendary soundtrack, to the parodies on every corner, and even to the title alone, in that ridiculous vibrant font.
If you have not played this game before, definitely pick it up and play it. Turn on the radio, (Emotion 98.3 or Wave 103 are the best choices in my opinion) and have fun. Just, try not to get your suit wet.

This is a very solid digital card game; if you’re new to the CCG world and Hearthstone’s Warcraft theme doesn’t interest you too much, Shadowverse is a great alternative. It’s addictive and fast-paced, it has nice art, and it’s pretty easy to get a lot of free packs. If you’re a Hearthstone veteran, this is definitely a Hearthstone clone to the core. The presentation, the card crafting system, the game mechanics (Battle Cry is now called Fanfare, Taunt is called Ward, etc.), the mission log, the card rarity tiers, and so on are all 99% the same. Heck, it even has an Arena mode. I think it’s still worth playing even if you’ve played Hearthstone, though; it has just enough unique stuff going on that it’s different in interesting ways. I’ll write a bit here about how Shadowverse is different from Hearthstone, so that you can differentiate between them and see what you think.
- Shadowverse does have a few mechanics that you won't find in Hearthstone. One of the game's unique mechanics is the ability to “Evolve” your units. After a few opening turns, you'll get a small number of Evolve points that you can use on any of your units in the field – when a unit Evolves, it gets a stat boost, it sometimes gains an additional power or triggered ability, and it gets to attack on the same turn that it entered the field (a.k.a. Haste or Charge). This adds a nice extra level of strategy to the battle, because you have to consider whether or not your opponent is going to pop his or her Evolve and ruin your plans.  Every unit even has alternate Evolved art, which is a nice touch.
- I was never super-attached to the Warcraft universe (though I loved Warcraft 2 back in the day), so I prefer the anime art and setting of Shadowverse over Heathstone. Shadowverse's art is really good – some of it is too “~~kyaaaaaa~~” for my taste but for the most part it looks great. The best art in the game is reserved for the character portraits of the major character classes (I especially like Erika, the Swordcraft hero) and the legendary cards. There are quite a few animations in the game as well. When you use the Evolve power, your character will leap out of his or her emblem and do an animated flourish that looks awesome. The English voice acting is a bit cheesy at times, but it's not that bad...honestly, the English voices are actually quite solid. If you can use Japanese voice mode, though, that's much better.
- It’s quite easy to get free packs. When you start the game for the first time, you’ll get about 40 free packs from both the standard card pool and the latest expansion. I got a few nice legendaries, and I was quickly able to craft a couple more. While playing Hearthstone, I felt that the path to getting packs was a bit of a slog...Shadowverse is much more friendly about giving you packs and making legendaries that much more accessible.
- One of the biggest and most welcome differences from Hearthstone is that Shadowverse has a story mode! The story stuff here isn't going to set the world on fire, but it's a really nice supplement to the multiplayer game. If you like card games with a single player mode or you just want to get in some AI practice with a bit more context to it, this is going to be right up your alley. Every class gets its own story, and playing through the story nets you a few story mode-exclusive cards. Some of these story mode cards are really great and can form the foundation of a good deck, so make sure that you take the time to play through every story.
- Hearthstone is definitely more polished all around. It has that Blizzard sharpness to it that most other studios just can't fake, and Shadowverse is no different. Shadowverse started life as a a mobile game and it shows. The interface is a little clunky and awkward. This isn't a huge deal and Shadowverse is very playable...it's just not as user-friendly and easy to navigate as its high profile competition.
- While Shadowverse might not have Hearthstone's polish, the online matchmaking here is actually *excellent*. It's really easy to find a game, and I never encountered any lag. It seems like the community for this game is pretty big and growing larger, which is great. My only complaint is that a surprising numbher of people would rather concede than play out a match and see what happens. It's like, come on...you've still got 10 health and 5 cards in your hand. See what happens!

FOREWORD: I have played quite a few different zombie games, enjoyed some and hated others. They all have similarities and then the different things that make them a unique experience for better or worse.  Comparing them side by side is unfair as each must be taken as a whole experience. That said my Review:
I LOVE this game. The pace, the combat, the skill system and the crafting. I have minor disagreements with certain aspects of the story line and character interaction with some of the smaller role NPC.s but overall it's a fun story despite these hang ups.
COMBAT:    The speed and fluidity of combat is awesome and the use of the environment to overcome huge odds always produces an amazing outcome. Many, many " Holy @#!% " moments. Some of the combat abilities are weak but the majority of others are so so good. The shooting in this game is pretty satisfying too, though the pure joy is melee.
SKILLS & CRAFTING:   As stated there's a few skills that aren't especially helpful  but there are more that can be game changers.  The crafting is not overly complex and somewhat shallow but the results are effective.
So TLDR? BUY This Game! It's fast and nervewracking , you smash a variety of zombies in a bunch of different ways and at the end of the day - what really matters - IT'S FUN AS %$@#.

As an old school fan of the Resident Evil series [culling the infected since '96], I have to say that this series has definitely had its ups and downs. I still remember the completely game changing shocker that was Resident Evil 4, shying away from the traditional Survival Horror we were used to. After that, the franchise seemed to have lost its way a little. Resident Evil 5 was atrocious, both in the way of the plot, and in the character development. [Chris became a giant steroid monkey, and Wesker loses it completely and goes over the top, a terrible ending to one of my favourite video game bad guys] Operation Raccoon City was a very enjoyable non-canon romp through Raccoon City during the height of the T-Virus that stood apart from the rest of the franchise. Revelations was an interesting game, and 6 was... okay. It had its moments, but felt like it was trying to be too many things.
Revelations 2 however, hits the nail on the head. On one hand, you've got the ever brave Claire Redfield, sister to franchise protagonist Chris, fighting alongside Moira, daughter to Barry Burton, whom also was in the original game from way back in 1996. The two women have been kidnapped and are being held on an island somewhere near Russia, and are being monitored by someone called the Overseer as they try to find a way of escape. Unfortunately for the ladies, they are part of an experiment on a new virus called T-Phobos; a variant of the Uroborous virus, which is triggered in states of extreme fear. On the other hand, you've got Barry Burton himself, alongside a strange young girl named Natalia, trying to track down Moira and Claire on the island.
Each campaign has a distinct feel to it. Claire and Moira's made me feel constantly under pressure; Why have you been brought here, what the hell are these things trying to kill you, and who the hell is the Overseer and what is her end game? It is a very fast paced campaign, with quick enemies, boss monsters o'plenty and a defined goal: Escape. Barry and Natalia's campaign is more a slower paced, creeptastic crawl through the horror. Shambling zombies [although some who can pick up speed quickly, and some with extremely long reach!], more firepower, monsters that change depending on how you previously defeated them as Claire and Moira [I'm talking about normal enemies, not boss monsters!]
Each campaign has its own sidekick gimmick. Moira has a flashlight which can be used to blind enemies [setting them up for a strong melee knockdown] and can attack foes with her crowbar, whereas Natalia can sense and detect enemies through solid objects, and can throw bricks. [Don't knock the brick throwing, sometimes it's hilarious to hoss a brick at a zombie and watch it crumple] Each of these bring a different style of gameplay. If playing solo, you can jump back and forth between your character and their sidekick. So you can jump to Moira, use her flashlight to stun the quickly advancing Hammer Dude, so Claire can run forward, kick him to the ground, and you can quickly run up as Moira and implant your crowbar directly into his chest, weakening [not killing] him considerably. Whereas Moira can be a hindrance to her foes, with blinding lights and crowbar stuns, Natalia can be a very very helpful little lady! Using her ability to figure out where your foes are positioned can make for some very satisfying stealth clears, where it's possible to clear entire areas without being seen or heard.
I suppose I should try and wrap this up, as I could quite easily write an essay on this game.

Resident Evil is possibly one of my favorite series. While lots of people say that Resident Evil went down hill once 4 came out, I am one of the few old school Resident Evil players to actually have enjoyed all major Resident Evil releases, including 4 and up. Resident Evil Revelations 2 in my opinion is a decent mix of scary moments, with tense action horror. The co-op is extremely fun, and perhaps the most interesting in the series thus far. If you have someone willing to play a side character who doesn't get as many fun toys, but does get some interesting perks, then you or your partner should enjoy it.
One of the other positives to this game, at least on release, was it's cheap price. The game launched at 24.99, and for that price it's a great bang for your buck. The episodes are not extremely long, but they feel just right, and by the end of the game you will most likely feel like you got more than what you paid out of this game.
I do have some major gripes however. This game launched with no campaign co-op support on PC, and while they did fix that, there is still NO ONLINE campaign co-op. I pre-ordered this game assuming this would have been standard, as it was with all previous co-op RE titles, but sadly this game was not. I ended up having to split my 27" monitor screen with my best friend, and split screen in this day and age should be completely optional. LAN mode, or even online campagin should have been a no brainer, quite frankly it's pathetic it wasn't included. Yes I'm happy I get split screen, but still the developers should have done better.
Also a nitpick, as I mentioned above the side characters do not fire weapons, and have unique abilities. While this was interesting, and at times pretty damn fun, it would have been nice for them to have felt a little more useful, purley for higher fun factor for your co-op friends.
All in all, it was another fun Resident Evil game, if you don't mind the direction the series has moved in. Great value, just be sure to have a big screen for co-op play.

Lego games are a strange breed. I thought they had grown quite stale after releasing almost a dozen games with the same basic formula. I had given up on them myself around the time Lego Batman was released. However, I had to pick up Lego Marvel just to see if being able to play as a bunch of my favourite fictional characters would get me through the already stale Lego formula and thankfully the game felt extremely fun and fresh.
This could be entirely due to my time away but I had a ton of fun with Lego Marvel. There are a boatload of characters while they mostly fit into the same half dozen archetypes and you see the same ones in the story missions a bit too often for my tastes, the levels are all well made and varied so you stop caring about which characters you’re using. There are 15 main story levels in total that take you to a bunch of different Marvel locations including the Baxter building, Asgard and Latveria. After beating a level you unlock it in free play which allows you to replay the level with any character you have unlocked, which is necessary to collect all of the mini-kits or Stan Lees in the game.
The controls are incredible which is a necessity for this game. You never feel like you aren’t in control and you have a lot of movement during jumps which can be essential as there are a few sections in the levels and in the hub world where you need to be pretty on-par with the jumping.
One thing worth noting is how good this game looks. I would have thought you would be quite limited with what you can do to a Lego game but this game is gorgeous and the animations are top-notch. Seeing telekinetic characters build Lego objects is a particular highlight every time. It’s obviously not going to win any awards but considering the source I’m surprised how good it can look.
The biggest gripe I’ve had is with the hub world. While it is a nice thing to marvel at it has a whole bunch of extraneous side missions which reward gold bricks and don’t add anything fun to the experience but exist only to pad out the game’s playtime. This is only an issue if you plan on getting a 100% completion though.
If you haven’t played the Lego games in a while or if you fancy a really solid 3D Platformer then this is a definite get.
P.S. Next time please don’t lock the Guardians of the Galaxy as post-game content. Thanks.
P.P.S. I am Groot.

Valve's sequel to their early masterpeice. Often hailed as THE best game of all time, how does it hold up 11 years later? Lets find out
Pros: well, the game looks really nice. It shows its age almost always, but it also somehow doesn't. You look at it and conciously think it looks old but it also looks odly good. The story is WELL above average as you'd expect, and you don't really need to play the first one to understand this game (although you should, it helps you feel a LOT more invested in the story, which can be hard if you play this first). There is also GREAT variation, in both location and in gameplay. Ravenholm is basically a physics sandbox, allowing you to use the gravity gun (a gun that alows you to manipulate objects without touching them) to its full potential, while the next section is in a car. This helps make the game not feel repetitive and makes playing in long sessions posible, if not completly unavoidable. You start in a city, then go to a river, then to a buring city, then to the open roads, and then to a prison. The settings change almost always, and keep the game feeling always fresh.
Cons: the car and boat sections go on too long and they don't control very well. They aren't bad by ANY means, but really should have been cut down or had their controls tweeked. The shooting is good, but not impressive. It's perfectly fine, but from a game with this reputation you'd expect more. Most importatly, (simi-spoiler) when you're back in the city again and command a squad of soldiers, YOUR TROOPS ARE IDIOTIC! They are almost useless in battle and get in the way 90% of the time. Also, the enemies always seem to have an advantage, they may suprise you, have cover, or have the high ground. I'm sure this was done to make you feel like the odds aren't in your favor, but it ends up just being annoying.
In short, this is an AWESOME game, but also one that doesn't deserve the hype it gets. The first game was revolutunary in the way it told it's story, but this game didn't really have anything like that. Still, it's amazingly fun and any FPS fan MUST play it at least once in their lifetime!

If you liked Lego Star Wars or Lego Batman, this title may be right up your alley. As a lifelong Marvel comic nerd, this game brought two of my favorite franchises together. The gameplay is not revolutionary, since the formula has been used in many Lego games before, but Marvel Super Heroes benefits greatly from the constantly evolving mechanics of the series. The inclusions of so many different Marvel characters, both hero and villain, as well as the huge assortment of minigames and large hub world (basically all of Manhattan) makes the game feel really big. If you purchase the single DLC, you will be able to unlock some of the game content earlier than you would have otherwise, because required abilities are yours at the start.
My one knock on the game was that there was some glitch that caused me to be unable to earn a number of the achievements related to the Hulk. The only way I could get them was to download another person's save from the internet. My overall enjoyment was not all that hampered by this, though. I highly recommend the game to those who like either Marvel Comics or the Lego games.

I went into this game as a huge fan of the series. I was happy, although there could have been many improvements. The game does an EXCELLENT job of offering fan service by including basically every character and tons of little trinkets and things from the entire series. There are some genuinely funny parts and you can tell the creators put a lot of work into it. I will list some of the problems. For story and comedy especially, the game uses a lot of the same tropes from the series, instead of inventing new things. My favorite thing about south park is tuning in every week to see what great point they will make next or what thing they will skewer from pop culture, and instead of that, the game is mostly a retread. It is doing mongolians/city wok, manbearbig, the two sides are from the game of thrones, mr slave/lemmiwinks/and so on. It would have been nice for more innovation instead of just repeating the same jokes from the show. The main storyline is new and original in many parts, and definitely funny. No new characters are introduced really.
Now the gameplay. It uses turn based gameplay, which is pretty meh. The problem is with the execution. It relies on quicktime/button execution combat for the turn based action, which although makes it more exciting, but is very hit or miss. Tons of times I would press the button to block and it would not count me as blocking, and other times would. Other times, with certain spells, it would say hold button until your guy loses control, and every single time I would let go around when he starts to lose control, and the game always said I was late, but I had no idea what I was doing wrong, as I was just following directions. For another spell I had to press a certain button when the wires were touching, but they just touch for an instant and stop, so there was no way to react in time, you had to try and anticipate, which didn't really work. With using magic with your weapons, it says to press W when it lights up, and every single time I did what it said and it never once worked. With so many things being poorly explained and finnicky, I just never did like half my spells, which is a mistake by their system. Another problem is the individualism. You can pick from multiple guys and multiple companions, but everyon who plays 1 character progresses the same. You unlock 1 set spell at a time and just upgrade slight things about that spell. There is no variation or creation of your character or playstyle. There are tons of weapons. and the story is good length. It is nice being able to go around the entire town and see things. Another problem is lack of direction. Sometimes I would need to use a certain ability to get through something, but it would be to use a companion ability you hadn't used in the world yet and you didn't know could solve the problem. There could have been better explanation. Also, there are tons of parts you cant do for a while and just have to wait forever to get the ability then go back to finish side quests you got early on, which is annoying. They tried to be metroid a little too much. The magic doesn't work, as you only get it from buying and using potions, which you never remember to do. Would be nice to fill it up through victory. It is nice how you can use potions and attack, as that is fair and takes away wasting turns because someone went first.I like the game mostly for the characters and fan service, while the gameplay was just ok, and quite annoying at times.  8/10

Take the irreverant antics of South Park, mix in some light RPG and you get South Park the Stick of Truth.
This game is a must have for fans of the long running animated series.  The best part is that the game isn't some lame adaptation but rather a faithful complement to the TV series.  If you remember the great PS4 versus Xbox1 conflict of 2013 then you have the backstory for this game.
It was co-developed with South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone with game voice overs performed by the current series cast.  In short playing "The Stick of Truth" is like having the starring role in the TV series.
Gameplay is typical RPG but greatly simplified.  There's ample options to customize your character,  level him/her up, collect ever more powerful items and choose your destinty be it good or evil.
Don't expect bragging rights or leaderboards though.  That's not what this game's about.  Enjoy the 20 or so hours like you would a season of South Park.

If you're looking for a faithful recreation of Shadowrun themes, complete with gloomy cyberpunk-ish cities, violent gangs running the streets, folk tales mixed into the 1990s sci-fi aesthetic, and a healthy dose of awkward pulp novel prose, then this is is exactly what this game offers. The pace of the plot is decent, and the minimum requirements for an engaging story are met. While all characters I've met were very one-dimensional, at least they had motivations I could understand, and there was something tangible at stake.
Unfortunately, this isn't really what I was looking for.The best thing about old-school RPGs in my opinion was that they didn't hold your hand. You could go more or less anywhere. You could snoop around people's houses. You could choose which gang to side with. You could try frontal assault, or go through the sewers and pick the backdoor lock. You could travel alone, or gather a party. You could farm random encounters for loot. You could explore the wilderness. In the best games of the genre, your choices regarding development of your character would unlock new experiences.
Shadowrun Returns has none of that. I'm sure the authors knew it should, because it sometimes creates pretenses, token interactions that create the illusion of agency - but the veil is very thin. Underneath, everything is preset and linear. For instance, you can customize your character, but there never seems to be any opportunity to see if your choices affect anything (except for unlocking dialogue options - but the outcomes of conversations seem to be predetermined anyway, so what's the point?). Environements are pretty much non-interactive, except for quest-related interaction spots and occasional theft freebies. Combat is simplistic in that it the best option is always to just concentrate fire. The use of tactics is severely limited by the very simple topology of combat arenas and the fact that many objects that offer cover are not recognised as such (you can't lean against a wall next to a door frame, for example).
I believe if you're looking for a pulp novel, then you'll be better off buying an actual novel, because then you won't be risking that some enemy scores a critical hit, kills you, and forces you to read the same paragraph again.

Hello there, you shiny little gem! What do we have here? Our age old, classic card game that we practically grew up with since Windows 3.0 - or as your grandmother's generic hobby - combined with a pretty fairytale and collectibles? I'm in!
The scene opens up to the realm of fairies, threatened by an unspeakable conspiracy. A dark, evil force that we fail to identify enslaves the inhabitants of the realm for its own dark purposes. A kindly old wizard approaches, and declares us as the only possible candidate to save fairies from their torment... with our solitaire skills? (I owe this joke to my friend
. It was originaly in his review, but I couldn't bear myself not to include it, due to the joke being perfectly definitive.) Yes, it is solitaire. Yes, it has a story... and the story actually ends with a huge cliffhanger, so you'll be anticipating for Faerie Solitaire 2 before you know.
Aside from your usual solitaire gameplay, Faerie Solitaire contains some surprises. You earn cash as you progress through various levels of the story - or in any casual game - to obtain upgrades for your gameplay. The gameplay also sets some goals for you in each level, that raises the stakes a bit more, either with time limits or a certain number of cards that you have to make a combo with. You are also entitled to collect some magical eggs that will hatch into various magical beasts. These beasties gain experience as you play and they may be raised into adulthood for their own achievement set.
All in all, it is a good game for a low price that you can pick to pass some mindless time, with interesting features. I also gotta mention that the art is surprisingly beautiful for a casual game. I adored the profile backgrounds and emoticons! I know, I know, it is girly... But I am a girl anyhow. So I am entitled to my fairies, damn it!

Antichamber is very fun for the first half of the game. However, once it starts introducing puzzles that rely on game mechanics that you simply have to *know*, without any proper introduction to them, and begins to regularly rely on puzzles that revolve around trying random crap and hoping it will work, all fun goes out the window and the game becomes an exercise in tedium.
Often, I was reminded of the infamous NES game "Milon's Secret Castle," whose gamplay involved searching every area of the screen, in every level, hoping to find secret doors that would allow you to continue. However, in Antichamber you are searching a fully interactive 3D world, only compounding the issue of where hidden areas might be located.
A prime example of this is a puzzle to reach a certain area, which has nothing but an enclosed area with a blank wall as your cue for access. To enter, you look in the opposite direction of the blank wall and walk backwards. Then, turn around, turn around again and the entrance you went through has disappeared, walk backwards again, and walk around the enclosed area. The blank wall has been replaced by a pit, which you drop into, which traps you in a small area. To get out, you look at the ceiling, jump, and fall through the floor. Then you go through a series of further trick jumps to continue. And all of this has no hints, no clues, no nothing for what you are supposed to do. If that sounds like fun, you'll love Antichamber.
Some of the puzzles involving blocks and switches are rather fun, and I would have loved it if the game had focused on them more, rather than disappearing walkways, illusionary walls, and paths leading nowhere. Antichamber is very clever, but perhaps a bit too clever for its own good. It took my puzzle solving enthusiasm, and squashed it to a bloody pulp. By the end, I just didn't care any more. There is very little to encourage you to move forward, except that you might finish at some point. Antichamber is simply one annoying puzzle after another, with no story, no "good job," no rewards of any kind. Finish one headache-inducing puzzle, and you're right smack in the middle of another one. It is wearisome.

Faerie Solitaire is nothing more than what promises to be: a solitaire card game. The game itself, though, is wrapped up in a nice setting with beautiful drawings, pleasant music and sound effects, and a sort of story (don't expect to get hooked on it, though: it's nothing spectacular). The adventure mode presents you with objectives that you need to achieve in order to progress (all related to your solitaire games).
In order to keep you interested, there are also collectable eggs dropped randomly (as far as I can tell) while you play, that you can hatch and evolve into creatures. I think that this is a sort of missed opportunity, because in fact those eggs and creatures have no effects whatsoever on the game play. It would have been nice to get something out of them! On the other hand, the gold that you collect by playing can be used to buy upgrades that will make it easier to reach the objectives of the various levels.
All in all, I recommend this game, as each of its levels is a nice way to spend 15, 20 minutes while you are waiting for something like your meal to be ready, or just before going to bed.

The gameplay is not revolutionary, since the formula has been used in many Lego games before, but Marvel Super Heroes benefits greatly from the constantly evolving mechanics of the series. The inclusions of so many different Marvel characters, both hero and villain, as well as the huge assortment of minigames and large hub world (basically all of Manhattan) makes the game feel really big. If you purchase the single DLC, you will be able to unlock some of the game content earlier than you would have otherwise, because required abilities are yours at the start.
My one knock on the game was that there was some glitch that caused me to be unable to earn a number of the achievements related to the Hulk. The only way I could get them was to download another person's save from the internet. My overall enjoyment was not all that hampered by this, though. I highly recommend the game to those who like either Marvel Comics or the Lego games.

Lego Batman 2 was quite an achievement in Traveller's Tales' long-running Lego series with its large sandbox city filled with tons of collectibles and an equally large roster of colorful and varied heroes and villains. The storytelling aspect got a major writing overhaul by officially leaving the 'mime' humor behind by bringing in the A-team of voicework that made the game able to tell its own, unique story rather than simply act out a film's plot.
Lego Marvel Super Heroes does what any sequel should and expands on everything its predecessor was and more.
The sandbox of New York city is positively ginormeous and filled to the brim with personality,
be it in the faithfully constructed Marvel landmarks or the various quirky side-quest granting citizens and puzzles. There are even secret stages to uncover if you search hard enough!
The stages themselves have also taken a boost and are more layered,
boasting strong location variety and quirky creativety.
The creators also managed to finally truly nail the length of the stages so that they go on just long enough while throwing encounters and thrills at you around every corner to satisfy
without overstaying their welcome and just becoming stale.
There are boss-fights a plenty in this game, even more than ever before
and, while they are all fairly unique, few bosses actually change their tactics mid-fight,
leaving what will initially strike many players as impressive and fun fights
to become rather repetitive by the time they land the final hit.
One thing that has taken a hit since the last game, however, is the combat.
Unlike Lego Batman 2, which used a miniaturized version of the Arkham games' combat
by allowing you to unleash special moves when your multiplier was high enough,
in this game, those moves now just randomly happen.
It certainly adds visual flair to the fights,
but feels even more button-mashy than previous incarnations.
Still, all is not lost, most characters now have unique moves
that can be triggered by pressing B at any time
(it used to be a generic grab-button in LB2), which does add some much needed variety.
Speaking of variety, Lego Marvel Super Heroes boast one of the largest rosters in any Lego game and all the characters look, move, fight and feel like they should, which is a large plus for comic-book fans who can finally say their favorite characters have a game that does them justice.
Unfortunately, this game is not without glitches,
on a 100% playthrough, you're sure to run into some sooner or later.
In my experience, I had situations were certain NPCs wouldn't load,
NPCs wouldn't jump into your Taxi and the game wouldn't accept 100%
until I re-beat the final stage again.
In all cases, simply continuously resetting the game until it worked eventually prevailed,
so luckily, there is no truly gamebreaking glitch that'll make 100% impossible.
Ultimately, Lego Marvel Super Heroes is superior to its predecessors in almost every way,
though, as it IS more of a simple
(unless you set your eyes upon the lofty goal of achieving 100% completion)
and quirky puzzle-game by nature,
I'd recommend to pay with caution if you expect something grander.
However! If you like the Marvel universe, collect-a-tons that keep you playing long after the credits roll, puzzles or large sandboxes to roam around in and explore,
then you can do little better than Lego Marvel Super Heroes.

A fun excellent piece of entertainment hindered by tedious mission structure, false challenges and terrible controls. I will only recommend this game for people with patience or who simply crave a tongue-ahd-cheek, low-key adventure.
Story: Great
The amount of creativity gone into structuring the crazy insane scenarios for these characters to endure is a charm amongst itself, and the tongue and cheek episodic style of the missions suits the Marvel Universe very well. All the characters are spot on in this adaptation. Spider-Man is a charming smart♥♥♥♥♥ Captain America is a cheesy boy scout, Dr. Doom is arrogant but intelligent, etc. My only complaint is that some of the missions don't add anything narratively, but this isn't the kind of game that's trying to tell a deep story. It's more about being lossed in the insanity and action of it all.
Graphics: Appealing "in places."
While the characters themselves are impressive, it’s the environments apart from New York City itself that really enrapture my attention. Levels with Lego contraptions embedded into them are the high point of the visual appeal for this game. Unfortunately, New York City itself isn't very impressive looking. Outside the park area and the S.H.I.E.L.D. Helicarrier, the city is not worth looking at.
Gameplay: Simple but . . . .SIMPLE
Don't expect this game to be challenging or engaging. People play Lego games to relax or just to enrapture themselves in a toy store like state of mind. I wouldn't call the puzzles "PUZZLES." The puzzles in this game are fairly straight forward and there is no requirement for the player to have to analyze or take into account a different perspective on the objective at hand. The Puzzles are more like Quick Time Events without the "Quick" part. And combat is . . . well what do you expect? Just press a button till they get hurt. Targeting is broken as ever and the circle reticle does nothing to improve the aiming in the game. Thank goodness for the auto lock feature in this game, otherwise there would be no way to beat some of the missions or challenges. Also, it still disappoints me that there is very few actual "building" gameplay in a game based around a property that's all about building. Shame on you Lego video games. I know non-Lego games that have more building gameplay than the games based around your product.
Controls: Terrible
Ok this really is a breaking point for me. A game can be phenomenal, but poor controls can ruin the entire experience, and believe me these controls did for me. Flying feels too complicated for what it is. Imaging having to motivate a sleeping dog and the only way you can is if you inject them with rabies. That's how flight and sometimes walking feels. There's too big of a jump from slow movement to insanely fast movement, so precision is non-existent in this game. Also to note, often times some puzzles will  require the player to move objects with the control sticks and since the camera is always fixed during these situations, there were a multitude of times where I had to restart the entire mission because pieces would get stuck together and there was no way to reverse it. For a game that's not about challenge and aims to relax players, the controls are very frustrating at times that may even infuriate some people.
Sound: Sound Effects = Meh, Music = Awesome!
The sound effects are nothing to discuss. Sometimes they're there, sometimes they're not. The game gets very quiet at times that might be annoying or off-putting to some players. However, when the music plays, it really gets me pumped up. From simple quirky tunes to epic rifts that rival the movies' soundtracks, the soundtrack for this video game is definitely something to check out if you like fun, intense, or even quirky relaxing tunes.
Final Verdict: Play if you wish.

Now, let me start by saying this game can be enjoyed, and if you like rogue-like games like Binding of Isaac or Spelunky, you'll more then likely enjoy this game... However it does has it's faults.
The biggest issue I have with it is the way it handles difficulty. Now while I feel like the time based system in place,  where the longer you play, the harder it gets, is good on paper, in play it just proves to be more annoying. The game discourages level exploration considering these levels are huge, but have nothing in them, save for the teleporter and the chests/shops/alters, but the way the levels are generated make it so you HAVE to explore a level, and sometimes do it twice if you want any items. Some levels in this game practically force you to go a certain way each time you play through them, espicially in the Water Level, where you have to almost always go from right to left, get up to the surface, and find the teleporter.
The Levels in this game really start feeling same-y, and soon, boring, and saddly, the combat follows this. This game likes to swarm you with enemies, which you may have seen in the trailers. However, the trailer is misleading in the fact that you are very unlikely to get this many items unless you basically go back to the first level of the run, and do everything all over again, keeping your past items and difficulty. This means you'll often be running away, turning to chip away at one monster's HP, occasionally all with the few skills that have pierce or AOE, rince, and repeat. This gets old very quickly and if that wasn't bad enough, considering how slowly you kill enemies, espicially without drones which again are random spawns, it causes things to become more and more difficult for you. The enemies health also grows with difficulty, as well as the spawn rate, making the problem become worse and worse with time.
Now that wouldn't be so bad... if it wasn't for two things. The fact that to progress from level to level, you have to kill every single enemy, and this game revolves around kiting enemies.  The former brings out the issue of the player not being at fault for the game forcing you to waste time. Usually by the time the teleporter is ready, the player is ready to leave, maybe still has to kill the boss, but there's nothing left that they care for. However, with this game design choice, it goes against the games nature of Risk Vs Reward. At that point, you either need to accept the wasted time, and then money because going from level to level turns your money into a very miniscule amount of EXP, which is terrible in comparison to the Items that give your run a winning chance.
Now, for kiting enemies... this just leads into HORRIBLE character design. Each character has it's own unique set of abilities, but over half of them aren't designed well enough for the game's play style. Take the Sniper for example. His specialty is taking out bosses, which, yes, he can do exceptionally well. What he can't do however is handle the horde of enemies on his tail thanks to the fact he only has one half decent escaping move, the Backflip, which is the opposite of the Commando's Combat roll, where you dive in the opposite direction you're facing. First thing's first, DO NOT buy this game if you don't have a Nvidia graphics card. That's the only one that will even kind of run this game.
There's only two bad things I can say about this game. It's a bit laggy, even on high end PCs, (though the game seems to be seeing regular updates and should be optimized soon) and the only unique thing about it is it's exact combination of elements stolen from other games; Essentially Mirrors Edge's combat and parkour, Dead Island's combat, crafting and inventory, with Farcry 3's skill tree (and antenna scaling missions), Skyrim's lockpicking, Escape From New York's music, etc. But I'll be damned if this isn't exactly the way to do it. Dying Light serves to prove something doesn't have to be original to be innovative.
Aside from that, everything about this game is great. Combat and parkour are seamless, elements therein blending together fluidly when properly executed, even before your more advanced combat moves and parkour moves are even unlocked. It's fast, intuitive and practically bug free. Every texture, every model and every particle effect I've seen so far was perfect, even though this is undoubtedly why the game runs too slow for many to play. There's tons to do, nearly every character offering quests and spontaneous scripted (and unscripted) events simply littering the playscape. Harran, the city Dying Light takes place in, certainly feels alive because of it. Items are scarce, (There are guns, they're just rare, as are their ammunition) zombies are hard to kill, the price of everything is cranked to hundreds of times their real price, making every moment of gameplay a challenge, giving it a realistic feel.
Right up until you get stuck on a timed mission, and your continual loss of the mission gets progressively worse because your weapon's sturdiness carries over into your respawn so you break weapon after weapon over the head of the same zombie into eternity, because you can't go back.

Well, Where to begin with Dying Light.
After finishing the main storyline with plenty of side quests that I missed, I can safely say that this game was quite something.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I'm not quite sure where to start with this review so I'll just start with the good stuff first.
It holds good variety in weapons and zombies, As well as various human enemies, Both military and non-military. The parkour is, in my opinion, pretty smooth, Maybe not to Mirror's Edge standard but it gets the job done nicely. Combat feels very satisfying and well done, Especially with the dismemberment of body parts. Graphics aren't too bad, Even at a low resolution, The game still looked very pretty on my computer, though others may disagree. The variation between day and night offers a nice change in the gameplay, One minute you're a zombie killing badass, The next you're a wimpy baby hiding from corners and climbing rooftops as if your life depends on it, Because 9 times out of 10, it does.
A few very small but noticable features in the game add to it's charm, Such as the three seperate skill trees, Survivor, Agility and Power, Each having unique perks that help improve the way you play the game (If you're not too busy dropkicking Zomboids off the rooftops to notice them). The menu's are similar to Dead Island, So those who played that should instantly be used to it, Though it's easy for new people to understand. Certain NPC's in the game can offer some valuable loot and a weapon completely for free,  Crafting feels very well done with the different varieties of blueprints you can find throughout the world or earn through quests (Flaming, Electrifying Sledgehammers FTW!) And it's open world gameplay with two different areas to explore: The Slums, where you start the game off and play about 70% of the game, The other being The City, Where you travel to during the main storyline and has much, much bigger buildings.
I personally haven't played Multiplayer with any of my friends who also own the game but from the few random dudes who have joined my game whilst I play, I would say that the Multiplayer runs quite smoothly. As the host, It gives you plenty of oppertunities to set up challenges for you and your friends to complete, Such as kill the most zombies or find the most loot and whatever else the game decides. I do have a personal recommendation if you intend to go public online when you're playing so random people and friends can join you, TURN OFF ZOMBIE INVASION. If you don't want to be CONSTANTLY invaded by super zombies trying to munch your face off, Turn this off. If not, You'll most likely find yourself being invaded every 5 minutes with NO ONE to help you, You'll be left alone and have quite a disadvantage, Though if that's your kind of thing, Go right ahead.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Plenty of good stuff to say about this game, Now for the bad stuff...
The story isn't great. Pretty much throughout the entire thing, You can already see what will happen from miles away and most times they do. The characters aren't too interesting and some are completely forgettable, Even though this game tries at times to make you feel something for the characters and make you feel connected to them (I'm looking at you, Rahim.)
The game takes a little while to bring out the different enemy variations, Which mainly consists of you having to play through the main storyline before you even see mutated zombies in the world and even then, You rarely notice any or don't pay enough attention to notice them, the most I've seen is the normal snappy bitey zombies, Some Viral zombies which come when you make noise (The super fast ones in daylight) and the big hulking fellas with metal rebars usually standing around in one place.
And I cannot finish off this review without mentioning The Final Boss of the game, The psychopathic dude who has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, Killed your comrades and ultimately made your life terrible in this zombie apocalypse. It comes down to that final moment, you finally reach the top of his mighty tower after scratching and clawing your way past zomboids and virals and falling to the dirt many, many times. A cutscene comes along, You and your enemy face off and what do you know? QUICK TIME EVEEEEENT!!!!
You could see it coming a mile away, A God Damn Quick Time Event for the final boss. Please bear in mind that other bosses in the game that you fight, The Main Boss's Right Hand Man being just one of them, You fight all of those in the game normally, Dodging and leaping and slashing and dying a lot. But oh no, Not with this final boss, They treat you with a nice little QTE right at the end and you could EASILY see it coming a mile off. A dissapointing ending, In my opinion.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Well, If you could be bothered to read through all my rubbish, Welcome to the end! ~Confetti and Fanfare~
So, Final opinion on Dying Light.
Although it has a few faults in the game that can be noticed with ease and may annoy a lot of players, Especially that damn final boss, Does it make Dying Light a bad game? Not. At. All.
It's Fun, It's Satisfying and it certainly lived up to my personal expectations when I first heard about it and got excited to play it.
If you're a Zomboid fan, A Parkour Fan or you just like to slice dudes up and dropkick them from rooftops like a total boss, I HIGHLY recommend Dying Light to you. Some may argue about the asking price of this game but from what I've played and seen, I personally think it's worth it.
Dying Light has been, In my opinion, A great start to a new year of gaming, I only hope that developers can keep this up for the months to come.
Until Then, Catch ya later, Folks!

A steam holiday sale bet I was not expecting to like as much as I do.
XCOM is a turn based strategy game. So something within the same realm to final fantasy tactics, if you ever played that cult classic. Except, with aliens and guns.
What really surprised me wasn't the combat, though there are some nice little surprises there too, but how hard the game will hit you over the head for a mistake. Especially in the beginning. You dont worry enough about money in the beginning, youll be watching your poor shabby soldiers get decimated near the mid to endgame. Worry too much, youll end up with a great big bank account, but still end up with shabby soldiers near the mid to endgame. Timing plays a more important role in any game I have seen since Starcraft or warcraft, which is really really wierd in a Turn Based Strategy game, but in a good way. You get off your beat just a lilbit, youll almost certainly, suffer. The good news is since its turn based, you can take your time. So grow out your chin stroking beard and be ready to sit and wonder what in the world your gonna do now.
Though the game does have a plateau effect in difficulty, that is really nothing new in this genre of games. Its normally something I would complain about but really, after struggling like mad in the beginning to keep from treading water, outright failing, or even backing yourself into a incompletable game, a nice coast to the finish is just gravy as far as I am concerned. Asides, if your really looking for punishing through and through, there are a host of modes to get you there. Especially after you are done with your first playthrough and get the "New game +" bonus options. (called second wave in the game, but they are new game + bonuses.)Turn it on insane difficulty, activate ironman, (only one save that is not in control of the player,) and every second wave option, and see how long you last.  (I got past the first mission and thats it.)
If you do decide to get this game, which I wholeheartedly recommend to anyone who likes aliens, soldier games or strategy games, I do make one more suggestion and splurge on XCOM: enemy within as well. Mainly because its in essence, the same game and story, only with more story added, more game options, more tactical variety and mission variety than the original. Might as well get the full experience right outta the gate.
Also! Turning on Autosave helps allot. Its not necissary, (pointless in ironman mode,) but so helpful.

Are you Tired of the Ye Olde RPG games?
Are you sick of medieval settings?
High mountains?
Talking Trees?
Knights and Sorcerers?
Armies of the undead?
Maybe you're sick of swords and crossbows but you're just not ready to give up on Orks, Trolls, Dwarves, Elfs and Wizzards?
Well then chum, throw away your flail and pick up a handgun instead!
Play Shadowrun! Replace bandits with Gangers! Throw away the world of Magic for the world of the Matrix! A cyberpunk adventure awaits!
Its 21st century Seattle and magic has come back. People have become awakened wizards, mutated into orcs and some have woken up with elf ears. The year is 2050-something and you are a shadowrunner, a person without a past and without an ID. With no microchip under your skin, big brother can't see you, and you are away from the spotlight of government or police. You are a shadowrunner! A person living in the gray existence of no-records. Doing illegal jobs for legal people who can afford it.
The story begins when you suddenly get a call from a friend. A person like you has been murdered! And that person has a job for you, from beyond the grave.
Delve into the underworld of the dystopian future to investigate a legendary murderer. Infiltrate the ranks of a seemingly good-natured cult. Discover a conspiracy that may destroy the world.
This game is a classic attempting to make a come-back. Think D&D with neon lighting. An enjoyable single-player campaign of turn based RPG goodness. Its a thinker's game. A Reader's game. No action or skill required. Just planning and luck. The campaign it self is engaging, if a little bit short but if that's not enough for ya there's a whole workshop full of more missions and mods. The graphics are simple but you'd be surprised how much can be achieved with so little. This game is gorgeous. The setting as mentioned earlier is a little hard to swallow if you're a hard-core fan of medieval settings, but you may find it to your liking if you're a more sci-fi guy, or girl. An excellent game for any player who enjoys Sci-fi, action, strategy, plot, and in-character voice acting.
1. A true science fiction that has a what if scenario. The what if aliens invaded, and they are not friendly. This game's story focuses on Humanities fight for survival against a vastly superior alien force. Very nice technology, meshed with modern equipment.
2. Action and strategy are in every mission, though it can be dragged out at times. Once you advance in the game a little, you will find yourself drawn into the world of X-Com. The interface is easy to use, and the tutorial explains everything during a main mission. A number of mods exist to make the game either more difficult or easier; depending on what your after.
3. Graphics are impressive, though mods drastically improve options, making the game able to utilize a PC's full ability, rather than limiting it to a console.
4. The overall plot is interesting, sadly there are still a number of unanswered questions; however, that does leave us wanting to play future expansions, (one of which Enemy Within, is already out). In-character voice acting is top notch, with good accents matched to the characters.
In the end, X-Com is one of the best modern strategy games for the PC. With a number of enhancements made by fellow users available on the internet, this will make an excellent addition to any gamer's collection.

Antichamber is very fun for the first half of the game. However, once it starts introducing puzzles that rely on game mechanics that you simply have to *know*, without any proper introduction to them, and begins to regularly rely on puzzles that revolve around trying random crap and hoping it will work, all fun goes out the window and the game becomes an exercise in tedium.
Often, I was reminded of the infamous NES game "Milon's Secret Castle," whose gamplay involved searching every area of the screen, in every level, hoping to find secret doors that would allow you to continue. However, in Antichamber you are searching a fully interactive 3D world, only compounding the issue of where hidden areas might be located.
A prime example of this is a puzzle to reach a certain area, which has nothing but an enclosed area with a blank wall as your cue for access. To enter, you look in the opposite direction of the blank wall and walk backwards. Then, turn around, turn around again and the entrance you went through has disappeared, walk backwards again, and walk around the enclosed area. The blank wall has been replaced by a pit, which you drop into, which traps you in a small area. To get out, you look at the ceiling, jump, and fall through the floor. Then you go through a series of further trick jumps to continue. And all of this has no hints, no clues, no nothing for what you are supposed to do. If that sounds like fun, you'll love Antichamber.
Some of the puzzles involving blocks and switches are rather fun, and I would have loved it if the game had focused on them more, rather than disappearing walkways, illusionary walls, and paths leading nowhere. Antichamber is very clever, but perhaps a bit too clever for its own good. It took my puzzle solving enthusiasm, and squashed it to a bloody pulp. By the end, I just didn't care any more. There is very little to encourage you to move forward, except that you might finish at some point. Antichamber is simply one annoying puzzle after another, with no story, no "good job," no rewards of any kind. Finish one headache-inducing puzzle, and you're right smack in the middle of another one. It is wearisome.

I couldnt decide what to write in this review , so im gonna share with you guys my favorite apple pie recipe Enjoy! :D
Pastry
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons shortening
4 to 6 tablespoons cold water
Filling
1/3 to 1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/8 teaspoon salt
8 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples (8 medium)
2 tablespoons butter or margarine
1) In medium bowl, mix 2 cups flour and 1 teaspoon salt. Cut in shortening, using pastry blender (or pulling 2 table knives through ingredients in opposite directions), until particles are size of small peas. Sprinkle with cold water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with fork until all flour is moistened and pastry almost cleans side of bowl (1 to 2 teaspoons more water can be added if necessary).
2) Gather pastry into a ball. Divide in half; shape into 2 flattened rounds on lightly floured surface. Wrap in plastic wrap; refrigerate about 45 minutes or until dough is firm and cold, yet pliable. This allows the shortening to become slightly firm, which helps make the baked pastry more flaky. If refrigerated longer, let pastry soften slightly before rolling.
3) Heat oven to 425°F. With floured rolling pin, roll one pastry round into round 2 inches larger than upside-down 9-inch glass pie plate. Fold pastry into fourths; place in pie plate. Unfold and ease into plate, pressing firmly against bottom and side.
4) In large bowl, mix sugar, 1/4 cup flour, the cinnamon, nutmeg and 1/8 teaspoon salt. Stir in apples until well mixed. Spoon into pastry-lined pie plate. Cut butter into small pieces; sprinkle over filling. Trim overhanging edge of pastry 1/2 inch from rim of plate.
5) Roll other round of pastry into 10-inch round. Fold into fourths and cut slits so steam can escape. Unfold top pastry over filling; trim overhanging edge 1 inch from rim of plate. Fold and roll top edge under lower edge, pressing on rim to seal; flute as desired. Cover edge with 2- to 3-inch strip of foil to prevent excessive browning.
6) Bake 40 to 50 minutes or until crust is brown and juice begins to bubble through slits in crust, removing foil for last 15 minutes of baking. Serve warm if desired.

I've played all the Lego games and they've all had little irritating things about them, either something with the gameplay or something with the controls, or lacking interesting characters, or all characters feeling the same. Usually because each new Lego game were trying new game mechanics and they didn't quite get them right the first time; in the next Lego game it would be perfected, but then they were trying something new again that didn't quite work, so there was always something wrong. And depending on the universe of the Lego game, sometimes there just weren't enough characters to make it feel varied and interesting (Indiana Jones was particularly bad about this).
This is the first Lego game that has felt completed and polished. I have no criticisms whatsoever. All the game mechanics work, they're not overly complicated to use, and there's so much variation in the characters' abilities that you really do want to play through with all of them. The game world is also large enough that you want to explore it all, AND you have character abilities that let you do so without wasting time walking. Only this game and the previous Harry Potter ones feel like 100% completion is not a chore :)

is the 4th and final entry in the
franchise, developed by Rocksteady, who developed the first two games in the series,

After the incredibly disappointing
, the final game is back in the hands of the original developers, and ready to “be the Batman” as it were.
Set one year after
, the plot begins with now main villain Scarecrow teaming up with all of Batman’s greatest foes, Two Face, Penguin, the Riddler, Harley Quinn and the newly introduced Arkham Knight. Scarecrow forces a mass evacuation of Gotham after threatening to unleash his new fear toxin on the entire city, and now the streets of Gotham are ruled by thugs and criminals. It’s the standard comic book Batman storyline, and would have been a rather average story if not for the inclusion of a particular character, who singlehandedly carries the entire game.
Outside of the spoiler character mentioned above, the rest of the villains were disappointingly utilised. Unlike
, where secondary villains (Penguin, Mr. Freeze, Ra's al Ghul, Harley Quinn) were integrated seamlessly into the main plotline, most of the villains are treated as afterthoughts and dealt with in secondary missions, with the exception of Harley, who gets her own fantastic section in the story. It was disappointing to see most encounters with these villains end up with you doing the same side mission over and over until you finally catch them.
Honestly, most of my complaints with the story is due to its weak main villains, Scarecrow and the Arkham Knight. The Scarecrow sections in
were some of the most memorable, and arguably the best parts of that game. Here, Scarecrow doesn’t have the charisma or interesting personality of the Joker to stand as the main antagonist of the game. He puts on a menacing voice, threatens Batman everywhere he goes, but when you actually meet him in the game, he runs away with a “I’ll get you next time Batman!” Arkham Knight on the other hand is so laughably incompetent through the story, it’s cringeworthy. In nearly every scene where he has Batman cornered, he will walk out of the room and leave his militia to deal with Batman, who surprise surprise, deals with them with ease. Even more laughable was the way the Arkham Knight was introduced as a new character, when anyone who even knew a little bit about the comics would be able to guess his identity straight away.
Overall, the story isn’t bad, but it doesn’t go out with the bang it should have. My comparison would be the game is like
to
it’s not as good as the previous title, but it’s still okay overall. And it’s infuriating that you need to 100% the entire game (which means all Riddler trophies too) to get the true ending. Don’t. Do. That.♥♥♥♥♥♥
If you’ve played any of the previous games, you’ll know how to play this one. The Freeflow combat system is still the same and satisfying as ever, easy to learn, while still able to provide a fair challenge, especially in the late game. Unlike
which was a step down, did nothing new and had arguably worse combat than
,
combat feels like a natural evolution, while still being familiar. There is more emphasis on utilizing gadgets in combat, where in previous titles it was rarely necessary,
adds new enemies which require the use of gadgets to safely defeat. I felt this change was for the better, fights now require paying attention to certain types of enemies instead of button pressing from one to the other.
The inclusion of Dual Play was a nice inclusion. In certain parts of the game, you can play as two characters, where you switch from Batman to Catwoman/Nightwing/Robin mid-combat. The ability to play as those characters was nice for a change, and gave a lot of spice to the combat, particularly the Batman/Catwoman missions, where both characters could only attack a certain type of enemy. It’s far from innovative, but it was a nice addition.
Rather disappointingly was the reduced amount of investigation scenes. While they were never complex, searching an area for clues and reconstructing crime scenes was always a neat feature in the previous Arkham games, bringing out the detective side of Batman. There’s far less of them in
than previous games, which is shame since I thought they did a good job of making the player feel like Batman.
Probably the most controversial addition to the game was the Batmobile. While the Batmobile was fun to drive around in and battle with, it became FAR too overused in the story. The first 3 drone battles were cool, the next 30 were not. Somehow, they even have you doing pseudo stealth with it. More bizarrely, some Riddler missions now have you driving timed races with the damned thing. Even worse is the way the game forces you to use it for more than half of the main story. It was infuriating when the final fight with two main villains ended with a tank battle, rather than a proper boss fight. It could have been a neat addition to the game, but it far outstays its welcome.
Graphically, it’s hella impressive, one of the best looking games on the market. Despite its disastrous launch, the game runs well now, for the most part. On an i5-4460, GTX 970, 8GB RAM, I maintained 70-80+ fps consistently when maxed out. However, driving around in the Batmobile will make your game stutter worse than King George VI. Just keep those NVIDIA effects off.
Artistically,
returns to the style of the first 2 games. While
looked drab and boring, the Arkham games always were surprisingly colourful, and Knight is a return to form in that regard. The character designs are fantastic, Scarecrow in particular, looks suitably menacing.
The soundtrack was average, outside of the main theme no song jumped out at me
What did jump though out at me was the reuse of songs from
and
even when it made no sense in the context. Perhaps they should have gotten Hans Zimmer to score at least one Arkham game.
Voice acting was fantastic, a return to form after the average
If you enjoyed the previous Arkham games, you’ll probably enjoy this one too, though
is still the best. Though the game is let down by its average villains and overuse of the Batmobile, the improved combat, impressive graphics and return to form after the awful
makes this worth picking up if you liked
and

First thing's first, DO NOT buy this game if you don't have a Nvidia graphics card. That's the only one that will even kind of run this game.
There's only two bad things I can say about this game. It's a bit laggy, even on high end PCs, (though the game seems to be seeing regular updates and should be optimized soon) and the only unique thing about it is it's exact combination of elements stolen from other games; Essentially Mirrors Edge's combat and parkour, Dead Island's combat, crafting and inventory, with Farcry 3's skill tree (and antenna scaling missions), Skyrim's lockpicking, Escape From New York's music, etc. But I'll be damned if this isn't exactly the way to do it. Dying Light serves to prove something doesn't have to be original to be innovative.
Aside from that, everything about this game is great. Combat and parkour are seamless, elements therein blending together fluidly when properly executed, even before your more advanced combat moves and parkour moves are even unlocked. It's fast, intuitive and practically bug free. Every texture, every model and every particle effect I've seen so far was perfect, even though this is undoubtedly why the game runs too slow for many to play. There's tons to do, nearly every character offering quests and spontaneous scripted (and unscripted) events simply littering the playscape. Harran, the city Dying Light takes place in, certainly feels alive because of it. Items are scarce, (There are guns, they're just rare, as are their ammunition) zombies are hard to kill, the price of everything is cranked to hundreds of times their real price, making every moment of gameplay a challenge, giving it a realistic feel.
Right up until you get stuck on a timed mission, and your continual loss of the mission gets progressively worse because your weapon's sturdiness carries over into your respawn so you break weapon after weapon over the head of the same zombie into eternity, because you can't go back.

If you like over the top gore effects and zombie/mutant wave survival then this game is the right thing to buy. In the state the game is right now it's as good as the first game. Well, Where to begin with Dying Light.
After finishing the main storyline with plenty of side quests that I missed, I can safely say that this game was quite something.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I'm not quite sure where to start with this review so I'll just start with the good stuff first.
It holds good variety in weapons and zombies, As well as various human enemies, Both military and non-military. The parkour is, in my opinion, pretty smooth, Maybe not to Mirror's Edge standard but it gets the job done nicely. Combat feels very satisfying and well done, Especially with the dismemberment of body parts. Graphics aren't too bad, Even at a low resolution, The game still looked very pretty on my computer, though others may disagree. The variation between day and night offers a nice change in the gameplay, One minute you're a zombie killing badass, The next you're a wimpy baby hiding from corners and climbing rooftops as if your life depends on it, Because 9 times out of 10, it does.
A few very small but noticable features in the game add to it's charm, Such as the three seperate skill trees, Survivor, Agility and Power, Each having unique perks that help improve the way you play the game (If you're not too busy dropkicking Zomboids off the rooftops to notice them). The menu's are similar to Dead Island, So those who played that should instantly be used to it, Though it's easy for new people to understand. Certain NPC's in the game can offer some valuable loot and a weapon completely for free,  Crafting feels very well done with the different varieties of blueprints you can find throughout the world or earn through quests (Flaming, Electrifying Sledgehammers FTW!) And it's open world gameplay with two different areas to explore: The Slums, where you start the game off and play about 70% of the game, The other being The City, Where you travel to during the main storyline and has much, much bigger buildings.
I personally haven't played Multiplayer with any of my friends who also own the game but from the few random dudes who have joined my game whilst I play, I would say that the Multiplayer runs quite smoothly. As the host, It gives you plenty of oppertunities to set up challenges for you and your friends to complete, Such as kill the most zombies or find the most loot and whatever else the game decides. I do have a personal recommendation if you intend to go public online when you're playing so random people and friends can join you, TURN OFF ZOMBIE INVASION. If you don't want to be CONSTANTLY invaded by super zombies trying to munch your face off, Turn this off. If not, You'll most likely find yourself being invaded every 5 minutes with NO ONE to help you, You'll be left alone and have quite a disadvantage, Though if that's your kind of thing, Go right ahead.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Plenty of good stuff to say about this game, Now for the bad stuff...
The story isn't great. Pretty much throughout the entire thing, You can already see what will happen from miles away and most times they do. The characters aren't too interesting and some are completely forgettable, Even though this game tries at times to make you feel something for the characters and make you feel connected to them (I'm looking at you, Rahim.)
The game takes a little while to bring out the different enemy variations, Which mainly consists of you having to play through the main storyline before you even see mutated zombies in the world and even then, You rarely notice any or don't pay enough attention to notice them, the most I've seen is the normal snappy bitey zombies, Some Viral zombies which come when you make noise (The super fast ones in daylight) and the big hulking fellas with metal rebars usually standing around in one place.
And I cannot finish off this review without mentioning The Final Boss of the game, The psychopathic dude who has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, Killed your comrades and ultimately made your life terrible in this zombie apocalypse. It comes down to that final moment, you finally reach the top of his mighty tower after scratching and clawing your way past zomboids and virals and falling to the dirt many, many times. A cutscene comes along, You and your enemy face off and what do you know? QUICK TIME EVEEEEENT!!!!
You could see it coming a mile away, A God Damn Quick Time Event for the final boss. Please bear in mind that other bosses in the game that you fight, The Main Boss's Right Hand Man being just one of them, You fight all of those in the game normally, Dodging and leaping and slashing and dying a lot. But oh no, Not with this final boss, They treat you with a nice little QTE right at the end and you could EASILY see it coming a mile off. A dissapointing ending, In my opinion.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Well, If you could be bothered to read through all my rubbish, Welcome to the end! ~Confetti and Fanfare~
So, Final opinion on Dying Light.
Although it has a few faults in the game that can be noticed with ease and may annoy a lot of players, Especially that damn final boss, Does it make Dying Light a bad game? Not. At. All.
It's Fun, It's Satisfying and it certainly lived up to my personal expectations when I first heard about it and got excited to play it.
If you're a Zomboid fan, A Parkour Fan or you just like to slice dudes up and dropkick them from rooftops like a total boss, I HIGHLY recommend Dying Light to you. Some may argue about the asking price of this game but from what I've played and seen, I personally think it's worth it.
Dying Light has been, In my opinion, A great start to a new year of gaming, I only hope that developers can keep this up for the months to come.
Until Then, Catch ya later, Folks!

8 hours in and I'm still enjoying it! If you like Killing Floor 1, this feels very similar but with updated graphics, familiar zeds, new perks, awesome cosmetics and very difficult boss fights!
