Now, let me start by saying this game can be enjoyed, and if you like rogue-like games like Binding of Isaac or Spelunky, you'll more then likely enjoy this game... However it does has it's faults.
The biggest issue I have with it is the way it handles difficulty. Now while I feel like the time based system in place,  where the longer you play, the harder it gets, is good on paper, in play it just proves to be more annoying. The game discourages level exploration considering these levels are huge, but have nothing in them, save for the teleporter and the chests/shops/alters, but the way the levels are generated make it so you HAVE to explore a level, and sometimes do it twice if you want any items. Some levels in this game practically force you to go a certain way each time you play through them, espicially in the Water Level, where you have to almost always go from right to left, get up to the surface, and find the teleporter.
The Levels in this game really start feeling same-y, and soon, boring, and saddly, the combat follows this. This game likes to swarm you with enemies, which you may have seen in the trailers. However, the trailer is misleading in the fact that you are very unlikely to get this many items unless you basically go back to the first level of the run, and do everything all over again, keeping your past items and difficulty. This means you'll often be running away, turning to chip away at one monster's HP, occasionally all with the few skills that have pierce or AOE, rince, and repeat. This gets old very quickly and if that wasn't bad enough, considering how slowly you kill enemies, espicially without drones which again are random spawns, it causes things to become more and more difficult for you. The enemies health also grows with difficulty, as well as the spawn rate, making the problem become worse and worse with time.
Now that wouldn't be so bad... if it wasn't for two things. The fact that to progress from level to level, you have to kill every single enemy, and this game revolves around kiting enemies.  The former brings out the issue of the player not being at fault for the game forcing you to waste time. Usually by the time the teleporter is ready, the player is ready to leave, maybe still has to kill the boss, but there's nothing left that they care for. However, with this game design choice, it goes against the games nature of Risk Vs Reward. At that point, you either need to accept the wasted time, and then money because going from level to level turns your money into a very miniscule amount of EXP, which is terrible in comparison to the Items that give your run a winning chance.
Now, for kiting enemies... this just leads into HORRIBLE character design. Each character has it's own unique set of abilities, but over half of them aren't designed well enough for the game's play style. Take the Sniper for example. His specialty is taking out bosses, which, yes, he can do exceptionally well. What he can't do however is handle the horde of enemies on his tail thanks to the fact he only has one half decent escaping move, the Backflip, which is the opposite of the Commando's Combat roll, where you dive in the opposite direction you're facing. Characters like these make me wonder how pollished this game was. It really gives the illusion of choice, because only about 3 or 4 characters are actually worth using if you want to get anywhere.
In the end, this game really fell short of expectations, and doesn't do a good job of making me feel like a death was my fault, unless I just up and kill myself out of sheer boredom or overly difficult enemies. This game is best enjoyed when you have people to play it with, and saddly the game still falls short in that department, given the fact that you can't host games without a seperate program like Hamachi or Evolve.

When the game first came out it had a few problems. Bugs and the whole co-op offline thing. Now after patching and all the episodes are out, the game is really one of the best in the Resident Evil Series. The controls are more like Resident Evil 6, but without the melee meter. The inventory system is MUCH better than RE6, and it's more like the earlier Resident Evil with limited bag space you can upgrade over time. The story while somewhat short (around 8 hours casual) has multiple ways to replay it in different modes and difficulties. The story itself is pretty good! Lots of twists and while it feels weird at first to have to switch between the two characters, you begin to realize their strengths and see the advantages of team work.
Raid mode is where this game really shines though. The Raid mode is a ramped up version of Mercenaries from the earlier games. There are a large variety of enemies, including some enemies from previous titles. (Excutioner, i'm looking at you.) If you thought these enemies were bad before, now they get buffs, everything from invisibility, on fire, super speed, toxic gas to one that makes you die if you get too close and don't kill it within 30 seconds. Oh, and the buffs stack on the enemies when you get higher level. When you are fighting a Scagdead that can kill you in one hit that is invisible, on fire, and has super speed suddenly things get very tense. It's definitely challenging. A great thing about Raid mode is every character possesses certain skills that the other don't, for example, Cipher gets a katana to replace the knife. If you level up the Sword skill to max, you can pay again to unlock it for all other raid character to buy. Then that character can buy and use that skill. This is great because if you have a favorite character but they don't have the skills you want them to, now you can give them those skills. With the Dailies it's fairly easy to level up the characters to max out the skills you want.
The only negatives about this game really are the in game purchases for hearts and toolbox space. Hearts you earn by doing the daily missions which are easy enough if you are accustomed to raid mode. The Hearts are what you use to revive during Raid mode matches. Your partner cannot get you back up in Co-op. You won't really use them until you get to around level 100, that's when they game gets really crazy and very hard. It might take you a while to build back up your hearts so you can do more high level stuff unless you want to pay for them. Toolbox space you don't really need unless you are a pack rat because you can combine the parts.
All in all, this story reminds me more of Resident Evil 2, with the parallel storylines in the same areas but offset by time, with all the options and gameplay of the newer Resident Evil titles. That's a combo I like very much.

This game is great.  Buying in for the Episodes (1-4, and the two bonus episodes) is great, gives plenty of play time.  The other DLC?  Cosmetic costumes, two extra characters for Raid Mode (and they're the only way to get certain skills...), and slot expansions (completely unneeded if you plan and pay attention).
Raid Mode, like in Revelations 1, is the shining point of this game.  While this game's campaign is much stronger than its predecessor, it's still not perfect.  Raid Mode gives the replayability and balance needed for long term play.  Capcom has still been updating the game, and releasing more and more map packs.
If you're playing campaign, there's three difficulties and three gamemodes.  The "easy" and "normal" difficulties are rather easy, and turn the game into more a survival action game; think of Resident Evil 5 or 6 here, loosely.  The hardest difficulty, Survival, is where the game shifts back towards a more classic feel, with ammo conservation being important and more work on utilizing the game's melee combo mechanics; think of your first Resident Evil 4 playthrough when the ammo was scarce and you had to really THINK to get around/through bosses.
All in all, this game is another step forward in the right direction for the franchise.  If the main numbered games stay "action-y" and the Revelations games continue in a slower, more deliberate manner, I'll be satisfied for a long time.

While this doesn't equate to many non-players of this series, it is the most direct evidence that this game is a great purchase for strategy minded gamers. You will find yourself cursing barbarians and other civs quite often. You'll notice at the higher difficulty levels, how much of a head start is given the AI. You may or may not get upset at this. I tend to look at it as a challenge to be overcome.
Without a doubt, the expansions are practically neccessary to get the true experience, as changes made to the systems make you wonder how you played without that layer.

1) In the mission "Guardian Angels" the guy in the passenger seat who is supposed to hand over the suitcase with money just gets off the car, starts running into it and dies...

nothing can go faster than light. allow me to prove, theoretically, time dilation.
consider a traincar with an experiement setup within. the experiement consists of a mirror on the roof and a laser on the ground, pointing at the mirror. we fire the laser and take the time it takes to hit the mirror and come back down. we call the height of the traincar h, so the distance traveled by the laser beam is 2h times its velocity since velocity is distance over time. but we want the time, so the time recorded is 2h over the velocity, which we found experimentally to be c (the speed of light)
now consider an observer looking upon this experiment from the ground (assume the side of the trainbox is missing, so as to see inside properly). he notices the same experiment taking place and clocks the time it takes for the laser to return to the ground. for him, the length  the laser traveled was not vertically straight, but slanted. we can call these slants L and observe that one leg of the right triangle the slant makes is the height of the traincar, h, while the other leg is half of the base where the base is given by the velocity of the moving train times the time recorded for the whole experiement. this gives us h and (1/2)(v)(T) where v is the velocity of the train and T is the time the observer recorded. using pythagoreans theorem, we conclude that L is equal to sqrt( h^2 + (1/4)(v^2)(T^2) ). since the velocity is distance over time, and we want to solve for time again, we conclude that the time T is 2L over velocity, which once again was found experimentally to be c.
as a recap, let us see the three equations we have found.
t = (2h)/c   (time elapsed for the observer on the train)
T = (2L)/c   (time elapsed for the observer on the ground)
L = sqrt( h^2 + (1/4)(v^2)(T^2) )   (distance the laser traveled for the observer on the ground)
we now solve the first equation for h and plug it into the third equation. the first equation becomes h = (1/2)(c)(t). this gives us
L = sqrt( (1/4)(c^2)(t^2) +  (1/4)(v^2)(T^2) )  (our fourth equation)
we now solve the second equation for L, and set it equal to the fourth equation, giving us
(1/2)(T)(c) = sqrt( (1/4)(c^2)(t^2) +  (1/4)(v^2)(T^2) )

after a bit of algebra, that fifth equation reduces to
T = t / sqrt(1 - (v/c)^2)
keeping in mind that T is the outside observers time, t is in inside observers time, v is the velocity of the train, and c is the speed of light.
notice from the equation that if the train were going at the speed of light, c, the equation would be undefined as there would be a 0 in the denominator. if we viewed a graph of the equation, there would be an asymptote at v = c, with all of the usual implications thereof.
therefore, this equation predicts that nothing can move faster than the speed of light and is has thus far been shown via countless experiments to be the case.
the equation also explains how the time we experience (around us) depends upon the velocity we travel at. use that equation to find the difference in time observed between two observers if one is within an inertial reference frame (t) with respect to the experiment being conducted and the other is not (T).

Do you like Arkham City and Asylum? You'll like this game.
Didn't like Arkham City? You probably won't like this game.
That's the short version.
The long version:
Knight is a mixed bag of mostly really good things. The game loks fantastic, easily one of the best looking games I have ever played. The combat is as fun as ever with a couple new enemy types to keep you on your toes and prevent you from spamming the counter button to win every encounter - it's the only game in the Arkham series that really forces you to use all of the tools in Batman's arsenal. The story is generally good and, in my opinion, the best executed in the series.
The open world is much better utilized than in City. Arkham Knight has several quest lines with objectives that you will come across while traversing to other missions whereas in City the open world was mostly just a means to get a bunch of Riddler trophies. Speaking of Riddler trophies, probably one of the worst things about Knight is to see the true ending you have to collect 200+ trophies strewn throughout the game. I put over 30 hours into the game and only got about 50 trophies. Just watch the full ending on Youtube, it's a better use of your time.
Other than the trophy fiasco, there's only a few other things that bothered me about this game. The Batmobile is completely useless when it comes to traversal since gliding around Gotham is a way faster and more efficient way to get around. I do have to say the Batmobile is actually well used in terms of some of the puzzles and combat. I've seen a lot of people complain about the car combat, but I found it to be fun, just a little overused. Second, there are these parts of the game where Batman goes into detective mode to reconstruct how a scene happened in order to find clues of where to go next, there are maybe 3-4 uses of this in the whole game and I would've liked to see more of it in the last third of the game. My last main complaint is how the game's level/mission design takes a massive nose dive towards the last 5 or so main missions and it just results in a lot areas that have you fighting waves of guys and tanks without any thoughtful use of your tools.
Overall a very fun game with plenty of highs and only a few real lows.

Mirror's Edge can be described in one word, and only one word really seems to fit. "Unique". Everything from the visual style of a bleached white city (which is hardly as boring to look at as it sounds) to the gameplay are some thing that I've never seen before, and am sad I haven't.
The gameplay is hard to explain, and fits no real genre. "First person parkour shooter puzzle game" is probably the closest. When you reach that point in the game where you play flawlessly, able to launch over and under any obstacle you see it's something that feels... right.
Combat is somewhat important, but most encounters can be avoided. Moving into combat comes as seamlessly as moving through parts of the level, and you can bring the same momentum and speed you feel in the parkour elements right into the battles.
That's not to say the game is *all* gameplay. The story is also interesting, and the comic book style cutscenes do a great job portraying every important character in the game.
It's not the world's longest game, but it's got immense replay value. Time trials, and the satisfaction of nailing each section with perfect landings and non stop running kept brining me back to the game.
I recommend this game to fans of puzzle games (searching for paths to objectives up and down buildings and rooftops), and action game fans (because of the hectic movement and combat) alike. Every element seems to fall into place together, and it makes this a true classic that every fan of gaming should own a copy of.

If you could get beyond the art style, you will discover a tcg with surprising depth. Here's some pro's and con's to help you decide whether this is a game for you.
Cons:
- Art Style [this depends on individual preference]
- It's pretty obvious that this is a PC port from mobile device. Not saying that it's a bad port, it is simply not good either, it simply is. There is 60 fps support but then no new UI to cater to PC users.
- There is certain downsides to playing on Steam/PC, namely rerolling [more on that below]
Pros:
- f2p-friendly [This is the most generous tcg I've played, giving you 35 packs, each giving you 8 cards, from completing the tutorial]
- Reroll [This trick is so prevalent, it might as well be a feature of the game. Basically, being on the phone allows the user to delete system data and start afresh, combine that with the generosity of the game with free packs, one could technically restart until one get the desired cards from the get-go. Now this is a lot more tedious through Steam, since steam locks user data. Not saying it's impossible, you just gotta go through emulator and stuff]
- Vialibility of archetypes [Due to unique feature like evolve and flexibility of most cards, one could play most archetypes on all class. There's still decks that are prevalent in meta snapshot, but they don't leave the rest of the gang in the dust]

If you're looking for action-packed combat or deep RPG character evolution, you won't find it here, but if you enjoyed X-Com, you should like this X-Com meets Bladerunner game. It starts as a detective story but ends up as revenge quest. Those who have described this as simply an interactive novel do it an injustice - yes, the story is linear, but it's none the worse for that and you do have room to build different teams for each setpiece when it comes along. The storytelling is high class and the exploration is fun. The one weak point to me was the visits to cyberspace which seemed a bit perfunctory and over simplified. We still haven't really progressed beyond the first Tron in depicting cyberspace.
All in all, for an indie game, it's excellent and well worth the money.

The following is a review of the game from a long-time Resident Evil fan.
Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a decidedly low-budget affair, it's not particularly graphically impressive and there is a level of jank to it all. However, behind this lays what may be one of the stronger Resident Evil games in years that manages to be a solid episodic title, a solid survival-action game, and more atmosphere and horror-oriented and feeling more like 'Resident Evil' than probably the last several RE games combined.
Now I say that as someone who actually liked Resident Evil Umbrella+Darkside Chronicles, RE5, Revelations 1, and Resident Evil 6 well enough for what they were. RE5 and RE6 were fun action co-op games for me, RE5 was a fun arcade shooter with some fun monsters, RE6 had some fun combat mechanics with a sort of uneven-quality campaign but great Mercenaries. Revelations 1 was okay, I enjoyed it well enough, but its handheld origins showed strongly and really, the design of the game was kind of dull at times, and it never quite gave that classic Resident Evil feel it claimed it would.  But Raid Mode was a joy for me.
However, I think with this title it's helped me better understand what element is missing from those games, besides the obvious flaws that something like Resident Evil 6 has, Revelations 2 comes as something of a reminder of elements of RE I deeply appreciate and love that have been mostly absent in recent years. That's not to say this is some complete return to form or a classic-styled survival-horror game, but it recalls back to the older series while also not quite feeling it's living in the past.
While the graphics leave some things to be desired, the sound design is well-handled. It doesn't quite have the memorable moody tunes of the original series, but the dynamic shifts of the music, the audio design of ambiance and monsters is well-handled, with good depth of audio for headphone users, and a good layer of subtlety which help propel the title further to a more engaging experience.
This is a much slower experience than recent Resident Evil's. That's not to say it doesn't have its action-full moments, but even those comparatively to recent RE titles feel more constrained and leveled, and a lot of the time you find yourself scouting locations, looking for hidden items, sneaking past or onto enemies with a new stealth system (that's a bit flawed sometimes, but functional).
Before I continue, I shall mention like I do with most Resident Evil titles, I played this game on the hardest difficulty available from the start, Survival. I did my first run in Revelations 1 on Infernal, I played RE6 on Professional on the 360 before No Hope existed. However, this is probably tied for me right now with Code Veronica as the most challenging RE on Hard difficulty. Revelations 1 had some artificial difficulty spikes on Infernal (the first chapter and final boss fight come to mind), but this feels more like a challenge. I've discovered Survival both lowers the amount of ammo you get, and adds specific trickier enemy placements. I wouldn't recommend it for the easily frustrated, but for those who like a challenge and an amplified survival element, I would recommend it.
And maybe in part to this I found the game to have a bigger survival aspect than the recent RE's, I found myself struggling more for ammo and health than I can recall in any recent survival-action, horror, or the like games. Even in a lot of older RE's I would be stockpiled with a lot of supplies past the very beginning, but here I found myself aching for specific ammo types and herbs on a number of occasions. But not to my lament, I found it a joy, with the slower-pace. The lack of constant action with more of a focus on survival and playing more intelligently and preservative brought back certain feelings I haven't felt from the series in a while.
The element I was most surprised by though was the story. This isn't some masterfully crafted tale, but the story feels like a Resident Evil story. One of the single most disappointing elements of RE6 and Revelations 1 for me happened to be their narratives, the characters lacked playfully fun tones often, the files were a bore, the stories delved into the ridiculous, and not in a good way, and often came up as boring and forgettable. This game has single-handily pushed Barry as one of my favorite characters in the series, had a child character in Natalia that is actually not annoying and enjoyable, the ridiculous cussing of Moira actually didn't totally turn me off from her character and she became likable by the end of it, and it has what in my opinion is the best villain the series has had in years. Claire unfortunately is missing some of her charm from RE2 and Code Veronica, but I also find herself in this game fairly unoffensive. Unlike the first 'Revelations', this game actually feels super connected with the rest of the series, episodes end with actually impactful cliffhangers, and the overall story feels like actual revelations to the series that makes me interested to see where they take it in the future. The story managed to be enjoyable throughout, make me care, make me laugh, and unexpectedly delivered a few moments that put me on the bit of the edge of feelsy and realizing I actually like these characters, something no recent RE has been able to afflict on me.
It's also notable that there's only a small handful of QTEs in the game, that aren't harmful, and it happens to be the only game I can think of that got forced walking sections correctly. That's usually a huge game design sin for me, but the moments are very rare and when it happens it both makes sense and actually works.
One of the game's finer strengths is its monster design and encounters. Some of the monsters found in the game are among some of my favorites in recent RE's, and they're backed with memorable and some of the most tense encounters I feel in the series history. Boss encounters are infrequent, but the few that are here managed to be good ones in my opinion, with a few maybe being some of my favorite tense boss encounters in the series. While not specifically a chainsaw, this game probably has my favorite 'chainsaw enemy' since Dr. Salvador, and a boss fight in Claire's Chapter 3 is a fun and wonderfully RE-styled boss fight. I even thought the final boss was the best final boss the series had seen in the last few years, and I agree with others, the good ending was probably the best ending a Resident Evil game has had in over a decade.
Then there's small touches that bring the game together. Certain things you do in Claire's scenario affects Barry's, some being as subtle as picking up ammo and herbs not making it available for Barry/Natalia, to minor cool things, like turning on the flamethrower to aid Claire in episode 1 causes there to be an additional obstacle in Barry's episode 1, to nice subtle things like a certain monster you can fight or run from in one of Claire's episodes will change completely what Barry has to do or encounter... The episodes get progressively better in my opinion, and some of the later stuff feels a lot like older RE, including a few light, easy, but fun puzzles in episode 3, and a certain fun section in the last episode...
One disappointing thing is, despite spending hours in it already and enjoying it well enough, I think I've concluded that Raid Mode in Revelations 2 I don't find as enjoyable as Raid Mode in Revelations 1. There's aspects I like about it more, like character-specific abilities, the new monster buffs, the higher number of stages... But most of the stages being from RE6, as well as just not as well designed or varied as Revelations 1, and the whole thing lacking an over-arching fun challenge like Ghost Ship, I think is deeply felt.

Best .49 I ever spent.
It's a solitaire card game.  If you're expecting something more, you're looking at the wrong game.  If you're expecting just that - a solitaire card game - you are going to be pleasantly surprised.
- Gameplay is simple and easy to learn.  Each game takes 1-2 minutes, each level has 9 games and a level-specific goal to achieve.  The goals are easy to achieve, but perfection is not.
- The adventure mode has a story which is cute but fairly generic.  It's a card game, after all.  Still, I enjoyed it.  The voice acting was even decent.
- The resources and pet gathering was fun.  It doesn't affect the outcome of the game in any way but if you enjoy collecting pets/achievements, you'll find some entertainment in it.
All in all, it's a simple but smooth card game that can be played by kids or adults and can be fairly addicting.  It's likely worth the 10 bucks it costs normally but if you can catch it for .49, even better.   Then you can buy it for your friends, too, and feel better about your own addiction.

Finally a game that lets you play as the Avengers,the Xmen, the Guardians of the Galaxy or if you fancy it you can play as one of the bad guys like the Green Goblin or Loki. This is another brilliant game from the Lego series and like previous Lego games it's a lot of fun and a game that has appeal to both casual and hardcore gamers. This game sees you through various missions where you will play a variety of Marvel characters each with their unique abilities and advantages. So Hulk can lift heavy objects while Iron Man can destroy them with rockets.
The levels are the usual types that you'll see in a Lego game i.e collecting studs, using different characters abilities to progress and so on. When your not playing a level you have a nice open-world Manhatten to explore where you can solve puzzles, do quests and races to unlock gold bricks or more characters. The game also introduces driveable vehicles which although are not utilized much in the levels are still a fun distraction in the open-world section.
The story isn't bad either with all the villains teaming up under Loki and Dr.Doom to collect cosmic bricks which the heroes have to stop them. One of the great things about the characters in this game is they are all brilliantly voiced in the game which really brings the characters to life in the game.
The Good:
-has pretty much every Marvel hero and villian from the more famous like Iron Man and the Hulk to the more obscure.
-fun gameplay that can be enjoyed by anyone.
-open-world Manhatten is a great feature with the ability to fly around or even drive.
-characters are brilliantly voiced in this game (Deadpools commentary in the extra levels is fantastic)
The Bad:
-gameplay can feel a bit repetetive at times
- AI can be terrible at times particularly in freeplay
Overall Lego have pulled off another brilliant game that anyone with even a passing interest in the Marvel Universe should check out. 9/10

This is a fantastic turn based RTS that I heavily recommend.
-Nice variety of units, civs, benefits, and management (resources, tiles, money, science, etc)
-Several different ways to play each civ. Most are good at two or three victory routes.
-Mechanics like science and culture bend to your playstyle more than you bend to their limitations.
-Maps are randomly generated, but never feel unbalanced or unplayable.
-The DLC bundle is only $50, and really enhances the game experience.
I consider this to be a mid to high strategy focused game. It has far more depth than your average strategy game, but can't compare to something like EU (which isn't turn based).
There are some slight issues.
-Some civs (ie Japan, Russia) are clearly better than others.
-Team battles with AI partners can be an upredictable experience. They declare war, you march your army to the enemy, they negotiate peace, then they declare war on an enemy that's next to your capital but your whole army is across the map... Thanks, AI.
-You can have some pretty awful start locations. Start in the center of a desert, a civ to your north and south, ocean east and west, and only incense and iron? Have fun with that!
-Gandhi. I shall never again trust you and your war mongering ways.
There are some ways to overcome the game. For example, building on tundra or desert limits your city's potention. Building on snow literally gives it no potential. Great engineers, merchants, and scientists can construct on all but water tiles, making even snow tiles productive.
All in all, 10/10 with all DLC. If you're hesitant, get the bundle on sale. It's worth $50; it's theft at $10. :)

This review is from a long time Hearthstone player who only recently started playing Shadowverse. I was quite on the fence about trying Shadowverse due to hesitation about having to learn an entirely new card game, new mechanics, new interface, new classes, etc. For anyone feeling the same hesitation about trying Shadowverse out, this review is for you.
1) The graphics, card art, and animations.
If you like (or don't mind) anime style artwork, this game is going to blow your mind, especially if you're coming from Hearthstone. The animations, card art (2 versions of artwork for each card due to the evolve mechanic), hero animations, game maps... it's just all so well done. As a fan of anime myself, I think they did an absolutely amazing job in this department. The UI (user interface) can take a little bit of getting used to, but this game is highly polished and very well made.
On the flip side, if you don't enjoy anime-style artwork, you should skip this game because it's all done anime style.
2) Tutorials. (And hesitation about learning a new game)
The in-game tutorials are pretty well done provided you take your time to read and examine everything that is presented to you. Much like Hearthstone, special abilities and things are listed in the card text in bold fonts. Clicking these bold fonts will give you more detail about what it means/does/etc. It took me a while to figure out that I could click on this bold text to get that additional info (they might want to make the bold text a different color or something so that it is more apparent for new players that it is a clickable thing that provides more information).
3) Mechanics.
For the most part, many of the base card mechanics are identical to Hearthstone except they are simply named differently. For example, Ward = Taunt, Fanfare = Battlecry, Last Words = Deathrattle, etc. There are no hero powers, as they have been replaced with the Evolve mechanic (which is awesome and seems to add a good deal of depth to the game) along with Amulet cards which are kind of like spells, but different. Instead of there only being Minion, Weapon & Spell cards, like in Hearthstone, there are Minion, Spell, and Amulet cards, some of which have second level classifications similar to tribe cards in Hearthstone. While this paragraph probably does little to give you a good picture of it all, once you're in game and running through the story modes it will all become clear pretty quickly. This is another area I think they have done a fanstastic job in. Oh, and I see a lot, and I mean a LOT less RNG baked into the cards, unlike Hearthstone were the majority of cards produce random effects.
4) Single Player Mode.
Currently still going through all the stories of each character (each character contains 8 chapters!) and it is a great deal of fun. It's been a while since I started playing a game and had trouble putting it down, but even just playing the story mode, Shadowverse is very hard to turn off. They could just have the game be nothing but story modes and I would still play it non-stop.
5) Starting your collection
Coming from Hearthstone, I was absolutely floored by how much free stuff is given to new players to help get them started. Lots and lots of packs, gold, and dust from the story mode. The developers seem to have been*extremely* generous in this department, almost as if they care more about customer satisfaction than milking every penny possible from their players (what a concept, huh?!).
6) System Requirements.
I currently only game on a laptop that wasn't built for that purpose, so after seeing how smooth and rich the graphics for Shadowverse were in videos and trailers, I was pretty worried that the game wouldn't run on this crappy laptop with generic Intel HD graphics. I decided to give it a go anyway and downloaded the game. Not only does the game run on my crappy laptop, but it actually runs smoother than Hearthstone despite Shadowverse having 3D type map elements, fast action, hero animations, evolve animations, and so on. The game looks and runs great, which was a pleasant surprise.
7) Misc Notes.
- Heroes have 20hp as opposed to Hearthstone's 30hp. Haven't noticed much of a difference in terms of game play due to the way Shadowverse cards and mechanics were designed, but I haven't started playing against other players yet.
- Decks contain 40 cards and allow 2x duplicates as opposed to Hearthstone's 30 cards and 1 duplicates.
8) Closing Thoughts
While I'm still new to the game and learning everything it has to offer, I'm absolutely having a blast with it. It is extremely well made. Playing this game made me realize that nearly all of my recent Hearthstone play hours were done out of sheer boredom with little to no enjoyment gained from playing the game, simply because I hadn't found a good alternative. Should the game be even *half* as good as it has been from my newbie experience, I highly doubt I will ever log into FrustrationStone again.
So, if you're on the fence about this one. Do yourself a big favor and at least give it a try. Complete a couple of the character's story lines and you're gonna be hooked. Good luck out there.

This game makes me rage.. But I love it!
Firaxis studios' remaking of the older XCOM franchise is a great game all around without a shadow of a doubt. It has aliens, guns, global terror and addictive tactical play that I just can't leave alone.
The premise is simple enough, you're an operative for the XCOM organisation, and it's your job to direct the forces at your disposal to best serve the interests of humanity in fighting off the alien menace (more on them in a mkinute). You do this through turn based tactical combat scenarios and a metagame of base management and decision making that overarches the main gameplay by forcing you to choose which options you want to research, what facilities you want to construct to better your force or gear, and which missions you want to send your recruits on to shoot the aliens to bits.
At the basic level, that's what the game is all about really - decision making. It's why it works so wonderfully, and also why it will make you rage but keep coming back for more. The turn based nature of the gameplay means you can weigh the odds of different approaches as you go and take your time to figure out the various angles and opportunities you have at each point. Squad cohesion is important in mission gameplay, and a poor choice of action or missed opportunity could see you paying for it down the line with your squad members, when alien plasma fries them. It forces you to adapt and overcome your enemies, predict the outcome of your options and make the best choices, whether that involves a squad wide attack to wipe out the enemy or (occasionally) sacrificing one member to allow the others to move to a safer position or escape (though you'll find that this is a painful lesson when it's a high level unit with helpful abilities that you lose however).
There's plenty to keep track of and experiment with too. Your different units have classes that affect their weaponry loadout (heavy units being armed with an LMG and Rocket launcher at the first level for example) and abilities that go along with them (in the case of the aforementioned heavy, suppression fire and usage of the launcher etc), so making sure that the different specialisations are utilised well is wise to be keep in mind while on a mission. You are free to choose who you want to field however, so if you find you don't really enjoy using a particular class or would rather take another sniper than a support unit for example, it's your choice.
Outside of mission play the decision making is just as important if not more so. You'll create a base layout with facilities to upgrade or improve your arsenal and construct your gear between missions, and keeping appropriate facilities close gives benefits so juggling everything or putting one plan on hold to get a different module placed first can provide bigger bonuses down the line. The different research tiers as the game progresses ramp up in power quite nicely and are satisfying to play with when you finally get to top tier weaponry and armor (higher tier armors especially offering some interesting options in terms of gameplay, IMO). All important research unlocks all these goodies so taking advantage of your time at the base to figure out which projects you want to take next is the other main aspect between mission play to keep in mind - neglecting any one aspect ofyour squad's equipment can leave you underequipped for some missions but researching the alien tech and recovered corpses etc is also important so as to discover their weak points, making it a fine balancing act.
So yeah, as the title said, it'll make you rage. When Corporal Bloggs pops his head round a blind corner only to get it melted by alien plasma fire unexpectedly you might want to shout, or swear, whatever floats your boat. But it's so satisfying to play that you'll just want to keep coming back to try again. Maybe Corporal Bloggs' brother will have better luck on point instead..

This game can be summerized into one word: hard. This game is tough as I've logged in roughly 6 hours and I haven't beaten the first level (which is named hard...). YET, I still enjoy this game. Here's why:
Music:
Honestly, if you're not a huge fan of EDM music, or just music games in general, then this game is not for you. This game is a very simple one (all you need is just a way to go left or right, enter, and exit), which means it doesn't have a lot to offer aside from its music and graphics. With that said, I really enjoy the soundtrack as it definitely adds to the mood of the game. I'll admit that it does get repetitive, and it would be nicer if they had more variety in each level, but it's still enjoyable to hear.
Gameplay:
Very simple controls, yet they're able to give you a headache when playing. I like the concept of the game, but I don't like how sensetive the controls are. I have probably died a lot of times due to being off by just a hair. Although, they have variety of controls. You can use the left and right keys, the mouse, or a gamepad to play. I also don't like how you can't really predict the patterns at times. Sure you can recongize what will happen, but the pattern is always different each play through. This'll lead to a lot of frustration. But on the bright side, it's easy to manage time with this game. With the level only lasting a minute at the most, you're able to play through the level at least 5 times in around 5 minutes. Definitely a game to play when you have the urge to play something, but don't have a lot of time to play. It's also good for the gamer who wants to challenge themselves, like me.
Graphics:
Again, simple. The color changing looks cool and is very smooth. You can easily tell what you need to avoid and where you are despite the flashing/changing colors around you. The game has a cool "tilt" that gives it a slight (only slight) 3D look to it, which is nice too. It does change directions, which always trip up my eyes. It definitely has a look of a simple yet futuristic-like game.
Over all, the game is good, but not amazing. If you find this game for a cheap price, then I would recommend getting it. The game offers a challenge that I rarely see in most games, and is super trippy, which I like... A LOT. If you can master the levels like a boss, then you'll easily be a boss to everyone you know... Or at least my mind will be blown...

I'm pleased to say that Revelations 2 is one of the best games in the Resident Evil franchise, and I think I enjoyed this game more than any other except RE1. Set after Revelations 1 and before RE6 (but not really connected to either story), Claire Redfield has been abducted along with Barry Burton's daughter Moira, and Barry is trying to rescue them with the help of a mysterious young girl called Natalia.
Each of the four episodes has a Claire/Moira chapter followed by a Barry/Natalia chapter, and the player can switch control between the characters at will. Claire and Barry are the primary characters for combat against the undead. Moira and Natalia both have a melee weapon, but neither can use guns. They can find hidden items (mostly ammo and gems) that Claire/Barry can't see, and Natalia can "sense" the presence of monsters, which is useful to check ahead for danger. There's also one particular enemy that requires the use of this ability in a very interesting way (I won't spoil the surprise).
Combat is mostly the slower pace associated with traditional survival horror, where you fight small groups of strong enemies and have limited ammo. There are a few action focused set pieces, where you'll get locked in a room with lots of monsters, especially with Claire. Barry has some areas where the layout allows him to sneak up behind enemies and perform instant kill stealth takedowns. The guns are the usual handgun, magnum, shotgun, smg, rifle, and you can also craft a few different types of throwables such as molotovs and smoke bombs.
The downside of having two characters working together is that it negates the impact of horror. Being alone is always scarier. But on the other hand, some of my favourite parts of this game were sections that required the use of both characters to solve puzzles. And the dialogue between the characters helped to keep the story moving. The story is pretty good and voice acting is superb.
After each chapter there's a basic upgrade system, where you can exchange points earned from your performance (quicker completion time, fewer deaths and better accuracy equals more points) and finding gems for stronger passive skills (more weapon damage, herbs heal more, etc).
It took me 13 hours to finish the main story plus two "bonus episodes". Graphics are an upgrade from Revelations 1 (probably that game's weakest point) and I had no problems with framerate, bugs or crashes. Controls are mostly rebindable and work well with mouse and keyboard, however it wouldn't detect my mouse thumb buttons which forced me to find unusual keys for some commands.
Revelations 2 is a must play for any fan of Resident Evil, and even if you're not a fan, its a really good game that's worth checking out.

Most people think this game is similar to Portal. In some ways, yes, I suppose it is. But it's also very different. The game utilises an interesting block gun mechanic which is actually really fun to use and makes for a unique puzzle experience (similar to how Portal's mechanics make it unique). Another mechanic used in this game involves, basically, thinking out of the box. One may come across a wall which isn't really as it seems. You may have to look at the picture from a different angle before you can make sense of your area. These blend together well to create a fulfilling experience that doesn't tug at your nerves and can be solved at a leisurely pace.
Now, having said that, there are some points in the game which I felt to be...less of what I wanted the game to give. For example, one would have to time him/her-self at just the right time to get past the puzzle and that, I feel, removed me from the experience the other puzzles gave. It felt more like a game (which is a good thing!) but I was already satisfied with the uniqueness of simply thinking my way out of a puzzle. Adding a trivial game mechanic into it felt disjointed but these instances happened so rarely that it may simply be overlooked when taking the whole game into account.
I won't spoil the story but I just have to say that it was pretty...decent. Not great by any means but not dull either. It was satisfying and open to interpretation (which, depending on perspective, is either a good or a bad thing). All in all, I felt that Antichamber was money well spent (though I got this at a very cheap price). It's an experience that most people would want to go through and I certainly didn't regret giving up my two assignments to finish the game in two days.

This is a fantastic turn based RTS that I heavily recommend.
-Nice variety of units, civs, benefits, and management (resources, tiles, money, science, etc)
-Several different ways to play each civ. Most are good at two or three victory routes.
-Mechanics like science and culture bend to your playstyle more than you bend to their limitations.
-Maps are randomly generated, but never feel unbalanced or unplayable.
-The DLC bundle is only $50, and really enhances the game experience.
I consider this to be a mid to high strategy focused game. It has far more depth than your average strategy game, but can't compare to something like EU (which isn't turn based).
There are some slight issues.
-Some civs (ie Japan, Russia) are clearly better than others.
-Team battles with AI partners can be an upredictable experience. They declare war, you march your army to the enemy, they negotiate peace, then they declare war on an enemy that's next to your capital but your whole army is across the map... Thanks, AI.
-You can have some pretty awful start locations. Start in the center of a desert, a civ to your north and south, ocean east and west, and only incense and iron? Have fun with that!
-Gandhi. I shall never again trust you and your war mongering ways.
There are some ways to overcome the game. For example, building on tundra or desert limits your city's potention. Building on snow literally gives it no potential. Great engineers, merchants, and scientists can construct on all but water tiles, making even snow tiles productive.
All in all, 10/10 with all DLC. If you're hesitant, get the bundle on sale. It's worth $50; it's theft at $10. :)

There's a lot of work to be appreciated the first time you get to fly around as the caped crusader in Arkham Knight, just like 'Arkham City' the open-world map is detailed in a way most games take for granted. Most of the buildings look uniquely handcrafted and store information in a way that's easily accessible at first glance.
The player ends up soaking in the identity of Gotham without feeling overwhelmed, few games on the market acheive visual storytelling to the degree 'Arkham Knight' does, the city is littered with nods towards hardcore fans. But they're all laid out in such a fashion where newcomers can join in without hassle.
I'd catch myself smirking with what's considered a bountiful mass of easter eggs by many video game standards. Everything is treated with a professional amount of love and respect to the lore that's absent from remakes/spin-offs thats an industry standard today. This is all supplemented by the now iconic Arkham Theme delivered by Composers "Nick Arundel, David Buckley" there's a tense feeling that the town needs saving, making you feel like you have a score to settle.
It's nice to see someone understand a License to a degree where they actually stay loyal to the source material, while still creating something of their own.
The combat is simple where anyone can pick up and play but delicate enough for those who enjoy racking up combos. With a system dominated by a two button setup for punching/countering. You will be encouraged the use of gadgets for variation bonuses with XP rewards that fit into a flimsey and trivial skill tree that could've been made more rewarding with less frequent skillpoints rewarded.
Everything is solely focused on giving the player a cinematic superhero experience while fistfighting, the extra layer of complexity comes into play through stealth sections.
Taking out tricky opponents with takedowns before intiating combat can help rough fights. Some sections force you to go full Tom Clancy, picking people off until nobody remains. this is shown very rewardingly with fluent animations that have enough diversity to be entertaining each time.
There's a sense of speed that's absent from most stealth games, in 'Arkham Knight' it's entirely possible to take out 5 people in quick succesion while flying through airducts and scoping through the map laid out for you. It really feels impowering when you start getting a hold on the game mechanics.

That brings us to the most tricky addition, this third installment introduces the batmobile.
While it's refreshing to drive around in something that handles way different to most racing games, with tactile drifting and a wildy destructible environment there's just too many sections that involve needlessly switching back and forth from batman just to pull something off a wall or lower a bridge to walk across.
it brings moments of tension to a grinding halt which ultimately just drags you out of the experience. It overstays it's welcome, but i wouldn't say you should steer clear of playing the game just because of it.
Without getting into the story too much, The main focus is presented as Batman fighting odds stacked up against him, the writing doesn't get incredibly deep but overall the game does show Bruce from new angles that are interesting to visit.
Even as a third installment of the Arkham series, there's an easy possiblity for people to jump into this game without having played previous releases.
Personally i'd recommend starting from the first 'Arkham Asylum' to get the full experience.
Skip the spin-off 'Arkham Origins' due to the huge thematic gap that doesn't fit well in contrast to the games as a trilogy.
If you haven't played it yet it's a great experience and very few deliver quite the blend of gameplay it has to offer.

Before I get to the good I want to talk about the bad.
First off, the controls for this game are designed for a controller, not mouse and keyboard. Not a huge deal, but occasionally things will happen and you'll have to spam a random button (w, a, s or d) with no warning and it'll give you a .75 second window to hit it five times times. Doesn't sound too hard, but in the heat of battle it is. Most of the time I'd fail a challenge, learn what to do, then redo it with my right hand over the wasd keys. In some instances failing these button mashing sequences is game ending.
Second, the gear progression in this game sucks. If you shop around you can buy weapons and armor that is better than anything you will find for many levels, and around the time you find something better there will be a new shop with something even better still. I don't think I found a single piece of equipment throughout the entire game that was actually an upgrade from what I had already. Even the level 13-15 weapons found in the final stage are inferior to the ones you can buy as soon as you reach Jimbo's shop (at like level 5). Another example, near the end of the game there are a few new areas that are unlocked in sequence. Each area has a new set of armor to find. The armor in area 1 is better than the armor in area 2, and area 2's armor is better than area 3's. None of them were better than what I already had. Just useless junk.
Third, you have no control over your buddies gear or progression. By the end of it your character is decked out and lugging around lethal weapons, while your buddies are still packing a claw hammer or a golf club. Lame.
Fourth, all the 'junk' you find in the game (it's an actual loot category) has no purpose other than to be sold. Cool, free money. BUT by the time you get to a shop you will have hundreds of items to sell, and there is no 'sell all' button. You can sell stacks of junk, but even then it is tedious. I resorted to just spam clicking junk until it was all gone. Sometimes it would take 4-5 minutes to do. If the game was designed properly it would take around 3 seconds.
Fifth, when enemies die the loot drops in the world and you have to pick it up manually. Not a big deal, but you'll consistently have the max stock of cure and health potions, so when you click the 'take all' button you'll then have to click another button to close the interface. Esc won't do it. Then that cure potion that you left laying there will be on top of another loot pile, and you'll just have to leave it because every time you try to pick it up it tries to get the cure potion again. Could have been avoided by just putting the loot in your inventory after battle and dropping what you couldn't carry. Not a big deal I guess, but it was annoying.
Sixth, magic serves no purpose in combat at all. The only way to restore mana is to use mana potions. Ain't no one got time for that. The only thing that magic does is allow you to access new areas.
Seventh, summons serve no purpose either. They can't be used against boss's, and normal encounters are so weak that they die in a couple of turns anyway. Then, if you do use a summon you'll have to go back to where you got it and get another one. Waste of time. I feel like this feature was added just so they could say 'Game features blah blah blah summons blah blah blah.'.
Eighth, each buddy has a special command. Through out the entire game I remember using four of them. Stan and Jimmy's buddy command was used once each. Butters and Kenny's buddy command were each used a handful of times. I have no idea what Kyle or Cartman's buddy commands even do.
Now let's talk about the GOOD parts of this game and why I recommend it.

Dying light is what you get when you combine Mirror's edge and Dead island, then mix in a bit of Farcry.
As soon as load the game the graphics look very nice, and seem to be well optimized for high FPS.
The combat for the most part feels very fluid and fun, being able to chain hits together and decapitate multiple zombies with one handed weapons. Although early on in the game, you run out of stamina pretty quick from swinging a pipe around, so you might just want to stick to running around on rooftops untill you get better skills and gear.
I love the freerunning in this game, it feels very Mirrors edge-y. You can outrun common zombies (Biters) easily, so they aren't too threatening. The skill trees are nicely designed and, instead of choosing your favorite skill tree to put all your points into, you get skill points for the different trees by doing things related to them (eg. Climing to get agility points).
The crafting system is pretty generic, but it works. You can craft quite a variety of weapon mods that let you create some pretty cool looking weapons. In addition to weapons, you can also craft tools such as explosive shurikens, grenades, sheilds, ect. You'll learn how to craft new items as you level up.
You feel pretty safe in the day, what with there being few zombies that can chase you, but at night, the game changes from running rooftop to rooftop, looting, and killing weak zombies, to a stealth action game, where you hide from demonic spawn that can chase you down and rip you to pieces (Volatiles). However you do get double XP at night, giving you an insentive you stay out late.
Well overall, I'd say I really enjoy this game. I know this review dosn't cover everything in the game, but its just to give people an idea of what its like. If you like games like Farcry or Dead island, or maybe you're entertained by dropkicking zombies off of buildings of various hights, then I would recommend this game.

I recently beat Mirrors Edge (in about 6 hours of gameplay)
The game is unlike any other, which you'll find out as you're jumping around actually avoiding enemies. You don't run into fights like in most games nowadays, you die too easily. You can take out one enemy easily, but they always move in two or more. If you're able to knock out or kill an enemy with your kickass martial arts skills you can pick up his gun, but you only have the magazine that is currently in it. The gunfights aren't exactly interesting, as its not a shooting game, but sometimes I found them necessary because I couldn't get around the enemies in that particular level. Of course the focus of the game is hardcore parkour essentially, you feel superhuman as you run across walls and jump across buildings. One bad step and you can find yourself plummetting toward the ground in a stomach churning fall ending with a sickening crack of bones and a splat. The cutscenes aren't interesting, they use an animation style that literally makes you feel like you're watching an esurance commercial. Honestly I would be sucked into the game, having a lot of fun when a cutscene reared its ugly head, and I didn't feel like playing anymore.
Overall, the graphics are nice, the gameplay is fresh but sometimes repetetive, the story is generic and uninteresting, and the game is moderately hard to run.

Dead space. A singleplayer horror, sci-fi. I must admit that I had not personally played the dead space games before, but due to watching a few let's players, i decided to have a look at the game myself. After finishing the second chapter, I decided to give my own opinion about the game.
However, like every other game out there, there are good things and bad things.
Lets start with the things the game did well:
In my personal opninion, it has mostly to do with the admosphere and overal feeling of what is happening around you.
The ship truly feels like a living place, where crewmembers and people used to live and work before and during the time that everything went wrong.
A lott of detail has gone into the many rooms and haunting corridors of the ship, with lights popping out, the distant noises and the few screams and people you encounter, driving home the horror aspect. And from the moment you encounter your first enemy, you will be sitting on the edge of your seat, scanning every area you will enter for what will happen next. Combined with the music and some good placed effects, make it quite a good and scary experience.
However, I think it is now time to talk about the elephant in the room:
While the atmoshpere itself was done beautifully, I could not help but struggle with the controls and the gameplay. There seemed to be somekind of delay with every movement of my character and  mouse when you look around. Although this can be something one can get used to, it can also mess up your day when you are constantly thrown out of your rhythm due to a jump scare and unable to aim at your attacker.
Does this mean it's a good game?
That is entirely up to you. While I will give Dead Space a thumbs up, it is mostly due to being a good horror game.
But if you decide to buy the game, then be aware that there will be some minor gameplay difficulties.

This game makes me rage.. But I love it!
Firaxis studios' remaking of the older XCOM franchise is a great game all around without a shadow of a doubt. It has aliens, guns, global terror and addictive tactical play that I just can't leave alone.
The premise is simple enough, you're an operative for the XCOM organisation, and it's your job to direct the forces at your disposal to best serve the interests of humanity in fighting off the alien menace (more on them in a mkinute). You do this through turn based tactical combat scenarios and a metagame of base management and decision making that overarches the main gameplay by forcing you to choose which options you want to research, what facilities you want to construct to better your force or gear, and which missions you want to send your recruits on to shoot the aliens to bits.
At the basic level, that's what the game is all about really - decision making. It's why it works so wonderfully, and also why it will make you rage but keep coming back for more. The turn based nature of the gameplay means you can weigh the odds of different approaches as you go and take your time to figure out the various angles and opportunities you have at each point. Squad cohesion is important in mission gameplay, and a poor choice of action or missed opportunity could see you paying for it down the line with your squad members, when alien plasma fries them. It forces you to adapt and overcome your enemies, predict the outcome of your options and make the best choices, whether that involves a squad wide attack to wipe out the enemy or (occasionally) sacrificing one member to allow the others to move to a safer position or escape (though you'll find that this is a painful lesson when it's a high level unit with helpful abilities that you lose however).
There's plenty to keep track of and experiment with too. Your different units have classes that affect their weaponry loadout (heavy units being armed with an LMG and Rocket launcher at the first level for example) and abilities that go along with them (in the case of the aforementioned heavy, suppression fire and usage of the launcher etc), so making sure that the different specialisations are utilised well is wise to be keep in mind while on a mission. You are free to choose who you want to field however, so if you find you don't really enjoy using a particular class or would rather take another sniper than a support unit for example, it's your choice.
Outside of mission play the decision making is just as important if not more so. You'll create a base layout with facilities to upgrade or improve your arsenal and construct your gear between missions, and keeping appropriate facilities close gives benefits so juggling everything or putting one plan on hold to get a different module placed first can provide bigger bonuses down the line. The different research tiers as the game progresses ramp up in power quite nicely and are satisfying to play with when you finally get to top tier weaponry and armor (higher tier armors especially offering some interesting options in terms of gameplay, IMO). All important research unlocks all these goodies so taking advantage of your time at the base to figure out which projects you want to take next is the other main aspect between mission play to keep in mind - neglecting any one aspect ofyour squad's equipment can leave you underequipped for some missions but researching the alien tech and recovered corpses etc is also important so as to discover their weak points, making it a fine balancing act.
So yeah, as the title said, it'll make you rage. When Corporal Bloggs pops his head round a blind corner only to get it melted by alien plasma fire unexpectedly you might want to shout, or swear, whatever floats your boat. But it's so satisfying to play that you'll just want to keep coming back to try again. Maybe Corporal Bloggs' brother will have better luck on point instead..

This game can be summerized into one word: hard. This game is tough as I've logged in roughly 6 hours and I haven't beaten the first level (which is named hard...). YET, I still enjoy this game. Here's why:
Music:
Honestly, if you're not a huge fan of EDM music, or just music games in general, then this game is not for you. This game is a very simple one (all you need is just a way to go left or right, enter, and exit), which means it doesn't have a lot to offer aside from its music and graphics. With that said, I really enjoy the soundtrack as it definitely adds to the mood of the game. I'll admit that it does get repetitive, and it would be nicer if they had more variety in each level, but it's still enjoyable to hear.
Gameplay:
Very simple controls, yet they're able to give you a headache when playing. I like the concept of the game, but I don't like how sensetive the controls are. I have probably died a lot of times due to being off by just a hair. Although, they have variety of controls. You can use the left and right keys, the mouse, or a gamepad to play. I also don't like how you can't really predict the patterns at times. Sure you can recongize what will happen, but the pattern is always different each play through. This'll lead to a lot of frustration. But on the bright side, it's easy to manage time with this game. With the level only lasting a minute at the most, you're able to play through the level at least 5 times in around 5 minutes. Definitely a game to play when you have the urge to play something, but don't have a lot of time to play. It's also good for the gamer who wants to challenge themselves, like me.
Graphics:
Again, simple. The color changing looks cool and is very smooth. You can easily tell what you need to avoid and where you are despite the flashing/changing colors around you. The game has a cool "tilt" that gives it a slight (only slight) 3D look to it, which is nice too. It does change directions, which always trip up my eyes. It definitely has a look of a simple yet futuristic-like game.
Over all, the game is good, but not amazing. If you find this game for a cheap price, then I would recommend getting it. The game offers a challenge that I rarely see in most games, and is super trippy, which I like... A LOT. If you can master the levels like a boss, then you'll easily be a boss to everyone you know... Or at least my mind will be blown...

Most people think this game is similar to Portal. In some ways, yes, I suppose it is. But it's also very different. The game utilises an interesting block gun mechanic which is actually really fun to use and makes for a unique puzzle experience (similar to how Portal's mechanics make it unique). Another mechanic used in this game involves, basically, thinking out of the box. One may come across a wall which isn't really as it seems. You may have to look at the picture from a different angle before you can make sense of your area. These blend together well to create a fulfilling experience that doesn't tug at your nerves and can be solved at a leisurely pace.
Now, having said that, there are some points in the game which I felt to be...less of what I wanted the game to give. For example, one would have to time him/her-self at just the right time to get past the puzzle and that, I feel, removed me from the experience the other puzzles gave. It felt more like a game (which is a good thing!) but I was already satisfied with the uniqueness of simply thinking my way out of a puzzle. Adding a trivial game mechanic into it felt disjointed but these instances happened so rarely that it may simply be overlooked when taking the whole game into account.
I won't spoil the story but I just have to say that it was pretty...decent. Not great by any means but not dull either. It was satisfying and open to interpretation (which, depending on perspective, is either a good or a bad thing). All in all, I felt that Antichamber was money well spent (though I got this at a very cheap price). It's an experience that most people would want to go through and I certainly didn't regret giving up my two assignments to finish the game in two days.

An incredibly fun, yet punishing top-down space simulator.
Upon entering, you'll find that you are the last hope of the Federation, carrying vital information key to crippling the Rebellion. On your first few playthroughs, you'll be lucky to get past the first few sectors, but the hopes of unlocking different ships or variations of what you already have beckons you to press on.
Until, at long last, salvation! You've made it to 'The Last Stand' -- The final sector of the game, you encounter the Rebel Flagship for the first time, and you are decimated by it. This process repeats, each time you learn more and more about this seemingly impossible adversary. Then finally! Success!! You destroy the monstrosity... But, wait... It didn't explode, it just jumped away... OH FOR ♥♥♥♥S SAKE!!
You fight the flagship once more, but with it's power now altered to drones. Ultimately, the damage you took from your first run is your undoing, and you fail once more.
Trying and trying again, you finally defeat the flagship's demonic drone phase, only to find it has one final form for you to face off against. Surely you're capable enough to fell the beast, right?
Wrong. In a blaze of blood, sweat and tears, you are destroyed.
Everything seems hopeless, you want to give up, you feel your sanity slipping. But you must kill this ship. You need to save the Federation.
Painstakingly, you try more and more, until you finally discover a combination that works. Wether it be brute force, or just a clever intrication of teleporters, bombs and lasers, you bring the flagship to it's final square of hull. You pause your game triumphantly as you fire the last laser, savouring the moment. But all good things must come to an end... You hit spacebar and watch as the flagship crumbles, when you realise... You forgot to teleport your crew back, and now only your pilot is alive to celebrate... ♥♥♥♥... And did I mention that was just 'Easy' mode?

After avoiding this game like the plague because of bad reviews for the PC version I caught it on sale. I went ahead and bought it. And the season pass. It's late, it means I get it all. I haven't been dissapointed by it. And also that it has had time to be updated. I'm an early adopter of lot's of things, games are usually not on that list.  It has the same feel as the other games in this run. The art is good, the gameplay is what you'd expect out of a somewhat sandbox game. If you are the  type of person who wants completion... it's that kind of game. The story runs flat in a few spots, but so did the other games in some degree or another.
On the art and graphics I give it an 8.5 out of 10. It's dark and the rain looks good. I just recently got my hands on a new i5 mid-to-upper processor and GTX 970. I get to run it full on at 1080 and it looks good at 60-75fps. The usual wear and tear on the character model through the game is there and unique to this game. The new suit is nice.  The design of the batmobile is rugged and tough feeling. Hands down the DLC for the Mad Hatter is the best art style I've seen in a while... and after just 14 hours and around 37% completion... yeah, it's pretty.
On the gameplay I give it 9 out of 10. It has the same feel as the other large scale Batman games in the run. There are things to do but the random "I'm gonna go fight a group of people at random" feels diminished because of the batmobile's toughness. There are though plenty of good fights in the main gameplay and the big ol' VR missions section if that's what ya want. The DLC adds a bit of extras but it's not a whole lot. Just enough to round out the game, but I'm not even at 40 percent yet. The riddler challenges are definitely hit or miss as always. They do make you think about it, and much like the others those reflexes and repitition are gonna be there. The batmobile in general has changed the landscape of this game series. The "tank mode" makes it feel much better in terms of control for a vehicle but it can be a bit off-putting in the beginning. Even after 14 hours I still hit the left trigger for the brake instead of the x button in "pursuit mode". I am learning game design and programming and I honestly couldn't suggest a better control scheme, so it's just one of those things. A few new surprises in the gadgets.
On the tech side I give it a 6 out of 10. Sorry the early adopters suffered, and even I ran into some issues this late on. It would crash before launch. And I do mean I got a splash screen and then a crash. No fix the resolution pre-game menus... just a crash. I think mine was the DX installers or something that I usually see before every new Steam install that were missing. Luckily I fix PC's for side cash and managed to get it fixed in under 20 minutes after 3 out of 4 methods. For the non-technical PC gamers I'm sure this is still a problem. Search the Steam forums for a couple of good tips if it happens to you. This is the exact reason I waited to purchase this game. (as in you didn't get good mark up on the sell because I will not pay full price for buggy software). PC hardware is getting pretty standard and these are near unforgivable issues. I expected better after this long. A lot of new games suffer nowadays at launch and it's not acceptable. Once it was up and running though... not a crash to be seen except while attempting to allow background downloads while playing. Framerate suffered horribly for my next game greed while wanting to play some Batman.
In summary, it's like the others. Fans of this series will likely be pleased by the "back to it" feel of Arkham Knight if the game runs "out of the box", and will enjoy it as much if not more than other games. If you have the hardware to run it full tilt it will look good if not a bit "shiny" due to the shaders. But most modern games have that. It's a button mashing good time in fights and there are things to do and it still breaks patterns now and then. If you just want a story it may let you down (I like it), but if you want that 100% it will make you try for it and you will get your dollars worth... race what is basically a tank through a shifting maze under a timer and you will have to try at it more than once but not 20 times and most times not more than 5 times on some of the harder puzzles. I'll admit that I'm impressed by a good bit of this game and the difficulty feels about right so far. The amount of dialogue and random pop up remakrs make this game better overall if you take the time to explore and press A alot. I don't regret waiting for it but would have been let down if I bought this early with all the fixings and had to deal with the tech issues more than I did.

Dying light is what you get when you combine Mirror's edge and Dead island, then mix in a bit of Farcry.
As soon as load the game the graphics look very nice, and seem to be well optimized for high FPS.
The combat for the most part feels very fluid and fun, being able to chain hits together and decapitate multiple zombies with one handed weapons. Although early on in the game, you run out of stamina pretty quick from swinging a pipe around, so you might just want to stick to running around on rooftops untill you get better skills and gear.
I love the freerunning in this game, it feels very Mirrors edge-y. You can outrun common zombies (Biters) easily, so they aren't too threatening. The skill trees are nicely designed and, instead of choosing your favorite skill tree to put all your points into, you get skill points for the different trees by doing things related to them (eg. Climing to get agility points).
The crafting system is pretty generic, but it works. You can craft quite a variety of weapon mods that let you create some pretty cool looking weapons. In addition to weapons, you can also craft tools such as explosive shurikens, grenades, sheilds, ect. You'll learn how to craft new items as you level up.
You feel pretty safe in the day, what with there being few zombies that can chase you, but at night, the game changes from running rooftop to rooftop, looting, and killing weak zombies, to a stealth action game, where you hide from demonic spawn that can chase you down and rip you to pieces (Volatiles). However you do get double XP at night, giving you an insentive you stay out late.
Well overall, I'd say I really enjoy this game. I know this review dosn't cover everything in the game, but its just to give people an idea of what its like. If you like games like Farcry or Dead island, or maybe you're entertained by dropkicking zombies off of buildings of various hights, then I would recommend this game.

Sci-fi and horror is my favourite combination, and Dead Space is a third-person shooter that does this setting well. Arriving on a dead ship, only to find it broken and full of ugly monsters that are best killed by tearing them apart, limb by limb. You'll be delivering this carnage as Isaac Clarke, a silent protagonist wearing one of the coolest game suits of armor ever. Creepy religions and mad scientists are also involved. The spooky atmosphere is much helped by a total lack of a conventional UI, your health and power are shown on your armor and ammo is shown on the weapons themselves.I just played the game for the first time, and it still really holds up. Highly recommended.
(The PC port is not really great, missing various graphics-related stuff one would expect, and mouse aiming is terrible thanks to really horrid forced acceleration. Fortunately, all of these are fixable, and within the Guides section on Steam you'll find everything you need.
